digest:
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** De Castro v. Judicial and Bar Council (JBC)
**Full Official Caption:** Arturo M. De Castro, Petitioner, vs. Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) and President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, Respondents (G.R. No. 191002); Jaime N. Soriano, Petitioner, vs. Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), Respondent (G.R. No. 191032); Philippine Constitution Association (PHILCONSA), Petitioner, vs. Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), Respondent (G.R. No. 191057); In Re Applicability of Section 15, Article VII of the Constitution to Appointments to the Judiciary, Estelito P. Mendoza, Petitioner (A.M. No. 10-2-5-SC); John G. Peralta, Petitioner, vs. Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), Respondent (G.R. No. 191149); Atty. Amador Z. Tolentino, Jr. (IBP Governor-Southern Luzon) and Atty. Roland B. Inting (IBP Governor-Eastern Visayas), Petitioners, vs. Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), Respondent (G.R. No. 191342); Philippine Bar Association, Inc., Petitioner, vs. Judicial and Bar Council and Her Excellency Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, Respondents (G.R. No. 191420).
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. Nos. 191002, 191032, 191057, 191149, 191342, 191420, and A.M. No. 10-2-5-SC; Promulgated March 17, 2010; En Banc; Ponente: Bersamin, J. Concurring: Puno, C.J., Carpio, Corona, Velasco, Jr., Leonardo-De Castro, Peralta, Del Castillo, Abad (with Concurring Opinion), Villarama, Jr., Perez, and Mendoza, JJ. Dissenting: Carpio Morales, J. (with Dissenting Opinion). Separate Opinions: Nachura, J. (concurring in dismissal for lack of justiciable controversy); Brion, J. (concurring in part that the President may appoint Supreme Court Members, but dissenting as to lower courts).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Arturo M. De Castro, John G. Peralta, and PHILCONSA:** Petitioners in G.R. Nos. 191002, 191149, and 191057; sought to compel the JBC via mandamus to submit a list of nominees for Chief Justice to incumbent President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo.
**Estelito P. Mendoza:** Petitioner in A.M. No. 10-2-5-SC; former Solicitor General who sought an administrative ruling/guidance on whether the election appointment ban applies to the Judiciary.
**Jaime N. Soriano:** Petitioner in G.R. No. 191032; sought to prohibit the JBC from screening candidates, theorizing that the Supreme Court En Banc, not the President, appoints the Chief Justice.
**Atty. Amador Z. Tolentino, Jr. and Atty. Roland B. Inting:** Petitioners in G.R. No. 191342; IBP Governors who petitioned for prohibition to enjoin the JBC from submitting nominees to the incumbent President during the election ban.
**Judicial and Bar Council (JBC):** Respondent constitutional body tasked with vetting and recommending nominees for judicial vacancies.
**President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo:** Respondent incumbent President of the Philippines whose term ended on June 30, 2010.
**Intervenors-Oppositors:** Various public interest groups, bar leaders, and attorneys (e.g., Peter Irving Corvera, Christian Robert S. Lim, Alfonso V. Tan, Jr., NUPL, Marlou B. Ubano, IBP-Davao del Sur, Mitchell John L. Boiser, BAYAN, COURAGE, KADAMAY, ANAKBAYAN, Walden F. Bello, Loretta Ann P. Rosales, WTLOP) opposing presidential appointment during the election ban.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Consolidated Petitions for Certiorari, Mandamus, and Prohibition under Rule 65 of the Rules of Court, alongside an Administrative Matter (A.M. No. 10-2-5-SC), directly filed with the Supreme Court En Banc to resolve the constitutional impasse between the midnight appointment prohibition in Section 15, Article VII and the mandatory 90-day vacancy-filling directives in Sections 4(1) and 9, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Executive Department & Judicial Department → Appointment Process and Qualifications (Midnight Appointments Ban vs. Mandatory Period to Fill Judicial Vacancies).
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Special Civil Actions → Rule 65 (Certiorari, Prohibition, and Mandamus) & Judicial Review (Locus Standi and Ripeness/Justiciability).
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article VII, Section 15, 1987 Constitution:**
"Two months immediately before the next presidential elections and up to the end of his term, a **President or Acting President shall not make appointments**, **except temporary appointments to executive positions when continued vacancies therein will prejudice public service or endanger public safety**."
**Article VIII, Section 4 (1), 1987 Constitution:**
"The Supreme Court shall be composed of a Chief Justice and fourteen Associate Justices. It may sit en banc or in its discretion, in division of three, five, or seven Members. **Any vacancy shall be filled within ninety days from the occurrence thereof**."
**Article VIII, Section 9, 1987 Constitution:**
"The Members of the Supreme Court and judges of lower courts **shall be appointed by the President from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the Judicial and Bar Council for every vacancy**. Such appointments need no confirmation.
For the lower courts, the President shall issue the appointments within ninety days from the submission of the list."
**Historical Landmark Rule:** In **In Re Appointments Dated March 30, 1998 of Hon. Mateo A. Valenzuela and Hon. Placido B. Vallarta** (A.M. No. 98-5-01-SC, 1998), the Supreme Court had previously held that Section 15, Article VII prohibited the President from making judicial appointments during the election ban, ruling that Section 15 prevailed over Section 4(1) and Section 9 of Article VIII because it was couched in stronger negative language ("shall not"). The present decision explicitly **overrules and reverses** the **Valenzuela** doctrine.
**Factual Trigger:** Chief Justice Reynato S. Puno was set to reach compulsory retirement on May 17, 2010—seven days after the May 10, 2010 presidential election and during the constitutional two-month election ban ending June 30, 2010. Facing conflicting constitutional mandates, the JBC began the vetting process but deferred determining when and to whom it would submit its shortlist of nominees, triggering multiple petitions to compel, enjoin, or clarify the appointment process.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**December 22, 2009:** Congressman Matias V. Defensor, an ex officio member of the JBC, sends a letter to the JBC requesting that the nomination process for the office of the Chief Justice be commenced immediately in anticipation of Chief Justice Reynato S. Puno's mandatory retirement on May 17, 2010.
**January 18, 2010:** The JBC En Banc unanimously passes a resolution agreeing to start the process of filling up the position of Chief Justice. It resolves to publish the opening, deliberate on candidates, accept public comments, conduct interviews, and prepare a shortlist, but explicitly leaves open the question of when to submit the shortlist to the proper appointing authority in light of constitutional questions. On the same date and on January 25, 2010, Associate Justices Presbitero J. Velasco, Jr. and Antonio Eduardo B. Nachura decline their automatic nominations as senior Associate Justices.
**January 20, 2010:** The JBC officially publishes the announcement opening the position of Chief Justice for applications or recommendations, with a deadline set for February 4, 2010.
**February 8, 2010:** The JBC evaluates applicants and nominees. Associate Justices Renato C. Corona, Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro, Arturo D. Brion, and Sandiganbayan Associate Justice Edilberto G. Sandoval accept their nominations unconditionally; Associate Justices Antonio T. Carpio and Conchita Carpio Morales accept conditionally (stipulating that their nominations be submitted to the next President). Former Deputy Ombudsman Victor Fernandez, Atty. Henry Villarica, and Atty. Gregorio M. Batiller, Jr. withdraw or decline, while former Judge Florentino Floro and Special Prosecutor Dennis Villa-Ignacio are disqualified. The JBC announces the list of qualified candidates for public comment.
**February 9 to March 8, 2010:** Various petitions are filed with the Supreme Court En Banc: G.R. No. 191002 (De Castro) on February 9, 2010; G.R. No. 191032 (Soriano) on February 10, 2010; G.R. No. 191057 (PHILCONSA) on February 11, 2010; A.M. No. 10-2-5-SC (Mendoza) on February 15, 2010; G.R. No. 191149 (Peralta) on February 23, 2010; and G.R. No. 191342 (Tolentino and Inting) on March 8, 2010.
**February 16, 2010:** The Supreme Court directs the JBC and the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) to comment on the consolidated petitions.
**February 25–26, 2010:** The JBC files its Comment, stating it has not taken a definitive position on when to submit the shortlist and manifests that it will be guided by the Court's ruling. The OSG files its Comment, maintaining that the President has the constitutional power and duty to appoint the next Chief Justice, as Section 15, Article VII does not apply to the Judiciary.
**March 9, 2010:** The Supreme Court consolidates G.R. No. 191342 with the other cases and admits several oppositions and comments-in-intervention from various attorneys and civil society groups.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments (De Castro, Peralta, PHILCONSA, Mendoza) & OSG
**Main Thesis:** The constitutional ban on presidential appointments under Section 15, Article VII applies strictly to appointments in the Executive Department and does not restrict appointments to the Judiciary, specifically the Supreme Court, which is governed by the independent 90-day mandate under Section 4(1) and Section 9, Article VIII.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Textual Separation & Placement: Sections 14, 15, and 16 of Article VII deal exclusively with executive appointments. Had the framers intended the prohibition to cover the Judiciary, they would have placed it in Article VIII (specifically under Section 4(1) or Section 9).
 Mandatory Nature of Section 4(1), Article VIII: The phrase "shall be filled within ninety days from the occurrence thereof" is an imperative constitutional command imposed upon the President. It cannot be overridden by negative inferences.
 Flaws of Valenzuela Precedent: In Re Valenzuela was poorly reasoned, ignored the intent of the Constitutional Commission as confirmed by Commissioner (later Senior Associate Justice) Florenz D. Regalado, and rested on conjectures that should now be formally overruled.
 Depoliticization via the JBC:** The evils of "midnight appointments" articulated in **Aytona v. Castillo (vote-buying, hasty appointments, partisan considerations) are completely neutralised in the Judiciary by the creation of the independent JBC, which vets, screens, and shortlists candidates.
 Mathematical Impossibility: Regular elections occur between May 8 and May 14, creating an election ban period of 109 to 115 days. If the ban applied to the Supreme Court, any vacancy arising during the ban would deprive the outgoing President of complying with the 90-day constitutional command, creating an absurd constitutional contradiction.
 Public Interest & Stability: The Supreme Court serves as the Presidential Electoral Tribunal (PET). An incomplete Court during an election period involving automated balloting threatens constitutional stability.
 Mandamus vs. Discretion: Mandamus lies to compel the JBC to submit its shortlist because its duty to submit nominees is ministerial, while its selection of who to include is discretionary.
B. Petitioners for Prohibition (Soriano, Tolentino, Inting) & Intervenors-Oppositors
**Main Thesis:** The prohibition in Section 15, Article VII is absolute, categorical, and admits of only one exception (temporary appointments in the executive department), thereby strictly prohibiting the outgoing President from appointing the next Chief Justice or any member of the Judiciary between March 10, 2010 and June 30, 2010.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Lack of Actual Controversy / Prematurity: There is no ripe controversy because the position of Chief Justice is not yet vacant (compulsory retirement is on May 17, 2010) and the JBC has not yet finalized a shortlist. The petitions improperly seek an advisory opinion.
 Plain Meaning (Verba Legis) and Exclusivity:** Section 15 uses absolute negative phrasing ("shall not make appointments") without distinguishing among branches (**ubi lex non distinguit nec nos distinguere debemus**). The sole exception for temporary executive positions excludes all others (**expressio unius est exclusio alterius).
 Stare Decisis (**Valenzuela**):** The En Banc ruling in **Valenzuela settled that the constitutional ban on appointments takes precedence over the 90-day period to fill judicial vacancies, as the prevention of vote-buying and midnight appointments outweighs delays in filling court vacancies.
 Availability of an Acting Chief Justice: Section 12 of the Judiciary Act of 1948 (R.A. No. 296) provides that in case of a vacancy, the duties of the Chief Justice devolve upon the most senior Associate Justice first in precedence. The Court can function smoothly en banc or in divisions with 14 members; a full court is not indispensable.
 No Usurpation by Incoming President: The 90-day period under Section 4(1) would lapse on August 15, 2010. Upon the incoming President assuming office at noon of June 30, 2010, 46 days would still remain to make the appointment without violating the Constitution.
 Soriano's Separate Theory (G.R. No. 191032): The power to appoint the Chief Justice belongs to the Supreme Court itself, not the President, because Section 9, Article VIII refers only to "Members of the Supreme Court" (allegedly meaning Associate Justices).
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the petitioners possess **locus standi** to maintain their respective actions challenging or compelling the actions of the JBC regarding the appointment of the next Chief Justice.
2. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the petitions present an actual case or controversy that is ripe for judicial determination, despite the fact that Chief Justice Puno has not yet retired and the JBC has not yet finalized its shortlist.
3. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the constitutional prohibition against presidential appointments under Section 15, Article VII of the Constitution applies to appointments to fill a vacancy in the Supreme Court and other judicial positions.
4. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the power to appoint the Chief Justice is vested in the Supreme Court En Banc rather than the President of the Philippines.
5. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Section 12 of the Judiciary Act of 1948, providing for an Acting Chief Justice, obviates the imperative necessity for the incumbent President to appoint a permanent Chief Justice within the 90-day period under Section 4(1), Article VIII.
6. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not a writ of mandamus lies to compel the JBC to submit its shortlist of nominees to the incumbent President.
7. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not a writ of prohibition lies to restrain the JBC from vetting candidates and submitting a shortlist to the incumbent President.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Locus Standi of Petitioners
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the petitioners possess legal standing (**locus standi**). **YES.** The petitioners demonstrated adequate personal and public interest, and in any event, the Court relaxed technical standing rules due to the transcendental importance of the constitutional controversy.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Locus standi** requires a personal stake in the outcome to ensure concrete adverseness (**Agan, Jr. v. PIATCO**; **People v. Vera**). A citizen suing for a public right acts as an instrument of public concern (**David v. Macapagal-Arroyo**).
2.  Petitioners De Castro, Soriano, and Peralta sued as citizens and taxpayers; PHILCONSA is a civic organization dedicated to upholding the Constitution; Mendoza is a former Solicitor General and bar member; Tolentino and Inting are IBP Governors directly interested in the supervision and leadership of the bar.
3.  The issues affect the entire nation, the administration of justice, and the stability of the Judiciary, which is plagued by widespread trial court vacancies. Under settled jurisprudence (**Araneta v. Dinglasan**; **Aquino v. COMELEC**), the Court exercises broad discretion to waive procedural standing requirements when a petition presents issues of transcendental importance.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Standing is a peculiar concept in constitutional law because in some cases, suits are not brought by parties who have been personally injured by the operation of a law or any other government act but by concerned citizens, taxpayers or voters who actually sue in the public interest. But even if, strictly speaking, the petitioners 'are not covered by the definition, it is still within the wide discretion of the Court to waive the requirement and so remove the impediment to its addressing and resolving the serious constitutional questions raised.'"
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Supreme Court held that all petitioners have standing because every citizen and lawyer has a stake in who heads the Judiciary and whether the Constitution is being followed. Even if strict injury was questionable, the Court waived the technicality because resolving the appointment deadlock before a looming presidential election was of transcendental importance to the entire nation.
Issue 2: Justiciability and Ripeness
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the controversy is ripe for judicial determination prior to the actual occurrence of the vacancy on May 17, 2010. **YES.** An actual justiciable controversy exists because the JBC had already initiated the selection proceedings and was at an impasse on whether it could lawfully submit a shortlist to the incumbent President.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  Ripeness does not require the Court to wait until the vacancy actually occurs on May 17, 2010. The JBC had already opened the nomination process, published candidate lists, and received public objections, but halted at the submission stage due to conflicting constitutional interpretations.
2.  Opposing claims had crystallized: petitioners demanded submission to the incumbent President, while intervenors insisted that submission during the election period violated the midnight appointment ban.
3.  Under constitutional review principles (**Buckley v. Valeo**; **Regional Rail Reorganization Act Cases**), a reasonable certainty of a perceived threat to a constitutional interest affords a basis for judicial challenge when the facts are established and only legal questions remain.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"We need not await the occurrence of the vacancy by May 17, 2010 in order for the principal issue to ripe for judicial determination by the Court. It is enough that one alleges conduct arguably affected with a constitutional interest, but seemingly proscribed by the Constitution. A reasonable certainty of the occurrence of the perceived threat to a constitutional interest is sufficient to afford a basis for bringing a challenge, provided the Court has sufficient facts before it to enable it to intelligently adjudicate the issues."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Court refused to wait until May 17, 2010, because the JBC was already in the middle of screening nominees and frozen by legal uncertainty. When an institutional clash over a constitutional duty is certain to occur, the Court does not need to wait for the actual vacancy to happen before interpreting the Constitution and preventing a judicial crisis.
Issue 3: Inapplicability of Section 15, Article VII to Judicial Appointments (Reversal of **Valenzuela**)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the Section 15, Article VII election appointment ban applies to vacancies in the Supreme Court and the Judiciary. **NO.** The prohibition against midnight appointments applies exclusively to the Executive Department; appointments to the Judiciary are governed exclusively by Article VIII, and **In Re Valenzuela** is expressly reversed.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Constitutional Architecture and Placement:** The Constitution is meticulously arranged by departments (separation of powers). Article VII governs the Executive; Article VIII governs the Judiciary. Sections 14, 15, and 16 of Article VII all address presidential appointments within the Executive branch. If the framers intended to extend the Section 15 prohibition to the Judiciary, they would have written it into Article VIII, specifically under Section 4(1).
2.  **Mandatory 90-Day Duty Under Section 4(1), Article VIII:** Section 4(1) commands that "[a]ny vacancy shall be filled within ninety days from the occurrence thereof." The word "shall" is imperative, creating an enforceable, non-discretionary constitutional duty for the President. Deliberations of the Constitutional Commission (speeches by Commissioners Lerum and Concepcion) reveal that the 90-day period was deliberately inserted to end the 30-year historical practice of the Court operating with chronic vacancies.
3.  **Reversal of Valenzuela: In Re Valenzuela** erroneously held that Section 15 prevailed merely because it used stronger negative language ("shall not"). This was an arbitrary rule of construction that defeated the framers' true intent. Moreover, **Valenzuela** ignored the formal clarification made to the JBC by Senior Associate Justice Florenz D. Regalado (a former Constitutional Commissioner), who confirmed that the election ban was never intended to apply to judicial appointments.
4.  **The JBC Eliminates the Evil of Aytona:** Section 15 was adopted to curb **Aytona**-style midnight appointments—mass appointments made in haste, for vote-buying or partisan advantage. That evil cannot occur in the Judiciary because the 1987 Constitution established the independent JBC, which depoliticizes judicial appointments through transparent public screening and vetting.
5.  **Mathematical Conflict Demonstrating Intent:** A presidential election occurs between May 8 and May 14, making the ban last 109 to 115 days. If Section 15 applied to the Supreme Court, any vacancy occurring during the ban would completely extinguish or unlawfully reduce the 90-day window given to the President to fill it, causing an absurd constitutional contradiction that the framers could never have intended.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Had the framers intended to extend the prohibition contained in Section 15, Article VII to the appointment of Members of the Supreme Court, they could have explicitly done so. They could not have ignored the meticulous ordering of the provisions. They would have easily and surely written the prohibition made explicit in Section 15, Article VII as being equally applicable to the appointment of Members of the Supreme Court in Article VIII itself, most likely in Section 4 (1), Article VIII... A misinterpretation like **Valenzuela** should not be allowed to last after its false premises have been exposed... Consequently, **Valenzuela** now deserves to be quickly sent to the dustbin of the unworthy and forgettable. We reverse **Valenzuela**."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Supreme Court held that the "midnight appointments" ban belongs strictly to Article VII (Executive Department) to stop outgoing presidents from packing executive agencies. It does not apply to the Judiciary under Article VIII because the Constitution commands that vacancies in the Supreme Court **must** be filled within 90 days, and the independent Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) already prevents political rush-appointments by screening every nominee beforehand.
Issue 4: Power to Appoint the Chief Justice
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the Supreme Court En Banc, rather than the President, has the power to appoint the Chief Justice. **NO.** The President possesses the exclusive power to appoint all Members of the Supreme Court, including the Chief Justice, from the shortlist prepared by the JBC.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  Soriano's contention rests on a flawed reading of Section 9, Article VIII, which states that "[t]he Members of the Supreme Court and judges of lower courts shall be appointed by the President." Soriano argued that "Members" excludes the Chief Justice.
2.  Section 4(1), Article VIII expressly defines the Court's composition: "The Supreme Court shall be composed of a Chief Justice and fourteen Associate Justices. It may sit en banc or in its discretion, in division of three, five, or seven Members."
3.  Textually, historically (**Vargas v. Rillaroza**), and jurisprudentially, the Chief Justice is a **Member** of the Supreme Court, acting as **primus inter pares** (first among equals). The appointing power has always resided in the Chief Executive across all Philippine constitutions.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"A review of Sections 4(1) and 9 of Article VIII shows that the Supreme Court is composed of a Chief Justice and 14 Associate Justices, who all shall be appointed by the President from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the JBC for every vacancy... With reference to the Chief Justice, he or she is appointed by the President as Chief Justice, and the appointment is never in an acting capacity."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Chief Justice is legally a "Member" of the Supreme Court, albeit the first among equals. Since the Constitution explicitly gives the President the power to appoint all Members of the Supreme Court from the JBC shortlist, the Supreme Court cannot appoint its own Chief Justice.
Issue 5: Judiciary Act of 1948 and Acting Chief Justice Status
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not Section 12 of the Judiciary Act of 1948 excuses the President from appointing a permanent Chief Justice within 90 days. **NO.** The 1987 Constitution envisions a permanent Chief Justice and does not allow an Acting Chief Justice to replace the constitutional mandate to fill vacancies within 90 days.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  Section 12 of R.A. No. 296 (Judiciary Act of 1948) allows the most senior Associate Justice to temporarily discharge the duties of Chief Justice in case of vacancy or disability.
2.  This statutory rule was enacted under the 1935 Constitution to cover the interregnum while presidential appointments underwent confirmation by the Commission on Appointments. Under the 1987 Constitution, judicial appointments need no legislative confirmation.
3.  Relying on statutory devolution to keep the head of the Judiciary temporary undermines judicial independence. The Chief Justice has vital constitutional roles—presiding over the En Banc, heading the Presidential Electoral Tribunal (PET), chairing the JBC, and presiding over presidential impeachment trials.
4.  An Acting Chief Justice leaves the Court with only 14 members, increasing the risk of split deadlocks and impairing institutional stability. Statutory succession cannot defeat the explicit constitutional command of Section 4(1), Article VIII to fill the post permanently within 90 days.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The express reference to a Chief Justice abhors the idea that the framers contemplated an Acting Chief Justice to head the membership of the Supreme Court. Otherwise, they would have simply written so in the Constitution. Consequently, to rely on Section 12 of the Judiciary Act of 1948 in order to forestall the imperative need to appoint the next Chief Justice soonest is to defy the plain intent of the Constitution."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Having an Acting Chief Justice under an old 1948 statute is an emergency stopgap, not a constitutional substitute for an appointed Chief Justice. Leaving the Judiciary headless during an election season harms judicial independence and risks tie votes; therefore, the President has an imperative constitutional duty to make a permanent appointment.
Issue 6: Propriety of Mandamus Against the JBC
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not a writ of mandamus lies to compel the JBC to immediately submit its shortlist to President Arroyo. **NO.** The petitions for mandamus are premature because the JBC had until May 17, 2010 (the date of the actual vacancy) to submit its list, and had not unlawfully neglected its duty.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  Mandamus requires: (a) a clear legal right in the petitioner; (b) an imperative legal duty on the respondent; (c) unlawful neglect of duty; (d) that the act is ministerial, not discretionary; and (e) no other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy.
2.  The JBC's duty to prepare and submit a shortlist of at least three nominees for every vacancy is mandatory and ministerial; however, its selection of **which** candidates to nominate is purely discretionary.
3.  Unlawful neglect requires unjustified delay. Because the vacancy would not materialize until Chief Justice Puno compulsorily retired on May 17, 2010, the JBC still had time to finalize its shortlist and submit it on or before that date. Hence, no unlawful neglect had occurred, rendering mandamus premature.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The duty of the JBC to submit a list of nominees before the start of the President's mandatory 90-day period to appoint is ministerial, but its selection of the candidates whose names will be in the list to be submitted to the President lies within the discretion of the JBC... Accordingly, we find no sufficient grounds to grant the petitions for mandamus and to issue a writ of mandamus against the JBC. The actions for that purpose are premature, because it is clear that the JBC still has until May 17, 2010, at the latest, within which to submit the list of nominees to the President..."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Mandamus only lies when an official unlawfully refuses or delays performing a mandatory, non-discretionary duty. While the JBC is legally required to send a shortlist to the President, it had until May 17, 2010 (Chief Justice Puno's retirement day) to do so; therefore, filing a petition before that deadline was premature.
Issue 7: Propriety of Prohibition Against the JBC
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not a writ of prohibition lies to restrain the JBC from vetting and submitting nominees. **NO.** The JBC acted squarely within its constitutional authority, and petitioners in G.R. No. 191342 lacked standing to assail the JBC's congressional voting composition.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  Prohibition requires demonstrating that a tribunal or body acted without or in excess of jurisdiction, or with grave abuse of discretion.
2.  Because Section 15, Article VII does not apply to judicial appointments, the JBC's vetting of applicants to fill the upcoming vacancy was entirely within its constitutional mandate under Section 8(5), Article VIII.
3.  Regarding Tolentino and Inting's attack on the JBC's composition (allowing both a Senator and a Congressman to have one full vote each), petitioners failed to show direct injury or standing because neither petitioner was an applicant or nominee prejudiced by the JBC voting rules.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The challenge mounted against the composition of the JBC based on the allegedly unconstitutional allocation of a vote each to the ex officio members from the Senate and the House of Representatives, thereby prejudicing the chances of some candidates for nomination by raising the minimum number of votes required in accordance with the rules of the JBC, is not based on the petitioners' actual interest, because they have not alleged in their petition that they were nominated to the JBC to fill some vacancies in the Judiciary. Thus, the petitioners lack locus standi on that issue."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Prohibition was denied because the JBC was simply carrying out its constitutional duty to screen nominees. Furthermore, the claim that Congress improperly had two votes in the JBC could not be decided in that petition because the lawyers suing were not applicants whose nominations were blocked by that voting structure.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Appointment process and qualifications | Applied Lens: Remedial Law & Evidence.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
 Requisites for Mandamus under Rule 65, Section 3:
1.  Clear legal right of the petitioner: Citizen/bar standing recognized, but right to immediate transmittal had not accrued.
2.  Imperative legal duty of respondent: JBC must submit a list of at least 3 nominees (**Present**).
3.  Unlawful neglect of duty: None, as JBC still had until May 17, 2010 to submit (**Absent / Failed**).
4.  Ministerial character of act: Submission of list is ministerial, but candidate selection is discretionary (**Partially Present**).
5.  No other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy: (**Present**).
 Constitutional Elements for Presidential Appointment to Supreme Court (Art. VIII, Secs. 4[1], 8[5], 9):
1.  Vacancy in the Supreme Court.
2.  Screening and shortlist of at least three nominees prepared exclusively by the JBC.
3.  Selection and appointment issued exclusively by the President.
4.  Mandatory timeframe: Within 90 days from the occurrence of the vacancy.
5.  Exemption: No confirmation by Commission on Appointments required; completely exempt from the Section 15, Article VII midnight appointments ban.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Midnight appointments ban (Sec. 15, Art. VII)
 Mandatory 90-day period (Sec. 4[1], Art. VIII)
 Primus inter pares (First among equals)
 Ministerial duty vs. Discretionary act
 Ripeness and Justiciable Controversy
 Transcendental importance
 Overruling of Valenzuela
**Remedial Law & Evidence Lens Analysis:**
 Procedural Remedy & Jurisdiction Audit: The Court resolved the dispute using its extraordinary supervisory jurisdiction over the JBC under Section 8(1), Article VIII, coupled with its power of judicial review under Rule 65. Although the petitions for Mandamus were dismissed as premature and Prohibition was dismissed for lack of merit, the Court treated A.M. No. 10-2-5-SC as a proper administrative petition invoking its supervisory authority, thereby bypassing ordinary procedural dismissals to settle the constitutional impasse definitively.
 Evidentiary & Quantum of Proof Analysis: The Court took judicial notice under Rule 129 of official JBC publications, resolutions, press releases, and the known compulsory retirement date of Chief Justice Puno. Because the issues were purely legal and constitutional questions based on undisputed public facts, no evidentiary hearing or trial was required; the legal presumption of the regularity of constitutional duties applied.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**De Castro v. JBC** establishes that the constitutional ban on "midnight appointments" under Section 15, Article VII applies strictly to the Executive Department and never to vacancies in the Supreme Court or the Judiciary. The Supreme Court explicitly overruled **In Re Valenzuela**, holding that the mandatory command in Section 4(1), Article VIII requiring the President to fill Supreme Court vacancies within 90 days is independent and imperative, insulated from the election ban by the vetting mechanism of the Judicial and Bar Council.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Abad, J., Concurring:** Concurred fully. Stressed that the independent screening, public interviews, and non-negotiable shortlists of the JBC completely eliminate the danger of vote-buying or political patronage identified in **Aytona v. Castillo**. Noted that the JBC is under the Supreme Court, not the Executive, making it impossible for an outgoing President to use judicial posts for election influence.
**Carpio Morales, J., Dissenting:** Dissented vigorously. Argued that constitutional draftsmanship placement is the weakest construction tool and that Section 15, Article VII uses absolute negative phrasing ("shall not make appointments") with only one explicit exception (temporary executive posts), which excludes all others (**expressio unius est exclusio alterius**). Contended that the JBC does not eliminate political appointments, that **Valenzuela** was correctly decided En Banc, that the 90-day period under Section 4(1) is simply suspended during the election ban, and that the Court can function effectively under an Acting Chief Justice pursuant to the Judiciary Act of 1948.
**Nachura, J., Separate Opinion:** Voted to dismiss all petitions for lack of an actual justiciable controversy. Maintained that the petitions were premature and conjectural because the JBC had not yet prepared a shortlist and the President had not made an appointment; cautioned that the Court was rendering an impermissible advisory opinion.
**Brion, J., Separate Opinion:** Agreed with the majority that the President can appoint the Chief Justice and Associate Justices of the Supreme Court during the election ban pursuant to Section 4(1), Article VIII, but dissented from extending this exception to the rest of the Judiciary. Maintained that appointments to lower courts under Section 9, Article VIII do not carry the same constitutional urgency and remain subject to the Section 15, Article VII ban under the **Valenzuela** doctrine.
**Verbatim/Near-Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the Court:
1. Dismisses the petitions for certiorari and mandamus in G.R. No. 191002 and G.R. No. 191149, and the petition for mandamus in G.R. No. 191057 for being premature;
2. Dismisses the petitions for prohibition in G.R. No. 191032 and G.R. No. 191342 for lack of merit; and
3. Grants the petition in A.M. No. 10-2-5-SC and, accordingly, directs the Judicial and Bar Council:
(a) To resume its proceedings for the nomination of candidates to fill the vacancy to be created by the compulsory retirement of Chief Justice Reynato S. Puno by May 17, 2010;
(b) To prepare the short list of nominees for the position of Chief Justice;
(c) To submit to the incumbent President the short list of nominees for the position of Chief Justice on or before May 17, 2010; and
(d) To continue its proceedings for the nomination of candidates to fill other vacancies in the Judiciary and submit to the President the short list of nominees corresponding thereto in accordance with this decision.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo and the JBC prevailed on the core substantive constitutional question. While the petitions for mandamus were dismissed as premature and the petitions for prohibition were dismissed for lack of merit, the Court granted the petition in A.M. No. 10-2-5-SC and ordered the JBC to finalize its shortlist and submit it to incumbent President Arroyo on or before May 17, 2010, confirming her constitutional authority to appoint the next Chief Justice despite the ongoing presidential election ban.

digest:
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Republic v. Sereno (Quo Warranto Case)
**Full Official Caption:** Republic of the Philippines, represented by Solicitor General Jose C. Calida, Petitioner, v. Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 237428; May 11, 2018; 831 Phil. 271; En Banc; Ponente: Associate Justice Noel Gimenez Tijam.
**Voting Breakdown:**
Concurring (8): Tijam (Ponente), Leonardo-De Castro, Peralta, Bersamin, Jardeleza, Martires, A. Reyes, Jr., Gesmundo.
Concurring and Dissenting / Separate Opinions (2): Velasco, Jr., Del Castillo.
Dissenting (4): Carpio, Perlas-Bernabe, Leonen, Caguioa.
Inhibited/No Part (1): Sereno (Respondent).
Separate Opinions Filed: Dissenting Opinions by Carpio, Leonen, Caguioa; Concurring and Dissenting Opinions by Velasco, Jr., Del Castillo; Concurring Opinions by Leonardo-De Castro, Bersamin; Separate Concurring Opinion by Peralta; Separate Opinions by Perlas-Bernabe, Martires.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Petitioner:** Republic of the Philippines, represented by Solicitor General Jose C. Calida, invoking the sovereign right of the State to institute **quo warranto** proceedings against an allegedly unqualified occupant of a public office.
**Respondent:** Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno, incumbent Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines, whose title and qualifications are directly challenged.
**Judicial and Bar Council (JBC):** The constitutionally mandated body tasked with screening and nominating applicants to judicial vacancies, operating under the supervisory authority of the Supreme Court.
**University of the Philippines (UP) / UP College of Law / UP HRDO:** Respondent’s former public employer (faculty member from 1986 to 2006) whose human resource and custodian records established the missing Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs).
**Office of the Ombudsman:** The constitutional repository agency of public officials' SALNs that issued official certifications regarding respondent’s unfiled SALNs.
**Movant-Intervenors:** Groups of citizens, taxpayers, organizations, and legislators—including Capistrano **et al.**, Zarate **et al.**, the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP), and Senators Leila De Lima and Antonio Trillanes IV—seeking intervention to dismiss the petition.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Direct invocation of the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction under Section 5(1), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution in relation to Rule 66 of the Rules of Court (Special Civil Action for **Quo Warranto**), commenced by the Republic through the Solicitor General following letter-requests and disclosures made during House Committee on Justice impeachment proceedings.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Department → Appointment Process and Judicial Qualifications (Article VIII, Section 7).
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Special Civil Actions → **Quo Warranto** (Rule 66) → Direct Attack on Title to Public Office vs. Impeachment.
**Verbatim Text of Governing Constitutional and Statutory Provisions:**
**Article VIII, Section 7, 1987 Constitution:**
"SECTION 7. (1) No person shall be appointed Member of the Supreme Court or any lower collegiate court unless he is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines. A Member of the Supreme Court must be at least forty years of age, and must have been for fifteen years or more a judge of a lower court or engaged in the practice of law in the Philippines.
(2) The Congress shall prescribe the qualifications of judges of lower courts, but no person may be appointed judge thereof unless he is a citizen of the Philippines and a member of the Philippine Bar.
(3) **A Member of the Judiciary must be a person of proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence.**"
**Article XI, Section 2, 1987 Constitution:**
"SECTION 2. The President, the Vice-President, the Members of the Supreme Court, the Members of the Constitutional Commissions, and the Ombudsman **may be removed from office on impeachment for, and conviction of, culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust.** All other public officers and employees may be removed from office as provided by law, but not by impeachment."
**Article XI, Section 17, 1987 Constitution:**
"SECTION 17. **A public officer or employee shall, upon assumption of office and as often thereafter as may be required by law, submit a declaration under oath of his assets, liabilities, and net worth.** In the case of the President, the Vice-President, the Members of the Cabinet, the Congress, the Supreme Court, the Constitutional Commissions and other constitutional offices, and officers of the armed forces with general or flag rank, the declaration shall be disclosed to the public in the manner provided by law."
**Section 7, Republic Act No. 3019 (Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act):**
"SECTION 7. **Statement of assets and liabilities.** — **Every public officer, within thirty days after assuming office, thereafter, on or before the fifteenth day of April following the close of every calendar year, as well as upon the expiration of his term of office, or upon his resignation or separation from office, shall prepare and file** with the office of the corresponding Department Head, or in the case of a Head of department or Chief of an independent office, with the Office of the President, **a true, detailed sworn statement of assets and liabilities**, including a statement of the amounts and sources of his income, the amounts of his personal and family expenses and the amount of income taxes paid for the next preceding calendar year..."
**Section 8(A), Republic Act No. 6713 (Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees):**
"SECTION 8. **Statements and Disclosure.** — Public officials and employees have an obligation to accomplish and submit declarations under oath of, and the public has the right to know, their assets, liabilities, net worth and financial and business interests including those of their spouses and of unmarried children under eighteen (18) years of age living in their households.
(A) **Statements of Assets and Liabilities and Financial Disclosure.** — **All public officials and employees, except those who serve in an honorary capacity, laborers and casual or temporary workers, shall file under oath their Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth and a Disclosure of Business Interests and Financial Connections**...
**The documents must be filed: (a) within thirty (30) days after assumption of office; (b) on or before April 30, of every year thereafter; and (c) within thirty (30) days after separation from the service.**"
**Section 1 & Section 11, Rule 66, Rules of Court:**
"SECTION 1. **Action by Government against individuals.** — An action for the usurpation of a public office, position or franchise may be commenced by a verified petition brought in the name of the Republic of the Philippines against: (a) A person who usurps, intrudes into, or unlawfully holds or exercises a public office, position or franchise; (b) A public officer who does or suffers an act which, by the provision of law, constitutes a ground for the forfeiture of his office..."
"SECTION 11. **Limitations.** — Nothing contained in this Rule shall be construed to authorize an action against a public officer or employee for his ouster from office **unless the same be commenced within one (1) year after the cause of such ouster, or the right of the petitioner to hold such office or position, arose**..."
**Factual Trigger:** The controversy erupted when congressional hearings on an impeachment complaint filed by Atty. Larry Gadon revealed that Sereno, throughout her 20-year government service as a UP College of Law faculty member (1986–2006), failed to file her annual SALNs for 11 years and subsequently submitted only three SALNs (2009, 2010, 2011) to the JBC when applying for Chief Justice in 2012—despite the JBC’s explicit published mandate requiring government applicants to submit all previous SALNs (later adjusted to at least 10 years). This omission led the Solicitor General to file a direct **quo warranto** petition challenging her constitutional eligibility for lack of proven integrity.

### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's (The Republic through OSG) Arguments
**Main Thesis: Quo warranto** is the appropriate and legally available remedy to test an appointee's title and constitutional eligibility. Respondent's chronic failure to file her mandatory annual SALNs as a UP Law professor and her failure to submit the required SALNs to the JBC demonstrate a complete absence of the constitutional qualification of "proven integrity" under Article VIII, Section 7(3), rendering her appointment as Chief Justice void **ab initio**.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Remedy and Exclusivity:** Impeachment is designed to remove a validly appointed officer for wrongdoing in office; **quo warranto** tests the legal validity of the appointment itself. Section 2, Article XI uses the permissive term "may," meaning impeachment is not the exclusive mode of removing an impeachable officer whose title is defective.
2. **Prescription:** The one-year prescriptive period under Section 11, Rule 66 does not run against the State under the ancient maxim **nullum tempus occurrit regi** (no time runs against the King/State) and Article 1108(4) of the Civil Code. Alternatively, the period is reckoned from the **discovery** of the defect during the 2018 House hearings, not the date of appointment.
3. **Reviewability of JBC Action:** The JBC is an office under the Supreme Court's supervision. Its nomination is not an unreviewable political question when it acts in violation of constitutional minimum qualifications.
4. **Substantive Ineligibility (Proven Integrity):** Filing SALNs is a mandatory constitutional (Art. XI, Sec. 17) and statutory (R.A. 3019 and R.A. 6713) duty governed by principles of **malum prohibitum**. Repeated, chronic failure to file SALNs (11 missing SALNs) constitutes dishonesty, negates proven integrity, and cannot be cured by the President’s discretionary appointment.
5. **Deceit and Concealment:** Respondent actively misled the JBC in her July 23, 2012 letter by claiming academic files were "infeasible to retrieve" due to age, concealing that she simply failed to file them. She also suppressed massive earnings from the **PIATCO** arbitrations (P32.4 million gross), evading tax declarations and distorting her net worth statements.
B. Respondent's (Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno) Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Under Section 2, Article XI of the 1987 Constitution and settled jurisprudence (**Lecaroz, Cuenca, In Re Gonzales**), an incumbent Member of the Supreme Court can be ousted from office **only** through the constitutionally exclusive mechanism of impeachment by the Senate. **Quo warranto** against an impeachable officer is unconstitutional, time-barred, and usurps the sole jurisdiction of the Senate.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Exclusivity of Impeachment & Hierarchy:** Allowing **quo warranto** against high magistrates eviscerates judicial independence, bypasses the cumbersome impeachment framework designed to protect constitutional officers from harassment suits, and creates an absurdity where a Regional Trial Court judge could potentially oust a Supreme Court Justice under concurrent Rule 66 jurisdiction.
2. **Prescription:** The petition is fatally time-barred under Section 11, Rule 66. The one-year period commences strictly from the "cause of ouster" (which occurred, at the latest, upon her appointment on August 24, 2012—nearly six years prior), not from "discovery." **Agcaoili v. Suguitan** establishes that prescription runs against the State when expressly fixed by statute.
3. **Political Question and JBC Discretion:** Whether an applicant possesses "proven integrity" is a subjective, value-laden determination textually committed to the wisdom and discretion of the JBC and the President, constituting an unreviewable political question absent a direct petition establishing grave abuse of discretion.
4. **Presumption of Regularity & Evidentiary Failure:** As a public officer, she enjoys the presumption of regular performance of duty. Under **Concerned Taxpayer v. Doblada, Jr.**, missing records in repository archives do not prove non-filing. She recovered 11 SALNs, proving a pattern of compliance. The burden of proof rests entirely on petitioner, who failed to produce categorical proof of non-filing.
5. **Excuses and Exceptions:** Under R.A. 6713, officers on leave without pay are exempt from filing because they receive no government compensation. Furthermore, UP HRDO issued administrative clearances in 2006, confirming the regular performance of all duties. The JBC waived complete filing and accepted her substantial compliance when it shortlisted her.
6. **Forum Shopping:** The Solicitor General engaged in forum shopping because the charges of SALN non-filing and tax evasion replicate the allegations pending before the House Committee on Justice.
