### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Santiago v. Bautista**
**Full Official Caption:** TEODORO C. SANTIAGO, JR., Minor, Represented by his Mother, Mrs. Angelita C. Santiago, **petitioner-appellant**, vs. MISS JUANITA BAUTISTA, ROSALINDA ALPAS, REBECCA MATUGAS, MILKITA INAMAC, ROMEO AGUSTIN, AIDA CAMINO, LUNA SARMAGO, AURORA LORENA, SOLEDAD FRANCISCO and MR. FLOR MARCELO, **respondents-appellees**.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. L-25024; March 30, 1970; 143 Phil. 209; En Banc; Barredo, **J.** (Concurring: Concepcion, **C.J.**, Reyes, J.B.L., Dizon, Makalintal, Zaldivar, Castro, Fernando, Teehankee, and Villamor, **JJ.**).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Teodoro C. Santiago, Jr. (Petitioner-Appellant):** A graduating Grade Six pupil at Sero Elementary School in Cotabato City, awarded third honor, suing through his mother (Mrs. Angelita C. Santiago) and assisted by his father (Atty. Teodoro M. Santiago) as legal counsel.
**Aurora Lorena (Respondent-Appellee):** School Principal of Sero Elementary School and Chairman of the "Committee on the Rating of Students for Honor."
**Juanita Bautista, Rosalinda Alpas, Rebecca Matugas, Milkita Inamac, Romeo Agustin, Aida Camino, and Luna Sarmago (Respondents-Appellees):** Grade Six classroom teachers at Sero Elementary School and members of the "Committee on the Rating of Students for Honor."
**Soledad Francisco (Respondent-Appellee):** District Supervisor of the Bureau of Public Schools in Cotabato City.
**Flor Marcelo (Respondent-Appellee):** Academic Supervisor of the Bureau of Public Schools in Cotabato City.
**Socorro Medina & Patricia Liñgat (Non-party Graduating Pupils):** Graduating pupils awarded first honor and second honor, respectively, by the respondent committee.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Direct appeal from the June 4, 1965 Order of the Court of First Instance (CFI) of Cotabato (Civil Case No. 2012) dismissing, on respondents' motion to dismiss, appellant's petition for **certiorari**, injunction, and damages for failure to state a cause of action, and from the subsequent order denying his motion for reconsideration.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Judicial Power & Jurisdiction → Nature of Judicial and Quasi-Judicial Functions vs. Administrative School Functions
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Special Civil Actions → Petition for **Certiorari** (Rule 65) → Requisites and Subject Matter of **Certiorari**
**Full Text of Governing Provisions:**
**Rule 65, Section 1, 1964 Rules of Court (now Rule 65, Section 1 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure):**
"Section 1. **Petition for certiorari.** — **When any tribunal, board, or officer exercising judicial functions, has acted without or in excess of its or his jurisdiction, or with grave abuse of discretion** and there is no appeal, nor any plain, speedy, and adequate remedy in the ordinary course of law, a person aggrieved thereby may file a verified petition in the proper court alleging the facts with certainty and praying that judgment be rendered annulling or modifying the proceedings, as the law requires, of such tribunal, board or officer.

**The petition shall be accompanied by a certified true copy of the judgment or order subject thereof, together with copies of all pleadings and documents relevant and pertinent thereto.**"
**Historical Landmark Rule (Article VIII, Section 1, 1935 Constitution vs. Article VIII, Section 1, 1987 Constitution):**
**1935 Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 1:** "The Judicial power shall be vested in one Supreme Court and in such inferior courts as may be established by law."

**Modern Provision (1987 Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 1):** "The judicial power shall be vested in one Supreme Court and in such lower courts as may be established by law. **Judicial power includes the duty of the courts of justice to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable, and to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government.**"
**Factual Trigger:** A graduating sixth-grade public school pupil, dissatisfied with being ranked third honor behind two female classmates, filed a petition for **certiorari** and injunction before the CFI against his teachers and school supervisors to annul the final graduation honor roll three days before commencement exercises, claiming teacher bias and irregularities in grading.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Summer Vacation, 1964:** Sixth-grade English teacher Rosalinda Alpas privately tutored and coached pupil Socorro Medina.
**School Year 1964–1965:** Teodoro Santiago, Jr., Socorro Medina, and Patricia Liñgat competed as close academic rivals in Grade Six at Sero Elementary School in Cotabato City.
**May 1965 (Close of School Year):** Principal Aurora Lorena constituted the "Committee on the Rating of Students for Honor," composed exclusively of Grade Six teachers (Lorena as Chairman, alongside Bautista, Alpas, Matugas, Inamac, Agustin, Camino, and Sarmago). Following committee deliberation, the final honors were resolved: Socorro Medina (1st honor), Patricia Liñgat (2nd honor), and Teodoro Santiago, Jr. (3rd honor).
**Mid-May 1965:** Discontented with placing third, Santiago, Jr. orally protested the ranking to Principal Lorena, District Supervisor Soledad Francisco, and Academic Supervisor Flor Marcelo, claiming the officials passed the matter to one another without resolving his grievance.
**May 18, 1965:** Three days before graduation, Santiago, Jr. instituted Civil Case No. 2012 in the CFI of Cotabato—a special civil action for **certiorari**, preliminary injunction, and P10,000.00 damages against the committee members, the District Supervisor, and the Academic Supervisor. He claimed the committee was illegally constituted under the Bureau of Public Schools Service Manual for Teachers (which allegedly required Grade V and VI teachers to sit jointly), that test scores of rivals were improperly elevated from 80% to 85%, that unadvisable district examinations were counted, and that a past Grade I certificate had been altered to read "second place" instead of "first place."
**May 20, 1965:** The CFI of Cotabato denied the prayer for preliminary injunction, ruling that restraining the graduation exercises scheduled for the next day would shock the school authorities, parents, and community.
**May 21, 1965:** Graduation exercises proceeded as scheduled at Sero Elementary School, with honors conferred according to the contested committee ranking.
**May 24, 1965:** Respondents filed a Motion to Dismiss Civil Case No. 2012, asserting that **certiorari** was improper and that the graduation having taken place, the issue had become academic. Santiago, Jr. opposed the motion.
**June 4, 1965:** The CFI of Cotabato granted the Motion to Dismiss on three grounds: (1) petitioner failed to attach a certified true copy of the questioned judgment or order under Rule 65, Section 1; (2) failure to exhaust administrative remedies within the Department of Education; and (3) allegations involved mere errors or irregularities rather than jurisdictional grave abuse of discretion.
**Subsequent Date, 1965:** The CFI denied petitioner's motion for reconsideration.
**Subsequent Date, 1965:** Petitioner appealed the orders of dismissal directly to the Supreme Court.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner-Appellant's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The CFI erred in dismissing the petition because the respondent teachers committed grave abuse of official discretion in rating graduating honor students, depriving him of his rightful academic standing without an adequate administrative remedy.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Procedural Compliance: Failure to attach formal copies of the ranking order was excused because the official graduation program was delivered only on the morning of graduation day.
 Exhaustion of Remedies: He personally protested to the Principal, District Supervisor, and Academic Supervisor, but they "passed the buck to each other," making recourse to higher educational authorities too late to prevent irreparable injury prior to graduation.
 Illegal Committee Constitution: The grading committee was formed in violation of the Service Manual for Teachers of the Bureau of Public Schools because it excluded Grade V teachers and comprised Grade VI teachers only.
 Grave Abuse and Fraud: Teachers altered the grading sheets of Socorro Medina and Patricia Liñgat from 80% to 85%, assigned petitioner starting grades of 75% to depress his standing, counted unauthorized district examinations, and awarded Medina an unnatural perfect score due to favoritism stemming from summer tutoring.
B. Respondent-Appellees' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The petition states no cause of action because the committee of teachers is not a tribunal exercising judicial functions, the procedural requisites of Rule 65 were ignored, administrative remedies were bypassed, and the controversy became entirely moot upon the holding of graduation exercises.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Absence of Judicial Functions:** Under Section 1 of Rule 65, **certiorari lies only against a tribunal, board, or officer exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions. A committee of schoolteachers rating pupils acts purely in an administrative capacity without statutory authority to resolve legal controversies or adjudicate property/personal rights.
 Violation of Mandatory Rule Requirements: The petition lacked certified true copies of the judgment or order complained of, as well as copies of the Service Manual, altered grade sheets, and relevant records, rendering the petition fatally defective.
 Non-Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies: Petitioner bypassed the established hierarchy of the Department of Education, lodging only informal oral complaints before rushing to court.
 Mootness: The graduation exercises having been concluded on May 21, 1965, the ranking could no longer be enjoined.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the "Committee on the Rating of Students for Honor" constituted by public schoolteachers exercises judicial or quasi-judicial functions within the contemplation of Section 1, Rule 65 of the Rules of Court so as to be subject to the corrective writ of **certiorari**.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the petitioner's failure to accompany his petition for **certiorari** with a certified true copy of the judgment or order complained of, together with copies of relevant pleadings and documents, is fatal to his cause of action.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Applicability of **Certiorari** to School Honor Rating Committees
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the committee of teachers rating honor students exercised judicial or quasi-judicial functions amenable to **certiorari**. **NO.** Evaluating and rating pupils for graduation honors involves purely administrative academic discretion, not the adjudication of legal rights by a body exercising judicial power.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Definition and Three-Part Test for Judicial Functions:** For **certiorari** to lie under Rule 65, the respondent must be a tribunal, board, or officer performing judicial acts. Drawing from established jurisprudence (**Ruperto v. Torres**; **State ex rel. Board of Commrs. v. Dunn), the Court synthesized three cumulative conditions:
1.  There must be a specific controversy involving rights of persons or property brought before the tribunal for hearing and determination of adverse claims;
2.  The tribunal must have the statutory power and authority to pronounce judgment by construing and applying the law to the controversy; and
3.  The body must pertain to the judicial department or exercise sovereign power not belonging to the legislative or executive branches.
 Application to Grading Committees: Public schoolteachers meeting to assess the comparative merits of graduating pupils do not interpret or apply the law to resolve conflicting legal rights. There is no statute creating an enforceable legal property right in academic honors prior to an official award.
 Discretion vs. Judicial Character: The mere exercise of thought, deliberation, judgment, and discretion does not transform an administrative act into a judicial function. Executive and administrative duties of the highest order require judgment, but they remain non-judicial because they do not involve legal adjudication between adverse parties under statutory mandate.
 Analogy to Academic and Literary Contests (**Felipe v. Leuterio**):** The Court reaffirmed **Felipe v. Leuterio**, which barred judicial interference in oratorical, literary, and beauty contests. Contestants possess merely an inchoate privilege to compete; no demandable right to a prize or honor vests until proclaimed by the designated arbiters. An error by evaluators in assessing comparative excellence is not an actionable legal "wrong" (violation of a right), but at most **damnum absque injuria.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"[B]efore [a] tribunal, board, or officer may exercise judicial or quasi judicial acts, it is necessary that there be a law that gives rise to some specific rights of persons or property under which adverse claims to such rights are made, and the controversy ensuing therefrom is brought, in turn, before the tribunal, board or officer clothed with power and authority to determine what that law is and thereupon adjudicate the respective rights of the contending parties."
"No rights to the prizes may be asserted by the contestants, because theirs was merely the privilege to compete for the prize, and that privilege did not ripen into a demandable right unless and until they were proclaimed winners of the competition by the appointed arbiters or referees or judges."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** An elementary school honor committee does not act like a court. Teachers assessing pupils' grades are exercising administrative educational discretion, not resolving a legal lawsuit between parties over vested legal or property rights. Because there is no law giving a student a demandable right to an academic honor before it is officially awarded, teachers do not exercise judicial or quasi-judicial functions, making **certiorari** completely unavailable.
Issue 2: Effect of Non-Attachment of Questioned Documents under Rule 65
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the failure to attach certified true copies of the questioned order, relevant pleadings, and referenced documents was fatal to the petition. **YES.** Compliance with the second paragraph of Section 1, Rule 65 is mandatory, and its omission leaves the petition without an identifiable, reviewable record.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Mandatory Requirement of Form:** Rule 65 explicitly requires that a petition for **certiorari must be accompanied by a certified true copy of the judgment or order subject thereof, along with all pertinent documents.
 Precedential Enforcement (**Alajar** and **NAWASA**):** Under **Alajar v. Court of Industrial Relations** and **NAWASA v. Municipality of Libmanan**, failure to attach the specific orders, records, and decisions alleged to have been violated renders a petition for **certiorari insufficient in form and substance.
 Rejection of Appellant's Excuse: Appellant claimed he could not attach the graduation program because it was distributed only on graduation day. The Court rejected this excuse, observing that appellant knew of the committee's decision days earlier when he made oral appeals. Furthermore, appellant wholly failed to attach copies of the Service Manual for Teachers, the alleged altered grade sheets, or his Grade I certificate upon which his claims of fraud were founded.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"It is striking, indeed, that this petition has not been accompanied by a certified true copy of the judgment or order complained of, together with all pleadings and documents which are relevant thereto, as required by the second paragraph of the aforequoted rule. This violation renders the petition extremely indefinite and uncertain. There is no written formal judgment or order of respondents that is submitted for revision or correction of this Court. This violation is fatal to the petition."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** You cannot ask a court to strike down a decision under Rule 65 without showing the court the actual written decision and the official documents being attacked. Santiago, Jr. sued to invalidate an honor roll without attaching the committee's official written rating, the Service Manual he claimed was violated, or the allegedly altered grading sheets. This omission rendered his petition fatally defective.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Assigned Syllabus Topic: c. Jurisdiction | Applied Lens: Remedial Law & Evidence
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
**Requisites for an Entity to Exercise "Judicial Functions" (Subject to Certiorari under Rule 65):**
1.  **Specific Controversy:** Must involve legal rights of persons or property brought before the entity for determination. → **Absent:** Students have no vested personal or property rights in class honors; rating pupils is an internal school evaluation.
2.  **Authority to Adjudicate under Law:** Entity must be clothed with power to declare what the law is, construe written law, and pronounce an enforceable judgment. → **Absent:** Teachers evaluate scholastic performance based on educational guidelines, not statutory interpretation or legal dispute arbitration.
3.  **Sovereign Judicial Character:** The function must pertain to the judicial department or a quasi-judicial body outside the purely administrative/executive hierarchy. → **Absent:** Public school teachers operate strictly within the administrative hierarchy of the Bureau of Public Schools.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Judicial Function vs. Discretion: Deliberation and judgment do not equal judicial power; executive and ministerial officers routinely exercise high discretion without acting judicially.
 Damnum Absque Injuria: Damage without legal injury. A student who loses an honor roll position due to non-fraudulent teacher evaluation suffers no compensable legal wrong because no vested right was violated.
 Privilege to Compete vs. Demandable Right: An academic contestant holds only a privilege to strive for an award; no enforceable right exists unless and until declared a winner by the appointed arbiters.
 Fatal Defect (Rule 65 Form): Failure to annex certified copies of the questioned judgment or documents leaves the court without subject-matter jurisdiction to modify or annul an administrative act.
**Procedural Remedy & Jurisdiction Audit:**
 Propriety of Vehicle:** Rule 65 **certiorari** was fatally defective **ab initio. The respondent teachers and supervisors were not an inferior court, board, or officer exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions. An administrative appeal within the Department of Education, followed by an ordinary civil action for damages if fraud were proven against specific individuals, was the only viable path.
 Hierarchy of Courts & Administrative Remedies: The CFI lacked subject-matter jurisdiction under Rule 65 to act as an appellate academic board of judges over public elementary school ratings.
**Evidentiary & Quantum of Proof Analysis:**
 Evidence on Motion to Dismiss: In resolving a motion to dismiss for failure to state a cause of action, well-pleaded factual allegations are hypothetically admitted, but legal conclusions (such as "grave abuse of discretion") are not.
 Missing Evidentiary Corpus: Because appellant failed to annex the primary documentary evidence (the Service Manual, the altered grading sheets, and the certificate), the complaint remained legally indefinite, rendering the alleged fraud non-actionable under Rule 65.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**Santiago v. Bautista** is placed under "Jurisdiction" because it delineates the constitutional boundary of judicial and quasi-judicial functions subject to court review via **certiorari**. The Supreme Court held that trial courts have no jurisdiction under Rule 65 to review the academic ranking of honor students by public school teachers. Teachers evaluating students exercise administrative educational discretion—not judicial power—because contestants hold merely a privilege to compete rather than a vested legal right, rendering any perceived grading error **damnum absque injuria**.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed. (All concurring En Banc).
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"FOR THE FOREGOING CONSIDERATIONS, the judgment appealed from is affirmed, with costs against appellant."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court completely affirmed the dismissal of Teodoro Santiago, Jr.'s petition. The school teachers and educational authorities prevailed; the contested Grade Six graduation honor roll remained valid and undisturbed; and the student was assessed court costs.

No. 207132; intervenor before the trial court; an association of non-GAMCA Philippine medical clinics conducting health examinations for overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), advocating for the strict enforcement of the statutory ban on the "referral decking system."
**Hon. Enrique T. Ona (Secretary of Health) / Alexander A. Padilla (Undersecretary of Health, Health Regulation Cluster) / Department of Health (DOH):** Petitioner in G.R. No. 207205; the executive regulatory agency tasked under Republic Act (RA) No. 10022 to regulate OFW medical examination clinics and enforce the prohibition against referral decking.

Cangco:** Respondents in both petitions; an association of selected Philippine medical clinics accredited by the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) States' Executive Board of the Health Ministers' Council (HMC), which operates a mandatory, centralized "referral decking system" where GCC-bound OFWs are farmed out exclusively to GAMCA member clinics.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
These are consolidated Petitions for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court filed separately by AMCOW and DOH Secretary Ona directly challenging the **August 10, 2012 Decision** and **April 12, 2013 Order** of the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Pasay City, Branch 108 (Sp. Civil Action No. R-PSY-10-04391-CV). The RTC had granted GAMCA's Rule 65 petition for certiorari and prohibition, declaring null and void **ab initio** the DOH Cease and Desist Orders (CDO letters) dated August 23, 2010 and November 2, 2010, permanently enjoining their enforcement against GAMCA, and ruling that Section 16 of RA No. 10022 does not apply to GAMCA under international law.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Department → Jurisdiction → Expanded Jurisdiction vs. Traditional Rule 65 Certiorari
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Special Civil Actions → Rule 65 (Certiorari and Prohibition) → Jurisdiction Over Quasi-Judicial Agencies (Sec. 4, Rule 65; Sec. 9, BP 129); Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies and Ripeness; Police Power vs. Sovereign Equality of States.
**Verbatim Text of Governing Provisions:**
**Article VIII, Section 1, Paragraph 2, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Judicial power includes the duty of the courts of justice to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable, and to determine whether or not there has been a **grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government**."
**Section 4, Rule 65, 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure (as amended):**
"Sec. 4. **When and where petition filed.** — The petition shall be filed not later than sixty (60) days from notice of the judgment, order or resolution...
The petition shall be filed in the Supreme Court or, if it relates to the acts or omissions of a lower court or of a corporation, board, officer or person, in the Regional Trial Court exercising jurisdiction over the territorial area as defined by the Supreme Court. It may also be filed in the Court of Appeals whether or not the same is in aid of its appellate jurisdiction, or in the Sandiganbayan if it is in aid of its appellate jurisdiction.
**If it involves the acts or omissions of a quasi-judicial agency, unless otherwise provided by law or these Rules, the petition shall be filed in and cognizable only by the Court of Appeals.**"
**Section 16, Republic Act No. 10022 (amending Section 23, Republic Act No. 8042):**
"(c) Department of Health. — The Department of Health (DOH) shall regulate the activities and operations of all clinics which conduct medical, physical, optical, dental, psychological and other similar examinations, hereinafter referred to as health examinations, on Filipino migrant workers as requirement for their overseas employment. Pursuant to this, the DOH shall ensure that:
...
(c.3) **No group or groups of medical clinics shall have a monopoly of exclusively conducting health examinations on migrant workers for certain receiving countries;**
(c.4) **Every Filipino migrant worker shall have the freedom to choose any of the DOH-accredited or DOH-operated clinics that will conduct his/her health examinations and that his or her rights as a patient are respected. The decking practice, which requires an overseas Filipino worker to go first to an office for registration and then farmed out to a medical clinic located elsewhere, shall not be allowed;**"
**Factual Trigger:**
Following the enactment of Section 16 of RA No. 10022 expressly criminalizing and prohibiting the "decking practice," the DOH issued administrative cease and desist orders (CDO letters) on August 23, 2010 and November 2, 2010 directing GAMCA to immediately halt its referral decking operations within three days. Instead of exhausting internal executive appeals or filing a Rule 65 petition before the Court of Appeals, GAMCA filed a petition for certiorari and prohibition directly before the Regional Trial Court of Pasay City to enjoin the DOH and invalidate the statutory ban, prompting the RTC to void the DOH orders and exempt GAMCA on grounds of foreign state sovereignty.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**March 8, 2001:** The DOH issues Administrative Order No. 5, Series of 2001 (AO 5-01), permitting and directing the equal distribution ("decking") of migrant workers among GAMCA-member clinics to accommodate GCC States' embassy visa pre-requisites.

**July 16, 2004:** The DOH issues AO No. 159, Series of 2004, reiterating the suspension of the referral decking system.
**August 30, 2004:** The DOH issues AO No. 167, Series of 2004, formally repealing and revoking AO 5-01, concluding that the GAMCA referral decking system neither assures nor guarantees migrant workers' rights to safe, quality healthcare and reliable medical test results.
**September 26, 2008:** DOH Secretary Francisco T. Duque III issues Department Memorandum No. 2008-0210, ordering all DOH/PhilHealth-accredited OFW clinics belonging to GAMCA to forthwith stop, terminate, and end the referral decking system.
**January 14, 2010:** Acting on GAMCA's administrative appeal, the Office of the President (OP) renders a decision nullifying DOH Memorandum No. 2008-0210.
**March 8, 2010:** Republic Act No. 10022 lapses into law without presidential signature, amending Section 23 of RA No. 8042. Section 16 expressly mandates patient freedom of choice and provides that **"The decking practice, which requires an overseas Filipino worker to go first to an office for registration and then farmed out to a medical clinic located elsewhere, shall not be allowed"** and forbids any monopoly of medical clinics.
**August 13, 2010:** The Omnibus Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of RA No. 8042, as amended by RA No. 10022, officially take effect.
**August 23, 2010:** DOH Undersecretary Alexander A. Padilla issues a letter-order directing GAMCA to cease and desist from implementing the referral decking system and to wind up its decking operations within three days from receipt. GAMCA receives the order on August 25, 2010.
**August 26, 2010:** GAMCA files a Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition with prayer for TRO/Preliminary Injunction before the Regional Trial Court of Pasig City (later transferred/re-raffled to RTC Pasay City, Branch 108), docketed as Sp. Civil Action No. R-PSY-10-04391-CV, asserting grave abuse of discretion and challenging the constitutionality of Section 16 of RA No. 10022.
**November 2, 2010:** The DOH issues a reiterating order commanding GAMCA to strictly comply with the cease and desist directive.
**November 23–24, 2010:** AMCOW files an urgent motion for leave to intervene and file an opposition-in-intervention. The RTC grants AMCOW's intervention without opposition from GAMCA or DOH.
**August 1, 2011:** The RTC of Pasay City, Branch 108, issues an order granting a writ of preliminary injunction restraining the DOH from enforcing its August 23, 2010 and November 2, 2010 CDO letters.
**August 10, 2012:** The RTC of Pasay City renders its Decision granting GAMCA's petition. It declares the DOH CDO letters null and void **ab initio**, makes the preliminary injunction permanent, and holds that while Section 16 of RA No. 10022 is constitutional on its face, it cannot apply to GAMCA because GAMCA is an adjunct of the GCC States' agent; applying it would violate the international customary principles of sovereign equality and independence of States.
**April 12, 2013:** The RTC denies the separate Motions for Reconsideration filed by the DOH and AMCOW.
**June 2013:** AMCOW (G.R. No. 207132) and DOH Secretary Ona (G.R. No. 207205) file separate Rule 45 petitions for review on certiorari directly with the Supreme Court.
**September 17, 2013:** The Supreme Court En Banc orders the consolidation of G.R. Nos. 207132 and 207205.
**April 14, 2015:** The Supreme Court denies GAMCA's urgent motions for injunctive relief and suspends the enforcement of the RTC's permanent injunction.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments (AMCOW and DOH Secretary Ona)
**Main Thesis:** The RTC committed grave jurisdictional and substantive legal errors in entertaining GAMCA's petition and exempting GAMCA from RA No. 10022. The CDO letters were valid exercises of police power regulating domestic health facilities, while GAMCA chose the wrong court, bypassed administrative remedies, and lacked legal basis to claim foreign sovereign immunity.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Improper Procedural Remedy and Lack of RTC Jurisdiction:** Certiorari and prohibition under Rule 65 lie only against judicial and quasi-judicial acts (and ministerial acts for prohibition). Since the DOH acted in a quasi-judicial capacity, Section 4 of Rule 65 and Section 9 of BP 129 vest exclusive jurisdiction in the Court of Appeals, completely depriving the RTC of subject-matter jurisdiction.
2.  **Violation of Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies and Ripeness:** GAMCA prematurely sought judicial intervention without first filing a motion for reconsideration before the DOH Secretary or an administrative appeal to the Office of the President—a remedy GAMCA was well aware of, having successfully utilized it against Memo No. 2008-0210 in 2010.
3.  **Valid Exercise of Police Power:** The statutory ban on referral decking under Section 16 of RA No. 10022 is a legitimate exercise of plenary police power designed to protect the health, welfare, and freedom of choice of Filipino migrant workers and dismantle monopolies in healthcare examinations.
4.  **Inapplicability of Sovereign Equality and Independence:** GAMCA and its member clinics are private domestic corporations operating in the Philippines under Philippine franchises and licenses. Foreign States cannot dictate domestic public health regulations within Philippine territory. State immunity belongs solely to sovereign States acting **jure imperii**, not to private commercial clinics (**jure gestionis**).
B. Respondents' Arguments (GAMCA and Christian E. Cangco)
**Main Thesis:** The DOH CDO letters are null and void for violating procedural due process and constituting an unconstitutional taking of property. Applying Section 16 of RA No. 10022 to GAMCA violates international law by unlawfully interfering with the sovereign visa prerogatives of the GCC States.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Undue Taking of Property & Due Process Violation:** The SEC approved GAMCA's Articles of Incorporation and By-laws sanctioning referral decking. GAMCA member clinics invested substantial capital to upgrade their facilities. The immediate summary CDO deprives them of property and business operations without a hearing, violating procedural due process and Article III, Section 1 of the Constitution.
2.  **Violation of Sovereign Equality and Independence (Par in Parem Non Habet Imperium):** GAMCA is an accredited adjunct and operational arm of the Health Ministers' Council (HMC) of the GCC States. Referral decking is an indispensable component of the GCC visa-granting process—an exercise of foreign sovereign power to protect their territories from health hazards. The Philippines cannot interfere with foreign immigration procedures.
3.  **Irreparable Injury to OFWs:** If GAMCA's decking system is shut down, GCC embassies will refuse to issue visas to Filipino workers lacking the GAMCA medical seal, paralyzing overseas employment deployment to GCC member states.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE] [Procedural / Jurisdiction Issue]:** Whether or not the Regional Trial Court legally erred in taking cognizance of and giving due course to GAMCA's petition for certiorari and prohibition challenging the DOH CDO letters, considering the requirements of subject-matter jurisdiction under Section 4, Rule 65 and Section 9 of BP 129, the doctrine of hierarchy of courts, and the doctrine of exhaustion of administrative remedies.
2.  **[Substantive / Constitutional Issue]:** Whether or not the DOH CDO letters enforcing the statutory prohibition against the referral decking system under Section 16 of RA No. 10022 violate the Constitution by amounting to an undue taking of private property without due process of law.
3.  **[Substantive / Constitutional & International Law Issue]:** Whether or not the application of Section 16 of RA No. 10022 to GAMCA violates the generally accepted principles of international law, specifically the customary international principles of sovereign independence and equality of States.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: RTC Jurisdiction and Propriety of Certiorari Against the DOH CDO Letters
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did the RTC legally err in taking cognizance of GAMCA's petition for certiorari and prohibition? **YES.** The RTC completely lacked subject-matter jurisdiction because the DOH acted in a quasi-judicial capacity, making its orders cognizable exclusively by the Court of Appeals under Section 4 of Rule 65 and BP 129; furthermore, GAMCA fatally bypassed the doctrine of exhaustion of administrative remedies.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Traditional Rule 65 vs. Expanded Article VIII, Section 1 Certiorari:** Under the traditional mode of Rule 65, certiorari lies exclusively to correct jurisdictional errors of tribunals, boards, or officers exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions where there is no appeal or plain, speedy, adequate remedy. In contrast, the second paragraph of Article VIII, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution established the "expanded certiorari jurisdiction" to determine whether any branch or instrumentality of government committed grave abuse of discretion. While the Court has ad hoc permitted Rule 65 as the procedural vehicle to invoke expanded review, the traditional requirements of justiciability—actual controversy, standing, ripeness, and hierarchy of courts—remain indispensable.
2.  **Quasi-Judicial Nature of the DOH CDO Letters:** Determining whether an administrative act is quasi-judicial depends on the **nature of the act performed**, not the nature of the office. An agency acts quasi-judicially when it investigates facts, holds hearings, applies legislative standards to particular individuals or groups, and draws conclusions regarding rights or violations. In issuing the CDO letters, the DOH investigated facts (finding that GAMCA operates the decking system) and applied the legislative policy of Section 16 of RA No. 10022 to command GAMCA to cease operations. A cease and desist order is inherently quasi-judicial, functioning akin to a judicial injunction.
3.  **Exclusive Appellate/Certiorari Jurisdiction Vested in the Court of Appeals:** Under Section 4, Rule 65 of the Rules of Court, if a petition for certiorari involves the acts or omissions of a **quasi-judicial agency**, it **"shall be filed in and cognizable only by the Court of Appeals."** This harmonizes with Section 9 of BP 129, which vests exclusive original and appellate jurisdiction over quasi-judicial bodies in the CA. The RTC of Pasay had no subject-matter jurisdiction over DOH quasi-judicial orders; its assumption of jurisdiction was a patent nullity, rendering its judgment void **ab initio**.
4.  **Fatal Non-Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies and Unripeness:** GAMCA failed to establish that there was no other plain, speedy, and adequate remedy. Under Book IV, Chapter 8 of EO No. 292 (Administrative Code of 1987) and Article VII, Section 17 of the Constitution, the DOH Secretary exercises supervision and control over the department, and the President exercises control over all executive departments. GAMCA should have sought reconsideration from the DOH Secretary or appealed directly to the Office of the President—as it had successfully done in 2010 against Memo No. 2008-0210. Failure to exhaust administrative remedies negates the ripeness of the constitutional challenge, depriving the courts of an actual justiciable controversy.
5.  **Absence of Grave Abuse of Discretion:** While the DOH technically erred in issuing the CDO letters without a prior hearing, this did not amount to grave abuse of discretion. The DOH had known GAMCA's decking system for nearly a decade (having previously regulated and suspended it under AOs 5-01, 106-02, and 167-04), and GAMCA had already extensively litigated the issue up to the Office of the President. Because RA No. 10022 expressly targeted this exact practice, and summary administrative CDOs are permissible when vital public health interests are at stake, the DOH's action was not whimsical, capricious, or despotic.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"If it involves the acts or omissions of a quasi-judicial agency, unless otherwise provided by law or these Rules, the petition shall be filed in and cognizable only by the Court of Appeals."

"Since the DOH is part of the Executive Department and has acted in its quasi-judicial capacity, the petition challenging its CDO letter should have been filed before the Court of Appeals. The RTC thus did not have jurisdiction over the subject matter of the petitions and erred in giving due course to the petition for certiorari and prohibition against the DOH CDO letters."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The RTC should have dismissed GAMCA's petition at the outset without asking for comment. Because the DOH issued a Cease and Desist Order by applying a statutory prohibition to GAMCA's specific factual operations, it acted as a quasi-judicial agency. Under Section 4, Rule 65 and BP 129, petitions for certiorari against quasi-judicial bodies belong exclusively to the Court of Appeals, not the Regional Trial Court. Furthermore, GAMCA violated the exhaustion doctrine because it jumped straight to court instead of appealing the Health Secretary's order to the Office of the President, making the case premature and unripe.
Issue 2: Validity Under Police Power vs. Undue Taking of Property
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Do the DOH CDO letters prohibiting referral decking violate the Constitution as an undue taking of property? **NO.** Section 16 of RA No. 10022 and the DOH CDO letters represent a valid, reasonable exercise of the State's police power to safeguard the health, general welfare, and freedom of choice of Filipino migrant workers.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Scope of Plenary Police Power:** Police power is the most pervasive, least limitable attribute of sovereignty, rooted in the maxims **salus populi est suprema lex** and **sic utere tuo ut alienum non laedas**. Private property, corporate charters, and business operations—especially those imbued with public interest such as healthcare services—are subordinated to reasonable state regulations promoting the general welfare.
2.  **The Lawful Subject and Lawful Means Test:** A valid exercise of police power requires: (1) the interests of the public generally require interference; and (2) the means employed are reasonably necessary and not unduly oppressive. Both requisites are present. The welfare and protection of OFWs against exploitative medical practices and exorbitant costs is an established public interest. Prohibiting monopolistic decking arrangements and securing patient freedom of choice to select any accredited clinic is a reasonable, non-oppressive means to ensure safe, quality medical examinations.
3.  **Inherent Regulatory Authority of DOH:** Under RA No. 4226 (Hospital Licensure Act), the DOH is expressly vested with the authority to suspend or revoke the licenses of health facilities that violate Philippine laws. The power to issue a cease and desist order against an illegal decking practice is a necessarily included lesser power of the statutory power to revoke licenses.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The State's police power is vast and plenary and the operation of a business, especially one that is imbued with public interest (such as healthcare services), falls within the scope of governmental exercise of police power through regulation. As defined, police power includes (1) the imposition of restraint on liberty or property, (2) in order to foster the common good."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
GAMCA cannot use its SEC corporate charter or private capital investments to block health regulations. Healthcare operations are deeply imbued with public interest and fully subject to the State's vast police power. Banning referral decking guarantees that OFWs are not treated as farmed-out commodities and can freely choose their doctors, satisfying the lawful subject and lawful means tests of due process.
Issue 3: Inapplicability of Sovereign Equality and Independence of States
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does exempting GAMCA from Section 16 of RA No. 10022 follow from the customary international principles of sovereign independence and equality? **NO.** Private clinics located in the Philippines are fully subject to Philippine territorial sovereignty and domestic regulatory statutes; sovereign immunity applies only to foreign States acting in a public capacity (**jus imperii**), which GCC States never extended to private domestic entities.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Territorial Sovereignty vs. Sovereign Immunity:** The principle of sovereign equality (**par in parem non habet imperium**) protects foreign sovereign States from being haled into Philippine courts without consent for sovereign, non-commercial acts (**jus imperii**). It does not grant foreign states, much less their domestic contractors or agents, immunity from observing Philippine domestic police regulations within Philippine territory.
2.  **Failure to Prove Customary Norm or Immunity Extension:** GAMCA presented zero evidence that international custom shields private state agents from complying with domestic police power laws. Moreover, sovereign immunity belongs strictly to the foreign State itself; it was never proven that the GCC States officially conferred sovereign status upon GAMCA.
3.  **Restrictive Immunity Doctrine:** Even assuming sovereign affiliation, the Philippines adheres to the restrictive theory of sovereign immunity, distinguishing sovereign acts (**jus imperii**) from commercial transactions (**jus gestionis**). Conducting clinic medical examinations for a fee is a purely commercial operation.
4.  **Domestic Scope of the Statute:** Section 16 of RA No. 10022 regulates domestic clinics and Philippine employers operating within the Philippines. It does not dictate foreign visa policies to GCC States. While GCC States remain free to grant or deny visas under their own domestic rules, they cannot enforce a prohibited decking cartel on Philippine soil.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"This recognition [of sovereign immunity] is altogether different from exempting governments whose agents are in the Philippines from complying with our domestic laws. We have yet to declare in a case that the principle of sovereign independence and equality exempts agents of foreign governments from compliance with the application of Philippine domestic law."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Sovereign immunity means you cannot drag a foreign State into our courts for its governmental acts; it does not mean foreign entities or their domestic agents can ignore Philippine laws while doing business in our country. GAMCA is a Philippine corporation operating clinics on Philippine soil. It is bound by Philippine statutes regardless of what visa requirements foreign GCC countries desire.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Topic: c. Jurisdiction | Lens: Remedial Law & Evidence
**Procedural Remedy & Jurisdiction Audit:**
 Defective Originating Vehicle: GAMCA filed a Rule 65 Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition in the RTC. This was fatal. A Cease and Desist Order issued by an administrative cluster head applying a statute to specific parties is a **quasi-judicial act**.
 Statutory Bar on RTC Subject-Matter Jurisdiction: Under Section 4, Paragraph 3 of Rule 65, and Section 9(3) of Batas Pambansa Blg. 129, original and supervisory jurisdiction to issue extraordinary writs against **quasi-judicial agencies** resides exclusively and originally in the **Court of Appeals**. The RTC lacked subject-matter jurisdiction; its assumption of jurisdiction and all subsequent injunctions were void **ab initio**.
 Proper Appellate Trajectory: GAMCA should have moved for reconsideration before the DOH Secretary, appealed the adverse ruling to the Office of the President (Administrative Code, Book IV, Chapter 8), and only thereafter elevated the final administrative determination to the Court of Appeals via Rule 43 (appeals) or Rule 65 (if grave abuse of discretion attended the executive action).
 Direct Rule 45 Review by SC: AMCOW and DOH properly utilized a Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 to bring pure questions of law directly from the RTC to the Supreme Court, bypassing the CA pursuant to Section 2(c), Rule 41.
**Evidentiary & Quantum of Proof Analysis:**
 Burden of Proving International Customary Law:** GAMCA asserted that international customary law recognized sovereign independence in a manner that immunizes state agents from local regulatory compliance. Under the Philippine rules of evidence and international law doctrine, customary international law is an evidentiary fact that must be proven through consistent, widespread state practice (**diuturnitas**) and **opinio juris sive necessitatis. GAMCA failed to introduce any evidence establishing that such a rule has crystallized into international custom.
 Proof of Sovereign Immunity Agency:** The party asserting sovereign immunity carries the burden of proving that it acted strictly as an organ of the foreign state performing sovereign (**jus imperii) acts and that immunity was formally extended to it. GAMCA presented no official diplomatic certification from the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) or GCC sovereign endorsements to substantiate its claim.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
 Requisites of Judicial Review (Constitutional Challenge):
1.  **Actual Case or Controversy:** Absent—GAMCA's challenge was premature due to failure to exhaust administrative remedies (unripeness).
2.  **Locus Standi:** Present for GAMCA as direct subject of the CDO; relaxed under expanded jurisdiction if grave abuse of discretion is prima facie shown.
3.  **Earliest Opportunity:** Raised in the RTC petition, but presented to the wrong tribunal.
4.  **Lis Mota:** The constitutional issue was not the very lis mota because the petition was dismissible on fundamental procedural and jurisdictional grounds.
 Police Power Reasonableness Test:
1.  **Valid Object:** Protection of migrant workers' health and elimination of oppressive monopolies (Passed).
2.  **Valid Means:** Ban on mandatory decking and preservation of patient freedom of choice (Passed).
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Expanded Certiorari Jurisdiction (Art. VIII, Sec. 1, Par. 2)
 Quasi-Judicial Act (Determination of facts + application of legislative standard)
 Exclusive Appellate/Supervisory Jurisdiction (Sec. 4, Rule 65; Sec. 9, BP 129)
 Doctrine of Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies
 Ripeness and Prematurity
 Par in parem non habet imperium
 Jus imperii vs. Jus gestionis (Restrictive Theory of State Immunity)
 Salus populi est suprema lex
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"Under the topic of Jurisdiction, **AMCOW v. GAMCA** establishes that a Cease and Desist Order issued by an administrative body like the DOH enforcing a statutory ban is a **quasi-judicial act**. Consequently, under Section 4, Rule 65 and BP 129, exclusive jurisdiction to issue writs of certiorari or prohibition against such quasi-judicial orders belongs **strictly to the Court of Appeals, not the Regional Trial Court**. The RTC's assumption of jurisdiction was void **ab initio**, further compounded by GAMCA's failure to exhaust administrative remedies by not appealing to the Office of the President, which left the constitutional challenge unripe for judicial review."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Leonen, J. (Concurring in the result):** Concurred that the RTC decision is null and void, but disagreed with the Ponencia's rationale. He maintained that: (1) An RTC writ under Section 21, BP 129 is territorially limited to its judicial region and cannot enjoin a nationwide CDO of the DOH; (2) The issuance of a CDO is an executive/administrative enforcement act, not a quasi-judicial act; thus, the proper remedy was a writ of prohibition, which GAMCA should have filed before the Court of Appeals due to the nationwide scope of the writ; (3) It is unnecessary and dangerous to bifurcate certiorari into "traditional" and "expanded" tracks, as this transforms the Court into an advisory super-legislature bypassing the indispensable requirement of an actual controversy; and (4) It was improper for the Court to suggest that customary international norms require prior judicial declaration before being recognized as binding under the doctrine of incorporation.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"**WHEREFORE**, in the light of these considerations, we hereby **GRANT** the petitions. Accordingly, we **REVERSE** and **SET ASIDE** the orders dated August 10, 2012 and April 12, 2013 of the Regional Trial Court of Pasay City, Branch 108, in Sp. Civil Action No. R-PSY-10-04391-CV.
Costs against respondent GAMCA.
**SO ORDERED.**"
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court ruled entirely in favor of AMCOW and DOH Secretary Ona, completely reversing the Pasay RTC. The RTC's permanent injunction shielding GAMCA was invalidated, and the DOH's Cease and Desist Orders were upheld as valid exercises of police power, meaning GAMCA's referral decking system remains strictly banned across the Philippines under RA No. 10022.
