Garcia-Codilla v. Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp., Ltd.
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Garcia-Codilla v. Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp., Ltd.
**Full Official Caption:** Governor Gwendolyn Garcia-Codilla, Petitioner, vs. Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp., Ltd., Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 255252, Promulgated December 4, 2023, 949 Phil. 730; Second Division; Ponente: Kho, Jr., J.; Concurred in by Leonen, SAJ. (Chairperson), Lazaro-Javier, M. Lopez, and J. Lopez, JJ. (Unanimous).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Governor Gwendolyn Garcia-Codilla (Garcia):** Petitioner; judgment obligor; individual doing business under the registered sole proprietorship names "GGC Enterprises" and "GGC Shipping" (GGC); former member of the House of Representatives and Governor.
**Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp., Ltd. (HSBC):** Respondent; commercial banking corporation; judgment creditor and issuer of the irrevocable commercial letter of credit.
**Sam Whan Phils. Trading Co. Ltd. (Sam Trading):** Seller/beneficiary under the documentary credit line from whom Garcia purchased a light cargo transit barge.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court assailing the June 30, 2020 Decision and January 7, 2021 Resolution of the Court of Appeals (CA) in CA-G.R. SP No. 159953. The CA had affirmed the September 17, 2018 and January 3, 2019 Orders of the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Makati City, Branch 57, which denied Garcia’s Urgent Motion to Quash the Alias Writ of Execution in Civil Case No. 00-863.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Article VIII (The Judicial Department) → Section 14 (Constitutional Requirement for Factual and Legal Bases of Decisions)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Civil Procedure → Rule 39 (Execution of Judgments; Writs and Alias Writs of Execution; Doctrine of Immutability of Final Judgments)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
Article VIII, Section 14, 1987 Constitution:
"SECTION 14. No **decision** shall be rendered by any court without expressing therein clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based.

No petition for review or motion for reconsideration of a decision of the court shall be refused due course or denied without stating the legal basis therefor."
Rule 39, Section 8, Rules of Court:
"SECTION 8. **Issuance, form and contents of a writ of execution.** — The writ of execution shall: (1) issue in the name of the Republic of the Philippines from the court which granted the motion; (2) state the name of the court, the case number and title, the dispositive part of the subject judgment or order; and (3) require the sheriff or other proper officer to whom it is directed to enforce the writ according to its terms, in the manner hereinafter provided:
(a) If the execution be against the property of the judgment obligor, to satisfy the judgment, with interest, out of the real or personal property of such judgment obligor;
(b) If it be against real or personal property in the hands of personal representatives, heirs, devisees, legatees, tenants, or trustees of the judgment obligor, to satisfy the judgment, with interest, out of such property;
(c) If it be for the sale of real or personal property to sell such property describing it, and apply the proceeds in conformity with the judgment, the material parts of which shall be recited in the writ of execution;
(d) If it be for the delivery of the possession of real or personal property, to deliver the possession of the same, describing it, to the party entitled thereto, and to satisfy any costs, damages, rents, or profits covered by the judgment out of the personal property of the person against whom it was rendered, and if sufficient personal property cannot be found, then out of the real property; and
(e) In all cases, the writ of execution shall specifically state the amount of the interest, costs, damages, rents, or profits due as of the date of the issuance of the writ, aside from the principal obligation under the judgment. For this purpose, the motion for execution shall specify the amounts of the foregoing reliefs sought by the movant."
**Factual Trigger:** After a monetary judgment ordering Garcia to pay HSBC attained finality, HSBC obtained an **ex parte** Alias Writ of Execution because the initial writ had lapsed unsatisfied. Garcia moved to quash the alias writ, arguing that it violated Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution for failing to state on its face the facts and law upon which it was based, and that issuing it without notice and hearing violated her right to procedural due process.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**November 19, 1996:** HSBC opens Documentary Credit Line No. DPCCEB960015 for USD 900,000.00 in favor of Sam Trading to finance the purchase of a light cargo transit barge by GGC, a registered sole proprietorship owned by Garcia. Under the irrevocable credit, HSBC agrees to pay Sam Trading in five semi-annual installments of USD 180,000.00 each from October 15, 1997 through October 15, 1999. Garcia secures the facility with a Real Estate Mortgage over two parcels of land, an October 15, 1997 Trust Receipt over the barge, and a General Surety Agreement Relating to Goods.
**Subsequent Defaults & Attachments:** Garcia and GGC default on reimbursing HSBC. HSBC terminates Garcia's USD 200,000.00 dollar time deposit to apply against the arrears and demands physical delivery of the barge, which goes unheeded. HSBC continues paying the installment obligations to Sam Trading under the irrevocable letter of credit.
**March 31, 2000:** Garcia’s unpaid balance reaches USD 720,000.00 principal plus USD 103,522.91 in accrued interest.
**July 17, 2000:** HSBC files a Complaint for sum of money with prayer for preliminary attachment against Garcia and her husband before Branch 57, RTC of Makati City (Civil Case No. 00-863). The RTC issues the writ of preliminary attachment and subsequently declares Garcia and her husband in default for failing to file a responsive pleading.
**December 21, 2001:** The RTC renders a default judgment ordering Garcia and her husband to pay HSBC: (1) USD 890,347.92 or its Philippine peso equivalent as actual damages; (2) PHP 1,000,000.00 as moral and exemplary damages; and (3) PHP 960,765.48 as costs of suit.
**October 17, 2006:** On appeal (CA-G.R. CV No. 75861), the CA affirms liability but modifies damages: reduces actual damages to USD 700,000.00; deletes moral and exemplary damages; reduces costs to PHP 650,503.90; and imposes 12% legal interest reckoned from November 17, 1998 until full payment.
**August 22, 2012:** The Supreme Court Third Division (G.R. No. 177734) denies Garcia's Petition for Review on Certiorari via Minute Resolution, further modifying the award: costs of suit are reduced to PHP 404,560.50, and the starting point for the 12% legal interest is re-anchored to July 17, 2000 (complaint filing date) due to insufficient proof of the earlier demand letter.
**February 25, 2013:** The Supreme Court denies Garcia's motion for reconsideration with finality. The judgment is entered in the Book of Entries of Judgment.
**September 20, 2013:** Pursuant to an RTC order granting HSBC's execution motion, the RTC issues a Writ of Execution commanding the sheriff to satisfy the judgment debt of USD 1,877,148.50 (inclusive of legal interest) and PHP 404,560.50 in costs. Three court sheriffs attempt personal service on Garcia at the Batasan Pambansa Complex. Following two unsuccessful attempts where staff claim lack of authorization, the sheriffs effect substituted service on the third attempt by leaving copies with her Protocol Officer and Head of Operations.
**February 22, 2018:** HSBC files an Urgent Ex-Parte Motion for the Issuance of an Alias Writ of Execution, as the original writ remained unsatisfied.
**February 23, 2018:** The RTC grants the motion and issues an Alias Writ of Execution directing the collection of USD 2,825,636.79 (inclusive of accumulated legal interest) and suit costs.
**June 13, 2018:** Garcia files an Urgent Motion to Quash the Alias Writ of Execution, claiming it violated procedural due process because HSBC's motion was not set for hearing.
**September 17, 2018 & January 3, 2019:** The RTC issues Orders denying Garcia's motion to quash and her subsequent motion for reconsideration.
**June 30, 2020:** The CA dismisses Garcia’s Rule 65 petition (CA-G.R. SP No. 159953), holding that Article VIII, Section 14 applies only to decisions on the merits and not execution writs; that alias writ issuance on a final judgment is ministerial; and that service at the Batasan office was valid.
**January 7, 2021:** The CA denies Garcia’s motion for reconsideration.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Gwendolyn Garcia-Codilla)
**Main Thesis:** The Alias Writ of Execution is void for failing to comply with constitutional content requirements and for having been issued **ex parte** in violation of procedural due process.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Constitutional Infraction:** Under Article VIII, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution, the Alias Writ must clearly and distinctly express the facts and law upon which it is based.
2. **Defective Service:** Service was void because the debt belonged to GGC, a sole proprietorship with registered offices in Ormoc and Cebu, not the Batasan. Furthermore, Rule 13, Section 7 rules on personal service of pleadings are mandatory and were violated.
3. **Lack of Notice and Hearing:** The motion for an alias writ is a litigious motion. Because HSBC filed it **ex parte** without a notice of hearing, it was a mere scrap of paper. Garcia was denied due process to challenge the calculation of the accumulated interest.
B. Respondent's Arguments (HSBC)
**Main Thesis:** The issuance of an alias writ of execution on an immutable final judgment is a non-litigious, ministerial act governed strictly by Rule 39, rendering constitutional content mandates and notice-of-hearing rules inapplicable.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Scope of Article VIII, Section 14:** The constitutional mandate applies exclusively to decisions and resolutions on the merits resolving controversies, not to interlocutory enforcement processes or writs of execution.
2. **Personality of Sole Proprietorship:** GGC has no separate juridical personality independent of Garcia. Service upon her office at the Batasan with responsible persons in charge complied with procedural rules.
3. **Ministerial Nature of Execution:** Execution of an entered, final, and executory judgment is an absolute matter of right. Motions for writs and alias writs of execution do not require advance notice or hearings, as the debtor's defenses on the merits are precluded by the doctrine of immutability.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the constitutional requirement under Article VIII, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution—mandating that decisions state clearly and distinctly the facts and law on which they are based—applies to a writ or alias writ of execution.
2. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not an **ex parte** motion for the issuance of an alias writ of execution is a litigious motion requiring prior notice and hearing under the due process clause.
3. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the service of the Writ of Execution and Notice of Demand to Pay at the judgment debtor's legislative office, rather than her sole proprietorship's registered business addresses, was procedurally defective under Rule 13 of the Rules of Court.
4. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the legal interest rate awarded in a 2012 final and executory judgment (12% per annum) may be reduced to 6% per annum pursuant to BSP Monetary Board Circular No. 799, Series of 2013.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Applicability of Article VIII, Section 14 to Writs of Execution
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does Article VIII, Section 14 apply to writs or alias writs of execution? **NO.** Writs of execution are ministerial enforcement orders, not decisions or judgments on the merits.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
The form and content of writs of execution are governed by Rule 39, Section 8 of the Rules of Court, which requires: (1) issuance in the name of the Republic; (2) designation of the court, case number, title, and the dispositive portion of the subject judgment; and (3) a direction to the sheriff to satisfy the judgment out of property. Nothing in Rule 39, Section 8 demands that the court specify the facts and law upon which the writ is based.
Textually, Article VIII, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution explicitly restricts its command to a "decision" or an order resolving a "petition for review or motion for reconsideration of a decision."
A writ of execution is an enforcement order issued after a judgment attains finality. It does not adjudicate rights or resolve the underlying merits of a dispute; it merely executes what was already resolved.
The factual and legal bases are already set forth in the underlying decision being enforced. Requiring them within the writ would be entirely redundant.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"A writ of execution is an order issued by the court upon motion once a judgment becomes final and executory. A writ of execution is not a decision or judgment. It is issued to enforce the terms of a final and executory decision or judgment. The facts and law on which the writ of execution is based should already be clearly set forth in the decision or judgment which it is enforcing."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution applies only to decisions resolving the merits of a lawsuit. A writ of execution is merely an administrative tool designed to carry out a final judgment; because it decides nothing new, it does not need to re-state the factual and legal background.
Issue 2: Due Process and Hearing Requirements for an Alias Writ of Execution
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Is a motion for an alias writ of execution a litigious motion requiring notice and hearing? **NO.** Execution of a final and executory judgment is a matter of right, making the issuance of an alias writ a ministerial duty that requires no advance notice or hearing.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Once a judgment becomes final and executory, the prevailing party is entitled to execution as a matter of right, and the court has the ministerial duty to issue the writ.
Settled jurisprudence establishes that motions for execution do not need to be served on the adverse party or set for hearing. The absence of advance notice does not violate due process because the obligor has already had her day in court.
Since an original writ of execution does not require a hearing, an alias writ—which merely reiterates the original writ that lapsed unsatisfied through no fault of the creditor—likewise does not require notice or hearing. It is not a litigious motion.
The debtor’s remedy is a motion to quash, which is strictly limited to exceptional grounds (e.g., change in situation making execution inequitable, controversy never submitted to court, improvident issuance, satisfaction of debt, or lack of authority). Garcia failed to prove any of these grounds and did not establish any specific mathematical error in the interest computation.
Entertaining dilatory challenges against ministerial writs violates the doctrine of immutability and unalterability of final judgments.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"When a prevailing party files a motion for execution of a final and executory judgment, it is not mandatory for such party to serve a copy of the motion to the adverse party and to set it for hearing. The absence of such advance notice to the judgment debtor does not constitute an infringement of due process... Since a motion for a writ of execution need not be set for hearing, it also follows that a motion for an alias writ of execution likewise does not need to be set for a hearing."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Once a decision is final, execution is a matter of right. A motion for an alias writ is non-litigious; setting it for hearing would merely invite dilatory tactics to stall the enforcement of an immutable judgment.
Issue 3: Validity of Service of the Writ of Execution
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Was the service of the writ improper because it was served at the Batasan rather than GGC's business addresses, or because it did not comply with Rule 13? **NO.** A sole proprietorship has no legal personality separate from its owner, and Rule 39—not Rule 13—governs the enforcement of execution writs.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
GGC is a sole proprietorship. Under Philippine law, a sole proprietorship does not possess an independent juridical personality distinct from its proprietor; Garcia and GGC are legally identical.
Garcia's invocation of Rule 13 is misplaced. Rule 13 governs the filing and service of pleadings, motions, and court papers. Writs of execution are governed by Rule 39, which dictates how writs are enforced against property and does not impose Rule 13 service formalities.
The record shows that the sheriffs attempted personal service twice at Garcia's official legislative office, and on the third attempt properly left copies with persons of suitable age and discretion having charge thereof (her Protocol Officer and Head of Operations). Garcia had actual knowledge of the writ.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Rule 39 enumerates only the manner by which the execution of a judgment may be enforced and does not provide strict requisites for a writ of execution's service. Significantly, the CA found that Garcia had been aware of the demand to pay and the Writ of Execution; she only claims—wrongly—that the Writ of Execution, Notice of Demand to Pay, and Alias Writ of Execution should have been served in accordance with Rule 13 of the Rules of Court."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Garcia cannot hide behind her trade name because a sole proprietorship has no separate personality from its individual owner. Furthermore, Rule 13 applies to pleadings, not to sheriffs enforcing execution writs under Rule 39.
Issue 4: Modification of Final Legal Interest Rates under BSP Circular No. 799
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Can the 12% legal interest rate fixed in a 2012 judgment be modified to 6% under BSP Circular No. 799? **NO.** Because the judgment became final and executory on February 25, 2013, before the circular took effect on June 30, 2013, the doctrine of immutability of judgments bars any modification.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
BSP-MB Circular No. 799, Series of 2013, lowered the legal interest rate from 12% to 6% per annum effective June 30, 2013.
However, the Supreme Court's Minute Resolution setting the interest rate at 12% per annum attained finality and was entered on February 25, 2013.
Under the doctrine of immutability of judgments, once a judgment attains finality, it becomes unalterable in all respects, even to correct perceived legal or factual errors, and even if applied to interest rate adjustments.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"However, since the Minute Resolution dated August 22, 2012 became final and executory on February 25, 2013, it can no longer be modified even as to the legal interest rate."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** A final and executory decision is carved in stone. Because the judgment became final months before the BSP circular took effect, the awarded 12% interest rate can never be altered.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I / Legal Method → Decisions and Resolutions - Factual and Legal Bases (Article VIII, Section 14)
**Constitutional & Political Law Mechanics:**
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:** Judicial Power (specifically the trial court’s enforcement power to execute final judgments) versus the procedural due process constraints and structural drafting mandates under Article VIII, Section 14 (requiring clear factual and legal expressions in decisions).
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny:** Standard of Grave Abuse of Discretion under Rule 65 (acted without or in excess of jurisdiction, or with whimsical, arbitrary, or capricious exercise of judgment).
**Constitutional Test Applied:** Textual and Functional Delimitation of "Decision." The Court interpreted "decision" strictly: Article VIII, Section 14 applies only to adjudications on the merits that resolve substantive controversies. It does not apply to interlocutory, ancillary, or enforcement orders (such as writs or alias writs of execution), whose factual and legal predicates are already settled in the underlying, immutable final judgment.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
**Constitutional Mandate of Art. VIII, Sec. 14 Requisites:**
1. Applicable Instrument: Must be a **Decision** on the merits, or an order/resolution resolving a **Petition for Review** or **Motion for Reconsideration of a decision**. (Trigger applied: A writ of execution fails this requisite—it is an enforcement order, not a decision).
2. Content Requirement: Must state clearly and distinctly the facts and law upon which it is based. (Trigger applied: Satisfied by the original final judgment; inapplicable to the secondary ministerial writ).
**Exceptions Allowing Quashal of an Alias Writ of Execution:**
1. Change in situation of parties making execution inequitable. (Absent)
2. Controversy never submitted to the judgment of the court. (Absent)
3. Writ improvidently issued, defective in substance, issued against the wrong party, or debt fully paid. (Absent)
4. Writ issued without authority. (Absent)
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Decision on the merits
 Ministerial duty
 Matter of right
 Non-litigious motion
 Immutability and unalterability of final judgments
 Sole proprietorship (lack of separate juridical personality)
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
This case falls under Article VIII, Section 14 because Garcia attempted to invalidate an Alias Writ of Execution by arguing that it failed to state the facts and the law on which it was based. The Supreme Court rejected this argument, ruling that the constitutional mandate applies strictly to "decisions" and resolutions on the merits. A writ of execution is an enforcement order issued as a ministerial duty pursuant to a final, immutable judgment; its legal and factual bases are already embedded in the judgment it executes, making Article VIII, Section 14 inapplicable to execution writs.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:** No separate opinions filed.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"ACCORDINGLY, the petition is DENIED. The Decision dated June 30, 2020 and the Resolution dated January 7, 2021 of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 159953 are hereby AFFIRMED. This case is hereby REMANDED to Branch 57, Regional Trial Court of Makati City for immediate execution of the Minute Resolution dated August 22, 2012 of the Supreme Court in G.R. No. 177734, which affirmed with modification the Decision dated October 17, 2006 of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. CV No. 75861.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court ruled in favor of HSBC and denied Garcia’s petition. The CA Decision and RTC Orders sustaining the Alias Writ of Execution were affirmed, and the case was remanded to the Makati RTC for immediate execution of the multi-million dollar judgment debt at the immutable 12% legal interest rate.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** People v. Bugarin (1997)
**Full Official Caption:** The People of the Philippines, Plaintiff-Appellee, v. Marcelino A. Bugarin, Accused-Appellant
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. Nos. 110817-22; June 13, 1997; 339 Phil. 570; Second Division; Mendoza, **J.** (Concurring: Regalado, Romero, Puno, and Torres, Jr., **JJ.**)
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Marcelino A. Bugarin:** Accused-appellant; biological father charged with multiple counts of rape and attempted rape.
**Maryjane Bugarin y Asuncion:** Private complainant and victim; minor daughter of accused-appellant (15 years old at the time charges were filed).
**Regina Bugarin:** Mother of Maryjane and wife of accused-appellant; prosecution rebuttal witness.
**Nena Padecio:** Maternal aunt of Maryjane to whom Maryjane first confided.
**Office of the Solicitor General (OSG):** Counsel representing plaintiff-appellee, People of the Philippines.
**Judge Oscar L. Leviste:** Presiding Judge of the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Quezon City, Branch 97, who penned the challenged two-page decision.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Direct ordinary criminal appeal from the Decision dated February 11, 1993, rendered by Branch 97 of the Regional Trial Court of Quezon City in Criminal Cases Nos. Q-92-28785 to 86 and Q-92-31157 to 31160, convicting Marcelino Bugarin of multiple counts of rape (sentencing him to **reclusion perpetua**) and one count of attempted rape.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department (Article VIII) → Requirements for Decisions and Resolutions → Factual and Legal Bases (Article VIII, Section 14)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Criminal Law & Procedure → Rule 120, Section 2 (Form and Contents of Judgment) → Sufficiency of Evidence in Incestuous Rape vs. Acts of Lasciviousness
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional & Statutory Provisions:**
**Article VIII, Section 14, Paragraph 1, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"No decision shall be rendered by any court without expressing therein **clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based**."
**Rule 120, Section 2, 1985 Rules of Criminal Procedure:**
"Sec. 2. **Form and contents of judgment.** — The judgment must be written in the official language, personally and directly prepared by the judge and signed by him and shall contain **clearly and distinctly a statement of the facts proved or admitted by the accused and the law upon which the judgment is based**.
If it is of conviction, the judgment shall state (a) the legal qualification of the offense constituted by the acts committed by the accused, and the aggravating or mitigating circumstances attending the commission thereof, if there are any; (b) the participation of the accused in the commission of the offense, whether as principal, accomplice, or accessory after the fact; (c) the penalty imposed upon the accused; and (d) the civil liability or damages caused by the wrongful act to be recovered from the accused by the offended party, if there is any, unless the enforcement of the civil liability by a separate action has been reserved or waived.
In case of acquittal, unless there is a clear showing that the act from which the civil liability might arise did not exist, the judgment shall make a finding on the civil liability of the accused in favor of the offended party."
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):**
After trial on six separate criminal informations charging a father with multiple counts of incestuous rape and attempted rape against his minor daughter, the trial judge rendered a bare two-page conviction that summarized testimonies and then laconically concluded—without legal analysis, without resolving evidential inconsistencies, without explaining the legal characterization of a digital/oral molestation, and with an outright contradiction between finding guilt for "three counts" in the narrative while imposing sentences for "four counts" in the dispositive portion—that the complainant was simply "credible." The accused appealed directly to the Supreme Court, assailing the complete absence of factual and legal bases in the judgment pursuant to Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**November 1989:** In their common family sleeping quarters in Payatas, Quezon City, while Maryjane Bugarin was lying down, Marcelino Bugarin embraced her, touched her body, stated that he was doing so so that when she grew up she would not be innocent, held her knees, spread her legs, placed his penis inside her vagina, and continued despite her pleas until she fainted, after which he withdrew and left.
**December 24, 1989:** Marcelino again assaulted Maryjane inside the family house by embracing and kissing her cheek, neck, and breast, spreading her legs, touching his penis to her vagina, and casting frightening looks at her when she cried. (This incident occurred near her brother's birthday, but was not among the dates specifically charged in the informations).
**June 1990:** Marcelino assaulted Maryjane in their house by embracing her, kissing her breasts and nipples, licking/kissing her vagina, and inserting his penis into her vagina.
**March 14, 1991:** On the day clearance was being issued near the end of the school year, Marcelino entered the bedroom, embraced Maryjane, forced her to lie down, kissed her vagina, and inserted his penis into her vagina.
**December 23, 1991:** Marcelino lay down beside Maryjane in the house, demanded that she accede to his desire, and had sexual intercourse with her against her will.
**January 17, 1992:** Marcelino molested Maryjane in the house by licking her vagina; Maryjane kicked him and pushed him away, and he desisted from further penetration while walking beside her and issuing threats.
**February 22, 1992:** Accompanied by her mother Regina Bugarin and maternal aunt Nena Padecio, Maryjane reported to the Central Police District Command that she had been repeatedly raped on nine different occasions between November 1989 and January 17, 1992. On the same date, she was examined by PNP Medico-Legal Officer Emmanuel I. Aranas, who certified that she was in a "non-virgin state physically."
**February 25, 1992:** Maryjane returned to the police station to file formal charges. The Quezon City Prosecutor found probable cause and filed two informations without bail recommendation: Criminal Case No. Q-92-28785 (attempted rape on January 17, 1992) and Criminal Case No. Q-92-28786 (consummated rape on December 23, 1991), both initially raffled to RTC Branch 88.
**May 7, 1992:** The prosecutor filed four additional informations against Marcelino for rape with the aggravating circumstance of relationship: Criminal Case No. Q-92-31157 (alleging rape in June 1990); Criminal Case No. Q-92-31158 (alleging rape in November 1989); Criminal Case No. Q-92-31159 (alleging rape on March 14, 1991); and Criminal Case No. Q-92-31160 (alleging rape in May 1990). These were raffled to Branch 97 and subsequently consolidated with the first two cases.
**Trial Phase (1992):** Marcelino entered pleas of not guilty to all six informations. During trial, Maryjane testified to the assaults and threats, explaining that her father carried out the acts while her mother worked from 3:00 p.m. to 11:00 p.m. and after sending her siblings out to play. Accused denied the accusations, asserting he was a God-fearing family man and that his wife fabricated the charges because she resented his financial neglect since 1989. On rebuttal, Regina Bugarin testified that no mother would sacrifice her child to public humiliation out of spite.
**February 11, 1993:** RTC Quezon City, Branch 97 (Judge Oscar L. Leviste) promulgated a two-page decision. After briefly summarizing the testimonies, the court laconically declared: **"The issue is simple. Is the private complainant credible in her story of how she was raped? The answer of this Court is an undoubtful and a definite yes."** In its dispositive portion, the trial court found accused guilty of "multiple (3 Counts) rape and one count of attempted rape," but sentenced him to **reclusion perpetua** "[f]or each of the four counts of the above rape" and an indeterminate term for attempted rape with P50,000 moral damages and P50,000 exemplary damages, without addressing the remaining charged counts or providing legal and factual explanations.
**Appellate Review Phase:** Accused-appellant appealed directly to the Supreme Court, invoking Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution and Rule 120, Section 2 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner / Accused-Appellant's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The trial court's decision is constitutionally and procedurally infirm for failing to express the factual and legal grounds on which it is based, and the evidence does not establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Constitutional & Procedural Nullity:** The trial court's two-page decision violates Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution and Rule 120, Section 2 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure because it contains no legal evaluation, fails to resolve obvious evidentiary inconsistencies, and contains glaring internal contradictions regarding the number of convictions (finding guilt for 3 counts in text, but sentencing for 4 counts).
**Witness Credibility Deficits:** Maryjane was not credible because on cross-examination she could not remember the exact time of day or specific dates when the alleged rapes occurred.
**Unreasonable Delay:** It took the complainant more than two years to report the alleged rapes, indicating the charges were fabricated.
**Lack of Force or Intimidation:** The prosecution failed to present competent proof that carnal knowledge was achieved through force and intimidation, especially inside a home where the sleeping area was separated only by a curtain.
**Failure to Present Medico-Legal Officer:** The prosecution failed to call PNP Medico-Legal Officer Emmanuel I. Aranas to the stand, rendering physical evidence of virginity loss unsubstantiated.
**Ill-Motive / Frame-up:** The charges were concocted by his wife, Regina Bugarin, who harbored deep resentment against him for failing to provide adequate financial support to the family since 1989.
B. Respondent / People of the Philippines' Arguments (Office of the Solicitor General)
**Main Thesis:** The trial court's assessment of credibility must be sustained, and the guilt of the accused for incestuous rape was proven beyond reasonable doubt.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Spontaneity and Minor's Credibility:** A 15-year-old daughter would not expose herself to public humiliation and concoct heinous charges against her own father if they were not true.
**Substitution of Moral Ascendancy for Force:** In incestuous rape committed by a father against his daughter, paternal moral ascendancy and physical dominance take the place of actual force and intimidation.
**Non-Prejudicial Failure to Call Doctor:** The testimony of the victim alone, when credible, is sufficient to convict in rape cases; presenting the examining physician is not an indispensable element of the crime.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the trial court's two-page decision violates Article VIII, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution and Rule 120, Section 2 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure by failing to state clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based, and if so, whether such violation warrants an immediate remand of the case.
2. **[Procedural / Substantive Issue]** Whether or not the prosecution established beyond reasonable doubt that the accused-appellant committed consummated rape against his minor daughter on the dates charged.
3. **[Substantive Issue]** Whether or not the act of the accused-appellant in licking his minor daughter's genital on January 17, 1992 constitutes attempted rape or acts of lasciviousness.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Compliance with Article VIII, Section 14 (Factual and Legal Bases of Judicial Decisions)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did the trial court's decision violate Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution and Rule 120, Section 2 of the Rules of Court by failing to state the facts and law upon which it was based? **YES.** The decision was an unacceptable **ipse dixit** ruling that disrespected the judicial function; however, to prevent further delay, the Supreme Court exercised review directly on the record rather than remanding the case.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Constitutional and Statutory Mandate:** Article VIII, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution and Rule 120, Section 2 of the Rules of Criminal Procedure strictly command that no decision shall be rendered without expressing clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based.
**Three Fatal Defects of the RTC Decision:** The Supreme Court identified three distinct ways in which the RTC decision fell short:
1. **Total Lack of Legal and Evidential Evaluation:** The decision contains no evaluation of the parties' conflicting evidence and zero discussion of the legal issues. It fails to explain why complainant was deemed credible despite failing to state the time of day, nor does it provide the legal classification for why licking the victim's genitalia constituted attempted rape rather than another offense.
2. **Unexplained Discrepancy in Counts Charged vs. Decided:** The complainant testified to five rapes and one molestation (six informations filed), but the RTC found accused guilty of only "four counts (which the trial court erroneously said three counts) and one count of attempted rape," without clarifying whether accused was acquitted of the remaining count.
3. **Blatant Internal Contradiction:** The decision was prepared so carelessly that its text found accused guilty of "three counts of consummated rape" while its dispositive portion sentenced him to **reclusion perpetua** "for each of the four counts of... rape."
**Core Functions of the Constitutional Requirement:** The requirement serves three vital constitutional functions:
1. **Due Process and Notice for Appeal:** It informs the parties of the precise reasons for the ruling so an appealing party can point out specific errors of fact and law to the appellate tribunal.
2. **Assurance of Deliberative Legal Reasoning:** It guarantees to the parties and the public that the judge reached the conclusion through disciplined legal reasoning, acting as a safeguard against judicial impetuosity and arbitrary decisions rendered by mere personal decree (**ipse dixit**).
3. **Democratic Legitimacy of Judicial Power:** Vested neither with the sword (the Executive) nor the purse (the Legislature), the Judiciary depends entirely on the power of reason for sustained public trust and confidence. The trial court's summary fiat disrespects this fundamental function.
**Exception to Remand Rule (Judicial Economy and Record Completeness):** Although such an invalid decision would normally be remanded to the trial court for compliance with Article VIII, Section 14, the Supreme Court opted to review the record directly to prevent further delay. Because the full transcript of stenographic notes (TSN), complainant's sworn statement, the prosecutor's resolution, and the police records were before the Court, it had sufficient basis to decide the case directly on the merits.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The requirement that the decisions of courts must be in writing and that they must set forth clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which they are based serves many functions. It is intended, among other things, to inform the parties of the reason or reasons for the decision so that if any of them appeals, he can point out to the appellate court the findings of facts or the rulings on points of law with which he disagrees. More than that, the requirement is an assurance to the parties that, in reaching judgment, the judge did so through the processes of legal reasoning. It is, thus, a safeguard against the impetuosity of the judge, preventing him from deciding by **ipse dixit**.
Vouchsafed neither the sword nor the purse by the Constitution but nonetheless vested with the sovereign prerogative of passing judgment on the life, liberty or property of his fellowmen, the judge must ultimately depend on the power of reason for sustained public confidence in the justness of his decision. The decision of the trial court in this case disrespects the judicial function."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
A trial judge cannot simply say "the witness is credible, therefore guilty" in a two-page summary. Under Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution, a decision must explain **how** the court evaluated the evidence and **why** the law applies, ensuring the judge reached the result through reasoned deliberation rather than personal whim (**ipse dixit**). While such a defective decision is usually remanded, the Supreme Court can bypass remand and decide the case on the merits if the complete evidentiary record is already before it, preventing unnecessary delays in the administration of justice.
Issue 2: Proof of Guilt Beyond Reasonable Doubt for Rape Charges
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did the prosecution prove accused-appellant guilty beyond reasonable doubt of the rape charges? **PARTIALLY MERITORIOUS.** The accused was proven guilty of four counts of consummated rape, but must be acquitted of Criminal Case No. Q-92-31160 (alleging rape in May 1990) due to failure of proof.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Minor's Testimony and Credibility:** When a minor victim of rape testifies that she was raped, she states all that is necessary to convict, provided her testimony is credible and candid. Maryjane's inability to state exact hours or dates does not impair credibility; it reflects the natural trauma of recounting humiliating events in open court. Date and precise time are not essential elements of rape.
**Explanation of Reporting Delay:** The two-year delay in reporting was reasonably explained by fear, confusion, shock, and the father's moral and physical control over his minor child. Studies and jurisprudence recognize that victims of incestuous rape take significantly longer to report assaults due to constant paternal authority, co-habitation, and fear of family disintegration.
**Presence of Force and Intimidation / Paternal Moral Ascendancy:** Force and intimidation were established: Maryjane testified that accused physically overpowered her, embraced her, cast frightening looks at her, and made threats. Even absent physical violence, a father's moral ascendancy over his young daughter substitutes for physical force and intimidation in incestuous rape.
**Dispensation of Medical Testimony:** A medical examination is not an indispensable element in rape prosecutions. The non-presentation of the PNP medico-legal officer does not weaken the prosecution's case.
**Analysis of Counts Charged:**
Accused is guilty beyond reasonable doubt of four counts of consummated rape: November 1989 (Q-92-31158), June 1990 (Q-92-31157), March 14, 1991 (Q-92-31159), and December 23, 1991 (Q-92-28786).
In Criminal Case No. Q-92-31160 (alleging rape in May 1990), Maryjane testified to an assault on December 24, 1989, but presented no evidence of an assault in May 1990. Because an accused cannot be convicted of an uncharged offense occurring on a completely different date, accused must be acquitted in Criminal Case No. Q-92-31160.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Nor is it entirely true that no evidence of force and intimidation had been adduced during the trial... Indeed, even if there was no violence or force employed against her, the moral influence of accused-appellant over the complainant sufficed to make the crime rape."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The victim's clear, consistent testimony established four distinct rapes. Exact dates and medical testimony are not essential elements of rape, and the delay in reporting was justified by the father's continuous moral and physical dominance over the household. However, because the prosecution completely failed to prove the alleged May 1990 rape—proving instead an uncharged December 1989 incident—the accused must be acquitted of that specific count to protect his constitutional right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation.
Issue 3: Legal Qualification of Genital Licking (Attempted Rape vs. Acts of Lasciviousness)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does the act of a father licking his daughter's genital constitute attempted rape? **NO.** Without proof that the accused placed himself on top of the victim or initiated acts directly aimed at penile penetration, the act constitutes Acts of Lasciviousness under Article 336 of the Revised Penal Code.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Requisites of Attempted Rape:** Attempted rape requires an overt act commencing the execution of carnal knowledge directly by external acts, stopped short of execution by causes other than spontaneous desistance. The intent to have sexual intercourse must be palpably evident from the overt act itself.
**Absence of Preparatory Acts for Intercourse:** Maryjane testified that on January 17, 1992, accused licked her genital, threatened her, and then walked beside her. The prosecution failed to show that accused attempted to lie on top of her or align his sexual organ with hers. Licking of the female genitalia alone cannot be legally deemed a direct overt act preparatory to sexual intercourse.
**Proper Legal Qualification:** The act demonstrates clear lewd designs accompanied by intimidation, satisfying all elements of Acts of Lasciviousness under Article 336 of the Revised Penal Code.
**Appreciation of Unalleged Aggravating Circumstance:** While the aggravating circumstance of relationship was not expressly alleged in Information No. Q-92-28785, it was fully proved during trial without objection, justifying the imposition of the penalty in its maximum period under the Indeterminate Sentence Law.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The intent to commit rape is not apparent from the act described. It cannot be inferred from this act (licking complainant's genital) alone that his intention was to have sexual intercourse with her because it has not been shown that he had at least placed himself on top of the complainant. The act imputed to him cannot be considered a preparatory act to sexual intercourse. Accused-appellant is instead guilty of acts of lasciviousness."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Licking a victim's genitalia, by itself, is not an attempted rape because it does not constitute an overt commencement of penile penetration; the perpetrator did not even position himself on top of her. Because lewd intent was undeniably present, the act constitutes acts of lasciviousness rather than attempted rape.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Decisions and Resolutions: Factual and Legal Bases (Article VIII, Section 14)
**Applied Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 State Power Exercised:** Judicial Power (Article VIII, Section 1)—specifically the sovereign prerogative of the trial court to adjudicate criminal guilt and deprive a citizen of liberty through **reclusion perpetua.
 Constitutional Check Invoked: Article VIII, Section 14, Paragraph 1 of the 1987 Constitution, which acts as a mandatory procedural and substantive limitation prohibiting courts from rendering decisions without clearly and distinctly expressing the factual and legal grounds upon which they rest.
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny & Doctrinal Tests Applied:**
 Constitutional Adequacy Test for Judicial Decisions: To satisfy Article VIII, Section 14, a judicial decision must exhibit:
1. An articulate evaluation of conflicting testimonial and physical evidence;
2. A clear legal qualification matching the proved acts to the specific statutory offenses; and
3. An absence of internal contradictions between the findings in the body and the dispositive portion (**fallo**).
 The "Ipse Dixit" Prohibition Test:** Courts are forbidden from deciding cases by mere assertion or personal fiat (**ipse dixit). A decision that merely declares a party "credible" without detailing the analytical steps of legal reasoning fails constitutional scrutiny.
 The Rule on Direct Review vs. Remand:** When a decision violates Article VIII, Section 14, the normal constitutional remedy is an order of remand. However, under the doctrine of exceptional judicial economy (citing **People v. Escober), the appellate court will dispense with remand if the record contains complete transcripts, sworn statements, and prosecution findings, enabling the Court to resolve the merits and prevent undue delay.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Ipse dixit (an assertion made without proof; deciding by arbitrary judicial decree).
 Clear and distinct statement of facts and law (the baseline constitutional benchmark under Art. VIII, Sec. 14).
 Disrespects the judicial function (the Court’s severe characterization of the trial judge's two-page summary ruling).
 Neither the sword nor the purse (Hamiltonian/Madisonian structural metaphor emphasizing that the Judiciary's power rests solely on the moral force of reason and public confidence).
 Moral ascendancy (the doctrinal substitute for actual physical force or intimidation in incestuous rape).
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**People v. Bugarin** is assigned under Article VIII, Section 14 to illustrate the constitutional mandate that every court decision must clearly and distinctly articulate its factual and legal bases. The Supreme Court condemned the trial judge's two-page decision as an unconstitutional **ipse dixit** because it failed to evaluate the evidence, offered no legal reasoning for the crimes charged, and contradicted itself between the narrative and the **fallo**. However, rather than remanding the case—which would cause undue delay—the Supreme Court established that appellate courts may review the complete evidentiary record directly and modify the judgment on the merits.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed. (All concurring: Regalado, Romero, Puno, and Torres, Jr., **JJ.**)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the decision dated February 11, 1993 of the Regional Trial Court of Quezon City is SET ASIDE and another one is RENDERED finding accused-appellant Marcelino Bugarin GUILTY of four counts of consummated rape in Criminal Cases Nos. Q-92-28786, Q-92-31157, Q-92-31158, and Q-92-31159 and SENTENCED to **reclusion perpetua** and ORDERED to INDEMNIFY the complainant Maryjane Bugarin in the amount of P30,000.00 in damages for each count of rape committed; and of acts of lasciviousness in Criminal Case No. Q-92-28785, for which he is SENTENCED to suffer imprisonment from 6 months of **arresto mayor**, as minimum, to six 6 years of **prision correccional**, as maximum.
In Criminal Case No. Q-92-31160, accused-appellant is hereby ACQUITTED.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The trial court's two-page conviction was set aside due to constitutional defects and replaced by the Supreme Court's own decision. Marcelino Bugarin was convicted of four counts of consummated rape (sentenced to four separate terms of **reclusion perpetua** plus P30,000 indemnity per count) and one count of acts of lasciviousness (instead of attempted rape, with an indeterminate prison term of 6 months of **arresto mayor** to 6 years of **prision correccional**). He was acquitted of the May 1990 rape charge because the prosecution failed to prove that any crime occurred on that date.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Dizon v. Lopez**
**Full Official Caption: Engineer Fernando S. Dizon, Complainant, vs. Judge Lilia C. Lopez, Regional Trial Court, Branch 109, Pasay City, Respondent.**
**Citation & Metadata:** A.M. No. RTJ-96-1338 (Formerly OCA IPI-95-21-RTJ); September 5, 1997; 344 Phil. 13; Second Division; Mendoza, **J.** (Concurring: Romero, Puno, and Torres, Jr., **JJ.**; On Leave: Regalado, **J.** [Chairman]).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Engineer Fernando S. Dizon (Complainant):** Accused in Criminal Case No. 91-0716 for Falsification of Private Document before the Regional Trial Court (RTC), Branch 109, Pasay City.
**Judge Lilia C. Lopez (Respondent):** Presiding Judge of RTC Branch 109, Pasay City, who rendered and promulgated a conviction consisting solely of an oral reading of the dispositive portion without releasing the full written decision until 20 months later.
**Bernardo P. Abesamis:** Deputy Court Administrator, Office of the Court Administrator (OCA), who evaluated the administrative complaint against respondent judge.
**Ma. Cleotilde Paulo:** Social Worker II and Officer-in-Charge (OIC) of Branch 109, tasked by respondent judge to type and incorporate the dispositive portion into the decision text.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
This case originated as a direct administrative complaint filed by Complainant Fernando S. Dizon before the Supreme Court against respondent Judge Lilia C. Lopez, charging her with violation of the Constitution, serious misconduct, inefficiency, and falsification of a judicial decision.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Department → Court Decisions → Requirement of Expressing Factual and Legal Bases (Art. VIII, §14) & Mandatory Period to Decide Cases (Art. VIII, §15)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Criminal Procedure → Rule 120 (Judgment: Definition, Form, Contents, and Promulgation) → Prohibition Against **Sin Perjuicio** Judgments
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional & Statutory Provisions:**
**Article VIII, Section 14, Paragraph 1, 1987 Constitution:**
"No decision shall be rendered by any court without expressing therein clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based."
**Article VIII, Section 15, Paragraph 1, 1987 Constitution:**
"All cases or matters filed after the effectivity of this Constitution must be decided or resolved within twenty-four months from date of submission for the Supreme Court, and, unless reduced by the Supreme Court, twelve months for all lower collegiate courts, and **three months for all other lower courts**."
**Rule 120, Section 2, Rules of Court (Rules on Criminal Procedure):**
"Sec. 2. **Form and contents of judgment.** — The judgment must be written in the official language, personally and directly prepared by the judge and signed by him and shall contain **clearly and distinctly a statement of the facts proved or admitted by the accused and the law upon which the judgment is based**."
**Rule 120, Section 6, Paragraph 1, Rules of Court (Rules on Criminal Procedure):**
"Sec. 6. **Promulgation of judgment.** — The judgment is promulgated by **reading the same in the presence of the accused and any judge of the court in which it was rendered**..."
**Factual Trigger:**
On April 22, 1993, respondent judge purported to promulgate a criminal conviction against complainant by merely reading the dispositive portion out loud in open court without providing or having finished the written decision stating the factual and legal bases of conviction; despite repeated demands and motions, complainant was not furnished a copy of the written decision until December 16, 1994—nearly one year and eight months later—revealing an incomplete, impermissible **sin perjuicio** judgment rendered well beyond the three-month constitutional deadline.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**January 18, 1992:** A fire destroys records at the Pasay City Hall, affecting pending cases in the local courts.
**August 18, 1992:** In Criminal Case No. 91-0716 (**People v. Engr. Fernando S. Dizon**), the prosecution and defense are required to simultaneously submit their respective memoranda, submitting the case for decision.
**April 22, 1993:** Judgment is purportedly promulgated. The promulgation consists solely of reading an oral dispositive portion convicting complainant of Falsification of Private Document under Article 172, paragraph 2, in relation to Article 171, paragraphs 2 and 4 of the Revised Penal Code, sentencing him to imprisonment of 2 years, 4 months, and 1 day to 6 years. No written copy of the decision is served on complainant or his counsel; they are instructed to return in a few days.
**April 23, 1993 – May 4, 1993:** Complainant and his father take turns visiting the court to secure a copy of the written decision, but court personnel repeatedly fail to produce it.
**May 5, 1993:** To protect his statutory right to seek relief, complainant files a partial motion for reconsideration, expressly reserving the right to submit a comprehensive motion upon actual receipt of the written decision.
**May 12, 1993:** The date scheduled for hearing the partial motion for reconsideration arrives. The case is not called because complainant’s counsel is informed that the written decision has not yet been finished.
**November 29, 1994:** Having waited over a year and a half without receiving the decision, complainant files an "Omnibus Motion to Annul Promulgation of Sentence and to Dismiss."
**December 16, 1994:** During the hearing on the Omnibus Motion, complainant is finally served a copy of the full written decision dated April 22, 1993. The text includes a penalty of imprisonment and adds an unexpected fine of ₱5,000.00 that was not part of the oral dispositive portion pronounced on April 22, 1993.
**December 26, 1994:** Upon reading the full decision, complainant files a second, comprehensive motion for reconsideration.
**January 3, 1995:** Complainant files a motion to disqualify respondent judge from acting on the pending motions for reconsideration. Respondent judge voluntarily inhibits herself and directs the case record to be forwarded to the Office of the Clerk of Court for re-raffle. (The case is re-raffled to Judge Manuel F. Dumatol of RTC Branch 113).
**Subsequent Administrative Proceedings:** Complainant files this administrative complaint charging respondent judge with violations of Article VIII, §§ 14 and 15, and Article III, § 14(2) of the Constitution, serious misconduct, inefficiency, and falsification.
**February 19, 1996:** Deputy Court Administrator Bernardo P. Abesamis submits a memorandum recommending the dismissal of the constitutional, misconduct, and falsification charges for lack of malice, but recommending an admonition for inefficiency due to unreasonable delay in releasing the decision.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Complainant's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Respondent judge violated core constitutional mandates, committed serious misconduct, demonstrated gross inefficiency, and committed falsification by orchestrating an empty promulgation, withholding the factual and legal bases of conviction for twenty months, and surreptitiously altering the sentence.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Violation of Article VIII, Section 14: Rendering an oral conviction on April 22, 1993 without expressing clearly and distinctly the facts and the law violated the constitutional ban against basis-less decisions.
 Violation of Article VIII, Section 15: Because the actual written decision was completed and released only on December 16, 1994, it was rendered twenty months after submission, far exceeding the three-month constitutional deadline for lower courts.
 Denial of Speedy Trial (Art. III, § 14[2]): The protracted withholding of the judgment subjected complainant to prolonged anxiety and denied him a speedy conclusion to his criminal trial.
 Falsification of Public Document: Respondent judge antedated the decision to "April 22, 1993" when it was only completed in late 1994, and altered the judgment by adding an unauthorized ₱5,000.00 fine not announced during the open-court promulgation.
B. Respondent Judge's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The decision was substantially prepared prior to April 22, 1993; the withholding of the dispositive portion until promulgation was a good-faith measure to prevent leaks; and subsequent release delays were unintentional and excused by heavy caseloads, staffing deficits, severe family tragedies, and debilitating personal illnesses.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Leak Prevention Practice: Withholding the dispositive portion until the day of promulgation is an approved judicial practice to avoid premature disclosure. The body of the decision was supposedly already drafted and merely given to the court social worker to incorporate the dispositive portion.
 Power to Modify Sentence:** Under **Abay, Sr. v. Garcia, an incomplete judgment can be modified prior to finality; thus, adding the ₱5,000.00 fine in the written text fell within judicial authority.
 Mitigating Difficulties & Personal Tragedies:** The branch had only two stenographers and no regular typist, requiring the Social Worker to type decisions; the court had a heavy caseload disposing of 285 cases in 1993 with daily morning and afternoon hearings; her niece (raised from childhood) died in a hospital accident; her mother died on March 1, 1992 after an eight-year stroke; her father died on September 17, 1993 from diabetes and cardiac arrest; respondent was the sole caregiver; her family suffered financial ruin from an **estafa; and she suffered from severe diabetes and hypertension, forcing leaves of absence from September 27 to December 12, 1994.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not respondent judge violated Article VIII, Section 15(1) and Section 14 of the Constitution, as well as Rule 120 of the Rules of Court, by promulgating only the dispositive portion of a criminal conviction on April 22, 1993 and failing to render and release the complete written decision stating the factual and legal bases until one year and eight months later.
2.  **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondent judge's practice constituted a valid promulgation of judgment or an impermissible **sin perjuicio** judgment.
3.  **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the prolonged delay in releasing the full written decision deprived complainant of his constitutional right to a speedy trial under Article III, Section 14(2).
4.  **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondent judge is administratively guilty of falsification and serious misconduct for antedating the decision and including an additional ₱5,000.00 fine not orally read during promulgation.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Violation of Constitutional Deadlines and Factual/Legal Basis Requirements
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did respondent judge violate Article VIII, Section 15(1) of the Constitution and Rule 120 by failing to release a decision stating the facts and law within the mandatory 3-month period? **YES.** The promulgation of a criminal conviction requires the reading of the complete judgment containing the factual and legal grounds; reading merely an oral dispositive portion is void as a final decision and defers the actual date of rendition to the date of service of the full text.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Constitutional Mandate: Article VIII, § 15(1) requires lower courts to decide or resolve all cases within three months from submission.
 Judgment Defined under Criminal Procedure: Under Rule 120, §§ 1, 2, and 6, a judgment is the adjudication of guilt or innocence imposing proper penalties, which must be personally prepared, signed, and contain "clearly and distinctly a statement of the facts proved or admitted by the accused and the law upon which the judgment is based," promulgated by reading the same to the accused.
 Reading Dispositive Portion Insufficient:** Reading merely the dispositive portion does not satisfy the law. The accused is entitled to have the **judgment itself read, encompassing its factual and legal foundations.
 Failure to Decide on Time: Because the full written decision stating the facts and law was not completed and served until December 16, 1994, the case was not legally decided within the three-month period following submission in August 1992.
 Rejection of the "Incorporation" Excuse: Respondent's excuse that the body was ready on April 22, 1993 and merely needed the dispositive portion typed is belied by the passage of one year and eight months. If respondent could not finish the decision on time due to difficulties, the proper remedy was to formally request an extension from the Supreme Court and defer promulgation until the text was complete.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"It is clear that merely reading the dispositive portion of the decision to the accused is not sufficient. It is the judgment that must be read to him, stating the facts and the law on which such judgment is based. Since this was done only on December 16, 1994 when a copy of the complete decision was served on complainant, it is obvious that the respondent failed to render her decision within three months as required by Art. VIII, § 15 of the Constitution."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** A judge cannot pretend to beat the 90-day constitutional deadline by reading an oral conviction in open court while keeping the actual written text hidden or unfinished. Promulgation requires reading the complete judgment—facts, law, and dispositive portion together. If the complete decision is only finished and served twenty months later, the judge is guilty of violating the mandatory constitutional period to decide.
Issue 2: Validity of Promulgation and Prohibition Against "Sin Perjuicio" Judgments
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did the promulgation of April 22, 1993 constitute an invalid **sin perjuicio** judgment? **YES.** Pronouncing a disposition without supporting factual and legal findings, leaving the bases to be supplied later, is an impermissible **sin perjuicio** judgment explicitly disapproved by the Supreme Court since 1923.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Definition:** A **sin perjuicio judgment is an incomplete judgment that announces a dispositive conclusion without a statement of facts and law, under the implied or express reservation that an explanatory final judgment will be rendered later.
 Condemnation of the Practice:** The Court reiterates its long-standing rule dating back to **Director of Lands v. Sanz** (1923) disapproving **sin perjuicio judgments due to the intolerable uncertainty, confusion, and prejudice they cause to litigants whose appeal periods are left in limbo.
 Respondent’s Own Defense Confirms the Error:** Respondent invoked **Abay, Sr. v. Garcia** to argue that she had the power to modify the sentence by adding a ₱5,000 fine because the decision was "not complete." By this admission, respondent acknowledged that what she promulgated on April 22, 1993 was an incomplete **sin perjuicio judgment.
 Misapplication of Leak Prevention Rules:** While the Supreme Court in **Castaños v. Escaño** approved the internal practice of withholding the dispositive portion until the last moment of drafting to prevent leaks, that applies only to **drafting**. At the moment of **promulgation, the entire decision must be signed, finalized, and revealed. There is no justification for keeping the dispositive portion separate or keeping the rationale secret once judgment is pronounced.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"What respondent did in this case was to render what is known as a 'sin perjuicio' judgment, which is a judgment without a statement of the facts in support of its conclusion to be later supplemented by the final judgment... As early as 1923, this Court already expressed its disapproval of the practice of rendering 'sin perjuicio' judgments, what with all the uncertainties entailed because of the implied reservation that it is subject to modification when the decision is finally rendered."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** A judge cannot hand down a "disposition first, reasons later" ruling. The doctrine against **sin perjuicio** judgments mandates that a court must never convict an accused and figure out or write up the legal justifications months afterward. While keeping the dispositive portion confidential during drafting avoids leaks, the decision read and released on the day of promulgation must be 100% complete.
Issue 3: Deprivation of the Right to a Speedy Trial and Prejudice to Appeal
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did the twenty-month delay violate complainant's right to a speedy trial or prejudice his right to appeal? **NO.** The reading of the sentence on April 22, 1993 terminated the trial stage, the delay was not vexatious or oppressive, and complainant's appeal period was automatically preserved.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Speedy Trial Boundary:** Under **Que v. Cosico, a violation of the right to a speedy trial requires "vexatious, capricious, and oppressive delay." Despite court records burning in January 1992, the trial was concluded and the reading of the sentence on April 22, 1993 terminated the trial.
 Absence of Appellate Prejudice:** While an accused needs the written text of the decision to intelligently draft an appeal or motion for reconsideration, the rule established in **Director of Lands v. Sanz** holds that the statutory reglementary period to appeal does not begin to run until the accused **actually receives the complete written judgment. Because the period did not run until December 16, 1994, complainant suffered no loss of appellate remedies, though he did suffer anxiety.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The delay, if any, was not such 'vexatious, capricious, and oppressive delay' as to justify finding a denial of the right to a speedy trial. The fact is that the reading of the sentence on April 22, 1993, albeit not in compliance with the requirement for promulgation of judgments, nonetheless put an end to trial."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The constitutional guarantee of a speedy trial protects against oppressive delays during the trial process itself, which ends when the sentence is pronounced. Furthermore, the accused is not procedurally prejudiced by the court's delay in releasing the written text because the clock for his appeal or motion for reconsideration does not start ticking until he holds the complete written decision in his hands.
Issue 4: Falsification and Serious Misconduct Charges
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Is respondent judge guilty of falsification and serious misconduct? **NO.** Malice was absent; respondent's failures were rooted in administrative inefficiency and personal tragedy rather than corrupt intent.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Absence of Malice: The Office of the Court Administrator correctly found that the charges of falsification and serious misconduct fail because there was no fraudulent or malicious intent when respondent antedated the text to April 22, 1993 (the date of nominal promulgation) or added the fine.
 Mitigating Factors:** Under **Mangulabnan v. Tecson, administrative delays caused by heavy caseloads, health issues, and family grief warrant mitigation rather than harsh dismissal. Respondent had served 17 years in the NBI and DOJ, and over 13 years as an RTC judge with an unblemished record. The deaths of her niece and parents, her debilitating illnesses (hypertension and diabetes), and serious staffing shortages mitigated her culpability to simple inefficiency.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Except for this incident, respondent's record of public service as legal officer and agent of the National Bureau of Investigation, as State Prosecutor, and later Senior State Prosecutor, of the Department of Justice for 17 years and as Regional Trial Judge for more than 13 years now is unmarred by malfeasance, misfeasance or wrongdoing... Her failure to decide the case of complainant was brought about by factors not within her control..."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Falsification and serious misconduct require an evil intent or conscious corrupt purpose. Where a judge's failure to release a decision is caused by overwhelming dockets, lack of typists, personal illnesses, and multiple family deaths, the offense is inefficiency and negligence, which is mitigated by long, unblemished public service.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → Decisions and Resolution - Factual and Legal Bases (Art. VIII, § 14) in relation to Mandatory Decisional Deadlines (Art. VIII, § 15).
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
Constitutional and Statutory Requisites for a Valid Promulgation of Judgment (Art. VIII, § 14; Rule 120, §§ 1, 2, 6):
1.  **Direct Preparation & Form:** Written in the official language, personally prepared and signed by the judge. **(Partially observed; signed belatedly).**
2.  **Factual and Legal Foundations:** Must clearly and distinctly state the facts proved/admitted and the specific law relied upon. **(Violated: Omitted entirely during the April 22, 1993 promulgation; supplied only twenty months later).**
3.  **Complete Reading in Accused's Presence:** The complete judgment—not merely the dispositive conclusion—must be read during promulgation. **(Violated: Dispositive portion alone was read).**
4.  **Adherence to Mandatory Timelines (Art. VIII, § 15):** Promulgation and rendition of the full judgment must occur within 3 months of submission for lower courts. **(Violated: Case submitted August 1992; complete decision rendered December 16, 1994).**
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Sin Perjuicio Judgment: An impermissible judgment that pronounces a dispositive holding or sentence while reserving the statement of facts and legal reasoning to be drafted and supplied later.
 Promulgation of Judgment: The formal act of delivering, reading, and serving the complete written judgment (facts, law, and disposition) to the accused in open court.
 Vexatious, Capricious, and Oppressive Delay: The high standard required to prove a violation of the constitutional right to a speedy trial.
 Tolling of Appeal Period: The principle that the reglementary 15-day period to file an appeal or motion for reconsideration does not run until the accused receives the complete written decision stating the factual and legal bases.
**Constitutional & Political Law Lens:**
 State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation: The judicial power to adjudicate criminal guilt (Art. VIII, § 1) subjected to the structural constitutional mandates of Article VIII, Section 14 (due process requirement of factual/legal bases) and Section 15(1) (constitutional time limits to prevent judicial delay).
 Level of Judicial Scrutiny: Strict enforcement of procedural and constitutional judicial duties, subject to equitable mitigation when assessing administrative sanctions.
 Justiciability & Appellate Impact: The Court harmonized administrative fault with appellate due process: while the judge is administratively liable for violating the three-month deadline, the accused suffers no procedural forfeiture because his appeal period remains suspended until complete service.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"Under Article VIII, Section 14 and Section 15 of the Constitution, a trial court cannot comply with the 90-day decisional deadline by staging a nominal promulgation where only the dispositive sentence is read out loud while the written decision stating the facts and the law is withheld. In **Dizon v. Lopez**, the Supreme Court condemned this practice as an illegal **sin perjuicio** judgment. Promulgation requires reading the complete judgment; if the written factual and legal foundations are not released until twenty months later, the judge is guilty of violating the mandatory constitutional period to decide."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed. (All concurring members of the Second Division joined the **ponencia** of Mendoza, **J.**; Chairman Regalado, **J.**, was on official leave).
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"IN VIEW OF THE FOREGOING, respondent is hereby REPRIMANDED with WARNING that repetition of the same acts complained of will be dealt with more severely.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Respondent Judge Lilia C. Lopez was found guilty of inefficiency and violation of the constitutional deadline for failing to complete and release the full written criminal decision within three months, but the charges of serious misconduct, falsification, and denial of speedy trial were dismissed. In light of her unblemished 30-year public service, severe family deaths, and ill health, the Supreme Court mitigated her liability and imposed the penalty of **reprimand with a warning**.
