### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Yao v. Court of Appeals
**Full Official Caption:** George Yao, Petitioner, vs. Hon. Court of Appeals, and The People of the Philippines, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 132428; October 24, 2000; 398 Phil. 86 (2000); First Division; Davide, Jr., C.J. (**Ponente**); Puno, Pardo, and Ynares-Santiago, JJ., concurring; Kapunan, J., on leave.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
George Yao: Petitioner; President and General Manager of Tradeway Commercial Corporation (TCC), criminally charged and convicted of Unfair Competition.
Alfredo Roxas: Member of the Board of Directors of TCC; co-accused who was acquitted by the trial court.
Tradeway Commercial Corporation (TCC): Commercial enterprise whose Caloocan City warehouse was raided, yielding counterfeit General Electric (GE) fluorescent lamp starters.
Philippine Electrical Manufacturing Company (PEMCO): Private complainant; sole local subsidiary of GE-USA, represented by Castillo Laman Tan & Pantaleon Law Offices.
People of the Philippines: Public respondent; prosecuting sovereign represented by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) and the Caloocan City Prosecutor.
Court of Appeals (CA): Public respondent appellate tribunal (Eleventh Division) that dismissed Yao’s appeal and directed execution.
** Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Caloocan City, Branch 121 (Presiding Judge Adoracion G. Angeles): Appellate court that rendered a one-page decision affirming **in toto Yao's conviction.
Metropolitan Trial Court (MeTC) of Caloocan City, Branch 52 (Presiding Judge Delfina Hernandez Santiago): Trial court of origin that convicted Yao of unfair competition.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court assailing the CA Resolution dated April 25, 1995 (dismissing Yao’s appeal and remanding the records to the MeTC for execution) and Resolution dated January 26, 1998 (denying his Urgent Motion to Set Aside Entry of Judgment).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Judicial Department (Article VIII) → Decisions and Resolutions — Factual and Legal Bases (Section 14)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Criminal Procedure / Civil Procedure → Mode of Appeal & Liberal Relaxation of Procedural Rules
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article VIII, Section 14, 1987 Constitution:**
"SECTION 14. **No decision shall be rendered by any court without expressing therein clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based.**

No petition for review or motion for reconsideration of a decision of the court shall be refused due course or denied without stating the legal basis therefor."
**Section 40, Batas Pambansa Blg. 129 (The Judiciary Reorganization Act of 1980):**
"Sec. 40. **Form of decision in appealed cases.** — **Every decision or final resolution of a court in appealed cases shall clearly and distinctly state the findings of fact and the conclusions of law on which it is based which may be contained in the decision or final resolution itself, or adopted by reference from those set forth in the decision, order or resolution appealed from.**"
**Factual Trigger:** After petitioner was convicted by the MeTC of unfair competition, the RTC on appeal affirmed his conviction via a hollow, one-page decision that merely copied the MeTC’s dispositive portion and declared without elaboration that it found "no cogent reason to disturb the findings"; thereafter, petitioner mistakenly filed an ordinary Notice of Appeal instead of a Petition for Review to the CA, causing the CA to treat the RTC decision as final and executory.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**June 1990:** PEMCO notices an influx of GE lamp starters in the local market despite having imported or manufactured none since 1983. PEMCO commissions Gardsmarks, Inc. to run a market survey; its investigator, Martin Remandaman, finds 30 retail establishments selling GE starters, all tracing their supply to TCC. Remandaman buys 50 counterfeit starters directly from TCC.
**October 10, 1990 (Search and Seizure):** Armed with a search warrant issued by MeTC Caloocan Branch 49, authorities raid TCC’s Caloocan City warehouse, seizing eight boxes containing 15,630 counterfeit GE fluorescent lamp starters.
**Subsequent Indictment:** An Information for unfair competition under Article 189(1) of the Revised Penal Code is filed before MeTC Caloocan Branch 52 against George Yao (President and General Manager of TCC) and Alfredo Roxas (Director), docketed as Criminal Case No. C-155713.
**Trial Phase:** Prosecution presents trademark specialist testimony and PEMCO officials showing genuine GE starters feature stenciled silk-screen printing, a drumlike glowbulb, and an M&M-shaped capacitor (.006) priced at P7.00 wholesale, whereas TCC’s products had sticker jackets, improper capacitors, and sold at P1.60. Yao testifies as the sole defense witness, admitting overall managerial control and purchase approvals, but denying knowledge that the units delivered by suppliers were counterfeit.
**October 20, 1993:** MeTC renders a 13-page decision acquitting Roxas (prosecution failed to prove corporate directorship at seizure) but convicting Yao as principal, sentencing him to 4 months and 21 days of **arresto mayor** to 1 year and 5 months of **prision correccional**, plus P20,000 consequential damages and P20,000 attorney’s fees.
**March 7, 1994:** MeTC denies Yao’s Motion for Reconsideration.
**May 24, 1994:** The appeal is docketed as Criminal Case No. C-47255(94) before RTC Caloocan Branch 121. Presiding Judge Adoracion G. Angeles orders both parties to submit memoranda.
**July 4, 1994:** Yao files his Appeal Memorandum.
**July 27, 1994:** Without awaiting the prosecution’s memorandum (filed later on August 20, 1994), Judge Angeles issues a one-page Decision affirming the MeTC **in toto**, simply quoting the MeTC **fallo** and stating: **"After going over the evidence on record, the Court finds no cogent reason to disturb the findings of the Metropolitan Trial Court."**
**August 16, 1994:** Yao receives the RTC decision.
**August 30, 1994:** Yao files a Motion for Reconsideration before the RTC (14 days of his 15-day appeal period used).
**September 28, 1994:** RTC issues an order denying the motion for reconsideration for being devoid of merit.
**October 3, 1994:** Yao receives the RTC denial order, leaving him exactly one (1) day to appeal.
**October 4, 1994:** Yao files a Notice of Appeal by registered mail addressed to the CA (an erroneous mode under Rule 42, which requires a Petition for Review).
**October 28, 1994:** CA receives the transmitted records from the RTC Branch Clerk of Court; the case is docketed as CA-G.R. CR No. 16893.
**February 28, 1995:** Acting on Yao’s motion for extension, the CA grants him an extension until March 12, 1995, to file his Appellant’s Brief. Yao files the brief on March 2, 1995.
**March 24, 1995:** The City Prosecutor files a Manifestation asserting the appeal period lapsed on October 4, 1994, because Yao resorted to a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review.
**April 25, 1995:** The CA issues a Resolution declaring the RTC decision final and executory due to the wrongful and belated appeal, ordering the remand of the records to the MeTC for execution.
**May 26, 1995:** CA issues an Entry of Judgment.
**Subsequent Interlocutory Filings:** Yao files an Urgent Motion to Set Aside Entry of Judgment, arguing that the April 25, 1995 Resolution did not formally dismiss the appeal and that procedural defects were cured.
**January 26, 1998:** The CA denies Yao's Urgent Motion, ruling that the April 25, 1995 Resolution had in effect dismissed the appeal.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (George Yao)
**Main Thesis:** The CA’s Entry of Judgment was legally defective, procedural lapses were cured, and he was denied substantive due process when his conviction was upheld without an adjudication on the merits.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **No Formal Judgment Dismissing Appeal:** Under Section 1, Rule 11 of the Revised Internal Rules of the Court of Appeals, entry of judgment is premature because the CA Resolution of April 25, 1995, did not explicitly dismiss the appeal.
2. **Defects Cured by Appellate Action:** Any procedural defect in the appeal was cured when the RTC transmitted the records and the CA actively took cognizance, ordered the filing of an appellant's brief, and granted an extension of time.
3. **Equity Over Technicalities:** The invocation of a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review was a harmless procedural misstep; the Court should relax technical rules because none of the elements of unfair competition were proven, and strict adherence sacrifices substantial justice.
B. Respondent's Arguments (People of the Philippines / OSG)
**Main Thesis:** The petition is devoid of merit because Yao failed to perfect his appeal in the manner and time prescribed by law, rendering the RTC conviction final, executory, and beyond appellate jurisdiction.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Wrong Mode of Appeal Fatal:** The RTC was acting in its appellate capacity; pursuant to Section 1, Rule 42 of the Rules of Court, the exclusive mode of appeal was a Petition for Review. Yao filed a Notice of Appeal.
2. **Lapse of Reglementary Period:** When Yao received the denial of his motion for reconsideration on October 3, 1994, he had only one day left. By filing the wrong pleading on October 4, 1994, he failed to file the proper petition within the statutory period, divesting the CA of jurisdiction.
3. **Unambiguous Resolution:** While the April 25, 1995 CA Resolution did not state the word "dismissed" in the body, its declaration of finality and order to remand for execution operated as an effective and irrevocable dismissal of the appeal.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the petitioner perfected his appeal to the Court of Appeals when he filed a Notice of Appeal instead of a Petition for Review within the remaining reglementary period.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the one-page decision of the Regional Trial Court affirming **in toto** the MeTC conviction complies with the mandate of Section 14, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution requiring courts to state clearly and distinctly the factual and legal bases of their decisions.
3. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the procedural lapse committed by petitioner in choosing the wrong mode of appeal must yield to the demands of substantial justice in order to set aside the void RTC judgment.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Validity and Timeliness of the Mode of Appeal
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did Yao properly perfect his appeal to the Court of Appeals? **NO.** Yao availed himself of the wrong mode of appeal by filing an ordinary Notice of Appeal instead of a Petition for Review under Rule 42 within the remaining reglementary period.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Appeal is not a natural right or an inherent component of due process; it is a purely statutory privilege that must be exercised strictly within the conditions set by law.
Perfecting an appeal within the prescribed reglementary period and via the mandatory mode is both mandatory and jurisdictional. Non-compliance extinguishes appellate jurisdiction and leaves the judgment final.
Yao had 15 days from August 16, 1994, to appeal. His motion for reconsideration filed on August 30, 1994 (14 days elapsed), tolled the period. Upon receiving the denial on October 3, 1994, he had only one day left—October 4, 1994. By filing a notice of appeal rather than a petition for review, Yao lost the right to appeal under established procedural rules.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The right to appeal is not a constitutional, natural or inherent right. It is a statutory privilege of statutory origin and, therefore, available only if granted or provided by statute. Since the right to appeal is not a natural right nor a part of due process, it may be exercised only in the manner and in accordance with the provisions of law."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** An appeal from an RTC decision rendered in its appellate jurisdiction can only be elevated to the CA through a Rule 42 Petition for Review. Yao mistakenly filed an ordinary Notice of Appeal with only one day left in his appeal period, which fundamentally failed to toll or perfect an appeal.
Issue 2: Constitutional Validity of the RTC's One-Page Decision
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does the one-page decision of the RTC pass constitutional muster under Section 14, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution? **NO.** The RTC decision is an absolute nullity because it failed to state any facts or law upon which it was based, reducing judicial review to an empty formality.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Section 14, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution explicitly forbids any court from rendering a decision without expressing therein clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based. This is reinforced by Section 40 of B.P. Blg. 129 and procedural rules.
** While "memorandum decisions" are sanctioned for appellate courts under B.P. Blg. 129 to foster judicial efficiency, they must rigorously meet the conditions laid down in **Francisco v. Permskul:
1. The decision cannot incorporate findings of fact and conclusions of law only by "remote reference"; it must embody them directly in an annex attached to and made an indispensable part of the decision.
2. The decision being adopted must itself comply with Section 14, Article VIII.
3. Memorandum decisions must be sparingly used and confined to simple litigations where facts are largely undisputed and no complex doctrinal issues exist.
The RTC judgment did not even qualify as a memorandum decision. It merely copied the dispositive portion of the MeTC ruling and concluded, without a single factual summary or legal analysis, that there was no cogent reason to disturb the MeTC findings.
** The constitutional mandate is designed to ensure that the judge decides through legal reasoning rather than **ipse dixit. A decision devoid of factual and legal bases violates due process because it deprives the losing party of the ability to pinpoint judicial errors for meaningful appeal.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"Tested against these standards, we find that the RTC decision at bar miserably failed to meet them and, therefore, fell short of the constitutional injunction. The RTC decision is brief indeed, but it is starkly hallow, otiosely written, vacuous in its content and trite in its form. It achieved nothing and attempted at nothing, not even at a simple summation of facts which could easily be done. Its inadequacy speaks for itself."

"The parties to a litigation should be informed of how it was decided, with an explanation of the factual and legal reasons that led to the conclusions of the court. The court cannot simply say that judgment is rendered in favor of X and against Y and just leave it at that without any justification whatsoever for its action. The losing party is entitled to know why he lost... It is, thus, a safeguard against the impetuosity of the judge, preventing him from deciding **ipse dixit**."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** A court cannot simply copy-paste the dispositive portion of a lower court decision and declare that it finds no reason to disturb it. Section 14, Article VIII requires judges to explain how and why they decided, preventing arbitrary **ipse dixit** rulings and preserving the litigant’s due process right to know the precise grounds of conviction.
Issue 3: Substantial Justice vs. Procedural Technicality
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Can the Supreme Court relax technical rules on the wrong mode of appeal to strike down the constitutionally deficient RTC decision? **YES.** Where an appealed decision is a constitutional nullity, procedural rules of the most mandatory character must yield to prevent manifest injustice and the denial of due process.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
** While Yao resorted to the wrong mode of appeal, the judgment being appealed from was void **ab initio for direct disobedience to the fundamental law.
A void judgment produces no legal effects and can never attain finality.
Although the CA cannot strictly be faulted for enforcing procedural rules regarding appeals, the Supreme Court, in the exercise of equity and its primary duty to uphold the Constitution, may relax procedural rules where manifest injustice would otherwise result, particularly in a criminal case where an individual’s liberty is jeopardized.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"In the interest of substantial justice, procedural rules of the most mandatory character in terms of compliance, may be relaxed. In other words, if strict adherence to the letter of the law would result in absurdity and manifest injustice or where the merit of a party's cause is apparent and outweighs consideration of non-compliance with certain formal requirements, procedural rules should definitely be liberally construed."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Even though Yao committed a fatal error by using a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review, the Supreme Court excused the lapse because the RTC’s one-page decision was completely void under the Constitution. A void decision cannot become final and executory, especially when a person's liberty is at stake.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Department → Decisions and Resolutions — Factual and Legal Bases (Article VIII, Section 14).
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (The Francisco v. Permskul Memorandum Decision Test):**
1. **Form of Incorporation:** Findings of fact and conclusions of law cannot be incorporated by remote reference; they must be embodied in a statement directly attached as an annex and made an indispensable part of the decision.
→ **Applied to Facts:** FAILED. The RTC did not attach the MeTC decision as an annex nor did it reproduce the facts; it only copied the MeTC dispositive portion (**fallo**).
2. **Validity of Underlying Decision:** The decision being adopted must itself comply with Article VIII, Section 14.
→ **Applied to Facts:** While the MeTC decision contained findings, mere unattached adoption cannot cure an unconstitutional appellate decision.
3. **Threshold of Litigation:** Must be sparingly used only in simple litigations (e.g., ordinary collection cases) where the facts are largely undisputed and no complex doctrinal complications exist.
→ **Applied to Facts:** FAILED. This was a criminal prosecution for unfair competition involving technical intellectual property distinctions and disputed corporate knowledge.
4. **Direct Meeting of Issues:** The appellate decision must directly confront the assignments of error raised on appeal.
→ **Applied to Facts:** FAILED. The RTC decision failed to resolve or even mention a single issue raised in Yao’s appeal memorandum.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Ipse dixit (deciding purely by bare assertion without supporting reason).
 Memorandum Decision (a summary appellate decision adopting the findings/conclusions of the lower court).
 Clear and distinct statement of facts and law (the constitutional minimum for valid judicial adjudication).
 Remote reference (impermissible indirect adoption of another court’s findings without attaching them).
 Substantial justice over procedural technicality (the equitable doctrine relaxing strict adherence to rules of appeal to correct a void judgment).
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"In **Yao v. Court of Appeals**, the Supreme Court nullified a one-page RTC appellate decision that affirmed a criminal conviction for unfair competition by merely quoting the trial court's **fallo** and stating there was 'no cogent reason to disturb' the findings. The Court ruled that such a vacuous decision violates Section 14, Article VIII of the Constitution, which requires all courts to state clearly and distinctly the facts and law on which decisions are based. Furthermore, the decision failed to qualify as a valid memorandum decision under the **Francisco v. Permskul** doctrine because it did not annex the lower court's findings nor resolve the assigned errors. Even though the accused committed a fatal procedural error by filing a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review, the Court relaxed the rules because a void judgment can never become final."
**Constitutional & Political Law Lens Focus:**
 State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation: The Judicial power to convict and deprive an individual of liberty (Section 1, Article VIII) was exercised in contravention of the structural and procedural due process check embodied in Section 14, Article VIII (the requirement of reasoned decisions).
 Level of Judicial Scrutiny: Absolute invalidation. Failure to articulate factual and legal bases renders the judgment a constitutional nullity; expediency and brevity can never substitute for substance.
 Justiciability & Review Audit: The Court bypassed the procedural barrier of an unperfected appeal (jurisdictional finality) by invoking substantial justice to review and strike down an unconstitutional, void act of a trial court.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, in view of all the foregoing, the petition in this case is GRANTED. The questioned 25 April 1995 resolution of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. No. 16893 is hereby SET ASIDE and the 27 July 1994 decision of the Regional Trial Court, Branch 121 of Kalookan City rendered in its appellate jurisdiction is NULLIFIED. The records are hereby remanded to said Regional Trial Court for further proceedings and for the rendition of judgment in accordance with the mandate of Section 14, Article VIII of the Constitution.

No costs.

SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** George Yao prevailed. The Supreme Court set aside the Court of Appeals’ dismissal and declared the RTC’s one-page decision completely void for violating the Constitution; the case was remanded to the RTC to prepare a proper, reasoned judgment containing full factual findings and legal conclusions.

### Case Digest: Maternal v. Coca-Cola Bottlers Phils., Inc.
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Maternal v. Coca-Cola Bottlers Phils., Inc.** (or **Maternal v. CCBPI**)
**Full Official Caption:**
**Fernand O. Maternal, Raymundo Vinoya, Erwin S. Constantino, Edilberto F. Carzon, Lourdes V. Alibudbud, Gloria Bathan, Dioscoro Marla, Felicisimo Articona, Joseph E. Calingasin, Loreta D. Pagcaliwagan, Cris R. San Pedro, Larry B. Tabura, Emilio T. Genada, Edzel C. Noble, Helen T. Erasga, Menchito B. Recaro, Ariel T. Roncesvalles, Mauro M. Villadiego, Manuel A. Cantillan, Librado L. Landicho, Ferdinand Santiago, Eriberto P. Palencia, Ariel C. Lumio, Arnel D. Alcantara, Crispulo Del Mundo, Castor B. Isiang, Elvin G. Pacumo, Maximo M. Tuiza, Jose U. Villapando, Elmo L. Camalig, Rommel Torrente, Nathaniel A. Hernandez, Leo A. Sioson, Juanito D. Beato, Marvin M. Rodas, Tristan Hernandez, Randy B. Medianero, Rafael Ceazar C. Vargas, Andrew Sarmiento, Glen A. Azuelo, Roderick Perez, Dexter Corachea, Rolan Balo, Ruben Lazo, Dennis Eugenio, Elmer Guibao, Adelo Vergara, Monico Marasigan, Henry B. Lopez, Mariano G. Aguilar, Jr., August B. Buenaventura, Henry N. Sumague, Edwin R. Celzo, Prudencio J. Zurbito, Jr., Marlon L. Gamilla, Johnny A. Majerano, Levie B. Argon, Dionisio R. Mabalot, Gliendon I. Garcia, Regino P. Baterisna, Elvin A. Mane and Randy M. Queruela, Petitioners, vs. Coca-Cola Bottlers Phils., Inc. (now known as Coca-Cola FEMSA Phils., Inc.), Respondent (G.R. No. 218010);**
**consolidated with**
**Fernand O. Maternal, et al., Petitioners, vs. Coca-Cola Beverages Philippines, Inc. (CCBPI) formerly known as Coca-Cola FEMSA Philippines, Inc. (CCFPI), Respondent (G.R. No. 248662).**
**Citation & Metadata:** 935 Phil. 309; G.R. Nos. 218010 & 248662; Promulgated: February 6, 2023; Second Division; Ponente: J. Lopez, J.; Voting Breakdown: Concurred in by Inting, Gaerlan, and Kho, Jr., JJ.; Dissenting Opinion by Senior Associate Justice (SAJ) Leonen.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Fernand O. Maternal, et al. (Petitioners):** Regular rank-and-file employees of CCBPI's plant operations and members of the Sta. Rosa Coca-Cola Plant Employees Union claiming entitlement to an annual year-end/economic assistance bonus as a vested company practice.
**Coca-Cola Bottlers Phils., Inc. / Coca-Cola Beverages Philippines, Inc. / Coca-Cola FEMSA Phils., Inc. (Respondent / CCBPI):** Employer corporation engaged in the manufacture, distribution, and marketing of carbonated beverages in the Philippines; previously managed by San Miguel Corporation (SMC), Coca-Cola Amatil Ltd., and The Coca-Cola Company.
**Labor Arbiter Melchisedek A. Guan (Public Officer):** The Labor Arbiter of NLRC Regional Arbitration Branch IV who originally granted the employees' bonus claims and subsequently issued successive writs of execution.
**National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC):** Sixth Division (which modified the LA award on the merits) and Fourth Division (which annulled the second writ of execution).
**Court of Appeals (CA):** Special Fourteenth Division (CA-G.R. SP No. 126819, which reversed the NLRC merit award) and Tenth Division (CA-G.R. SP No. 137718, which dismissed the employees' challenge against the annulment of the second writ of execution).
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Two consolidated Petitions for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court:
1.  **G.R. No. 218010:** Assails the August 19, 2014 Decision and March 17, 2015 Resolution of the CA in CA-G.R. SP No. 126819, which granted CCBPI’s Rule 65 petition and voided the February 29, 2012 Decision and July 25, 2012 Resolution of the NLRC (Sixth Division) that had awarded the 2008–2010 bonuses.
2.  **G.R. No. 248662:** Assails the November 14, 2018 Decision and July 26, 2019 Resolution of the CA in CA-G.R. SP No. 137718, which dismissed petitioners' Rule 65 petition and affirmed the NLRC (Fourth Division) Resolutions dated June 23, 2014 and July 31, 2014 that annulled the Labor Arbiter's November 11, 2013 Order executing bonuses for the subsequent years 2011 and 2012.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department (Article VIII) → Effects of Decisions and Resolutions / Judicial Precedents (**Stare Decisis** vs. Minute Resolutions)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Labor Law → Book Three: Conditions of Employment → Wages and Non-Diminution of Benefits (Article 100, Labor Code) → Bonus Ripening into Company Practice
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provisions:**
**1987 Constitution, Article VIII, Section 4, Paragraph 3:**
"Cases or matters heard by a division shall be decided or resolved with the concurrence of a majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberations on the issues in the case and voted thereon, and in no case without the concurrence of at least three of such Members. When the required number is not obtained, the case shall be decided **en banc**: **Provided, that no doctrine or principle of law laid down by the court in a decision rendered en banc or in division may be modified or reversed except by the court sitting en banc.**"
**1987 Constitution, Article VIII, Section 14, Paragraph 1:**
"**No decision shall be rendered by any court without expressing therein clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based.**
No petition for review or motion for reconsideration of a decision of the court shall be refused due course or denied without stating the legal basis therefor."
**Labor Code of the Philippines (Presidential Decree No. 442, as amended), Article 100:**
"ART. 100. **Prohibition against elimination or diminution of benefits.** — **Nothing in this Book shall be construed to eliminate or in any way diminish supplements, or other employee benefits being enjoyed at the time of promulgation of this Code.**"
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):**
Between 1997 and 2007, CCBPI periodically distributed varying corporate bonuses under separate guidelines labeled as "One-Time Grant," "One-Time Economic Assistance," "One-Time Gift," or "One-Time Transition Bonus." When SMC transferred 65% of its shares back to The Coca-Cola Company in 2007, the new management announced that beginning in 2008, all bonuses (apart from the statutory 13th-month pay) would be discontinued and replaced strictly with performance-based incentive programs. Because no performance bonuses were distributed in 2008, 2009, and 2010, the employees sued for non-payment, arguing that the past decade of grants had ripened into a demandable company practice protected by the non-diminution rule.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**July 1, 1997:** Coca-Cola Amatil Ltd. of Australia acquires management of CCBPI from SMC.
**November 26, 1997:** Management grants a "One-Time Grant" (80% of basic salary rate for monthly non-commission personnel, sales OICs, monthly commission personnel [plus commission average], and daily-paid equivalents).
**1998 to 2000:** No economic assistance or one-time bonuses are distributed.
**2001:** SMC reacquires CCBPI.
**July 13, 2001:** SMC/CCBPI management grants a "One-Time Economic Assistance" (50% of basic salary or PHP 40,000.00, whichever is lower) to all regular employees except Officers and AVPs and above.
**June 2, 2002:** Management grants a "One-Time Economic Assistance" (50% [erroneously typed as 75% in text] of basic salary or PHP 40,000.00, whichever is lower) to all commission/non-commission personnel.
**November 5, 2002:** Management grants a separate "One-Time Gift" (75% of basic salary) to all commission/non-commission personnel.
**June 27, 2003:** Management grants a "One-Time Economic Assistance" (PHP 50,000.00 or 50% of basic salary, whichever is lower) to all regular employees below AVP.
**June 25, 2004:** Management grants a "One-Time Economic Assistance" (PHP 20,000.00 or 50% of basic salary, whichever is lower) to all Philippine-based regular employees of the San Miguel Group.
**December 2, 2004:** Management grants a "One-Time Gift" consisting of PHP 5,000.00 worth of SMC Gift Certificates and cash equivalent to 75% of basic pay.
**December 2, 2005:** Management grants a "One-Time Christmas Gift" consisting of PHP 7,000.00 worth of SMC Gift Certificates and cash equivalent to 50% of basic pay or PHP 50,000.00, whichever is smaller (no mid-year economic assistance granted).
**November 17, 2006:** Management grants a "One-Time Gift" consisting of PHP 8,000.00 worth of SMC Gift Certificates and cash equivalent to 50% of basic pay (no mid-year economic assistance granted).
**2007:** SMC sells 65% of CCBPI shares to The Coca-Cola Company, transferring operational control.
**December 7, 2007:** Management grants a "One-Time Economic Assistance / One-Time Transition Bonus" equivalent to one month pro-rated base pay to regular associates, while announcing that starting 2008, all bonuses aside from the 13th-month pay will be replaced by performance-based metrics.
**2008 to 2010:** CCBPI stops releasing the discretionary grants. Regular rank-and-file workers and the Sta. Rosa Coca-Cola Plant Employees Union file consolidated complaints (NLRC Case Nos. SRAB-IV-09-5179-10-L and SRAB-IV-09-5156-10-L) before the Labor Arbiter for unpaid bonuses and attorney's fees against CCBPI and its President, Bill Schultz.
**April 18, 2011:** Labor Arbiter Melchisedek A. Guan renders a Decision ordering CCBPI to pay yearly bonuses from 2008 to 2010 (based on 2007 monthly base pay multiplied by 3) plus 10% attorney's fees (PHP 469,245.10), while dismissing the claims of 10 employees for failure to substantiate.
**February 29, 2012:** NLRC (Sixth Division) dismisses the cross-appeals of CCBPI and the 10 excluded employees, affirming the LA's ruling that the 10-year unconditional grants constituted an established company practice.
**July 25, 2012:** NLRC modifies the LA Decision upon reconsideration, fixing the yearly bonus from 2008 to 2010 at 2/3 of basic monthly pay (the average benefit from 2001 to 2007).
**October 2012:** CCBPI files a Rule 65 Petition for Certiorari before the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 126819) with a prayer for TRO/Injunction.
**January 22, 2013:** While the CA petition is pending without an injunction, the Labor Arbiter issues a Writ of Execution for the 2008–2010 bonus award.
**March 11, 2013:** Following the denial of CCBPI's motion to quash and the NLRC's denial of CCBPI's petition for annulment of the execution order, CCBPI pays the judgment under execution by releasing two manager's checks amounting to PHP 3,677,577.40 (monetary award) and PHP 36,275.77 (execution fees) to the NLRC Sheriff. The Labor Arbiter orders the cases closed and terminated.
**July 10, 2013:** The Supreme Court issues a Minute Resolution in **SACORU v. CCBPI** (G.R. No. 206506), denying the union's petition challenging the CA's declaration that the identical CCBPI bonuses did not constitute a company practice.
**November 11, 2013:** Acting on a fresh motion filed by the employees claiming subsequent bonuses, the Labor Arbiter issues an Order granting a second writ of execution for the collection of bonuses for the years 2011 and 2012, attorney's fees, and interest totaling PHP 2,907,901.25.
**June 23, 2014:** The NLRC (Fourth Division) issues a Resolution granting CCBPI's Petition for Annulment of Judgment, annulling the Labor Arbiter's November 11, 2013 Order and commanding the sheriff and respondents to desist from enforcing any writ for 2011–2012 bonuses. The NLRC denies reconsideration on July 31, 2014.
**August 19, 2014:** In CA-G.R. SP No. 126819 (on the main merits), the CA renders a Decision reversing and voiding the NLRC’s February 29, 2012 Decision and July 25, 2012 Resolution, holding that the bonuses were discretionary, varied, non-continuous, and never ripened into a company practice, invoking the **SACORU** Minute Resolution under **stare decisis**.
**October 2014:** The employees file a Rule 65 petition before the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 137718) challenging the NLRC's annulment of the execution order for the 2011–2012 bonuses.
**October 15, 2014 & February 11, 2015:** The Supreme Court issues Minute Resolutions in **CCBPI v. Ustaris** (G.R. No. 214149), denying CCBPI's petition and affirming a CA ruling that had granted the bonuses to another group of CCBPI workers.
**March 17, 2015:** The CA denies the employees' Motion for Reconsideration in CA-G.R. SP No. 126819.
**May 2015:** The employees file a Petition for Review on Certiorari before the Supreme Court, docketed as **G.R. No. 218010**.
**November 14, 2018:** The CA Tenth Division renders a Decision in CA-G.R. SP No. 137718, dismissing the employees' petition on the ground that the Labor Arbiter exceeded the terms of the April 18, 2011 judgment by awarding 2011–2012 bonuses, and noting that the base decision was voided in CA-G.R. SP No. 126819. The CA denies reconsideration on July 26, 2019.
**August 2019:** The employees file a Petition for Review on Certiorari before the Supreme Court, docketed as **G.R. No. 248662**.
**January 11, 2023:** The Supreme Court consolidates G.R. No. 248662 with G.R. No. 218010.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' (Employees') Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The annual bonuses received continuously from 1997 to 2007 ripened into a legally protected company practice that formed part of their wages; thus, CCBPI's unilateral withdrawal in 2008 violates the non-diminution rule under Article 100 of the Labor Code, and the execution thereof cannot be disturbed.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Unconditional Nature:** The bonuses were granted voluntarily, consistently, and without performance conditions or profit-sharing prerequisites.
2.  **Variance Irrelevant:** Differences in names ("Grant," "Economic Assistance," "Gift," "Transition") or fluctuating monetary amounts do not defeat the establishment of a regular company practice; the law does not require uniformity of nomenclature or exactitude in formula (**citing Metropolitan Bank and Trust Company v. NLRC** and **MERALCO v. Quisumbing**).
3.  **Binding Effect of Ustaris:** Under the SC Minute Resolutions in **Coca-Cola Bottlers Philippines, Inc. v. Ustaris** (G.R. No. 214149, October 15, 2014 & February 11, 2015), the Court ruled with finality that the identical CCBPI bonuses are demandable rights; the Court must resolve conflicts by referring the matter En Banc.
4.  **Immutability of Judgment (G.R. No. 248662):** The original April 18, 2011 Decision of the Labor Arbiter (affirming entitlement to "yearly bonuses... multiplied by the number of years it remained unpaid") became final and executory, conferring a vested right to yearly bonuses for 2011–2012 that could not be modified or annulled at the execution stage.
B. Respondent's (CCBPI's) Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The past distributions were pure acts of employer generosity, explicitly labeled "one-time," subject to shifting management guidelines, and completely lacked the consistency and deliberateness required to ripen into an enforceable company practice under Article 100.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Absence of Contractual Basis:** The bonuses were never incorporated into any Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) or employment contract, and the company never promised an annual bonus.
2.  **No Regular Practice / Interrupted History:** There was a complete 3-year gap between 1998 and 2000 where no bonus was granted; some years had two grants (2002–2004) while others had none (mid-year grants omitted in 1997 and 2005–2007); the amounts trended downwards and were often tied to SMC gift certificates rather than straight salary.
3.  **Stare Decisis / Precedents via Minute Resolutions:** The Court had already settled the non-demandability of these exact bonuses with finality by dismissing petitions in **SACORU** (G.R. No. 206506), **Nido** (G.R. No. 214996), **Deris** (G.R. No. 215681), and **Briones** (G.R. No. 225144), which decisions are binding.
4.  **Mootness of Second Execution:** The LA's 2011 decision was limited strictly to 2008–2010; executing 2011–2012 bonuses was void **ultra vires**. In any event, the CA voided the underlying merit award in CA-G.R. SP No. 126819, extinguishing any legal basis for execution and entitling CCBPI to restitution under NLRC Rules.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Supreme Court is bound under the doctrine of **stare decisis** by its previous minute resolutions in **SACORU** (G.R. No. 206506), **Nido** (G.R. No. 214996), **Deris** (G.R. No. 215681), and **Ustaris** (G.R. No. 214149) resolving identical claims for CCBPI bonuses.
2.  **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the discontinuation of CCBPI's one-time grants, economic assistances, gifts, or transition bonuses constitutes a prohibited diminution of benefits under Article 100 of the Labor Code.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the entitlement to an annual bonus for the years 2011 and 2012 had already become final and executory under the doctrine of immutability of judgments.
4.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the NLRC committed grave abuse of discretion in reversing the Labor Arbiter's Order that executed the payment of bonuses for 2011 and 2012.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Binding Effect of Minute Resolutions under **Stare Decisis**
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Minute resolutions denying or dismissing petitions for review do not constitute binding judicial precedents under the doctrine of **stare decisis** as to non-parties or separate actions, because they do not satisfy the constitutional requirements of a full decision under Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Nature and Limitations of a Minute Resolution:** Citing **Phil. Health Care Providers, Inc. v. CIR** and **Philippine Pizza, Inc. v. Poras**, the Court reiterated that while a minute resolution dismissing a petition operates as an adjudication on the merits between the parties involved, it constitutes **res judicata only** with respect to the identical subject matter, identical issues, and identical parties.
2.  **No Precedential Weight for Non-Parties:** A minute resolution is not a binding precedent to subsequent litigations involving different persons who were never impleaded, even if the legal questions and factual settings are identical. Petitioners in this case were complete strangers to the proceedings in **SACORU**, **Nido**, **Deris**, and **Ustaris**. The principles of fundamental fairness and procedural due process dictate that their independent claims cannot be foreclosed by summary dispositions entered in actions where they had no opportunity to be heard.
3.  **Constitutional and Formal Distinctions:** Under Section 14, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution, a court **decision** must express clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based, is signed directly by the Justices, bears the certification of the Chief Justice, and is published in the Philippine Reports. In contrast, a **minute resolution** is signed only by the Clerk of Court by authority of the Justices, contains no full statement of facts or exposition of legal reasoning, and is not published in the official reports.
4.  **Stare Decisis Inapplicable:** The doctrine of **stare decisis et non quieta movere** enjoins adherence to rules established in formal **decisions** of the Supreme Court. Because the Court's minute resolutions in the prior CCBPI litigations were bereft of factual narratives and legal justifications, the Court of Appeals committed legal error when it mechanically anchored its judgment on **stare decisis** via the **SACORU** minute resolution. The Court had full authority to resolve Maternal's petition completely de novo.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"[A]lthough the Court's dismissal of a case via a minute resolution constitutes a disposition on the merits, the same could not be treated as a binding precedent to cases involving other persons who are not parties to the case, or another subject matter that may or may not have the same parties and issues. In other words, a minute resolution does not necessarily bind non-parties to the action even if it amounts to a final action on a case."
"The constitutional requirement under the first paragraph of Section 14, Article VIII of the Constitution that the facts and the law on which the judgment is based must be expressed clearly and distinctly applies only to decisions, not to minute resolutions... Indeed, as a rule, this Court lays down doctrines or principles of law which constitute binding precedent in a decision duly signed by the members of the Court and certified by the Chief Justice."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
A minute resolution merely closes the door on the specific litigants in that exact case; it does not set binding case law for the rest of the country. Because minute resolutions lack signed judicial reasoning, factual findings, and formal publication, they do not create **stare decisis**. The CA erred in treating the prior dismissal of another union's petition (**SACORU**) as an automatic bar against these petitioners.
Issue 2: Non-Diminution of Benefits (Article 100, Labor Code)
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The withdrawal of the bonuses does not violate Article 100 because the grants were sporadic, discretionary, conditioned on annual management guidelines, variable in amount and kind, and expressly designated as "one-time" aids, thereby negating the existence of an established, deliberate company practice.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **General Rule on Bonuses:** Under **Producers Bank of the Phils. v. NLRC**, a bonus is a management prerogative, representing an act of employer generosity above standard compensation. It becomes demandable only if expressly stipulated in a CBA/contract or when it ripens into a company practice. Custom or practice is not presumed; the burden of proof rests entirely on the employee to show that the benefit was granted consistently and deliberately over a long period.
2.  **Absence of Consistency and Regularity:** The record refutes the claim of unbroken continuity. No bonuses were granted between 1998 and 2000. In certain years (2002–2004), two separate bonuses were granted (economic assistance in June and a gift in December), whereas mid-year assistance was completely omitted in 1997 and from 2005 to 2007. This uneven, unpredictable distribution demonstrates management discretion rather than a deliberate corporate policy to treat the bonus as regular compensation. If employees truly believed these were mandatory wage supplements, they should have formally protested their non-grant in 1998–2000 and the omission of mid-year aids after 2004, which they failed to do.
3.  **Conditional and Discretionary Character:** Unlike mandatory wages, each grant required prior executive approval and was governed by temporary administrative guidelines fixing separate eligibility rules, coverage, and formulas.
4.  **Inconstancy of Amounts and Medium:** The bonuses were neither uniform nor fixed. Except for the 2007 transition bonus, their monetary value steadily declined over time. Furthermore, from 2004 to 2006, the bonuses were split between cash and San Miguel Corporation gift certificates.
5.  Distinction from Jurisprudence:
 Metrobank v. NLRC:** In **Metrobank, the employer entered into four distinct written memoranda coinciding with successive CBAs expressing an explicit commitment to grant retirement benefits. Here, no CBA provision, memorandum, or policy declaration exists reflecting a long-term corporate commitment.
 MERALCO v. Quisumbing:** In **MERALCO, the employer consistently distributed a Christmas bonus for an identical purpose year after year without communicating that it was temporary. Here, CCBPI explicitly styled every release as a "one-time" grant, leaving no reasonable expectation of permanence.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"To invoke the prohibition against diminution of benefits under the premise that the grant of bonus has ripened into a company practice, it presupposes the existence of a company practice favorable to the employees has been clearly established. The **onus** lies on the employee to prove such company practice."
"Clearly, the 'one-time' bonus, economic assistance, or gift previously given were merely acts of generosity of respondent that are beyond what is required by law to be given to the workers."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
An employer's repeated generosity does not automatically trap it into a permanent legal obligation. Because CCBPI missed several years (1998–2000), varied the amounts and formats (cash plus grocery gift certificates), changed the justifications, and explicitly stamped every grant as a "one-time" release, the employees failed to prove the deliberate, continuous custom required by Article 100. CCBPI was well within its rights to discontinue them.
Issues 3 & 4: Immutability of Final Judgment, Second Execution, and Grave Abuse of Discretion (G.R. No. 248662)
**(a) Short Answer: MOOT AND ACADEMIC.** Petitioners' invocation of immutability of judgment fails because the Labor Arbiter's original award was voided on certiorari by the CA; execution cannot stand without a valid underlying judgment. Under Section 18, Rule XI of the NLRC Rules of Procedure, CCBPI is entitled to restitution of sums prematurely executed.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Mootness via Annulment of the Base Award:** The entire procedural theory in G.R. No. 248662 presupposed an immutable, final judgment awarding yearly bonuses in perpetuity. However, the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 126819—acting within its constitutional certiorari power to supervise labor tribunals—expressly declared the NLRC's underlying merit decisions **void**. The Supreme Court herein affirms that CA decision. With the underlying premise extinguished, the issue of enforcing subsequent years' bonuses is completely moot.
2.  **Ultra Vires Execution by Labor Arbiter:** The Labor Arbiter's April 18, 2011 decision was confined strictly to the 2008–2010 bonuses. In issuing an execution order on November 11, 2013 for the unlitigated years 2011 and 2012, the Labor Arbiter exceeded his jurisdiction. The NLRC Fourth Division committed no grave abuse of discretion in issuing a writ of injunction and setting that execution aside.
3.  **Restitution of Premature Execution:** Pursuant to Section 18, Rule XI of the 2011 NLRC Rules of Procedure, where an executed judgment is reversed or annulled on certiorari by the CA or Supreme Court with finality, the Labor Arbiter is mandated, upon motion, to order the full restitution of the executed award (save for reinstatement wages, which are not involved here).
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"The issues of whether the decision awarding the workers' year-end bonus has been declared final and executory, and whether the National Labor Relations Commission committed a grave error in reversing the Order of the labor arbiter at the execution stage presupposes the existence of a final and executory decision in favor of the workers. However, as discussed above, the bonus given to the workers did not ripen into a company practice. Hence, they are not entitled to these bonuses."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
You cannot execute a ghost. The moment the Court of Appeals voided the NLRC's award on certiorari (which the SC affirmed), the foundation for any writ of execution vanished. Furthermore, the Labor Arbiter had no power to magically expand an award for 2008–2010 into an ongoing collection agency for 2011 and 2012. Because the workers lost the main case, they must return what they prematurely collected via restitution.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
Active Subject Context & Syllabus Focus
**Assigned Course:** Constitutional Law I
**Assigned Syllabus Topic:** The Judicial Department → Effects of Decisions and Resolutions → Principle of Precedent & Stare Decisis vs. Minute Resolutions
**Applied Analytical Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law (Article VIII, Sections 4(3) and 14)
Doctrinal Requisites Checklist: Precedential Binding Effect (**Stare Decisis**)
Under the Court's constitutional synthesis of Article VIII, Section 14, an issuance of the Supreme Court constitutes a **binding judicial precedent** under **stare decisis** only if the following legal requisites are met:
1.  **Form of Issuance:** It must be a formal **Decision** or signed Resolution resolving legal questions, not a summary Minute Resolution. (**Failed:** The prior **SACORU**, **Nido**, and **Ustaris** dispositions were all unsigned minute resolutions).
2.  **Constitutional Articulation of Facts and Law:** It must strictly comply with Section 14, Article VIII by stating clearly and distinctly the facts proven and the legal justification applied. (**Failed:** The minute resolutions merely dismissed petitions for lack of reversible error without analytical prose).
3.  **Signatures and Certification:** It must be duly signed by the deliberating Members of the Court and officially certified by the Chief Justice. (**Failed:** The minute resolutions were attested only by the Clerk of Court).
4.  **Official Publication:** It must be officially promulgated and published in the Philippine Reports as a repository of national jurisprudence. (**Failed:** Minute resolutions are excluded from official publication).
5.  **Identity Requirement for Non-Precedents:** If an issuance is a minute resolution, it binds **only** under the doctrine of **res judicata**, requiring strict identity of parties, subject matter, and causes of action. It cannot bind non-parties. (**Failed:** The **Maternal** petitioners were never parties to the earlier CCBPI cases).
Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words")
 Stare decisis et non quieta movere (stand by decisions and do not disturb settled matters)
Minute Resolution vs. Signed Decision
 Res judicata (bar by prior judgment / conclusive between actual parties only)
Section 14, Article VIII (constitutional mandate to express facts and law)
**   Section 4(3), Article VIII (doctrine modification exclusively **en banc)
Principle of Non-Diminution of Benefits (Article 100, Labor Code)
Company Practice (deliberate, consistent, unbroken over a considerable length of time)
Restitution of Executed Judgment (Section 18, Rule XI, NLRC Rules)
Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer)
"Under Constitutional Law, **Maternal v. CCBPI** clarifies that the doctrine of **stare decisis** applies **strictly to full, signed Decisions** meeting the criteria of Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution—which demand a clear and distinct statement of the facts and the law, signatures of the Justices, certification by the Chief Justice, and publication in the Philippine Reports. A **Minute Resolution**, even though a final disposition on the merits, creates **res judicata only between the immediate parties** to that specific lawsuit; it carries **no precedential authority** over non-parties litigating the same question. Consequently, the Supreme Court held that neither the workers nor CCBPI could bind the Court using prior conflicting minute resolutions (**Ustaris** vs. **SACORU**), freeing the Court to determine independently that CCBPI's sporadic, 'one-time' bonuses never ripened into an enforceable company practice."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
Separate Opinions Summary
**Senior Associate Justice Leonen (Dissenting Opinion):**
 Core Disagreement: SAJ Leonen dissents from the majority's finding on the merits. He votes to **GRANT** the petition and reinstate the NLRC award.
 Substantive Points:** Leonen emphasizes that the company gave out bonuses **at least once every year for seven consecutive years (2001 to 2007). He stresses that administrative factual findings supported by substantial evidence are entitled to finality. A review of the corporate memoranda reveals that the bonuses were never profit-sharing schemes, incentives, or performance-based rewards; rather, they were unconditional aids "to provide meaningful help" to regular employees. He asserts that a 7-year uninterrupted, unconditional distribution based on a fixed percentage of monthly base pay is more than sufficient to ripen into an established company practice, making its cancellation an illegal diminution under Article 100.
Verbatim Fallo
"**ACCORDINGLY**, the Petitions for Review on **Certiorari** are **DENIED**. The Decision and the Resolution of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 126819, and the Decision and the Resolution of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 137718 are **AFFIRMED**. The petitioners who are the employees of Coca-Cola Bottlers Phils., Inc. (now known as Coca-Cola Femsa Phils.), are **NOT ENTITLED** to the bonuses subject of the instant case.

**SO ORDERED.**"
Plain-Language Outcome
The Supreme Court ruled entirely in favor of CCBPI. The employees are declared **not entitled** to the disputed bonuses because the previous distributions were discretionary, one-time gifts rather than a binding company practice. The rulings of the Court of Appeals voiding the monetary awards are affirmed, the execution proceedings for the 2011–2012 bonuses are dismissed as moot, and CCBPI is entitled to seek restitution of the sums previously executed.
