### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Eizmendi v. Fernandez (Resolution on Motion for Reconsideration)
**Full Official Caption:** Francisco C. Eizmendi, Jr., Jose S. Tayag, Jr., Joaquin L. San Agustin, Eduardo V. Francisco, Edmidio V. Ramos, Jr., Albert G. Blancaflor, Rey Nathaniel C. Ifurung, Manuel H. Acosta, Jr., and Valle Verde Country Club, Inc., Petitioners, v. Teodorico P. Fernandez, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 215280; November 27, 2019; 866 Phil. 638; Special Third Division; Peralta, C.J. (**Ponente**); Leonen and J. Reyes, Jr., JJ., concurring; A. Reyes, Jr., J., dissenting; Gesmundo, J., on wellness leave.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Francisco C. Eizmendi, Jr., Jose S. Tayag, Jr., Joaquin L. San Agustin, Eduardo V. Francisco, Edmidio V. Ramos, Jr., Albert G. Blancaflor, Rey Nathaniel C. Ifurung, and Manuel H. Acosta, Jr. (Individual Petitioners):** Claimed newly elected members of the Board of Directors (BOD) of Valle Verde Country Club, Inc. (VVCCI) following the contested February 23, 2013 annual meeting.
**Valle Verde Country Club, Inc. (VVCCI) (Corporate Petitioner):** A non-stock sports and recreational club corporation whose leadership and board actions are disputed.
**Teodorico P. Fernandez (Respondent):** Member of VVCCI suspended for six months by the Individual Petitioners; plaintiff in the underlying intra-corporate complaint assailing the BOD's authority and his suspension.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Resolution resolving Respondent Fernandez's **Motion for Reconsideration** dated October 29, 2018, seeking to set aside the Supreme Court's Decision dated September 5, 2018.
The September 5, 2018 Decision granted Petitioners' Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45, reversed and set aside the Court of Appeals' (CA) Decision (June 30, 2014) and Resolution (October 24, 2014) in CA-G.R. SP No. 134704, and reinstated the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Pasig City, Branch 158 Order (January 28, 2014) in Commercial Case No. 13-202, which disallowed evidence concerning the February 23, 2013 BOD elections.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law / Remedial Law → Effects of Decisions and Resolutions → Stare Decisis / Precedential Effect of Minute Resolutions vs. Signed Decisions
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Special Proceedings / Commercial Law → Interim Rules of Procedure Governing Intra-Corporate Controversies (A.M. No. 01-2-04-SC) → Election Contests (Rule 6, Sections 2, 3, & 4)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article VIII, Section 4(3), 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Cases or matters heard by a division shall be decided or resolved with the concurrence of a majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberations on the issues in the case and voted thereon, and in no case without the concurrence of at least three of such Members. When the required number is not obtained, the case shall be decided **en banc**: **Provided**, that **no doctrine or principle of law laid down by the court in a decision rendered en banc or in division may be modified or reversed except by the court sitting en banc.**"
**Article VIII, Section 14, Paragraph 1, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"**No decision shall be rendered by any court without expressing therein clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based.**"
**Section 6(c), Rule 13, Internal Rules of the Supreme Court (A.M. No. 10-4-20-SC):**
"By **unsigned resolution**, the Court disposes of the case on the merits, but its ruling is essentially meaningful only to the parties; has no significant doctrinal value; or is minimal interest to the law profession, the academe, or the public."
**Section 2, Rule 6, Interim Rules of Procedure for Intra-Corporate Controversies (A.M. No. 01-2-04-SC):**
"**Definition.** — An election contest refers to **any controversy or dispute involving title or claim to any elective office in a stock or non-stock corporation, the validation of proxies, the manner and validity of elections, and the qualifications of candidates, including the proclamation of winners**, to the office of director, trustee or other officer directly elected by the stockholders in a close corporation or by members of a non-stock corporation where the articles of incorporation or by-laws so provide."
**Section 3, Rule 6, Interim Rules of Procedure for Intra-Corporate Controversies (A.M. No. 01-2-04-SC):**
"**Complaint.** — In addition to the requirements in section 4, Rule 2 of these Rules, the complaint in an election contest must state the following: (1) The case was filed **within fifteen (15) days from the date of the election** if the by-laws of the corporation do not provide for a procedure for resolution of the controversy, or within fifteen (15) days from the resolution of the controversy by the corporation as provided in its by-laws; and (2) The complainant has exhausted all administrative remedies provided in the by-laws."
**Factual Trigger:**
Following a disputed annual meeting on February 23, 2013 where the hold-over board declared a lack of quorum but the Individual Petitioners proceeded to declare a quorum and elect themselves as directors, the newly installed board suspended Respondent Fernandez from VVCCI for six months on October 18, 2013. On November 28, 2013—nine months after the election—Fernandez filed a complaint to nullify his suspension and the underlying corporate acts by challenging the board’s legitimate authority, prompting the RTC to bar any evidence questioning the election because the 15-day reglementary period for election contests had expired.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**February 23, 2013:** VVCCI convenes its scheduled annual membership meeting through its hold-over BOD. The hold-over board adjourns the meeting for lack of quorum. Immediately after adjournment, the Individual Petitioners (Eizmendi, Jr. et al.) take over the proceedings, determine quorum using 1,500 membership certificates as the base, declare the presence of a quorum (alleging 790 or 793 members present in person or by proxy), and elect themselves as the new BOD of VVCCI.
**October 14, 2013:** In G.R. No. 209120 (**Valle Verde Country Club, Inc., represented by its hold-over Board of Directors, etc. v. Francisco C. Eizmendi, Jr., et al.**), the Supreme Court issues an unsigned/minute resolution dismissing VVCCI's petition and holding that an action assailing the February 23, 2013 election based on lack of quorum and proxy validity constitutes an "election contest" under Section 2, Rule 6 of the Interim Rules.
**October 18, 2013:** The newly constituted BOD under the Individual Petitioners passes a resolution finding Respondent Fernandez guilty of less serious violations of the club's by-laws and penalizing him with a six-month suspension from VVCCI.
**November 28, 2013:** Fernandez files a Complaint for Invalidation of Corporate Acts and Resolutions with Application for Writ of Preliminary Injunction against the Individual Petitioners before the RTC of Pasig City, Branch 158 (Commercial Case No. 13-202), praying to nullify the February 23, 2013 meeting, invalidate subsequent board resolutions (specifically his suspension), and enjoin the board from acting.
**January 28, 2014:** During the injunction hearing, the RTC rules that Fernandez’s challenge against the legitimacy of the BOD composition is an election contest filed beyond the mandatory 15-day period under the Interim Rules. The RTC issues an Order disallowing the presentation of any evidence relating to the conduct and validity of the February 23, 2013 elections, limiting the trial solely to whether the six-month suspension complied with due process.
**June 30, 2014:** The CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 134704) reverses the RTC, ruling that Fernandez’s complaint is not an election contest but an ordinary intra-corporate action questioning the authority of the directors, thus making evidence of the election admissible.
**October 24, 2014:** The CA denies Petitioners’ Motion for Reconsideration.
**September 5, 2018:** The Supreme Court (Third Division) renders a Decision granting Petitioners' Rule 45 petition, reversing the CA, and reinstating the RTC Order of January 28, 2014. The Court applies the ruling in the October 14, 2013 **Valle Verde** Resolution, holding that Fernandez's challenge to the election constitutes an election contest barred by the 15-day prescriptive period.
**October 29, 2018:** Fernandez files the present Motion for Reconsideration assailing the September 5, 2018 Decision.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondent Fernandez's Arguments (Movant)
**Main Thesis:** The Court erred in applying **stare decisis** to his complaint; the October 14, 2013 Resolution in G.R. No. 209120 (**Valle Verde**) is an unsigned minute resolution that has no binding precedential or doctrinal value upon non-parties, and his complaint is an action to invalidate unauthorized corporate acts, not an election contest.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Lack of Doctrinal Precedent: Under Section 6(c), Rule 13 of the Internal Rules of the Supreme Court, unsigned minute resolutions are meaningful only to the immediate parties and carry no significant doctrinal value.
 Obiter Dictum:** The legal disquisitions in **Valle Verde** regarding what constitutes an "election contest" were mere **obiter dicta** and cannot bind subsequent litigation under the doctrine of **stare decisis.
 Inapplicability of Statutory Construction Maxim: The maxim "what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly" applies only when there is an explicit constitutional or statutory prohibition; it cannot be extended to procedural rules of court, such as a 15-day prescriptive period.
 Non-Applicability of 15-Day Period: The 15-day limitation under Section 3, Rule 6 of the Interim Rules cannot bind him because he was not a candidate in the February 23, 2013 election and had no cause of action until his suspension on October 18, 2013.
 Disregard of Prayer: The prayer of a complaint cannot create a cause of action and should be disregarded when determining the true nature of an action.
B. Petitioners' Arguments (Eizmendi, Jr. et al. & VVCCI)
**Main Thesis:** The complaint is a disguised election contest barred by the strict 15-day limitation of the Interim Rules, and the RTC correctly excluded evidence attacking the election.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Prescription of Election Challenge: Fernandez is a member of VVCCI; any challenge to the election of the board of directors had to be mounted within 15 days from February 23, 2013.
 Prevention of Collateral Attacks: Allowing a disciplined member to collaterally assail board authority months later by attacking the underlying election would open the floodgates to continuous disruption of corporate leadership.
 Harmonious Application of Procedural Rules: Rules of court have the force and effect of law; procedural rules setting strict periods must be enforced to ensure speedy intra-corporate adjudication.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the unsigned/minute Resolution in G.R. No. 209120 (**Valle Verde**) constitutes a binding precedent that governs the characterization of Fernandez's complaint under the doctrine of **stare decisis**.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the disquisitions in the **Valle Verde** Resolution defining an "election contest" constitute mere **obiter dicta**.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the statutory construction principle "what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly" applies to the interpretation of procedural rules, specifically the 15-day reglementary period for election contests under the Interim Rules.
4.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not a non-candidate member who sustained injury months after an election is exempted from the 15-day prescriptive period for filing an election contest under Rule 6 of the Interim Rules.
5.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the relief prayed for in the complaint must be considered in determining the true nature of the action and the court's jurisdiction.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Precedential Effect of the Unsigned "Valle Verde" Resolution
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** While ordinary minute resolutions do not create binding judicial precedent for third parties, an unsigned resolution that clearly and distinctly states the factual and legal grounds directly resolving a substantive issue of law creates a binding precedent on that specific legal characterization.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 General Rule on Minute Resolutions:** As reiterated in **Philippine Health Care Providers, Inc. v. CIR** and **Deutsche Bank AG Manila Branch v. CIR**, an unsigned minute resolution dismisses a petition on the merits, rendering the challenged decision final and operating as **res judicata** between the same parties on the same subject matter and issues. If different parties or different subject matters are involved, a typical minute resolution does not establish a binding precedent under **stare decisis, because it generally lacks constitutional exposition of facts and law, is signed only by the Clerk of Court, and is unpublished in the Philippine Reports.
 The Exception/Distinction in This Case:** The October 14, 2013 **Valle Verde Resolution was not a bare dismissal for failure to comply with formal or substantive procedural requirements. Rather, it set forth "clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based."
 Judicial Authority: Even though signed by the Division Clerk of Court, the resolution was promulgated under the explicit authority of the Justices who deliberated on the case. It directly determined the legal threshold under Section 2, Rule 6 of the Interim Rules, establishing that when a complaint’s averments and prayers assert that an election was unlawfully held due to lack of quorum and proxy invalidity, the dispute is an election contest. Hence, it operates as a binding legal standard for characterization of identical factual triggers.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Even if **Valle Verde** is an unsigned resolution, it still creates a binding precedent to the extent that the Court pointed out in the assailed Decision, **i.e.**, if the allegations and prayers in the complaint raise issues of validation of proxies, and the manner and validity of elections, such as the nullification of the election was unlawfully conducted due to lack of quorum, then such complaint falls under the definition of 'election contest' under the Interim Rules. This is because **Valle Verde** stated clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based, and it is not just a mere dismissal of a petition for failure to comply with formal and substantive requirements."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
A minute resolution usually does not set a universal precedent because it merely disposes of a case between specific parties without explaining the law. However, where an unsigned resolution actually contains a full legal analysis setting out clear facts and substantive statutory applications—as the Court did in the 2013 **Valle Verde** case—it carries authoritative legal weight. The Court held that it is bound to treat an identical challenge involving the same meeting and the same election in the exact same legal manner.
Issue 2: Whether the Pronouncements in "Valle Verde" Were Obiter Dicta
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The legal disquisitions were not **obiter dicta** because they directly addressed and adjudicated the core substantive question raised by the petitioner in that case.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Definition of Obiter Dictum:** Citing **Land Bank of the Philippines v. Suntay**, an **obiter dictum is an incidental or collateral opinion expressed by a court upon a point not directly before it or not necessary to the determination of the cause, made without full consideration or argument.
 Direct Adjudication:** In **Valle Verde, VVCCI specifically argued that its petition was not an election contest because the annual meeting was adjourned and no valid election occurred. The Court directly evaluated this argument against Section 2, Rule 6 of the Interim Rules and expressly held that asserting an election was void for lack of quorum directly places the validity and manner of the election in issue.
Because resolving that question was the central holding necessary to determine whether VVCCI’s complaint was viable, the pronouncement was an essential judicial determination, not an incidental remark.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"**Valle Verde** directly resolved the substantive issue raised by VVCCI as to whether its complaint is an election contest... The determination of the validity of the proxies and of the manner and validity of elections is necessary in adjudicating whether the respondents are the lawful directors and officers of Valle Verde... Valle Verde's assertion that there was no election is merely an effect of the declaration of the nullity of the election if the current petition would be found meritorious."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
A statement is only **obiter dictum** if it is an unnecessary, passing remark that has nothing to do with the judgment. In **Valle Verde**, the petitioner squarely asked the Court whether an action to stop persons claiming to be directors after an adjourned meeting was an "election contest." The Court had to answer that exact question to decide the case; therefore, its answer was a binding ratio decidendi.
Issue 3: Application of the Maxim "What Cannot Be Done Directly Cannot Be Done Indirectly" to Procedural Rules
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Rules of procedure promulgated under constitutional authority have the force and effect of law; statutory construction doctrines apply equally to procedural rules to prevent the circumvention of mandatory deadlines.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Force of Law:** Under Section 5(5), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution, the Supreme Court has the power to promulgate rules of pleading, practice, and procedure. Established jurisprudence (**Shioji v. Harvey) confirms that rules of court have the force and effect of law.
 Harmonious Construction:** As pronounced in **Blay v. Baña, general canons of statutory construction apply when interpreting procedural rules.
 Circumvention Prohibited: The Interim Rules impose a strict 15-day prescriptive period for election contests to quickly remove uncertainty surrounding corporate management. Allowing a party to challenge the validity of an election months or years later under the guise of an action to nullify board resolutions would permit an indirect circumvention of the 15-day bar, violating the core principle that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"To disallow the application of such principle would defeat the purpose of the Interim Rules which is meant to expedite the resolution of intra-corporate cases, and would sanction the circumvention of said rules. As stressed in the Court's Decision, the 15-day reglementary period to file an election contest under the Interim Rules aims to hasten the submission and resolution of corporate election controversies, so that the state of uncertainty in the corporate leadership is settled."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
Rules of Court promulgated by the Supreme Court carry the same weight as statutes. The Interim Rules require corporate election disputes to be filed within 15 days so corporations are not paralyzed by constant leadership doubts. A litigant cannot be allowed to bypass this strict 15-day rule by simply labeling his lawsuit as an "action to invalidate corporate acts" when the real substance of his claim requires proving that the board was never validly elected.
Issue 4: Application of the 15-Day Prescriptive Period to Non-Candidates
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The 15-day prescriptive period under Section 3, Rule 6 applies universally to any person questioning an election; the rule makes no distinction between candidates and non-candidates.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Objective Criteria:** Section 2 and Section 3 of Rule 6 determine an "election contest" solely by the **subject matter of the controversy (title to office, validation of proxies, validity and manner of election, qualifications), not by the status of the complainant.
 Member Status: Fernandez was a member of VVCCI at the time of the February 23, 2013 election. His right to assail the election accrued from the date the election was conducted.
 Policy Hazard: Creating an exception for non-candidates who are later disciplined would destabilize corporate governance. Any member subjected to corporate discipline could revive expired election challenges anytime by simply asserting that the disciplining board lacked legitimate authority due to an invalid election held months or years prior.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The definition of an election contest is clear; it hardly distinguishes whether the complainant is a participant in the election or not, and it is determined only by the nature of the controversy or dispute involved... Fernandez is a member of VVCCI, and the time to question their election is within 15 days from the election; to allow him to belatedly question their authority as members of the board would open the floodgate to any member who will be disciplined by petitioners or to question their act by questioning the validity of their election anytime."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
The 15-day deadline to challenge a corporate election applies to all members, not just those who ran for office. If the Court allowed members to wait until they were disciplined by the board to challenge the original election, the 15-day prescriptive rule would become meaningless, and no corporate board’s authority would ever be definitively settled.
Issue 5: Significance of the Prayer in Determining the Cause of Action
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The prayer for relief is an integral part of the body of the pleading under Rule 7 of the Rules of Court and must be considered alongside factual allegations to ascertain the true nature of the action and court jurisdiction.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Composition of Pleading: Under Section 2, Rule 7 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, the body of a pleading explicitly includes the relief prayed for.
 Jurisdictional Standard:** Citing **Spouses Trayvilla v. Sejas**, subject-matter jurisdiction and the nature of an action are governed by the relevant allegations in the complaint, the law in force, and the **character of the relief sought.
 Precedent on Election Contests:** In **Yujuico v. Quiambao, the Court directly relied on the relief sought in the complaint (nullification of an election conducted at an improper venue) to conclude that the action was an election contest governed by the Interim Rules. Because Fernandez's prayer expressly sought to nullify the February 23, 2013 annual membership meeting and board elections, the prayer itself confirmed that the action was partly an election contest.
 RTC Dismissal Valid: The RTC committed no grave abuse of discretion under Section 4, Rule 6 and Section 3, Rule 1 of the Interim Rules when it barred evidence on the election, as the election contest cause of action was barred on its face by prescription.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Section 2, Rule 7 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure provides that the body of the pleading sets forth its designation, the allegations of the party's claims or defenses, the relief prayed for, and the date of the pleading. Considering that the prayer in a complaint is a 'relief,' which is part of the body of such pleading, the prayer in Fernandez's complaint cannot be simply ignored in deciding his case."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
A court cannot ignore what a plaintiff explicitly asks for in the prayer of his complaint. Under the Rules of Court, the relief prayed for is part of the pleading and defines the nature of the lawsuit. Because Fernandez specifically prayed for the nullification of the election meeting, his complaint was undeniably an election contest, and the trial court correctly dismissed that portion of the case as time-barred.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I / Remedial Law | Effects of Decisions and Resolutions (Precedential Value of Minute/Unsigned Resolutions vs. Full Signed Decisions; **Stare Decisis**)
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
1.  Standard Minute Resolution (Non-Precedential):
Signed only by the Clerk of Court.
No statement of facts or legal disquisition (falls outside Section 14, Article VIII, Constitution).
Not published in the Philippine Reports.
 Legal Effect:** Operates as **res judicata **only** between identical parties, subject matter, and causes of action. Holds **no stare decisis** effect for third parties.
2.  Substantive Unsigned Resolution (Precedential Exception under Eizmendi):
Issued under the authority of the deliberating Justices.
Expresses "clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based."
Directly adjudicates and disposes of a substantive question of law (not dismissed on mere technical defects).
 Legal Effect: Operates as a **binding precedent** (**stare decisis**) on the specific legal issue resolved, even against subsequent actions involving different non-parties.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Minute Resolution / Unsigned Resolution
 Stare Decisis et non quieta movere
 Res Judicata
 Obiter Dictum** vs. **Ratio Decidendi
 Rule-Making Power of the Supreme Court (Sec. 5[5], Art. VIII)
 "What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly"
 Election Contest (Sec. 2, Rule 6, Interim Rules)
 15-Day Reglementary Period
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
Under the topic **Effects of Decisions and Resolutions**, **Eizmendi v. Fernandez** clarifies the exception to the rule that minute resolutions lack precedential value under **stare decisis**. While typical minute resolutions bind only the immediate parties as **res judicata**, an unsigned resolution that clearly and distinctly sets forth the factual and legal grounds resolving a substantive issue of law establishes a binding judicial precedent. Applying this, the Court held that its prior unsigned resolution in **Valle Verde** definitively established that any complaint assailing the validity of an election for lack of quorum is an "election contest"; thus, Fernandez’s subsequent complaint questioning the same election was barred by the mandatory 15-day prescriptive period.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Dissenting Opinion of Associate Justice Andres B. Reyes, Jr.:**
 Core Divergence: Voted to grant the Motion for Reconsideration, set aside the September 5, 2018 Decision, and reinstate the CA Decision.
 Reasoning:** Argued that a holistic reading of Fernandez’s complaint reveals its true nature as an action assailing the inherent validity of a corporate meeting for lack of quorum under Section 50 in relation to Section 52 of the Corporation Code, which is legally distinct from an "election contest" under Rule 6 of the Interim Rules (citing **Bernas v. Cinco** and **Lim v. Moldex Land). The prayer to invalidate the board is merely incidental to declaring the meeting void. Treating any challenge to a meeting as an election contest forces litigants into an impossible 15-day prescriptive window and sets a dangerous precedent. The RTC should have received evidence regarding the lack of quorum.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"**WHEREFORE**, the Motion for Reconsideration dated October 29, 2018 is **DENIED** for lack of merit.

**SO ORDERED.**"
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Respondent Fernandez’s Motion for Reconsideration was denied with finality, meaning Petitioners won. The Supreme Court upheld its September 5, 2018 Decision, keeping in force the RTC Order that completely barred Fernandez from introducing any evidence attacking the February 23, 2013 board elections; Fernandez's remaining trial in Commercial Case No. 13-202 was restricted purely to whether his six-month suspension violated due process.

digest:
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Buella v. People
**Full Official Caption:** Jovit Buella y Abalain, Petitioner, vs. People of the Philippines, Respondent
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 244027; April 11, 2023; 939 Phil. 537; Gesmundo, C.J. (Ponente); En Banc. Concurred in by Caguioa, Hernando, Lazaro-Javier, Inting, Zalameda, M. Lopez, Gaerlan, Rosario, J. Lopez, Dimaampao, and Marquez, JJ. Separate Concurring Opinion by SAJ Leonen. Kho, Jr. and Singh, JJ., took no part.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Jovit Buella y Abalain (Petitioner):** Accused in Criminal Case No. 2016-0281, charged with carrying a folding knife outside his residence during the 2016 election period without a COMELEC permit.
**Matea C. Obay, Jeffrey A. Esperas, Ruel A. Valencia, and Joel C. Pastorizo (Co-Accused before the RTC):** Indicted under separate Informations for possessing various bladed instruments/knives during the 2016 election period; did not personally join the Rule 45 appeal to the Supreme Court.
**People of the Philippines (Respondent):** Represented by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) and the Naga City Assistant City Prosecutors.
**Hon. Soliman M. Santos, Jr. (Presiding Judge, RTC Naga City, Branch 61):** Declared the assailed COMELEC provisions unconstitutional and dismissed the criminal cases.
**Commission on Elections (COMELEC):** Constitutional body that promulgated Resolution No. 10015.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Appeal by Certiorari under Rule 45 assailing the June 22, 2018 Decision and January 10, 2019 Resolution of the Court of Appeals (CA) in CA-G.R. SP No. 148051. The CA had granted the OSG's Rule 65 petition for certiorari, setting aside the July 29, 2016 Joint Resolution, three August 1, 2016 Orders, and the August 25, 2016 Joint Resolution II of the Naga City RTC, Branch 61 (which dismissed the five criminal cases on constitutional grounds), and remanding the cases for further trial.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Department → Effects of Decisions and Resolutions / Judicial Review (Direct vs. Collateral Attack & Stare Decisis)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Administrative Law & Election Law → Delegated / Quasi-Legislative Rule-Making Power → Ultra Vires Acts & Penal Construction
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
Article 8, Civil Code of the Philippines:
"ART. 8. **Judicial decisions applying or interpreting the laws or the Constitution shall form a part of the legal system of the Philippines.**"
Article VIII, Section 1, 1987 Philippine Constitution:
"Section 1. The judicial power shall be vested in one Supreme Court and in such lower courts as may be established by law.
Judicial power includes the duty of the courts of justice to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable, and to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government."
Section 32, Republic Act No. 7166:
"Section 32. **Who May Bear Firearms.** — During the election period, **no person shall bear, carry or transport firearms or other deadly weapons** in public places, including any building, street, park, private vehicle or public conveyance, **even if licensed to possess or carry the same, unless authorized in writing by the Commission.** The issuance of firearms licenses shall be suspended during the election period.
Only regular members or officers of the Philippine National Police, the Armed Forces of the Philippines and other enforcement agencies of the Government who are duly deputized in writing by the Commission for election duty may be authorized to carry and possess firearms during the election period: **Provided**, That, when in the possession of firearms the deputized law enforcement officer must be:
(a) in full uniform showing clearly and legibly his name, rank and serial number which shall remain visible at all times; and
(b) in the actual performance of his election duty in the specific area designated by the Commission."
Section 11(a), Rule 122, Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure:
"Section 11. **Effect of appeal by any of several accused.** —
(a) An appeal taken by one or more of several accused shall not affect those who did not appeal, **except insofar as the judgment of the appellate court is favorable and applicable to the latter**."
**Factual Trigger:** The Naga City Prosecutor filed five separate criminal Informations charging petitioner and four others with an election offense for possessing knives, blades, or an icepick in public without a written COMELEC permit during the 2016 election period, pursuant to COMELEC Resolution No. 10015 which defined "deadly weapons" to include "all types of bladed instruments." Two accused moved to dismiss the charges, arguing that the COMELEC had no statutory authority under R.A. No. 7166 to criminalize the carrying of bladed instruments.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**November 13, 2015:** The COMELEC promulgates Resolution No. 10015 to implement Sec. 261(q) of B.P. Blg. 881 and Secs. 32 and 33 of R.A. No. 7166 for the May 9, 2016 Synchronized National and Local Elections. Rule II, Sec. 1(a) bans bearing, carrying, or transporting firearms or deadly weapons without COMELEC authority, while Rule I, Sec. 1(f) defines "deadly weapon" as including "all types of bladed instruments... except when possession is necessary to the occupation or used as a tool for a legitimate activity."
**March 13, 2016 – June 1, 2016:** Five separate individuals are apprehended in Naga City while carrying bladed implements during the election period:
 March 13, 2016: Ruel A. Valencia is caught carrying a folding knife (TM: Mastiff, 4-inch blade).
 April 12, 2016: Matea C. Obay is caught carrying a red kitchen knife (7.5-inch blade).
 May 1, 2016: Jeffrey A. Esperas is caught carrying a knife (10.5 inches overall length).
 May 8, 2016: Jovit Buella (petitioner) is caught carrying a black folding knife (TM: Cardsharp).
 June 1, 2016: Joel C. Pastorizo is caught carrying two shaving blades and one icepick.
**Pre-Trial / Arraignment Phase:** Five separate Informations are filed before the RTC of Naga City, Branch 61. All five accused plead not guilty upon arraignment.
**July 1, 2016:** Accused Obay and Esperas jointly file a Motion to Dismiss their criminal cases (Crim. Case Nos. 2016-0211 and 2016-0254), attacking the constitutionality of Sec. 1(f), Rule I of COMELEC Resolution No. 10015 for expanding the scope of Sec. 32, R.A. No. 7166, violating due process, and imposing an impossible condition (requiring a permit that COMELEC only issues for firearms). The City Prosecutor files an Opposition/Comment, arguing that constitutionality cannot be assailed collaterally and that bladed weapons are deadly weapons.
**July 29, 2016:** RTC Branch 61 (Judge Soliman M. Santos, Jr.) issues a Joint Resolution granting the motion to dismiss of Obay and Esperas. The RTC declares Rule II, Sec. 1(a) in relation to Rule I, Sec. 1(f) of COMELEC Resolution No. 10015 unconstitutional insofar as it includes "all types of bladed instruments," dismisses their cases, and orders their immediate release.
**August 1, 2016:** The RTC issues three separate, identical Orders in Criminal Case Nos. 2016-0131 (Valencia), 2016-0281 (petitioner Buella), and 2016-0313 (Pastorizo). Invoking its own July 29, 2016 Joint Resolution in the Obay and Esperas cases, the RTC **motu proprio** dismisses the cases against Valencia, Buella, and Pastorizo on the basis of equal protection and orders their immediate release.
**August 10, 2016 – August 25, 2016:** The prosecution files a single consolidated Motion for Reconsideration challenging the July 29, 2016 Joint Resolution and the three August 1, 2016 Orders. On August 25, 2016, the RTC issues Joint Resolution II denying reconsideration.
**CA Certiorari Proceedings:** The People, through the OSG, file a Rule 65 Petition for Certiorari before the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 148051) against Judge Santos, Jr. and all five accused.
**June 22, 2018:** The CA grants the OSG's petition, annuls and sets aside all the RTC Joint Resolutions and Orders, and remands the cases for further proceedings. The CA holds that the RTC committed grave abuse of discretion by entertaining an impermissible collateral attack on a presumed valid rule via a motion to dismiss, ruling that constitutionality can only be challenged in direct proceedings like declaratory relief or prohibition.
**January 10, 2019:** The CA denies the motion for reconsideration filed by the Public Attorney's Office (PAO) on behalf of all five accused.
**Appeal to the Supreme Court:** Petitioner Buella alone verifies and files a Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 before the Supreme Court. The PAO informs the Court that co-accused Obay, Esperas, Valencia, and Pastorizo could no longer be contacted despite diligent efforts.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Jovit Buella y Abalain)
**Main Thesis:** The CA erred in reversing the trial court. Petitioner possesses requisite **locus standi**, the motion to dismiss was a legitimate direct attack on the penal provision, and COMELEC Resolution No. 10015 is **ultra vires** and unconstitutional for expanding statutory election offenses to include bladed instruments.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Legal Standing: Petitioner's personal liberty was at stake, having been arrested, detained without bail, and facing one to six years of non-probationable imprisonment; thus, direct injury was evident.
 Direct Attack & Lis Mota:** The motion to dismiss raised a pure question of law that formed the very **lis mota of the criminal prosecution, because without the challenged provision, no crime exists.
 Trial Court's Mandate: Under the 1987 Constitution, trial courts of general jurisdiction possess full judicial power to resolve the constitutionality of administrative regulations directly involved in cases before them.
 Ultra Vires / Separation of Powers:** Sec. 261(q) of B.P. Blg. 881 and Sec. 32 of R.A. No. 7166 restrict the gun ban to firearms and regulated weapons. Under **ejusdem generis, "other deadly weapons" must be of the same class as firearms. COMELEC usurped legislative power by creating a new crime out of possessing bladed instruments.
B. Respondent's Arguments (People of the Philippines / OSG)
**Main Thesis:** The CA correctly held that the RTC committed grave abuse of discretion. Challenging the validity of an administrative regulation through an incidental motion to dismiss constitutes a prohibited collateral attack, and the regulation was a valid exercise of COMELEC's delegated quasi-legislative powers.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Prohibited Collateral Attack: An administrative rule having the force of law enjoys a presumption of constitutionality and can only be invalidated through a direct, stand-alone action (e.g., declaratory relief under Rule 63 or prohibition under Rule 65), not via a motion to dismiss in a criminal case.
 Absence of Lis Mota: Constitutional adjudication was dispensable. The RTC should have resolved the case purely on statutory construction or sufficiency of evidence without touching the constitutional question.
 Quasi-Legislative Authority: The COMELEC has broad constitutional authority (Art. IX-C, Sec. 2) to ensure free, orderly, and honest elections. Prohibiting bladed instruments directly advances this policy by curbing fear and violence during elections.
 Contemporaneous Construction: COMELEC had consistently included bladed instruments in its gun-ban resolutions since 2007 (Resolutions 8298, 8714, and 9561-A), an administrative interpretation entitled to substantial judicial deference.
 No Equal Protection / Due Process Violation: Bladed instruments are inherently deadly weapons, and the resolution provides a fair exemption for individuals carrying them for work or legitimate occupation.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether decisions and resolutions rendered by lower trial courts declaring a rule unconstitutional constitute binding judicial precedents under the doctrine of **stare decisis** in other pending cases.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether the Court of Appeals erred in ruling that assailing the constitutionality of a penal regulation through a motion to dismiss in a criminal prosecution constitutes an impermissible collateral attack.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether petitioner had the requisite **locus standi** and properly invoked judicial review, and whether declaratory relief or prohibition were the exclusive remedies available.
4.  **[Substantive / Secondary Issue]** Whether COMELEC Resolution No. 10015 is **ultra vires** and invalid insofar as Rule I, Sec. 1(f) includes "all types of bladed instruments" within the definition of "deadly weapons" prohibited under Sec. 32 of R.A. No. 7166.
5.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether the favorable judgment secured by petitioner Buella alone in his Rule 45 appeal applies to his non-appealing co-accused (Obay, Esperas, Valencia, and Pastorizo) pursuant to Section 11(a), Rule 122 of the Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Lower Court Rulings as Judicial Precedents (Stare Decisis vs. Res Judicata)
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Lower court decisions are not judicial precedents and have no binding effect under **stare decisis**; only decisions of the Supreme Court form part of the legal system and constitute binding precedent.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Correction of RTC Procedure:** The Supreme Court observed that the RTC, after issuing its July 29, 2016 Joint Resolution in the Obay and Esperas cases, **motu proprio** dismissed the distinct, unconsolidated criminal cases of Valencia, Buella, and Pastorizo by citing its own prior resolution as precedent.
2.  **Scope of Stare Decisis (Civil Code, Art. 8):** Adherence to judicial precedents (**stare decisis et non quieta movere**) mandates courts to follow rules established in final decisions of the Supreme Court. Supreme Court rulings alone become judicial precedents that must be adhered to by all lower courts in the land.
3.  **Lower Court Judgments Limited to Res Judicata:** Citing **United Coconut Planters Bank v. Spouses Uy**, the Court emphasized that decisions of the CA and regional trial courts, regardless of whether they are legally sound, bind only the immediate parties under the principles of **res judicata** (bar by prior judgment or conclusiveness of judgment). They possess no binding precedent effect and are, at best, merely persuasive in other cases.
4.  **Non-Finality:** This caution is heightened where, as here, the RTC's declaration of unconstitutionality was non-final and pending appellate review. Lower courts cannot treat their own unconsolidated rulings as binding precedent to dispose of separate criminal dockets. However, because life and liberty were directly affected, the Supreme Court relaxed procedural rules to decide the substantive questions.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The doctrine of **stare decisis** applies only to judicial precedents of this Court, to the exclusion of the lower courts. This is true regardless of whether the decisions of the lower courts are logically or legally sound as only decisions issued by the Court become part of the legal system. At most, decisions of the lower courts only have a persuasive effect."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** An RTC judge cannot dismiss a criminal case simply by citing his own prior ruling in a different, unconsolidated case as if it were a binding precedent. Under Article 8 of the Civil Code, only decisions of the Supreme Court establish judicial precedent under **stare decisis**. Lower court decisions only bind the specific parties under **res judicata** and carry no legal authority over other proceedings beyond mere persuasion.
Issue 2: Propriety of Raising Unconstitutionality in a Motion to Dismiss (Direct vs. Collateral Attack)
**(a) Short Answer: NO (the CA erred).** Attacking the constitutionality of a penal rule via a motion to dismiss in a criminal case is a legitimate, direct challenge, not a collateral attack.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Survey of Jurisprudential Distinctions:** The Court traced the direct-versus-collateral doctrine across eight decades (**Cadwallader-Gibson**, **McGirr**, **Olsen**, **Vera**, **San Miguel Brewery**, **Philippine National Bank**, **Garcia v. Drilon**, and **Palencia**). A direct attack specifically seeks to annul, invalidate, or enjoin the enforcement of an enactment; a collateral attack occurs when invalidity is raised as an incidental matter in a suit seeking entirely independent relief.
2.  **Two Governing Criteria:** A constitutional challenge against an enactment is properly entertained—and will not be treated as a collateral attack—if: (a) the validity of the enactment is the **lis mota** of the case; and (b) the challenge is raised at the earliest opportunity.
3.  **Heightened Due Process in Criminal Prosecutions:** In criminal cases, life and liberty take precedence over procedural formalities. Citing **People v. Vera** and **Palencia v. People**, the Court reiterated that in criminal actions, the constitutionality of a penal statute or regulation may be raised at any stage of the proceedings, even for the first time on appeal.
4.  **The Motion to Dismiss was Facially Direct:** The motion filed by the accused specifically prayed for a declaration of unconstitutionality of Sec. 1(f), Rule I of Resolution No. 10015. Because the regulation was the sole source of criminal liability, mounting the constitutional challenge via a motion to dismiss was the earliest, most logical, and direct avenue to resist state prosecution.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"From the foregoing recitation of relevant jurisprudence, it may be observed that in determining whether a challenge against the constitutionality of a legislative act may be entertained by the courts, two requisites must be present: the validity of the enactment is the **lis mota** and the challenge must be raised at the earliest opportunity. Otherwise, the challenge will be treated as a collateral attack."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** When the government charges an individual with a crime based on an administrative resolution, the accused can directly challenge the constitutionality of that resolution inside the criminal prosecution using a motion to dismiss. Because life and liberty are at stake, and because the unconstitutional rule is the very basis (**lis mota**) of the charge, such a motion is a direct, permissible attack, not an impermissible collateral attack.
Issue 3: Requisites of Judicial Review and Exclusivity of Declaratory Relief or Prohibition
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** All four traditional requisites for judicial review were met, and the CA erred in holding that declaratory relief or prohibition were the exclusive procedural vehicles.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Actual Case or Controversy:** The State formally indicted petitioner under an Information alleging criminal carriage of a folding knife during the election period.
2.  **Locus Standi:** Petitioner suffered direct personal injury through warrantless arrest, confinement without bail, and exposure to a non-probationable prison term.
3.  **Earliest Opportunity:** Raised immediately via a motion to dismiss before trial; under criminal jurisprudence, it can be raised at any time.
4.  **Lis Mota:** The constitutional validity of the ban on bladed weapons was the core legal issue; petitioner's criminal guilt or innocence could not be determined without resolving it.
5.  Impropriety of Alternative Remedies:
 Declaratory Relief (Rule 63):** Inadmissible. Declaratory relief lies only **prior** to a breach or violation of a statute. Once an arrest and criminal charge occur, a breach has transpired, stripping courts of Rule 63 jurisdiction. Allowing it post-arrest would violate the rule against multiplicity of suits (**Sarmiento v. Capapas).
 Prohibition (Rule 65): Unnecessary. Prohibition requires the absence of any plain, speedy, and adequate remedy in the ordinary course of law. The motion to dismiss before the RTC provided precisely that adequate remedy.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"It must be filed before the breach or violation of the statute, deed or contract to which it refers; otherwise, the court can no longer assume jurisdiction over the action... In the instant case, a breach or violation of COMELEC Resolution No. 10015 had already occurred. This breach or violation is the reason why petitioner stands accused before the RTC. As such, a petition for declaratory relief is no longer available and resort to the same would have been improper."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** You cannot file for declaratory relief after you have already been arrested and charged, because declaratory relief requires that no breach of the law has yet occurred. Likewise, a separate petition for prohibition was unnecessary because filing a motion to dismiss before the trial court was already a plain, speedy, and adequate remedy to challenge the unconstitutional penal rule.
Issue 4: Validity of COMELEC Ban on "All Types of Bladed Instruments"
**(a) Short Answer: YES (the provision is void).** COMELEC acted **ultra vires** and violated the principle of separation of powers by expanding the definition of "deadly weapons" under Sec. 32 of R.A. No. 7166 to include bladed instruments.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Limits on Subordinate Legislation:** An administrative agency's quasi-legislative power is strictly subordinate to the enabling statute. Administrative regulations cannot amend, alter, expand, or enlarge statutory coverage, nor can they criminalize acts not made punishable by Congress.
2.  **Statutory Text of Sec. 261(q) and Sec. 32:** Sec. 261(q) of B.P. Blg. 881 is explicitly limited to "firearms." Sec. 32 of R.A. No. 7166 is entitled "Who May Bear Firearms" and restricts "firearms or other deadly weapons... even if licensed to possess or carry the same, unless authorized in writing by the Commission."
3.  **Doctrine of Ejusdem Generis and the "Regulation" Test:** Under **ejusdem generis**, the general term "other deadly weapons" is restricted by the specific term "firearms." Crucially, the phrases "even if licensed to possess" and "unless authorized in writing" qualify both firearms and other deadly weapons. Therefore, to be covered by Sec. 32, a deadly weapon must be **one subject to state licensing/regulation** and for which COMELEC can issue a carriage permit.
4.  **Bladed Instruments are Unregulated:** Bladed instruments are ordinary household, occupational, or recreational items. The State does not issue licenses for knives, and COMELEC issues no permits or Certificates of Authority for bladed instruments during elections.
5.  **Application of Orceo v. COMELEC:** In **Orceo**, the Court sustained the election ban on airsoft guns because they were regulated by PNP Circular No. 11, but struck down the ban on toy replicas and imitations because they were unregulated. The identical principle applies: unregulated bladed instruments cannot be shoehorned into an election ban on licensed/regulated weapons.
6.  **Strict Penal Construction:** Penal statutes must be strictly construed against the State and liberally in favor of the accused (**Centeno v. Villalon-Pornillos**). Administrative bodies cannot construct a new crime out of innocent conduct without express legislative mandate.
7.  **Failure of COMELEC Exemption:** The fact that COMELEC Resolution No. 10015 created an exception for bladed weapons carried as a "necessary tool of trade" cannot cure the defect. Congress never granted COMELEC the power to prohibit bladed weapons in the first place; hence, COMELEC cannot manufacture an administrative exemption to save an unauthorized prohibition.
8.  **Void for Vagueness (Leonen Concurrence adopted):** The term "all types of bladed instruments" lacks comprehensible standards, failing to provide fair notice and granting unbridled discretion to law enforcement (e.g., arresting citizens for carrying kitchen knives or shaving blades).
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The power of administrative officials to promulgate rules in the implementation of a statute is necessarily limited to what is provided for in the legislative enactment... The implementing rules and regulations of a law cannot extend the law or expand its coverage, as the power to amend or repeal a statute is vested in the legislature... Bladed instruments do not fall within the purview of R.A. No. 7166. Bladed instruments are not regulated since no license is issued for possession or carriage of such. Further, the COMELEC does not issue a permit for the possession or carriage of bladed instruments during the election period."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** COMELEC exceeded its rule-making authority when it banned all knives and bladed instruments during the election period. The statutory election gun ban in Section 32 of R.A. No. 7166 only applies to regulated deadly weapons—meaning weapons that require a government license and for which COMELEC can grant a written permit. Since knives and blades are not regulated and have no licensing mechanism, COMELEC cannot invent a new crime by expanding the statute to cover them.
Issue 5: Benefit of Favorable Judgment to Non-Appealing Co-Accused
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Pursuant to Section 11(a), Rule 122 of the Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure, the reversal and dismissal obtained by petitioner applies to all non-appealing co-accused because it is favorable and applicable to them.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Rule 122, Section 11(a) Mechanics:** While an appeal taken by one accused generally does not affect those who did not appeal, it operates as an express exception where the judgment of the appellate court is favorable and applicable to the non-appealing accused.
2.  **Identity of Factual and Legal Offenses:** Obay, Esperas, Valencia, and Pastorizo were charged with the exact same offense as petitioner under the same invalid provisions of COMELEC Resolution No. 10015. Their cases were consolidated in purpose, handled identically by the lower courts, and defended by the same PAO counsel.
3.  **Complete Destruction of Legal Basis:** Because the Court declared the inclusion of "bladed instruments" in Resolution No. 10015 null and void, the legal foundation for the criminal prosecution against all five accused collapsed. The dismissal of petitioner's case inured directly to the benefit of the four non-appealing co-accused, requiring their immediate release.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The appeal taken by petitioner shall be applied to Obay, Esperas, Valencia, and Pastorizo since it is favorable and applicable to them. As discussed, Obay, Esperas, Valencia, and Pastorizo all face a criminal charge of violating the prohibition on carrying bladed instruments without the necessary permit during the 2016 election period as provided for in COMELEC Resolution No. 10015. Thus, the decision in the appeal taken by petitioner is pertinent to their respective criminal cases."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Even though only Buella appealed to the Supreme Court while his co-accused could no longer be located, they all benefit from the dismissal. Under Rule 122, Section 11(a), whenever an appellate court renders a favorable ruling that strikes down the very penal rule under which multiple co-accused were indicted, that benefit automatically extends to the non-appealing co-accused, entitling them to immediate release.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Assigned Syllabus Topic: Effects of Decisions and Resolutions | Applied Lens: Constitutional & Political Law
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
 Binding Precedent Checklist (Stare Decisis vs. Res Judicata under Civil Code Art. 8):
1.  **Rendered by the Supreme Court: ABSENT in RTC ruling.** (The RTC erroneously treated its own prior Joint Resolution as binding precedent; only Supreme Court decisions form part of the legal system).
2.  **Final Judgment: ABSENT.** (The RTC's declaration of unconstitutionality was still actively contested on reconsideration and certiorari).
3.  **Same Legal Question Decided:** Present, but limited in effect solely to **res judicata** between identical parties, never **stare decisis** across separate dockets.
 Direct vs. Collateral Attack / Judicial Review Requisites Checklist:
1.  **Actual Case or Controversy: PROVEN.** (Petitioner and co-accused were formally charged, arrested, and held in jail).
2.  **Locus Standi: PROVEN.** (Direct injury to personal liberty and exposure to non-probationable imprisonment).
3.  **Earliest Opportunity: PROVEN.** (Raised via a motion to dismiss; criminal cases permit raising unconstitutionality at any stage, even on appeal).
4.  **Lis Mota: PROVEN.** (The constitutionality of the administrative penal clause was the core issue indispensable to determining criminal liability).
 Administrative Quasi-Legislative Subordination Checklist:
1.  **Conformity with Enabling Law: FAILED.** (Sec. 32, R.A. No. 7166 regulates only licensed weapons; COMELEC Resolution expanded the ban to unregulated bladed instruments).
2.  **No Usurpation of Law-Making Power: FAILED.** (Creating an election offense out of innocent possession of knives without clear statutory authorization is **ultra vires** and unconstitutional).
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Stare decisis et non quieta movere (stand by decisions and do not move that which is settled)
 Res judicata (bar by prior judgment / conclusiveness of judgment)
 Lis mota (the moving cause or very heart of the controversy)
 Ejusdem generis (of the same kind or class)
 Ultra vires (beyond the scope of delegated authority)
 Cessante ratione legis cessat ipsa lex (when the reason for the law ceases, the law itself ceases)
Direct attack vs. Collateral attack
**Constitutional & Political Law Audit:**
 State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation: COMELEC exercised delegated quasi-legislative power under Art. IX-C, Sec. 2(1) to regulate election conduct. Invoked against it were the Constitutional Non-Delegation/Separation of Powers doctrine, the Substantive Due Process guarantee (prohibition against arbitrary/oppressive rules), and the Void-for-Vagueness doctrine.
 Level of Judicial Scrutiny: Strict scrutiny in evaluating penal regulations affecting personal liberty, combined with strict construction of delegated administrative rule-making authority.
 Justiciability Audit: All four threshold requirements for judicial review were met. The Court expressly rejected the OSG's collateral attack objection, affirmed trial courts' power of judicial review in criminal proceedings, and held that post-arrest declaratory relief is legally impossible.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
Under the syllabus topic **Effects of Decisions and Resolutions**, **Buella v. People** establishes that **decisions of lower courts do not constitute judicial precedents under the doctrine of stare decisis; under Article 8 of the Civil Code, only final decisions of the Supreme Court form part of the legal system and bind all courts**. Consequently, an RTC judge errs when he **motu proprio** dismisses unconsolidated criminal cases by citing his own prior ruling as binding precedent. Furthermore, an accused may directly challenge the constitutionality of a penal regulation inside a criminal prosecution through a motion to dismiss—which is a permissible direct attack, not a collateral attack—because the unconstitutional penal rule constitutes the very **lis mota** of the case and personal liberty is at stake.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Senior Associate Justice Leonen (Concurring Opinion):** Fully concurred that COMELEC Resolution No. 10015 is **ultra vires**, but added that Rule I, Sec. 1(f) in relation to Rule II, Sec. 1(a) is **unconstitutional for being void for vagueness**. The blanket term "all types of bladed instruments" provides no comprehensible standards on what is "deadly," what is a "weapon," what is "necessary to an occupation," or what constitutes a "legitimate activity." This creates absurd liabilities (e.g., criminalizing the possession of ordinary shaving blades, kitchen knives, or decorative swords without requiring sharpness or lethality) and leaves law enforcement unbridled discretion to oppress citizens carrying tools for legitimate self-defense, completely unmoored from preventing election-related violence.
**Madame Justice Lazaro-Javier (Dissenting Views noted in Ponencia):** Maintained that "other deadly weapons" in Sec. 32 of R.A. No. 7166 should include bladed instruments based on **ejusdem generis**, statutes **in pari materia** (such as Act No. 1780), and COMELEC's contemporaneous construction. The majority explicitly refuted her dissent, holding that Act No. 1780 governed concealed carry under early American colonial rule and cannot be read **in pari materia** with modern election laws, and that COMELEC cannot legislate a licensing requirement where none exists by statute.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"**WHEREFORE**, the appeal is **GRANTED**. The June 22, 2018 Decision and the January 10, 2019 Resolution of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 148051 are **REVERSED** and **SET ASIDE**.

Bladed instruments are hereby **DECLARED** excluded from the term "deadly weapons" in COMELEC Resolution No. 10015.

Criminal Case No. 2016-0281 against Jovit Buella y Abalain, Criminal Case No. 2016-0211 against Matea Obay y Coros, Criminal Case No. 2016-0254 against Jeffrey Esperas y Alemania, Criminal Case No. 2016-0131 against Ruel Valencia y Adante, and Criminal Case No. 2016-0313 against Joel Pastorizo y Canlobo are **DISMISSED**. The Court **ORDERS** their **IMMEDIATE RELEASE** from detention unless they are confined for another lawful cause.

The Regional Trial Court of Naga City, Branch 61 is **ORDERED** to **FURNISH** a copy of this Decision to the appropriate penal or detention facility where Buella, Obay, Esperas, Valencia, and Pastorizo may be detained within five (5) days from receipt of this Decision. The head of such institution is **ORDERED** to report to this Court the action taken within five (5) days from receipt of this Decision.

Let a copy of this Decision be **FURNISHED** to the Commission on Elections for their information and guidance.

**SO ORDERED.**"
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Petitioner Jovit Buella prevailed completely. The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals, struck down the COMELEC's inclusion of "bladed instruments" in the 2016 election weapon ban as **ultra vires**, dismissed all five criminal cases pending before the Naga City RTC, and ordered the immediate release of Buella and all four non-appealing co-accused from detention.
