### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Office of the Court Administrator v. Judge Atienza-Turla**
**Full Official Caption: Office of the Court Administrator, Complainant, vs. Hon. Evelyn A. Atienza-Turla, Presiding Judge, Branch 40, Regional Trial Court, Palayan City, Nueva Ecija, Respondent.**
**Citation & Metadata:** 892 Phil. 61; A.M. No. RTJ-21-005 (Formerly A.M. No. 20-11-161-RTC); Promulgated December 9, 2020; En Banc; Ponente: Gaerlan, J.
**Voting Breakdown:** Concurring: Peralta, **C.J.**, Perlas-Bernabe, Leonen, Caguioa, Hernando, Carandang, Lazaro-Javier, Inting, Zalameda, Delos Santos, and Rosario, **JJ.** On Official Leave: Gesmundo, and Lopez, **JJ.** Separate Opinions: None filed.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Complainant:** Office of the Court Administrator (OCA), the constitutional supervisory arm of the Supreme Court tasked with monitoring judicial efficiency, court audits, and disciplinary compliance.
**Respondent:** Hon. Evelyn A. Atienza-Turla, former Presiding Judge, Branch 40, Regional Trial Court (RTC), Palayan City, Nueva Ecija (compulsorily retired on March 18, 2019; on terminal leave from November 1, 2018 until retirement).
**Acting Presiding Judge:** Hon. Eleanor Teodora Marbas-Vizcarra, designated Acting Presiding Judge of Branch 40, RTC, Palayan City, Nueva Ecija following respondent judge's retirement.
**Court Staff of Branch 40, RTC, Palayan City:** Catherine Valdez-Nad (Officer-in-Charge / Branch Clerk of Court); Harold Joseph Mones Rupac (Utility Worker); Shamin De Guzman-Madrid (Court Interpreter); Rubentito V. Alomia (Sheriff); Alma Villanueva-Eubank, Mary Grace Labiano-Mendoza, and Rosita Reyes-Caramancion (Court Stenographers); Mark Joseph Magdaong Legaspi (DEMO); Mark Bryan Avila Coguiz (Docket Clerk); and Alejandro Cabico Fabian (Process Server).
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
This administrative matter originated from a judicial audit and physical inventory of cases conducted by the OCA Audit Team from January 31, 2019 to February 23, 2019 pursuant to Travel Order No. 12-2019 dated January 18, 2019. The matter was submitted to the Supreme Court En Banc upon the OCA Memorandum dated October 26, 2020, which recommended re-docketing the judicial audit report as a regular administrative matter against retired Judge Evelyn A. Atienza-Turla and the imposition of administrative sanctions.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Judicial Review and Court Administration → Periods to Decide (Article VIII, Section 15)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Legal & Judicial Ethics → Code of Judicial Conduct → Canon 3, Rule 3.05 (Prompt Disposition of Court Business) | Administrative Law → Discipline of Judges (Rule 140, Revised Rules of Court)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional & Statutory Provisions:**
**Article VIII, Section 15, Clauses (1) and (2), 1987 Constitution:**
"Section 15. (1) **All cases or matters filed after the effectivity of this Constitution must be decided or resolved within twenty-four months from date of submission for the Supreme Court, and, unless reduced by the Supreme Court, twelve months for all lower collegiate courts, and three months for all other lower courts.**
(2) **A case or matter shall be deemed submitted for decision or resolution upon the filing of the last pleading, brief, or memorandum required by the Rules of Court or by the court itself.**"
**Article III, Section 16, 1987 Constitution:**
"Section 16. **All persons shall have the right to a speedy disposition of their cases before all judicial, quasi-judicial, or administrative bodies.**"
**Canon 3, Rule 3.05, Code of Judicial Conduct:**
"Rule 3.05 - **A judge shall dispose of the court's business promptly and decide cases within the required periods.**"
**Rule 140, Section 9(1) and Section 11(B), Revised Rules of Court:**
"Section 9. **Less Serious Charges.** — Less serious charges include:
1. Undue delay in rendering a decision or order, or in transmitting the records of a case; x x x

Section 11. **Sanctions.** — x x x
B. If the respondent is guilty of a less serious charge, any of the following sanctions shall be imposed:
1. Suspension from office without salary and other benefits for not less than one (1) nor more than three (3) months; or
2. A fine of more than P10,000.00 but not exceeding P20,000.00."
**Factual Trigger:**
An OCA judicial audit of RTC Branch 40, Palayan City revealed that Presiding Judge Evelyn A. Atienza-Turla left behind 2 criminal cases and 18 civil cases unresolved beyond the mandatory 90-day constitutional period to decide, failed to act upon multiple pending motions and incidents, rendered decisions in 32 civil cases long past the reglementary period without ever requesting an extension of time from the Supreme Court, and mismanaged the court's dockets, which was aggravated when the entire court staff abandoned the office during an official exit conference to attend an unauthorized morning marathon in a neighboring city.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**January 18, 2019:** Travel Order No. 12-2019 is issued directing an OCA audit team to conduct a comprehensive judicial audit and physical inventory of pending cases at Branch 40, RTC, Palayan City, Nueva Ecija.
**November 1, 2018 to March 18, 2019:** Judge Evelyn A. Atienza-Turla avails of terminal leave prior to her compulsory retirement from the judiciary, which takes effect on March 18, 2019. Hon. Eleanor Teodora Marbas-Vizcarra is subsequently designated Acting Presiding Judge of Branch 40.
**January 31, 2019 to February 23, 2019:** The OCA audit team conducts the judicial audit. The inventory reveals an overall court caseload of 833 cases (666 criminal cases and 167 civil cases). The audit team uncovers pervasive docket delays, unresolved matters, and administrative non-feasance:
1.  **Criminal Docket Delays:** Two criminal cases (Criminal Case Nos. 1626-P-06 consolidated with 1721-P-06, and Criminal Case No. 2168) remained submitted for decision well beyond the constitutional 90-day period. Fourteen criminal cases had pending interlocutory incidents unacted upon for an unreasonable period. Three criminal cases ripe for archiving and the issuance of alias warrants were unacted upon.
2.  **Civil Docket Delays:** Eighteen civil cases submitted for decision were unresolved beyond the reglementary period with no extension requested from the OCA. Eleven civil cases had no initial action or scheduling/setting. Twelve civil cases had pending motions or incidents unresolved. Thirty-two civil cases were decided by Judge Atienza-Turla well beyond the mandatory period without any request for extension of time.
3.  **Docket Mismanagement:** The audit team finds eleven structural deficiencies: total failure to observe continuous trial rules; absence of corresponding court orders; failure to state case statuses in hearing notices; non-production of minutes and stenographic notes within reasonable periods; non-use of case indexes to track incidents; missing pagination in court records; un-updated detainee notebooks; clerical inaccuracies in party names and pleading dates; absence of registry return receipts or proof of service on decisions and orders; persistent resettings on the court's own initiative due to official business or judge's absences while routinely granting party motions for postponement; and non-use of mandatory OCA docket inventory templates.
**February 22, 2019 (8:00 AM):** The audit team arrives at Branch 40 to conduct a formally scheduled exit conference to discuss the audit findings. No court employee is present in the courthouse except the utility worker, Harold Joseph Mones Rupac. Upon inspecting the court attendance logbook, the audit team observes that almost all personnel failed to sign in. When questioned regarding the staff's whereabouts, Rupac replies, **"nagmarathon po."** The audit team contacts Officer-in-Charge/Branch Clerk of Court Catherine Valdez-Nad by telephone, who confirms that the court staff left the court to join a marathon in Cabanatuan City, Nueva Ecija. The audit team photographs the empty office and photocopies the attendance logbook.
**March 18, 2019:** Judge Atienza-Turla reaches the compulsory retirement age of 70, leaving behind the unresolved docket backlog.
**October 2, 2020:** The OCA audit team formalizes its findings in an exhaustive Judicial Report submitted to the Court Administrator.
**October 26, 2020:** The Court Administrator submits a Memorandum to Chief Justice Diosdado M. Peralta recommending that the audit report be re-docketed as a regular administrative matter, that Judge Atienza-Turla be adjudged guilty of undue delay under Rule 140 of the Rules of Court and Canon 3, Rule 3.05 of the Code of Judicial Conduct, that a fine equivalent to three months of her final judicial salary be deducted from her retirement benefits, and that the absent court staff be ordered to show cause.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Complainant's Arguments (Office of the Court Administrator)
**Main Thesis:** Respondent Judge Atienza-Turla is guilty of gross inefficiency and undue delay in rendering decisions and orders under Rule 140 of the Rules of Court and the Code of Judicial Conduct, warranting a salary-equivalent fine in lieu of suspension due to her retirement, alongside disciplinary directives against the defaulting branch staff.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Violation of Mandatory Periods:** Under Article VIII, Section 15(1) of the 1987 Constitution, trial judges must decide cases within three months (90 days) from submission. Respondent failed to decide 2 criminal cases and 18 civil cases within the period, and belatedly decided 32 other civil cases.
2.  **Failure to Request Extensions:** While heavy caseloads are acknowledged, the Court routinely grants reasonable requests for extensions. Respondent never filed a single request for extension with the OCA, rendering her delays inexcusable.
3.  **Violation of Judicial Ethics:** Respondent's chronic delays breach Rule 3.05, Canon 3 of the Code of Judicial Conduct, which commands judges to dispose of court business promptly.
4.  **Staff Culpability & Office Mismanagement:** The court records were grossly mismanaged, and the entire court personnel abandoned their judicial posts during official hours on February 22, 2019 to attend an athletic event, necessitating formal administrative explanations.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Judge Evelyn A. Atienza-Turla)
**Main Thesis: Not expressly stated in the decision.** (The matter was initiated and resolved directly on the basis of the OCA judicial audit inventory and recommendations without an answer or counter-affidavit appearing on record).
**Specific Contentions: Not expressly stated in the decision.**
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not retired Judge Evelyn A. Atienza-Turla is administratively liable for gross inefficiency and undue delay in rendering decisions and orders under Article VIII, Section 15(1) and Article III, Section 16 of the 1987 Constitution, Rule 3.05, Canon 3 of the Code of Judicial Conduct, and Section 9, Rule 140 of the Revised Rules of Court, by failing to decide dozens of cases within the mandatory 90-day period and failing to request extensions of time.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the compulsory retirement of a trial judge divests the Supreme Court of jurisdiction to impose administrative sanctions, and if not, what is the appropriate penalty where the prescribed sanction is suspension from office.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the court employees of RTC Branch 40, Palayan City who were absent during the scheduled audit exit conference to participate in a marathon should be required to show cause why they should not be administratively disciplined.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
1. Administrative Liability for Undue Delay in Deciding Cases
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not respondent Judge is administratively liable for undue delay in rendering decisions and orders within the mandatory period? **YES.** The 90-day period prescribed by the Constitution is strictly mandatory, and a judge's failure to decide cases or pending incidents within the period—without obtaining a seasonable extension—constitutes gross inefficiency and undue delay punishable under Rule 140 and the Code of Judicial Conduct.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Constitutional and Ethical Demands of Prompt Disposition: The Supreme Court emphasized that the office of a judge demands faithful observance of the Constitution and the law. Under Article VIII, Section 15(1) of the 1987 Constitution, lower courts are commanded to decide or resolve all cases or matters within three months (90 days) from submission. Failure to observe this rule infringes Article III, Section 16, guaranteeing litigants the right to a speedy disposition of cases.
 Mandatory Nature of the 90-Day Period: Rules fixing prescriptive periods for judicial action are indispensable tools to avert needless delay. The 90-day reglementary timeframe is strictly mandatory to eliminate docket congestion. Any delay, however brief, magnifies litigation expenses, undermines public confidence in the judicial branch, and brings the administration of justice into disrepute.
 Canon 3, Rule 3.05 Infraction: Under Rule 3.05, Canon 3 of the Code of Judicial Conduct, judges are ethically obligated to dispose of the court's business promptly and decide cases within the required periods. Failing to do so amounts to gross inefficiency.
 Heavy Caseload Is No Absolute Defense: While the Court acknowledges that trial judges face heavy caseload burdens, it cannot exonerate them from their duties. The proper recourse is to file a timely and formal request for an extension of time with the Supreme Court through the OCA before the period expires. Because respondent Judge Atienza-Turla never requested an extension for the 2 criminal cases, the 18 overdue civil cases, or the 32 belatedly decided civil cases, her dereliction is inexcusable.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"Time and again, the Court has emphasized that the office of a judge exacts nothing less than faithful observance of the Constitution and the law in the discharge of official duties. Failure to resolve cases submitted for decision within the period fixed by law constitutes a serious violation of Article III, Section 16 of the Constitution, which guarantees the right to speedy disposition of cases. Likewise, Article VIII, Section 15(1) of the 1987 Constitution mandates that the first and second level courts should decide every case within three months from its submission for decision or resolution."

"We are not unmindful of the burden of heavy caseloads heaped on the shoulders of every trial judge. But that cannot excuse them from doing their mandated duty to resolve cases with diligence and dispatch. Judges burdened with heavy caseloads should request the Court for an extension of the reglementary period within which to decide their cases if they think they cannot comply with their judicial duty."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The Supreme Court held that the constitutional three-month period for trial judges to decide submitted cases is strictly mandatory. A heavy caseload cannot excuse judicial delay unless the judge formally asks the Supreme Court for an extension of time before the deadline expires. Because Judge Atienza-Turla let numerous cases sit undecided past the 90-day period and failed to ask for any extensions, she committed gross inefficiency and undue delay.
2. Effect of Compulsory Retirement on Penalties for Undue Delay
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the compulsory retirement of respondent judge precludes disciplinary action, and what sanction applies? **NO.** Retirement does not moot an administrative matter or strip the Court of disciplinary jurisdiction; where the maximum penalty of suspension can no longer be served due to retirement, a fine equivalent to three months' salary is properly imposed against retirement benefits.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Classification of the Offense: Under Section 9(1), Rule 140 of the Revised Rules of Court, undue delay in rendering a decision or order is classified as a less serious charge.
 Prescribed Penalties: Under Section 11(B) of Rule 140, a less serious charge warrants either: (1) suspension from office without salary and benefits for not less than one (1) nor more than three (3) months; or (2) a fine of more than P10,000.00 but not exceeding P20,000.00.
 Adjustment Due to Supervening Retirement: Considering the sheer volume of unresolved cases, unacted motions, and delayed judgments, the maximum penalty of three months' suspension was fully warranted. However, because respondent retired compulsorily on March 18, 2019, suspension from office was no longer executable. Consequently, the Court converted the three-month suspension into a fine equivalent to three months of her salary at the time of retirement, deductible directly from her accumulated retirement and gratuity benefits.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"In this case, considering the number of cases that were left unresolved and undecided, resolved and decided beyond the reglementary period, and motions or pending incidents that were unresolved or unacted upon, the maximum penalty of suspension from office for three (3) months, as recommended by OCA, is in order. However, considering that Judge Atienza-Turla has retired from service on March 18, 2019, a penalty of fine equivalent to three (3) months salary should be imposed."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
A judge cannot escape administrative liability simply by retiring. While the standard maximum penalty for serious delays is a three-month suspension without pay, that penalty cannot physically be served by a retired judge. Therefore, the Supreme Court converts the suspension into a monetary fine equal to three months of the judge's last salary, deducted straight from her retirement pay.
3. Administrative Liability and Directives Concerning Court Staff
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the non-appearing court personnel should be ordered to show cause and administrative operational directives issued? **YES.** Court employees who abandon their posts during work hours to participate in private sporting events compromise judicial administration and must show lawful authority or face disciplinary action.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Dereliction of Public Duty: Leaving the judicial workplace unmanned during official working hours—especially during a scheduled exit conference with Supreme Court audit examiners—constitutes serious operational non-feasance.
 Show Cause Order: Nine named court employees, led by the Officer-in-Charge Catherine Valdez-Nad, were ordered to formally explain their unauthorized absence and present proof of official leave or authorization.
 Corrective Directives: To remediate Branch 40's chronic record mismanagement, the Court directed the Branch OIC to update all missing minutes, steno notes, case indexes, and service proofs, and to submit regular quarterly docket status reports under Administrative Circular Nos. 76-2007 and 61-2001.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The following court employees are directed to EXPLAIN why they should not be held administratively liable for not being present on the scheduled exit conference last February 22, 2019 and to present their authority, if any, as to their absences on the said date: x x x The Officer-in-Charge is hereby DIRECTED to update all corresponding orders, minutes and stenographic notes; to attach to the case records updated indexes of case events and necessary proofs of service/mailing; to expedite the disposition of cases which have been pending in the docket of the court for an unreasonable length of time..."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Judicial employees owe full-time fidelity to their official duties and cannot abandon their desks during office hours to run a marathon. The Court compelled the absent staff to show cause why they should not be disciplined and ordered the branch clerk to systematically correct the mismanaged court dockets.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → g. Periods to Decide (Article VIII, Section 15, 1987 Constitution)
**Applied Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law (Judicial Department Powers, Mandated Periods, and Litigant Rights)
1. Constitutional Power vs. Constitutional Limitation
 Judicial Branch Power Exercised: The Supreme Court exercised its constitutional power of administrative supervision over all courts and personnel pursuant to Article VIII, Section 6 of the 1987 Constitution, implemented via the Court Administrator under Rule 140.
 Constitutional Limitation Enforced: The constitutional limitation operates as a strict, mandatory timetable against lower court judges under Article VIII, Section 15(1) (three-month / 90-day period to decide cases), harmonized with the litigant's fundamental right under Article III, Section 16 (speedy disposition of cases).
2. Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Periods to Decide)
For a lower court judge to comply with or be held liable under Article VIII, Section 15(1), the Court evaluates:
1.  **Submission of the Case/Matter:** Under Article VIII, Section 15(2), a case is deemed submitted upon the filing of the last pleading, brief, or memorandum required by the rules or the court. **(Proven: 2 criminal cases and 18 civil cases were fully submitted for decision).**
2.  **Lapse of the 90-Day Reglementary Period:** Three months elapsed without the promulgation of a judgment or resolution. **(Proven: The cases remained unresolved well beyond 90 days, and 32 civil cases had been decided months after the period expired).**
3.  **Absence of Timely Extension:** The judge failed to apply for an extension before the expiration of the original 90-day period. **(Proven: Judge Atienza-Turla never filed a single request for extension of time with the OCA).**
4.  **Non-Exonerative Defense:** Heavy caseloads and pending retirements do not excuse non-performance of this constitutional mandate without an authorized extension. **(Applied: Caseload acknowledged, but held unmeritorious as a defense).**
3. Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words")
**Article VIII, Section 15(1) Mandatory 90-Day Period:** The rule that lower trial courts have three months to decide submitted cases is strictly mandatory, not directory.
**Article VIII, Section 15(2) Deemed Submitted Rule:** A case is deemed submitted for decision immediately upon the filing of the last pleading, brief, or memorandum.
**Article III, Section 16 Speedy Disposition of Cases:** The constitutional guarantee violated whenever a judge permits unresolved backlogs to fester.
**Gross Inefficiency:** The administrative characterization of a judge's failure to decide cases within the reglementary period.
**Undue Delay:** Less serious charge under Rule 140, Section 9.
4. Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit
 Actual Case or Controversy:** Live administrative disciplinary matter initiated by the Court **motu proprio pursuant to its plenary administrative supervisory powers over inferior courts.
 Supervening Retirement / Mootness Exception: The compulsory retirement of a judicial officer does not strip the Court of administrative jurisdiction over offenses committed while in active service; the Court converts unexecutable suspensions into monetary fines deducted from accrued terminal/retirement benefits.
5. Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer)
"**OCA v. Atienza-Turla** falls squarely under 'Periods to Decide' because it operationalizes Article VIII, Section 15(1) and Article III, Section 16 of the 1987 Constitution against trial judges. The Supreme Court held that the three-month (90-day) period for first- and second-level courts to decide submitted cases is strictly mandatory. While trial courts endure heavy caseloads, heavy work is not a valid legal excuse for delay; rather, the judge must formally petition the Supreme Court for an extension before the period lapses. Because Judge Atienza-Turla left 20 cases undecided beyond 90 days and decided 32 others late without requesting extensions, she was found guilty of undue delay and gross inefficiency, and penalized with a fine equal to three months of her salary deducted directly from her retirement benefits."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, Judge Evelyn A. Atienza-Turla, formerly of Branch 40, Regional Trial Court, Palayan City, Nueva Ecija is hereby found GUILTY of the less serious charge of undue delay in rendering decision or order under Section 9, Rule 140 of the Rules of Court, and Rule 3.05 of Canon 3 of the Code of Judicial Conduct. Considering her retirement which took effect on March 18, 2019, a PENALTY OF FINE equivalent to three (3) months salary at the time of her retirement is hereby imposed, to be deducted from her retirement/gratuity benefits.

The following court employees are directed to EXPLAIN why they should not be held administratively liable for not being present on the scheduled exit conference last February 22, 2019 and to present their authority, if any, as to their absences on the said date:
a. Catherine Valdez-Nad (Officer-in-Charge/COC);
b. Shamin De Guzman-Madrid (Court Interpreter);
### c. Rubentito V. Alomia (Sheriff);
### d. Alma Villanueva-Eubank (Stenographer);
e. Mary Grace Labiano-Mendoza (Stenographer);
f. Rosita Reyes-Caramancion (Stenographer);
g. Mark Joseph Magdaong Legaspi (DEMO);
h. Mark Bryan Avila Coguiz (Docket Clerk); and
### i. Alejandro Cabico Fabian (Process Server);

The Officer-in-Charge is hereby DIRECTED to update all corresponding orders, minutes and stenographic notes; to attach to the case records updated indexes of case events and necessary proofs of service/mailing; to expedite the disposition of cases which have been pending in the docket of the court for an unreasonable length of time; to submit quarterly reports on the status of cases which have been pending in the court docket for a year or more; and to submit quarterly reports on the status of such cases. He is further DIRECTED to strictly comply with Administrative Circular No. 76-2007 (Submission of Semestral Docket Inventory Report) and Administrative Circular No. 60-2001 (Revised Rules, Guidelines, and Instructions on Accomplishing Monthly Report of cases).

SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court adopted the OCA's findings and found retired Judge Evelyn A. Atienza-Turla administratively guilty of undue delay. Because she had already retired, the Court penalized her with a fine equal to three months of her judicial salary to be deducted directly from her retirement benefits, issued a show cause order against nine court employees who abandoned the courthouse to join a marathon, and ordered the Branch OIC to immediately reorganize and report on the status of the court's delayed dockets.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Re: Problem of Delays in Cases Before the Sandiganbayan
**Full Official Caption:** Re: Problem of Delays in Cases Before the Sandiganbayan, A.M. No. 00-8-05-SC
**Citation & Metadata:** 422 Phil. 246; A.M. No. 00-8-05-SC; Promulgated November 28, 2001; En Banc; Pardo, **J.** (Ponente); Davide, Jr., **C.J.**, Bellosillo, Melo, Puno, Vitug, Kapunan, Mendoza, Panganiban, Quisumbing, Ynares-Santiago, Sandoval-Gutierrez, and Carpio, **JJ.**, concur; De Leon, Jr., **J.**, filed a Concurring and Dissenting Opinion; Buena, **J.**, took no part (on official leave).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP): Complainant body, acting through National President Arthur D. Lim and its Board of Governors; transmitted the resolution prompting the administrative inquiry.
Francis E. Garchitorena: Respondent Presiding Justice of the Sandiganbayan and Chairman of its First Division.
Associate Justices of the Sandiganbayan: Sitting across five divisions of the anti-graft court (including Senior Associate Justice Minita V. Chico-Nazario, designated interim head).
Office of the Court Administrator (OCA): Investigating judicial arm led by Court Administrator Alfredo L. Benipayo and Consultant Pedro A. Ramirez (Retired CA Justice), tasked with conducting judicial audits.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Initiated by a formal letter-resolution of the IBP Board of Governors requesting an inquiry into delays and the extension of Administrative Circular No. 10-94 to the Sandiganbayan. The Supreme Court treated the matter **ex mero motu** as an administrative complaint against Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Francis E. Garchitorena for serious delays in the decision of cases and resolution of motions, amounting to inefficiency and gross neglect of duty.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Periods to Decide (Article VIII, Section 15)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Judicial Ethics & Court Administration → Delay in Case Disposition (**Mora Decidendi**) → Special Courts (Sandiganbayan Jurisdiction & Rules)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article VIII, Section 15 (1) and (2), 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Sec. 15. (1) **All cases or matters filed after the effectivity of this Constitution must be decided or resolved within twenty-four months from date of submission to the Supreme Court, and, unless reduced by the Supreme Court, twelve months for all lower collegiate courts, and three months for all other lower courts.**
(2) **A case or matter shall be deemed submitted for decision or resolution upon the filing of the last pleading, brief or memorandum required by the Rules of Court or by the court itself.**"
**Section 6, Presidential Decree No. 1606 (Revising P.D. 1486, Creating the Sandiganbayan):**
"Sec. 6. **Maximum period for termination of cases** — As far as practicable, the trial of cases before the Sandiganbayan once commenced shall be continuous until terminated and **the judgment shall be rendered within three (3) months from the date the case was submitted for decision.**"
**Rule XVIII, Section 3, Revised Rules of the Sandiganbayan (promulgated Sept. 18, 1984):**
"Sec. 3. **Maximum Period to Decide Cases** — **The judgment or final order of a division of the Sandiganbayan shall be rendered within three (3) months from the date the case was submitted for decision.**"
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):**
The administrative conflict was triggered when the IBP transmitted a resolution exposing pervasive, long-standing delays across divisions of the Sandiganbayan, followed by Presiding Justice Garchitorena's formal compliance admitting that 415 cases remained undecided long beyond the reglementary period—some having languished submitted for decision for over a decade (dating back to 1990)—and an unresolved motion for reconsideration pending ten months beyond the statutory 30-day limit.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**June 29, 1994:** The Supreme Court issues Administrative Circular No. 10-94 directing all trial court judges to conduct physical docket inventories and submit bi-annual tabulations of pending cases.
**July 29, 2000:** The IBP Board of Governors passes a Resolution in Los Baños, Laguna, citing Section 16, Article III of the Constitution (speedy disposition of cases) and Canon 12 of the Code of Professional Responsibility, noting systemic delays in the Sandiganbayan and recommending an inquiry into delays and the application of SC Adm. Circular No. 10-94 to cases under the Sandiganbayan's original jurisdiction.
**July 31, 2000:** IBP National President Arthur D. Lim transmits the resolution to the Supreme Court.
**August 8, 2000:** The Supreme Court En Banc requires Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Francis E. Garchitorena to comment and submit a complete list of pending cases submitted for decision and motions for reconsideration pending resolution.
**September 27, 2000:** Presiding Justice Garchitorena submits his compliance report admitting to 415 undecided cases submitted for decision across all five divisions (First Division: 341; Second Division: 5; Third Division: 12; Fourth Division: 5; Fifth Division: 52; plus one pending motion for reconsideration in the Fifth Division), with some cases unresolved since May 24, 1990.
**October 10, 2000:** The Supreme Court En Banc issues a resolution noting that a motion for reconsideration remained unresolved over 30 days from submission and admonishing bench members that justice delayed is justice denied.
**October 20, 2000:** Presiding Justice Garchitorena submits a schedule of cases submitted for decision, reporting zero detained prisoners.
**October 26, 2000:** The IBP files a Reply pointing out that the First Division had unresolved cases dating back to 1990, that pending motions were omitted, that the Sandiganbayan as a trial court must submit trial court reports, and arguing that while collegiate courts have 12 months under Article VIII, Section 15(1), the Sandiganbayan, acting as a trial court, must resolve cases within 3 to 6 months.
**November 21, 2000:** The Supreme Court directs Court Administrator Alfredo L. Benipayo to conduct a formal judicial audit and physical inventory of the Sandiganbayan.
**December 4, 2000:** Presiding Justice Garchitorena writes the Chief Justice admitting a First Division backlog, but pleading that a single consolidated case (**People v. Corazon Gammad-Leaño**, involving 156 counts) accounted for over 50% of it, with promulgation set for December 8, 2000.
**January 26, 2001:** Court Administrator Benipayo submits a judicial audit report attributing Sandiganbayan delays to five systemic bottlenecks: (1) OSP failure to submit reinvestigation reports; (2) years-long unacted incidents/motions; (3) proceedings suspended due to pending SC petitions without injunctions; (4) lack of court calendar settings; and (5) the improper unloading of submitted cases to other divisions.
**November 14–16, 2001:** The Supreme Court directs an updated audit. OCA Consultant Pedro A. Ramirez submits an updated compliance report revealing that 138 cases remained undecided in the First Division alone (including 73 never assigned to a ponente), and showing an unresolved motion for reconsideration submitted January 11, 2001, in the **Leaño** case that had remained unacted upon by Garchitorena for ten months.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The Sandiganbayan suffers from serious, unacceptable delays violating litigants' constitutional rights to speedy disposition, necessitating SC intervention and administrative reporting mandates.
**Specific Contentions:**
Sandiganbayan divisions commit egregious delays in deciding cases and pending motions, with some cases pending decision since 1990.
Although the Constitution grants lower collegiate courts 12 months to decide cases under Article VIII, Section 15(1), the Sandiganbayan functions primarily as a trial court introducing evidence; hence, its period to decide should be reduced to 3 months (like RTCs) or at most 6 months.
SC Administrative Circular No. 10-94, which requires bi-annual docket inventories and monthly postings of submitted cases, should be made applicable to the Sandiganbayan for cases under its original jurisdiction.
B. Respondent Presiding Justice Francis E. Garchitorena's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Delays in the Sandiganbayan, specifically in the First Division, resulted from systemic structural reorganizations, moving disruptions, and mass-count single litigation, rather than culpable inefficiency.
**Specific Contentions:**
The court underwent major statutory reorganization in 1997, requiring newly appointed justices to undergo extensive orientations.
The Sandiganbayan relocated to a new physical building, forcing records to be packed into crates, some of which remained unexamined or unopened.
** Over 50% of the First Division's massive backlog was attributable to a single consolidated case (**People v. Leaño, Criminal Cases Nos. 9812–9967) comprising 156 counts, which, once promulgated, would halve the backlog.
Cases submitted before the 1997 reorganization were placed "under study," and certain delays were caused by unconfirmed deaths of accused parties.
### C. Office of the Court Administrator (OCA) Evaluation
**Main Position:** Sandiganbayan original jurisdiction cases are trial proceedings subject to a 3-month reglementary period, whereas appellate cases from the RTC are subject to the 12-month collegiate period. The practice of "unloading" submitted cases must cease.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the reglementary period within which the Sandiganbayan must decide cases submitted to it for decision is three (3) months or twelve (12) months.
2. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the Sandiganbayan, particularly its First Division under Presiding Justice Garchitorena, incurred unreasonable, sanctionable delay (**mora decidendi**) in failing to decide cases beyond the reglementary period.
3. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not Supreme Court Administrative Circular No. 10-94 is applicable to the Sandiganbayan.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Reglementary Period to Decide Cases in the Sandiganbayan
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the period to decide cases submitted to the Sandiganbayan is three (3) months or twelve (12) months?
**THREE (3) MONTHS.** Under its governing charter (P.D. No. 1606) and its own Revised Rules of Procedure, the Sandiganbayan must decide cases within three months from the date of submission, not the twelve months provided in Article VIII, Section 15(1) for regular lower collegiate courts.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
The Court rejected the proposition that the Sandiganbayan falls under the 12-month provision of Article VIII, Section 15(1) of the 1987 Constitution. That constitutional category refers strictly to regular lower collegiate courts, which in the Philippine judicial hierarchy applies solely to the Court of Appeals.
The Sandiganbayan is not a regular court; it is a "special court" possessing the same level as the Court of Appeals and exercising inherent judicial powers, but functioning inherently as a trial court. Special courts are judicial tribunals exercising limited jurisdiction over particular or specialized categories of actions (e.g., CTA, Sandiganbayan, Shari'a Courts). Under Article VIII, Section 5(5) of the Constitution, rules of procedure of special courts remain in force unless disapproved by the Supreme Court.
** The governing charter, Section 6 of P.D. No. 1606, explicitly mandates: "**the judgment shall be rendered within three (3) months from the date the case was submitted for decision."
** On September 18, 1984, the Sandiganbayan enacted its own Revised Rules of Procedure. Section 3, Rule XVIII unambiguously commands that judgment or final orders "**shall be rendered within three (3) months from the date the case was submitted for decision."
The Court expressly rejected the OCA's proposed distinction that original cases have a 3-month window while appealed cases have a 12-month window. The plain statutory text makes no distinction.
** Citing **DARAB v. Court of Appeals** and **Cabagnot v. COMELEC, the Court held that a tribunal cannot violate or suspend its own rules at whim. The Sandiganbayan must be the first to observe its own rules without making unilateral exceptions.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Given the clarity of the rule that does not distinguish, we hold that the three (3) month period, not the twelve (12) month period, to decide cases applies to the Sandiganbayan. Furthermore, the Sandiganbayan presently sitting in five (5) divisions, functions as a trial court. The term 'trial' is used in its broad sense, meaning, it allows introduction of evidence by the parties in the cases before it."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The 12-month period in the Constitution applies only to regular lower collegiate courts (the Court of Appeals). The Sandiganbayan is a special court functioning as a trial court that receives evidence. Because both its creating law (P.D. 1606, Sec. 6) and its own rules (Rule XVIII, Sec. 3) explicitly order all judgments to be rendered within three months from submission without making distinctions, the Sandiganbayan is strictly bound to decide all cases within three months.
Issue 2: Liability for Undecided Cases and Mora Decidendi
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not Presiding Justice Francis E. Garchitorena and the Sandiganbayan are guilty of gross neglect of duty and inefficiency for delay in deciding cases?
**YES.** Presiding Justice Garchitorena incurred inordinate and inexcusable delays (**mora decidendi**) in hundreds of cases, leaving matters undecided for up to ten years, constituting gross neglect of duty and inefficiency.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
** The official audit established that 415 cases across divisions remained undecided long past the 90-day reglementary period, with some submitted as early as May 24, 1990. In the First Division, 138 cases were still undecided, 73 of which were never even assigned to a **ponente.
** The Court discarded all of Garchitorena's defenses. A delay of three years in deciding even a single case is inexcusably long; therefore, multi-year delays are indefensible. The Latin maxim applies: "**para muestra, basta un boton" (for an example, one button suffices). Moving offices, crated records, judicial orientation, and court reorganizations do not excuse judicial inaction.
** The claim that the **Leaño** consolidated case wiped out 50% of the First Division's backlog was fallacious because a consolidated case is legally treated as a single case. Moreover, Garchitorena failed to act on the Motion for Reconsideration in **Leaño for 10 months, despite the strict 30-day limit to resolve motions for reconsideration.
** Failure to assign a case to a writer of the opinion (**ponente) does not toll or erase the backlog. The Court declared the rule: **It is the duty of the Presiding Justice or Division Chairman to assign the ponente immediately upon submission; if he fails to make the assignment, he is deemed by law to be the ponente.**
The improper practice in the First and Third Divisions of "unloading" submitted cases onto newly created Fourth and Fifth Divisions to shed workload was condemned. A division that hears and tries a case must decide it.
** Unreasonable delay (**mora reprobatur in lege**) violates the litigants' constitutional right to a speedy disposition of cases, paralyzes anti-graft efforts, and brings the judiciary into disrepute. Because Garchitorena previously received a warning in **Canson v. Garchitorena, disciplinary action was warranted.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"This Court has consistently impressed upon judges (which includes justices) to decide cases promptly and expeditiously on the principle that justice delayed is justice denied. Decision making is the primordial and most important duty of the member of the bench... It is the duty of the Presiding Justice and the Chairmen of divisions to assign the ponente as soon as the case is declared submitted for decision, if not earlier. If he fails to make the assignment, he shall be deemed to be the ponente."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Presiding Justice Garchitorena allowed hundreds of cases to sit undecided for up to a decade, and even left 73 cases unassigned so they wouldn't appear on individual dockets. The Supreme Court ruled that an unassigned case is automatically charged to the Presiding Justice as **ponente**, and held that trial reorganization or massive case consolidation never excuses delay in decision-making.
Issue 3: Applicability of Supreme Court Administrative Circular No. 10-94
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not Supreme Court Administrative Circular No. 10-94 applies to the Sandiganbayan?
**YES.** SC Administrative Circular No. 10-94 applies fully to the Sandiganbayan for both original and appellate jurisdiction cases.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Circular No. 10-94 requires trial judges to physically inventory dockets bi-annually and verify submitted cases to prevent delays and track court efficiency.
Given that the Sandiganbayan functions as a collegiate trial court introducing and weighing original evidence, the rationale of inventory, case-tracking, and transparency applies with equal force to it.
Consequently, the Sandiganbayan must implement bi-annual docket inventories and execute the certifications required by Circular No. 10-94.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Given the rationale behind the Administrative Circular, we hold that it is applicable to the Sandiganbayan with respect to cases within its original and appellate jurisdiction."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Because the Sandiganbayan functions as a trial court, it is not exempt from administrative transparency. It must perform bi-annual docket physical inventories and submit tabulations of submitted cases under Circular 10-94 just like any trial court.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Assigned Syllabus Topic: g. Periods to Decide
**Applied Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law Lens
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 Judicial Administration & Disciplinary Power (Art. VIII, Sec. 5[5], Sec. 6, Sec. 11): The Supreme Court exercised its administrative supervision over all courts and personnel to discipline an appellate-level Presiding Justice.
 Constitutional Counter-Guarantees Invoked: Art. III, Sec. 16 (Right to Speedy Disposition of Cases before judicial, quasi-judicial, or administrative bodies) and Art. VIII, Sec. 15 (Constitutional periods to decide cases).
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
 Strict Statutory & Regulatory Compliance / Non-Derogation Principle: The Court applied strict enforcement of mandatory decision periods. When a statute (P.D. 1606) and a court’s own rules prescribe a 3-month window, the tribunal cannot invoke constitutional periods meant for regular appellate courts to extend its time.
**Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:**
 Ex Mero Motu Administrative Jurisdiction:** The Court converted an IBP recommendation directly into an **ex mero motu administrative disciplinary proceeding against a sitting Presiding Justice without requiring formal third-party complainant verification, based on the respondent's judicial admissions and official audit records.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Periods to Decide & Special Court Application):**
** [x] **Classification of the Tribunal: Regular collegiate court vs. Special court. The Sandiganbayan is a "special court" with trial court functions, not a "regular lower collegiate court."
** [x] **Trigger Event for Period: Filing of the last pleading, brief, or memorandum, or expiration of time to file (Art. VIII, Sec. 15[2]; Adm. Cir. No. 28).
** [x] **Prescribed Reglementary Period: Three (3) months for Sandiganbayan judgments (Sec. 6, P.D. 1606; Rule XVIII, Sec. 3, Sandiganbayan Rules); thirty (30) days for motions for reconsideration.
** [x] **Assignment Rule for Ponente:** Presiding Justice/Division Chair must immediately designate a **ponente**; omission makes the Presiding Justice the constructive **ponente.
** [x] **Excuse Evaluation: Reorganization, court transfer, volume of counts in consolidated actions, and unassigned statuses are rejected as legal justifications for delay.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Mora decidendi (delay in deciding cases).
 Mora reprobatur in lege (delay is reprobated in law).
 Para muestra, basta un boton (for an example, one button suffices).
Special Court (tribunals of limited, specialized jurisdiction, distinct from regular courts under Art. VIII, Sec. 15).
Unloading of cases (the prohibited practice of shifting submitted cases to another division).
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"Under the syllabus topic **Periods to Decide**, this case establishes that the 12-month period in Article VIII, Section 15(1) applies only to **regular** lower collegiate courts (the Court of Appeals). The Sandiganbayan is a **special court** functioning as a trial court; hence, under Section 6 of P.D. No. 1606 and its own rules, its period to decide is strictly **three (3) months**, with 30 days for motions for reconsideration. Presiding Justice Garchitorena was fined and stripped of administrative/trial duties for gross neglect of duty due to decades-long backlogs, establishing the doctrine that failure of a division chair to assign a submitted case makes him the constructive **ponente** responsible for the delay."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**De Leon, Jr., J. (Concurring and Dissenting):** Dissented specifically on the 3-month ruling. Argued that under Article VIII, Section 15(1), "all lower collegiate courts" have 12 months unless reduced by the Supreme Court. Since the Sandiganbayan is a collegiate court of the same level as the Court of Appeals (R.A. 8249), requires three justices to decide, and sits in divisions where a dissent requires a special division of five, it is fundamentally different from a single-judge RTC. The Constitution must prevail over P.D. 1606 or court rules. He concurred in the rest of the resolution and sanctions.
**Verbatim/Near-Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, in view of all the foregoing, the Court resolves:
(1) To IMPOSE on Presiding Justice Francis E. Garchitorena a fine of twenty thousand pesos (P20,000.00), for inefficiency and gross neglect of duty.
(2) Effective December 1, 2001, to RELIEVE Presiding Justice Francis E. Garchitorena of his powers, functions and duties as the Presiding Justice, Sandiganbayan, and from presiding over the trial of cases as a justice and Chairman, First Division, so that he may DEVOTE himself exclusively to DECISION WRITING, until the backlog of cases assigned to him as well as cases not assigned to any ponente, of which he shall be deemed the ponente in the First Division, are finally decided. There shall be no unloading of cases to other divisions, or to the First Division inter se.
In the interim, Associate Justice Minita V. Chico-Nazario, as the most senior associate justice, shall TAKE OVER and exercise the powers, functions, and duties of the office of the Presiding Justice, Sandiganbayan, until further orders from this Court.
(3) To DIRECT Presiding Justice Francis E. Garchitorena and the associate justices of the Sandiganbayan to decide/resolve the undecided cases submitted for decision as of this date, within three (3) months from their submission, and to resolve motions for new trial or reconsiderations and petitions for review within thirty (30) days from their submission. With respect to the backlog of cases, as hereinabove enumerated, the Sandiganbayan shall decide/resolve all pending cases including incidents therein within six (6) months from notice of this resolution.
(4) To ORDER the Sandiganbayan to comply with Supreme Court Administrative Circular 10-94, effective immediately.
(5) To DIRECT the Sandiganbayan en banc to adopt not later than December 31, 2001 internal rules to govern the allotment of cases among the divisions, the rotation of justices among them and other matters leading to the internal operation of the court, and thereafter to submit the said internal rules to the Supreme Court for its approval.
This directive is immediately executory.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court disciplined Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Francis E. Garchitorena with a P20,000 fine and stripped him of his administrative and trial functions, ordering him to devote himself exclusively to writing decisions on all his unresolved backlogged and unassigned cases within 6 months. Senior Associate Justice Minita V. Chico-Nazario was designated Acting Presiding Justice, the 3-month period to decide was reaffirmed for the Sandiganbayan, and the anti-graft court was formally subjected to mandatory physical docket inventories under SC Administrative Circular No. 10-94.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Garcia v. Macaraig
**Full Official Caption:** Paz M. Garcia, Complainant, vs. Hon. Catalino Macaraig, Jr., Respondent
**Citation & Metadata:** Administrative Matter No. 198-J; Promulgated May 31, 1971; 148-A Phil. 93; En Banc; Ponente: Barredo, J.
**Voting Breakdown:** Concurring: Concepcion, C.J., Reyes, J.B.L., Dizon, Makalintal, Zaldivar, and Villamor, JJ.; Took No Part: Castro and Teehankee, JJ.; Separate Concurring Opinion: Fernando, J. (concurring fully, joined by Makasiar, J.).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Paz M. Garcia:** Complainant who initiated an administrative complaint charging respondent with dishonesty, grave incompetence, violation of oath of office, and violations of the Judiciary Act of 1948.
**Hon. Catalino Macaraig, Jr.:** Respondent; formerly appointed District Judge of the Court of First Instance (CFI) of Laguna and San Pablo City, Branch VI (stationed at Calamba), who subsequently served as Undersecretary of Justice.
**Secretary of Justice (Vicente Abad Santos):** Cabinet official who requested respondent to assist the Department of Justice (DOJ) while the physical courtroom in Calamba was being established.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** This is an original administrative complaint (A.M. No. 198-J) filed directly with the Supreme Court seeking disciplinary action against respondent judge for alleged dishonesty, moral bankruptcy, and non-compliance with statutory judicial duties.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Judicial Independence & Separation of Powers → Non-Judicial Work / Incompatibility of Administrative Detail
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Legal Ethics & Judicial Conduct → Administrative Liabilities of Judges → Collection of Salaries and Submission of Certificates of Service
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Judiciary Act of 1948 (Republic Act No. 296, as amended), Section 5:**
"District judges, judges of City Courts, and municipal Judges shall certify on their application for leave, and upon salary vouchers presented by them for payment, or upon the payrolls upon which their salaries are paid, that all special proceedings, applications, petitions, motions, and all civil and criminal cases which have been under submission for decision or determination for a period of ninety days or more have been determined and decided on or before the date of making the certificate and ... **no salary shall be paid without such certificate.**"
**Judiciary Act of 1948 (Republic Act No. 296, as amended), Section 55:**
Prescribes the requirement for district judges to hold court at the place of their permanent station.
**Judiciary Act of 1948 (Republic Act No. 296, as amended), Section 58:**
Prescribes the regular daily hours of court sessions to be observed by trial judges.
**Historical Landmark Rule (Modern Provision Cross-Reference):** Decided under the **1935 Constitution** (which distributed powers among the Legislative [Art. VI], Executive [Art. VII], and Judiciary [Art. VIII], without an express textual clause prohibiting non-judicial assignments). The Court's doctrinal warning against detailing judges to executive agencies served as the precursor to **Article VIII, Section 12 of the 1987 Constitution**, which strictly codifies:
"**The members of the Supreme Court and of other courts established by law shall not be designated to any agency performing quasi-judicial or administrative functions.**"
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):** Following his appointment as a newly created CFI judge, respondent had no physical courtroom, staff, or equipment in Calamba; upon being prevailed upon by the Secretary of Justice, he forewent his leave and rendered administrative assistance in the Department of Justice while collecting his judicial salary, which prompted a complainant to charge him with dishonesty, incompetence, and failure to submit statutory certificates of service.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**June 29, 1970:** Catalino Macaraig, Jr. takes his oath of office as District Judge of the Court of First Instance of Laguna and San Pablo City, Branch VI, with station at Calamba (one of 112 newly created branches under Republic Act No. 296). On the same date, he formally advises the Secretary of Justice by letter that he is entering upon the performance of his duties. By taking the oath, he automatically ceases to hold his previous positions as Chief of the Technical Staff of the DOJ (salary: P16,200/annum) and Member of the Board of Pardons and Parole (salary: P8,000/annum), and takes a leave of absence from his professorial lecturer post at the U.P. College of Law (earning ~P600/month).
**July 1970:** Respondent attempts to organize the Calamba sala from scratch. Under Section 190 of the Revised Administrative Code, the provincial government is mandated to furnish courtroom space, equipment, and supplies, but Laguna provincial officials inform him they lack the capacity to do so. The Municipal Mayor of Calamba offers space in the municipal building's west wing, but the municipal treasurer and several councilors object to vacating their offices. The mayor advises respondent to locate commercial rental space at municipal expense. Negotiations for the second floor of the Republic Bank branch fail when the owner refuses to reduce rent to P300 per month.
**July 1970 – August 1970:** Realizing that establishing the sala will take substantial time, respondent applies for an extended leave of absence (having accumulated 16 years of unused leave benefits at the DOJ). The Secretary of Justice prevails upon respondent to forego his leave and instead assist the Department, without formal detail, whenever respondent is not occupied with organizing his court.
**October 26, 1970:** After month-long negotiations, the Calamba municipal government executes a lease agreement for the second floor of the Laguna Development Bank building.
**November 1970:** The municipal government takes another month to release funds required to construct partitions and convert the large, unpartitioned hall into a courtroom and offices for court personnel and the assistant provincial fiscal.
**December 1970:** Respondent obtains an appropriation of P5,000 from the Laguna provincial government for supplies and materials. Early in December, he places an equipment requisition with the DOJ Property Officer. However, government funds for CFI equipment are not released until December 23, 1970, leaving procurement pending.
**July 1, 1970 – February 28, 1971:** Respondent does not submit monthly accomplishment reports or Certificates of Service (New Judicial Form No. 86) regarding ninety-day case dispositions, but collects his judicial salary (P19,000/annum). During this period, he actively divides his time between organizing the physical sala in Calamba and assisting the Secretary of Justice.
**Prior to May 31, 1971:** Paz M. Garcia files an administrative complaint with the Supreme Court against respondent (now Undersecretary of Justice) charging dishonesty, violation of his oath of office, gross incompetence, and violations of Sections 5, 55, and 58 of the Judiciary Act of 1948 and DOJ Circular No. 10. Respondent submits his Answer supported by official certifications from Judicial Superintendent Eulalio D. Pichay, Undersecretary Guillermo S. Santos, and the DOJ Financial Officer.
**May 31, 1971:** The Supreme Court En Banc promulgates its Resolution dismissing the administrative complaint, but emphatically condemning and directing the discontinuation of the practice of detailing judges to executive departments.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Complainant's Arguments:
**Main Thesis:** Respondent judge is guilty of gross incompetence, dishonesty, and moral bankruptcy for collecting public judicial salaries without having held a single court session or discharged judicial functions.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Violation of Reporting Directives: Failed from July 1, 1970 to February 28, 1971 to submit monthly reports of cases filed, decided, and pending, or hours of daily court sessions, violating DOJ Circular No. 10 (Feb. 6, 1952) and Sections 55 and 58 of the Judiciary Act of 1948.
 Illegal Collection of Salaries: Collected judicial salaries from July 1970 through February 1971 without submitting the mandatory Certificate of Service certifying that no cases remained undecided for over ninety days, in explicit violation of Section 5 of the Judiciary Act.
 Moral Bankruptcy & Perjury: On June 29, 1970, respondent falsely notified the Secretary of Justice that he was "entering upon the performance of the duties of the office," constituting a deliberate falsehood that demonstrated moral unfitness for the bench.
B. Respondent's Arguments:
**Main Thesis:** Inability to preside over hearings stemmed entirely from the physical non-existence of the newly created sala, an impediment beyond his control; collecting salaries while actively organizing the court and assisting the DOJ upon executive request did not constitute dishonesty or neglect.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Inapplicability of Statutes and Circulars: Sections 5, 55, and 58 of the Judiciary Act and Circular No. 10 logically apply only to judges presiding over functioning salas. A judge cannot certify the disposition of cases submitted for decision, observe session hours, or hold court at a station that does not physically exist.
 Absence of Incompetence or Dishonesty: Respondent was eager to preside, but local and national governments failed to provide facilities as required by Section 190 of the Revised Administrative Code. He diligently spent time and personal funds negotiating leases and securing appropriations.
 Entitlement to Salary & Legitimate Service: Having taken a valid oath pursuant to a confirmed appointment, he was entitled to salary. He gave up higher total compensation to accept the judicial post. Rather than remaining idle on accrued leave, he forewent leave upon the Secretary's request to assist the DOJ, thereby rendering legitimate public service.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondent judge is guilty of dishonesty, moral falsehood, or violation of his oath of office for collecting judicial compensation while physically unable to hold judicial trials.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondent judge violated Section 5, 55, and 58 of the Judiciary Act of 1948 and DOJ Circular No. 10 by failing to submit monthly reports and Certificates of Service before his courtroom had been physically established.
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the long-standing executive practice of detailing or assigning members of the judiciary to perform non-judicial administrative work in the Department of Justice violates the constitutional principle of separation of powers and compromises judicial independence.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Dishonesty, Falsehood, and Salary Collection
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not respondent judge committed dishonesty and moral falsehood by accepting his salary prior to presiding over trials. **NO.** A duly appointed judge who has taken his oath is legally entitled to compensation, and assisting another public office at the executive's request when local facilities are unavailable does not establish dishonesty.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Legal Vesting of Office: Upon taking a valid oath under a confirmed presidential appointment, respondent legally assumed the status and emoluments of a CFI Judge.
 Exogenous Impediments: Respondent's inability to preside was entirely due to the failure of provincial and municipal authorities to furnish a physical courtroom, furniture, and equipment pursuant to Section 190 of the Revised Administrative Code.
 Entitlement to Accrued Leave vs. Alternative Service: Respondent had a clear right to earn compensation, and could lawfully have taken extended accrued leave while waiting. Foregoing his leave at the request of the Secretary of Justice to assist the Department, while concurrently securing rental space, funding, and equipment for his sala, demonstrates commendable diligence rather than deceit or dishonesty.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"What is lost sight of, however, is that after taking his oath and formally assuming his position as judge, respondent had a perfect right to earn the salary of a judge even in the extreme supposition that he did not perform any judicial function for he could, while preparing himself for his new job or for any good reason, take a leave, as in fact, he had planned to do, were it not for the request of the Secretary of Justice for him to forego the idea and, instead, help the Department in whatever way possible..."
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** A judge who has taken his oath is fully entitled to his salary even if local officials have not yet built his courtroom. Working to set up his branch and helping the DOJ instead of sitting on paid leave is not dishonest, because the delay was completely beyond his control.
Issue 2: Failure to Submit Statutory Reports and Certificates of Service
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not respondent violated Sections 5, 55, and 58 of Republic Act No. 296 and DOJ Circular No. 10 by failing to submit case reports and Certificates of Service. **NO.** Statutory reporting duties and ninety-day clearance certificates apply exclusively to judges whose salas are physically organized and functioning.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Sensible Statutory Construction: Sections 5, 55, and 58 of the Judiciary Act, as well as DOJ Circular No. 10, clearly contemplate judges who are actually conducting court sessions, holding hearings, and taking cases under submission.
 Absurdity of Literal Compliance: A judge cannot be compelled to certify that cases submitted for decision for 90 days have been decided, or record hours of daily sessions, when no courtroom exists, no docket has been opened, and no cases have been submitted. The law does not mandate impossibilities.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Admittedly respondent has not prepared and submitted any of the reports of accomplishments and status of cases in his sala which are usually required of judges under existing laws as well as the corresponding circulars of the Department of Justice. The reason is simple. He has not yet started performing any judicial functions. None of those laws and circulars apply to him for all of them contemplate judges who are actually holding trials and hearings and making decisions..."
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** The statutory 90-day certification and session-reporting requirements exist to prevent trial backlogs. It makes no sense to punish a judge for failing to certify that he decided pending cases when his courtroom did not even physically exist yet.
Issue 3: Legality of Detailing Judges to Non-Judicial Administrative Work
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not detailing judges to perform non-judicial work in the Department of Justice violates the constitutional principle of separation of powers. **YES.** While respondent is exculpated due to established executive practice, the Supreme Court unequivocally condemned the practice as an impermissible encroachment that erodes the constitutional independence of the judiciary and must be discontinued.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Paramountcy of Separation of Powers: The constitutional tripartite division of authority and system of checks and balances are designed to protect individual liberty and the rule of law. These principles cannot be bypassed for passing administrative convenience or well-intentioned collaboration.
 Impermissible Executive Oversight: A judge occupies a constitutional office dedicated solely to adjudication. Allowing an active judge to assist an executive department head—where the judge's actions or recommendations are subject to executive review, approval, or reversal—subordinates the judicial office to the executive.
 Protection from Subordinate Relationships: The line dividing judicial adjudication from executive administration must be jealously guarded. No member of the bench may be placed in a subordinate posture where his official output is subject to administrative alteration by any authority other than an appellate court (the Court of Appeals or Supreme Court).
 Mandate of Discontinuation: The Court issued an express directive that the long-standing practice of assigning trial judges to the Department of Justice must cease.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The line between what a judge may do and what he may not do in collaborating or working with other offices or officers under the other great departments of the government must always be kept clear and jealously observed, lest the principle of separation of powers on which our government rests by mandate of the people thru the Constitution be gradually eroded by practices purportedly motivated by good intentions in the interest of the public service... It is thus of grave importance to the judiciary under our present constitutional scheme of government that no judge of even the lowest court in this Republic should place himself in a position where his actuations on matters submitted to him for action or resolution would be subject to review and prior approval and, worst still, reversal, before they can have legal effect, by any authority other than the Court of Appeals or this Supreme Court..."
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** Judges are independent adjudicators whose rulings can only be reviewed by higher appellate courts. Detailing a judge to an executive agency like the DOJ turns him into an executive subordinate subject to an administrative cabinet secretary, which violates separation of powers and undermines public trust in an independent bench.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → h. Non-judicial Work (Applied Lens: Constitutional & Political Law).
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
Under the doctrine of Separation of Powers governing the Judicial Department, any assignment or detail of a sitting judge to another branch is constitutionally prohibited if:
1.  **Non-Judicial Nature of Assignment:** The work entails executive, legislative, or administrative duties rather than adjudication (**Present:** Assisting the Secretary of Justice in administrative duties).
2.  **Impairment of Independence / Subordination:** The judge's official outputs or resolutions are subjected to executive approval, modification, or reversal (**Present:** The judge becomes an administrative assistant whose work is subject to review by the Secretary of Justice).
3.  **Absence of Appellate Character:** The reviewing authority is an executive official rather than a higher appellate tribunal (**Present:** Review by a Cabinet Secretary rather than the Court of Appeals or the Supreme Court).
**Application to Case:** Although the assignment violated these constitutional tenets, respondent was not penalized because he acted in good faith pursuant to a long-tolerated statutory and executive practice; however, the Court prohibited the practice prospectively.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Separation of powers (tripartite division of powers into coordinate and co-equal branches).
 Non-judicial functions / Non-judicial duties (tasks not incidental or ancillary to adjudication).
 Subordinate to executive review (impermissible condition where a judge's findings are subject to administrative alteration).
 Judicial independence (the requirement that courts remain free from executive influence in fact and in appearance).
**Constitutional & Political Law Lens Mechanics:**
 State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation: The Executive's statutory power of administrative supervision over inferior courts (under Section 83 of the 1917 Revised Administrative Code) versus the constitutional principle of Separation of Powers and Judicial Independence.
 Doctrinal Test Applied: The structural integrity test of Separation of Powers—whether an inter-branch assignment subordinates a judicial officer to executive control or dilutes the core judicial function of independent decision-making.
 Justiciability Audit: An administrative disciplinary complaint against an incumbent judicial officer over which the Supreme Court exercised direct disciplinary jurisdiction.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**Garcia v. Macaraig** is the seminal landmark under "Non-judicial Work" because it established that active trial judges cannot be detailed to executive departments like the DOJ. The Court held that while respondent could not be held administratively liable for dishonesty—since his sala was physically unequipped through no fault of his own and he acted in good faith under long-standing custom—the practice of detailing judges to executive agencies directly violates separation of powers. A judge must never be placed in a position where his official work is subordinate to, or subject to reversal by, an executive official rather than an appellate court.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Fernando, J., Concurring (joined by Makasiar, J.):**
 Repugnancy to Separation of Powers:** Affirms that detailing judges to executive posts fundamentally contradicts the tripartite system designed to secure human liberty. Citing Justice Cardozo in **In re Richardson** and Justice J.B.L. Reyes in **Noblejas v. Teehankee, he emphasizes that a judge’s essence is to decide; the judiciary cannot be charged with administrative functions unless strictly incidental to judicial duties.
 Unconstitutionality of Executive Oversight: Challenges the statutory scheme (Section 83, Revised Administrative Code of 1917) granting the Secretary of Justice executive supervision over inferior courts. He argues this supervisory power is of doubtful constitutionality because it forces judges to court the goodwill of an executive cabinet secretary, thereby compromising actual and perceived judicial independence. He expressly expresses hope that the upcoming 1971 Constitutional Convention will place court administration exclusively under the Supreme Court (which was later adopted in the 1973 and 1987 Constitutions).
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the herein administrative complaint is hereby dismissed. Let a copy of this resolution be furnished the Secretary of Justice."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Respondent Catalino Macaraig, Jr. completely prevailed; the administrative charges for dishonesty, incompetence, and statutory non-compliance were dismissed, but the Supreme Court formally notified the Department of Justice that the practice of detailing judges to executive agencies must immediately end.
