### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Office of the Court Administrator v. Atillo** (or **OCA v. Judge Atillo, Jr.**)
**Full Official Caption:** Office of the Court Administrator, Complainant, vs. Hon. Romeo M. Atillo, Jr., Executive Judge and Presiding Judge, Regional Trial Court, Branch 31, Agoo, La Union, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** A.M. No. RTJ-21-018 (Formerly A.M. No. 20-07-109-RTC); September 29, 2021; 911 Phil. 217; 120 O.G. No. 26, 6228 (June 24, 2024); Second Division; Ponente: Inting, **J.**; Voting Breakdown: Perlas-Bernabe, **S.A.J.** (Chairperson), Hernando, J. Lopez, and Dimaampao, **JJ.**, concur. No separate opinions filed.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Office of the Court Administrator (OCA):** Investigating, disciplinary, and administrative arm of the Supreme Court of the Philippines acting as the administrative complainant.
**Hon. Romeo M. Atillo, Jr.:** Respondent; Executive Judge and Presiding Judge of Branch 31, Regional Trial Court (RTC), Agoo, La Union.
**Anthony Yabes:** Respondent's Facebook connection/friend permitted to share content on Respondent's Facebook account profile page.
**Anonymous Sender:** The unidentified individual who obtained printed screenshots of Respondent's Facebook profile/cover photos and transmitted them to the OCA.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Administrative disciplinary proceeding initiated **motu proprio** by the OCA upon receiving printed social media screenshots, culminating in the OCA's Memorandum dated July 14, 2020 recommending administrative sanctions, which the Supreme Court re-docketed as a regular administrative matter pursuant to its constitutional disciplinary supervision over lower court judges under Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution and Rule 140 of the Rules of Court.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Disciplinary Power over Lower-Court Justices and Judges (1987 Const., Art. VIII, Sec. 6 & Sec. 11; Rule 140, Rules of Court).
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Fundamental Powers & Bill of Rights → Right to Privacy of Communication and Correspondence & The Exclusionary Rule (1987 Const., Art. III, Sec. 3) → Legal Ethics → New Code of Judicial Conduct (Canons 2 and 4) & OCA Circular No. 173-2017 (Proper Use of Social Media).
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article VIII, Section 6, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"The Supreme Court shall have administrative supervision over all courts and the personnel thereof."
**Article VIII, Section 11 (second sentence), 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"x x x The Supreme Court **en banc** shall have the power to discipline judges of lower courts, or order their dismissal by a vote of a majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberations on the issues in the case and voted thereon."
**Article III, Section 3, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"(1) The privacy of communication and correspondence shall be inviolable except upon lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law.
(2) **Any evidence obtained in violation of this or the preceding section shall be inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding.**"
**New Code of Judicial Conduct for the Philippine Judiciary (A.M. No. 03-05-01-SC), Canon 4:**
"SECTION 1. Judges shall avoid impropriety and the appearance of impropriety in all of their activities.
SECTION 2. As a subject of constant public scrutiny, judges must accept personal restrictions that might be viewed as burdensome by the ordinary citizen and should do so freely and willingly. In particular, judges shall conduct themselves in a way that is consistent with the dignity of the judicial office.
x x x x
SECTION 6. Judges, like any other citizen, are entitled to freedom of expression, belief, association and assembly, but in exercising such rights, they shall always conduct themselves in such a manner as to preserve the dignity of the judicial office and the impartiality and independence of the Judiciary."
**Factual Trigger:** The OCA received physical printouts of Facebook screenshots showing Judge Romeo M. Atillo, Jr. appearing half-dressed and displaying his tattooed upper torso and body, utilized as "profile pictures" and "cover photos" alongside official judicial regalia (robe and court seal), triggering an inquiry into whether his public social media presence violated the New Code of Judicial Conduct and OCA Circular No. 173-2017.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**August 11, 2019:** Respondent Judge Atillo, Jr.'s Facebook account was allegedly hacked, during which its privacy settings were purportedly switched without his authorization from "private" (or "friends only") to "public."
**Prior to January 28, 2020:** The OCA received printed copies of photographs originating from Respondent's Facebook account. The images depicted Respondent half-dressed, exposing tattoos covering his upper torso, posted as "profile pictures" and "cover photos" alongside pictures of him wearing his judicial robe with the official Court seal in the background.
**January 28, 2020:** The OCA issued a letter directing Respondent to submit his comment regarding the uploaded photographs, highlighting possible violations of the New Code of Judicial Conduct and OCA Circular No. 173-2017 (**Proper Use of Social Media**).
**February 11, 2020:** Respondent submitted his Comment. He admitted owning the account and the photos, but claimed his account had been hacked on August 11, 2019, causing privacy settings to flip to public. He asserted the images were intended solely for his personal viewing pleasure and for his Facebook friends. Furthermore, he raised an exclusionary objection, arguing that the photographs were obtained in breach of his constitutional right to privacy of communication and correspondence under Article III, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution and thus inadmissible.
**July 14, 2020:** The OCA released its Memorandum finding Respondent guilty of violating Sections 1 and 2, Canon 4 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct, OCA Circular No. 173-2017, and Conduct Unbecoming of a Judge. The OCA observed that juxtaposing a judge's robed image and court seal with half-naked, tattooed torso photographs creates skepticism among litigants and laypersons regarding judicial fitness. The OCA recommended re-docketing the complaint as a regular administrative matter, fining Respondent P15,000.00, and issuing a reprimand with a stern warning.
**September 29, 2021:** The Supreme Court Second Division promulgated its Decision adopting the OCA’s factual and administrative findings of guilt for Conduct Unbecoming of a Judge, but modifying the sanction to an admonition with a stern warning.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Complainant's Arguments (Office of the Court Administrator)
**Main Thesis:** Respondent's act of displaying public social media photographs showing his half-naked, tattooed body alongside his robed judicial persona impairs the dignity of the judicial office, fosters negative public skepticism, and breaches the standards of judicial propriety.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Breach of Canons and Circular: Respondent violated Sections 1 and 2, Canon 4 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct and OCA Circular No. 173-2017 by failing to exercise caution and circumspection in public social media postings.
 Harm to Judicial Image: While tattoos on an ordinary person are harmless, displaying a half-naked, tattooed torso on a profile page that simultaneously identifies the user as an RTC judge with a robed portrait and court seal creates a disreputable impression that damages public trust and litigant perceptions.
 Lack of Social Media Care: Had Respondent been circumspect and properly monitored his account and its access, the photographs would not have leaked to the general public.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Hon. Romeo M. Atillo, Jr.)
**Main Thesis:** Respondent did not deliberately broadcast the photographs to the public; the images were private, were leaked via account hacking, and are inadmissible under the constitutional exclusionary rule.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Hacking & Lack of Intent: Respondent's Facebook account was hacked on August 11, 2019, switching his privacy settings from "friends" to "public" without his knowledge or consent.
 Private Viewing Only: The images showing his tattoos were strictly intended for his personal viewing pleasure and for his direct Facebook friends, never for public consumption.
 Exclusionary Rule / Unlawful Search: The printed photographs submitted to the OCA were obtained illegally from his compromised Facebook account, directly violating his constitutional right to privacy of communication and correspondence under Section 3, Article III of the 1987 Constitution, rendering them strictly inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the printed Facebook photographs are inadmissible in an administrative disciplinary proceeding under the exclusionary rule of Section 3(2), Article III of the 1987 Constitution.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Respondent Judge incurred administrative liability under the Supreme Court's disciplinary power for posting half-dressed photographs showing his tattooed torso on his Facebook account, in violation of the New Code of Judicial Conduct and OCA Circular No. 173-2017.
3. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the penalty of a P15,000.00 fine and reprimand recommended by the OCA is the appropriate sanction under Rule 140 of the Rules of Court.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Admissibility of Facebook Pictures Under the Constitutional Exclusionary Rule
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the Facebook photographs are inadmissible under the exclusionary rule of Section 3(2), Article III of the Constitution. **NO.** The constitutional exclusionary rule operates solely as a restraint against state action and does not apply to evidence procured by private individuals without governmental involvement.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 State Action Requirement:** Drawing from established constitutional doctrine (**People v. Marti**, **Miguel v. People), the exclusionary rule under Section 3(2), Article III of the Constitution serves strictly as a protection against erring state officers who disregard constitutional procedures in effecting searches and seizures.
 Private Acts Not Covered: The Bill of Rights governs relationships between the individual and the State; it does not protect against private intrusions unless the private person acted under the color of a state-related function or as an agent of the government.
 Absence of State Participation: The record demonstrates that an anonymous private individual retrieved the images from Respondent's account and furnished them to the OCA. The State was in no way involved in accessing, retrieving, or printing the pictures.
 No Reasonable Expectation of Privacy on Facebook:** Even setting aside state action, under **Vivares v. St. Theresa's College, configuring an account to "Friends" provides no legal guarantee of privacy. A user's Facebook friends can tag, share, or redistribute content across expanding digital networks. Respondent admitted having a sizeable number of Facebook friends and allowed another individual (Anthony Yabes) to share posts on his profile. Thus, the uploaded content could not be deemed legally private.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"It is elementary that the exclusionary rule under Section 3(2), Article III of the Constitution only applies as a restraint against the State and cannot be extended to acts committed by private individuals, save for instances where such individuals are shown to have acted under the color of a state-related function. Clearly, the exclusionary rule finds no application in the case because the State was in no way involved in the retrieval of the subject pictures from Judge Atillo, Jr.'s Facebook account."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The exclusionary rule exists to stop abusive government searches, not private snooping. Because the government and the police had no hand in taking the screenshots from Judge Atillo's Facebook page, the photos can be used as evidence against him. Furthermore, once you share pictures on Facebook—even with privacy set to "Friends"—you lose any reasonable expectation of privacy because those friends can easily share and download your photos.
Issue 2: Administrative Liability for Breach of Judicial Propriety via Social Media Posts
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not Respondent Judge is administratively liable for Conduct Unbecoming of a Judge under the New Code of Judicial Conduct and OCA Circular No. 173-2017. **YES.** By posting half-dressed photographs displaying his tattooed upper torso on a social media profile identifying him as a judge, Respondent compromised the dignity of the bench and breached judicial propriety.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Judicial Standards of Conduct: Under Canons 2 and 4 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct, judges are held to exacting standards of integrity and propriety. A judge must avoid not merely actual impropriety, but the very appearance of impropriety in all activities, accepting personal restrictions that an ordinary citizen might consider burdensome.
 Extension to Cyberspace:** Under **Lorenzana v. Judge Austria, judges do not shed their judicial status when joining social networks. They carry their ethical responsibilities into cyberspace. Personal posts contribute directly to the public's perception of the judge and the entire Judiciary.
 Clarification Regarding Tattoos:** The Court explicitly held that having tattoos is a personal choice and does not constitute impropriety **per se. Rather, the administrative infraction stems strictly from the act of posting half-dressed images online in an accessible forum where the public and litigants could view them alongside his robed image and judicial title.
 Breach of OCA Circular No. 173-2017: The circular requires judicial personnel to be circumspect and cautious. By uploading highly personal, exposed photos visible to regular followers and acquaintances, Respondent exposed the bench to public scrutiny and ridicule, culminating in an anonymous report to the OCA.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The Court clarifies that the impropriety in this case relates solely on Judge Atillo, Jr.'s act of posting the subject pictures on social media, and it has absolutely nothing to do with his choice to have tattoos on his body. Simply put, by posting the pictures on Facebook, Judge Atillo, Jr. placed himself in a situation where he, and the status he holds as a sitting judge, became the object of the public's criticism and ridicule."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Court made it clear that having tattoos is perfectly fine, but posting shirtless photos of them on Facebook while presenting oneself as a sitting judge is not. Judges never stop being judges when they go online, and Judge Atillo violated judicial propriety by failing to maintain the dignity and decorum demanded by the bench, exposing his judicial office to public ridicule.
Issue 3: Proper Penalty Under Rule 140 of the Rules of Court
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the OCA's recommended sanction of a P15,000.00 fine and reprimand is proper. **NO.** Under amended Rule 140, Conduct Unbecoming of a Judge is classified as a light offense, and because this was Respondent's first administrative offense, the appropriate penalty is an admonition with a stern warning.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Offense Classification: Under Section 24, in relation to Section 25(C), of Rule 140 of the Rules of Court (as amended by A.M. No. 18-01-05-SC and A.M. No. 21-03-17-SC), Conduct Unbecoming of a Judge is a light charge.
 Prescribed Penalties: A light offense is punishable by: (a) a fine not less than P1,000.00 but not exceeding P35,000.00; (b) censure; (c) reprimand; or (d) admonition with warning.
 Mitigation / First Offense: Considering that this was Respondent's first administrative infraction, the Court reduced the OCA's recommendation from a fine and reprimand to an admonition, accompanied by a stern warning that repeating similar conduct would result in severe sanctions.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The Court finds that Judge Atillo, Jr.'s complained act constitutes Conduct Unbecoming of a Judge, which, under Section 24, in relation to Section 25(C), of Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 18-01-05-SC and A.M. No. 21-03-17-SC, is a light offense that is punishable by any of the following: (a) a fine of not less than P1,000.00 but not exceeding P35,000.00, and/or; (b) censure; (c) reprimand; or (d) admonition with warning. After a careful consideration of the peculiar circumstances of this case, the Court deems it proper to impose against Judge Atillo, Jr. the penalty of an admonition as this is his first offense."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Because Conduct Unbecoming of a Judge is classified as a light offense under Rule 140 and this was Judge Atillo's first time committing an administrative infraction, the Supreme Court showed leniency by imposing an admonition with a stern warning rather than fining or reprimanding him.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Assigned Syllabus Topic: iii. Disciplinary Power over Lower-court Justices and Judges | Applied Lens: Constitutional & Political Law
**Constitutional Mechanics (State Power vs. Bill of Rights Defense):**
 Governmental Power Exercised: The Supreme Court's constitutional administrative and disciplinary supervision over lower court judges and court personnel pursuant to Article VIII, Sections 6 and 11 of the 1987 Constitution, implemented via Rule 140 of the Rules of Court.
 Constitutional Limitation Invoked: Respondent invoked the Bill of Rights—specifically the Right to Privacy of Communication and Correspondence and its accompanying Exclusionary Rule (1987 Const., Art. III, Sec. 3(1) & 3(2))—in an attempt to suppress evidence obtained from his Facebook account.
 Judicial Scrutiny / Constitutional Resolution: The Supreme Court rejected the Bill of Rights defense by applying the **State Action Doctrine** (**People v. Marti**). The Bill of Rights restricts sovereign power, not private conduct. Because the State did not participate in the acquisition of the Facebook screenshots, Section 3(2) could not be triggered. Furthermore, the Court reaffirmed **Vivares v. St. Theresa's College**: internet users who post on social media lose an objective expectation of privacy once data is shared across digital networks.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Judicial Propriety in Cyberspace):**
1.  **Status as a Judicial Officer:** Proven. Respondent is the Presiding Judge of Branch 31, RTC, Agoo, La Union.
2.  **Conduct Subject to Public View:** Proven. Respondent uploaded half-dressed photos as his profile and cover pictures on a Facebook account featuring a sizeable friend network, allowed third-party sharing (via Anthony Yabes), and had his robed portrait on display.
3.  **Compromise of Judicial Dignity / Appearance of Impropriety:** Proven. The juxtaposition of a judge's official station with semi-nude, tattooed pictures creates skepticism in litigants and members of the public regarding the dignity and appropriateness of the bench.
4.  **Absence of Inherent Illegality of Body Art:** Proven. The Court explicitly isolated the act: tattoos are legally permissible personal choices; the administrative violation is strictly the **indiscreet publication and public presentation** of the half-dressed body on social media by a sitting judge.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Exclusionary rule as a restraint against the State
 Under the color of a state-related function
 Judges do not shed off their status as judges in cyberspace
 Appearance of impropriety
 Conduct Unbecoming of a Judge
 Light offense under Rule 140
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
Under its constitutional disciplinary power over lower court judges (Art. VIII, Sec. 6 & 11), the Supreme Court disciplined Judge Atillo for Conduct Unbecoming of a Judge after he uploaded public Facebook photos showing his half-naked, tattooed upper body juxtaposed with his robed official photos. The Court rejected his defense under the constitutional exclusionary rule (Art. III, Sec. 3), holding that the exclusionary rule applies exclusively against state action, not private screenshotting, and reaffirmed that judges carry their ethical duties of propriety and decorum into cyberspace (**Lorenzana**). Because having body tattoos is not an offense in itself, the infraction lay solely in the indiscreet public posting, warranting an admonition under Rule 140 for a first offense.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:** No separate opinions filed. (All participating members concurred unanimously).
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"**WHEREFORE**, the Court resolves as follows:
1) The Letter dated January 28, 2020 of the Office of the Court Administrator is **RE-DOCKETED** as a regular administrative matter;
2) Respondent Judge Romeo M. Atillo, Jr. is found **GUILTY** of Conduct Unbecoming of a Judge and is hereby **ADMONISHED** to be more circumspect in his professional and personal dealings in social media and **STERNLY WARNED** that a repetition of the same or similar acts shall be dealt with more severely; and
3) The Comment dated February 11, 2020 submitted by Respondent Judge Romeo M. Atillo, Jr. is **NOTED**.
**SO ORDERED.**"
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court adopted the OCA's finding that Judge Atillo breached judicial propriety by posting shirtless photos on Facebook, but modified the penalty from a P15,000.00 fine and reprimand down to an admonition with a stern warning because this was his first administrative offense. Judge Atillo was ordered to exercise greater circumspection in his social media use going forward.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Fider-Reyes v. Everglory Metal Trading Corporation**
**Full Official Caption:** Hon. Maria Amifaith S. Fider-Reyes, The Presiding Judge of Regional Trial Court, City of San Fernando, Pampanga, Branch 42, Petitioner, vs. Everglory Metal Trading Corporation, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 238709 | October 6, 2021 | 912 Phil. 755 | Third Division | Ponente: Carandang, **J.** | Voting Breakdown: Leonen (**Chairperson**), Rosario, and Dimaampao, **JJ.**, concur; Zalameda, **J.**, with a Separate Concurring Opinion.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Hon. Maria Amifaith S. Fider-Reyes:** Petitioner; Presiding Judge of the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of the City of San Fernando, Pampanga, Branch 42, who presided over the underlying patent infringement case and was cited for indirect contempt by the appellate court.
**Everglory Metal Trading Corporation (Everglory):** Respondent; defendant in the patent infringement case who initiated the indirect contempt petition against Judge Fider-Reyes before the Court of Appeals.
**Colorsteel Systems Corporation (Colorsteel) & Jose Rey S. Batomalaque:** Plaintiffs in the underlying patent infringement case (IPR Civil Case No. 005) before Judge Fider-Reyes.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court assailing the Decision dated August 23, 2017 and Resolution dated April 12, 2018 of the Court of Appeals (CA) in CA-G.R. SP No. 138756, which found petitioner Judge Fider-Reyes guilty of Indirect Contempt of Court and penalized her with a fine of P10,000.00.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Exclusive Disciplinary Power of the Supreme Court over Lower-Court Justices and Judges (Article VIII, Section 11 vs. Rule 71 Inherent Contempt Power)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Special Civil Actions → Rule 71 (Indirect Contempt) in Relation to Rule 65, Section 7 (Effect of Pendency of **Certiorari** & Judicial Courtesy)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional & Statutory Provisions:**
**Article VIII, Section 6, 1987 Constitution:**
"The Supreme Court shall have administrative supervision over all courts and the personnel thereof."
**Article VIII, Section 11, 1987 Constitution:**
"The members of the Supreme Court and judges of the lower courts shall hold office during good behavior until they reach the age of seventy years or become incapacitated to discharge the duties of their office. **The Supreme Court en banc shall have the power to discipline judges of lower courts, or order their dismissal** by a vote of a majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberations on the issues in the case and voted thereon."
**Rule 71, Section 3(b), Rules of Court:**
"Section 3. **Indirect contempt to be punished after charge and hearing.** — After a charge in writing has been filed, and an opportunity given to the respondent to comment thereon within such period as may be fixed by the court and to be heard by himself or counsel, a person guilty of any of the following acts may be punished for indirect contempt:
...
(b) **Disobedience of or resistance to a lawful writ, process, order, or judgment of a court**, including the act of a person who, after being dispossessed or ejected from any real property by the judgment or process of any court of competent jurisdiction, enters or attempts or induces another to enter into or upon such real property, for the purpose of executing acts of ownership or possession, or in any manner disturbs the possession given to the person adjudged to be entitled thereto[.]"
**Factual Trigger:** After a 60-day CA temporary restraining order expired without an injunctive writ being issued, trial judge Maria Amifaith S. Fider-Reyes proceeded with an intellectual property infringement case and rendered a decision on the merits, despite a pending, non-final CA decision ordering her to admit the defendant's expunged pleadings and receive its evidence. Litigant Everglory then filed an indirect contempt petition directly with the Court of Appeals against the sitting trial judge, and the CA found the judge guilty and fined her P10,000.00.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**August 16, 2013:** Colorsteel and its president Batomalaque filed a complaint for patent infringement and damages with an application for preliminary injunction against Everglory, docketed as IPR Civil Case No. 005, which was raffled to the RTC of San Fernando, Pampanga, Branch 42, presided over by petitioner Judge Fider-Reyes.
**September–October 2013:** Everglory filed two successive motions for extension of time to file its responsive pleading, citing the need for technical analysis and legal research.
**October 8, 2013:** Everglory filed its Answer with Ground for the Outright Dismissal of the Complaint and with Compulsory Counterclaim.
**October 25, 2013:** During a scheduled preliminary injunction hearing, Judge Fider-Reyes issued an open-court verbal order expunging all motions and pleadings filed by Everglory from the record, declared the injunction hearing terminated, and submitted the principal patent infringement case for decision.
**December 4, 2013:** Judge Fider-Reyes issued a Resolution denying Everglory’s Motion for Reconsideration.
**February 11, 2014:** Everglory filed a Petition for **Certiorari** with an application for a TRO/Preliminary Injunction before the CA, docketed as CA-G.R. SP No. 133942, assailing the RTC Orders of October 25, 2013 and December 4, 2013.
**April 22, 2014:** The CA issued a 60-day Temporary Restraining Order (TRO) enjoining Judge Fider-Reyes from conducting further proceedings in IPR Civil Case No. 005. Judge Fider-Reyes suspended proceedings upon receipt of the TRO.
**June 22, 2014:** The CA's 60-day TRO expired without any writ of preliminary injunction being issued.
**June 25, 2014:** The CA rendered a Decision in CA-G.R. SP No. 133942 granting Everglory's petition, finding grave abuse of discretion by Judge Fider-Reyes, setting aside the expunction orders, and directing the RTC to hear Everglory's evidence. Colorsteel and Batomalaque timely filed a Motion for Reconsideration before the CA.
**November 19, 2014:** In the absence of an injunctive writ and noting the expiration of the TRO, Judge Fider-Reyes issued an Order deeming the preliminary injunction application and the main infringement case submitted for decision.
**November 20, 2014:** The CA denied Colorsteel and Batomalaque's Motion for Reconsideration in CA-G.R. SP No. 133942, prompting them to appeal to the Supreme Court via Rule 45 (docketed as G.R. No. 215921).
**December 3, 2014:** Judge Fider-Reyes rendered a Decision on the merits in IPR Civil Case No. 005 in favor of Colorsteel and Batomalaque.
**December 15, 2014:** Everglory filed a Petition for **Certiorari** before the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 138410) challenging the RTC's refusal to voluntarily inhibit. Everglory also appealed the December 3, 2014 RTC Decision under Rule 43 (CA-G.R. SP No. 138582).
**January 15, 2015:** Everglory filed a Petition for Indirect Contempt of Court directly before the CA against Judge Fider-Reyes (docketed under CA-G.R. SP No. 133942, later re-docketed as CA-G.R. SP No. 138756), alleging that the judge contumaciously defied the CA’s June 25, 2014 Decision by proceeding with the main case.
**March 16, 2015:** The Supreme Court denied Colorsteel’s Petition for Review in G.R. No. 215921, which became final with Entry of Judgment directed on September 2, 2015 (the CA June 25, 2014 Decision formally attaining finality and executory status on January 25, 2016).
**September 10, 2015:** The CA consolidated CA-G.R. SP Nos. 138410 and 138582, annulled Judge Fider-Reyes's December 3, 2014 Decision and non-inhibition orders, and ordered the infringement case remanded and re-raffled to another branch.
**March 2, 2016:** Upon learning that the CA June 25, 2014 Decision had attained finality, Judge Fider-Reyes issued an **Order Ad Cautelam** undoing the default effects against Everglory and allowing it to participate, before the case was re-raffled to another judge.
**August 23, 2017:** The CA promulgated its Decision in CA-G.R. SP No. 138756 finding Judge Fider-Reyes guilty of Indirect Contempt of Court and imposing a fine of P10,000.00, ruling that she breached judicial courtesy and defied higher court authority.
**April 12, 2018:** The CA denied Judge Fider-Reyes's Motion for Reconsideration.
**May 2018:** Petitioner Judge Fider-Reyes filed the instant Petition for Review on **Certiorari** before the Supreme Court.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Hon. Maria Amifaith S. Fider-Reyes)
**Main Thesis:** The Court of Appeals lacked jurisdiction to entertain an indirect contempt petition aimed at disciplining a sitting trial judge for judicial acts, and petitioner did not willfully defy any final and executory order.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Lack of Jurisdiction over Disciplinary Sanctions: Under the Constitution, the Supreme Court possesses the exclusive authority to discipline lower court judges. The CA has no power to discipline judges through contempt citations.
 No Defiance of Final Judgment: The CA Decision dated June 25, 2014 was not yet final and executory when she decided the case on December 3, 2014, as it was subject to a timely motion for reconsideration and subsequent Rule 45 review before the Supreme Court.
 Legal Duty under Rule 65, Section 7:** Section 7, Rule 65 of the Rules of Court dictates that the pendency of a **certiorari petition does not stay proceedings in the absence of an injunctive writ; once the 60-day TRO lapsed without an injunction, she had the statutory obligation to proceed.
 Absence of Malice or Contemptuous Intent:** Petitioner acted in good faith, observed the TRO while effective, and immediately issued an **Order Ad Cautelam to comply as soon as the CA decision became final.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Everglory Metal Trading Corporation)
**Main Thesis:** The CA possesses the inherent contempt power to punish open defiance of its directives, and Judge Fider-Reyes's conduct constituted deliberate insubordination warranting an indirect contempt citation.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Immediately Executory Nature:** The CA Decision of June 25, 2014, having been rendered in an original **certiorari proceeding, was immediately executory upon the trial court.
 Inherent Contempt Power of the CA: The CA has the inherent judicial authority to enforce its own processes, maintain respect for its mandates, and cite lower court judges in indirect contempt under Rule 71.
 Willful Defiance & Breach of Judicial Courtesy: The judge received the CA Decision ordering her to receive Everglory's evidence on July 9, 2014. Proceeding to submit the case and render judgment on the merits on December 3, 2014 was an intentional, contumacious flouting of appellate authority and a violation of the precept of judicial courtesy.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Court of Appeals has the jurisdiction and authority to entertain an indirect contempt petition against a lower-court judge and discipline her for acts performed in her judicial capacity, in light of the Supreme Court's exclusive constitutional authority to discipline judges.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not petitioner Judge Fider-Reyes is guilty of indirect contempt of court for continuing with the proceedings and deciding the patent infringement case on the merits following the expiration of the appellate court's 60-day temporary restraining order.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: CA's Jurisdiction to Cite a Lower Court Judge in Contempt vs. SC Exclusive Disciplinary Power
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Can the Court of Appeals cite a lower-court judge in indirect contempt and impose a disciplinary fine for acts arising from judicial duties? **NO.** Under Section 11, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution, the Supreme Court has the exclusive power to discipline lower court judges; the Court of Appeals lacks authority to sanction judges through contempt proceedings, which open the floodgates to litigant harassment.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Constitutional Allocation of Disciplinary Power:** Under Section 11, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution, the Supreme Court **en banc exercises the exclusive power and authority to discipline judges of lower courts or order their dismissal. Section 6, Article VIII vests administrative supervision over all courts exclusively in the Supreme Court.
 Curtailment of Lower Courts' Contempt Jurisdiction over Judges: In lodging the power to discipline judges of lower courts exclusively with the Supreme Court (as reiterated in A.M. No. 10-4-20-SC and A.M. No. 18-01-05-SC), the Constitution simultaneously curtailed the inherent contempt power of the Court of Appeals. The CA has no authority to discipline judges or court personnel of lower courts; at most, the CA can only recommend disciplinary action to the Supreme Court.
 Personnel Administrator vs. Adjudicative Function: When the Supreme Court acts on complaints against judges, it acts as a personnel administrator imposing discipline, not as a court resolving justiciable controversies. Litigants cannot disguise an administrative grievance against a judge's judicial rulings as an indirect contempt petition before the CA.
 Public Policy Against Harassment Suits: Permitting litigants to file indirect contempt cases against judges for alleged failure to implement appellate orders would open the floodgates to attacks on judicial discretion, generate vexatious harassment suits, and render the judicial office untenable. A judge's erroneous legal interpretation in good faith does not incur administrative sanction.
 Exclusivity of Remedies:** If an appellate court's order is allegedly disobeyed in bad faith, the proper remedies are judicial review (**certiorari or appeal) or a direct administrative/disciplinary proceeding lodged exclusively with the Supreme Court.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"In lodging the power to discipline judges of lower courts exclusively with the Court, it curtailed in the same breath the inherent power of the CA to punish for contempt. The CA have no authority to discipline judges or even the court personnel of lower courts. At most, the CA can only recommend to the Court the necessary disciplinary action."

"Evidently, the CA overstepped the bounds of its authority when it took cognizance of the case and thereafter imposed a fine of P10,000.00 against petitioner."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Supreme Court alone has the constitutional power to discipline lower court judges. While appellate courts generally possess inherent contempt powers, they cannot use Rule 71 indirect contempt petitions to punish or fine trial judges for their judicial actions. If a litigant believes a judge maliciously disobeyed an appellate directive, the litigant cannot ask the Court of Appeals to hold the judge in contempt; the litigant must file an administrative complaint before the Supreme Court.
Issue 2: Liability for Indirect Contempt under Rule 65 and Principle of Judicial Courtesy
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did petitioner Judge Fider-Reyes commit indirect contempt by proceeding with the main case after the 60-day TRO expired? **NO.** A judgment in a **certiorari** case is not immediately executory, and under Section 7, Rule 65, the lower court is legally mandated to proceed absent an injunctive writ; furthermore, judicial courtesy did not apply because proceeding did not moot the CA petition.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Non-Finality of CA Judgment: The CA Decision dated June 25, 2014 was not immediately executory. It was challenged via a timely Motion for Reconsideration and elevated under Rule 45 to the Supreme Court (G.R. No. 215921). It did not achieve final and executory status until January 25, 2016—over a year after Judge Fider-Reyes rendered her December 3, 2014 judgment.
 Mandate of Rule 65, Section 7:** Under Section 7, Rule 65 of the Rules of Court, the mere pendency of a **certiorari petition does not stay proceedings in the court of origin without a temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction. Once the CA's 60-day TRO lapsed on June 22, 2014 without a writ of preliminary injunction being issued, there was no legal obstacle preventing the judge from proceeding.
 Inapplicability of Judicial Courtesy:** Judicial courtesy is an exception requiring the suspension of lower-court proceedings only if there is a strong probability that issues before the higher court would be rendered moot. Moving forward with the patent infringement case did not moot the CA **certiorari case.
 Absence of Contumacious Intent:** Petitioner demonstrated deference by suspending proceedings throughout the 60-day TRO. She issued an **Order Ad Cautelam to comply with the appellate ruling once it became final. Her actions reflected good-faith performance of duty, completely devoid of malice, bad faith, or contumacious defiance.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The earlier quoted Section 7 of Rule 65 provides the general rule that the mere pendency of a special civil action for Certiorari commenced in relation to a case pending before a lower court or court of origin does not stay the proceedings therein in the absence of a writ of preliminary injunction or temporary restraining order."

"From the foregoing, the Court finds that petitioner acted in accordance with her legal duty to proceed with the summary proceedings in the infringement case, in due deference and regard to the existing judgments, orders and issuances of the CA, and without any iota of malice or bad faith to defy them."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** An appellate court's decision in a **certiorari** case does not become executory right away if an MR or appeal is pending. Because the CA's 60-day TRO had already expired and no preliminary injunction was granted, Rule 65 commanded the trial judge to move forward. The judge’s failure to observe judicial courtesy did not constitute indirect contempt because proceeding did not moot the issues, and she acted in good faith without any intent to defy the higher court.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Assigned Syllabus Topic: iii. Disciplinary Power over Lower-court Justices and Judges
**Constitutional & Political Law Analytical Directives:**
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:** The Court examined the tension between the **inherent judicial power of appellate courts to punish for contempt** (Rule 71) and the **exclusive constitutional monopoly of the Supreme Court to discipline lower court judges** (Article VIII, Sections 6 and 11, 1987 Constitution). The Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional grant of exclusive disciplinary authority to the SC acts as an absolute structural limitation that curtails the CA's inherent contempt power whenever invoked against lower court judges for their judicial actions.
**Level of Scrutiny / Doctrinal Mechanism:** Structural-Jurisdictional Exclusivity. The Court enforced a strict jurisdictional demarcation: when a punitive sanction (such as a fine) is sought against a judge for acts performed in office, the proceeding is disciplinary in substance regardless of its label. Appellate courts are constitutionally stripped of adjudicative competence to impose such sanctions, retaining only the authority to **recommend** disciplinary action to the Supreme Court.
**Justiciability & Proper Forum Audit:** Litigants cannot weaponize Rule 71 against judges as a collateral attack on judicial rulings or to enforce interlocutory obedience. The sole constitutionally recognized mechanism to test whether a judge contumaciously defied an appellate order is an administrative complaint filed directly with the Supreme Court under Rule 140, or regular appellate/certiorari review.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Contempt vs. SC Exclusive Disciplinary Power):**
1.  **Identity of the Actor:** Is the respondent a justice, judge, or personnel under the administrative supervision of the Supreme Court? (Proven: Petitioner is an active RTC Presiding Judge).
2.  **Nature and Purpose of the Proceeding:** Is the dominant relief sought punitive or regulatory of judicial fitness, rather than remedial? (Proven: Everglory sought to penalize the judge for allegedly defying the CA; the CA imposed a punitive P10,000 fine).
3.  **Constitutional Gatekeeping:** Under Article VIII, Section 11, does any tribunal other than the Supreme Court **en banc** possess authority to discipline or fine judges? (Absent: The CA lacks this power; it is exclusive to the Supreme Court).
4.  **Requisite of Contempt (Willful Disobedience):** Was there an intentional disregard of a final, executory, and unambiguous directive? (Absent: The CA decision was non-final; the TRO had expired; Rule 65, Section 7 commanded the judge to proceed).
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Exclusive power to discipline judges of lower courts (Art. VIII, Sec. 11)
 Administrative supervision over all courts (Art. VIII, Sec. 6)
 Personnel administrator vs. adjudicator of justiciable controversies
 Inherent contempt power curtailed
 Judicial courtesy (narrow exception, not a substitute for an injunctive writ)
 Preservative vs. vindictive principle of contempt
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"Under Article VIII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution, the Supreme Court possesses the exclusive power to discipline lower-court judges. In **Fider-Reyes v. Everglory**, the Court of Appeals overstepped its jurisdiction when it entertained an indirect contempt petition and fined an RTC judge for continuing with an infringement case after a 60-day TRO lapsed. The Supreme Court held that the constitutional grant of exclusive disciplinary authority to the SC strictly curtails the CA's inherent contempt power over judges. Aggrieved litigants cannot use Rule 71 indirect contempt to sanction judges; they must file an administrative complaint before the Supreme Court. Moreover, on the merits, the judge was legally bound under Section 7 of Rule 65 to proceed with the case because the CA's decision was not yet final and no injunctive writ stayed the proceedings."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Zalameda, J. (Separate Concurring Opinion):** Concurred in clearing Judge Fider-Reyes of indirect contempt, agreeing that she did not willfully disobey any order since the CA decision was not final, the TRO had expired, and she had a statutory duty under Rule 65, Section 7 to proceed. However, Justice Zalameda **diverged strongly** from the **ponencia**'s constitutional holding on jurisdiction. He argued that the Supreme Court's exclusive power to administratively discipline judges does not curtail the inherent contempt powers of the Court of Appeals or lower courts. Disciplinary proceedings (which address fitness for office under Rules 138-140) and contempt proceedings (which preserve order and dignity under Rule 71) are distinct **sui generis** remedies with different purposes that can proceed independently. Section 9, Rule 65 expressly contemplates that disobedience by a lower court to an appellate **certiorari** judgment shall be punished as contempt. He warned that the **ponencia**'s sweeping rule would dangerously immunize court personnel (like sheriffs and stenographers) and judges from necessary contempt sanctions by reviewing courts.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is GRANTED. The Decision dated August 23, 2017 and the Resolution dated April 12, 2018 of the Court of Appeals in C.A.-G.R. SP No. 138756 are SET ASIDE. The complaint for indirect contempt against petitioner Judge Maria Amifaith S. Fider-Reyes is hereby DISMISSED.

SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Petitioner Judge Fider-Reyes prevailed. The Supreme Court set aside the Court of Appeals' decision and resolution that had cited her for indirect contempt and fined her P10,000.00, and completely dismissed Everglory's indirect contempt complaint. The Court established that appellate courts cannot use indirect contempt proceedings to discipline trial judges for acts committed in their judicial capacity, and affirmed that the judge properly complied with the Rules of Court in proceeding with the underlying litigation.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Tallado v. Racoma**
**Full Official Caption: Edgardo A. Tallado, Complainant, v. Judge Winston S. Racoma, Presiding Judge, Branch 39, Regional Trial Court, Daet, Camarines Norte, Respondent.**
**Citation & Metadata:** A.M. No. RTJ-22-022 [Formerly OCA IPI No. 20-5054-RTJ]; August 23, 2022; 929 Phil. 40; **Per Curiam**; Supreme Court En Banc (unanimous per curiam decision).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Edgardo A. Tallado:** Complainant; then incumbent Provincial Governor of Camarines Norte, who faced administrative/legal proceedings and filed the administrative complaint against respondent judge.
**Judge Winston S. Racoma:** Respondent; then Presiding Judge of Branch 39, Regional Trial Court (RTC), Daet, Camarines Norte (a multiple-sala station), accused of extortion, gross misconduct, and gross ignorance of the law.
**Office of the Court Administrator (OCA) / Judicial Integrity Board (JIB):** The administrative investigative bodies of the Supreme Court tasked with evaluating the complaint, docketing the disciplinary action, and recommending sanctions.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** This administrative disciplinary proceeding originated from a verified Complaint-Affidavit directly filed by Complainant Edgardo A. Tallado before the Office of the Court Administrator (initially docketed as OCA IPI No. 20-5054-RTJ, later re-docketed as administrative matter A.M. No. RTJ-22-022), seeking the disbarment, dismissal, and criminal prosecution of Respondent Judge Winston S. Racoma for Gross Ignorance of the Law, Gross Misconduct, and violations of the New Code of Judicial Conduct and the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (R.A. No. 3019). The Supreme Court En Banc exercised its direct constitutional disciplinary jurisdiction over lower court judges under Article VIII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution and Rule 140 of the Rules of Court, as amended.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Disciplinary Power over Lower-Court Justices and Judges (Art. VIII, Sec. 11, 1987 Constitution; Rule 140, Rules of Court).
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Provisional Remedies → Injunction and Temporary Restraining Orders (Rule 58, Sec. 5) → Gross Ignorance of the Law and Procedure; Legal and Judicial Ethics → New Code of Judicial Conduct (Canons on Integrity, Propriety, and Competence).
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional & Procedural Provisions:**
**Article VIII, Section 6, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"The Supreme Court shall have administrative supervision over all courts and the personnel thereof."
**Article VIII, Section 11, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"The Members of the Supreme Court and judges of lower courts shall hold office during good behavior until they reach the age of seventy years or become incapacitated to discharge the duties of their office. **The Supreme Court en banc shall have the power to discipline judges of lower courts, or order their dismissal by a vote of a majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberations on the issues in the case and voted thereon.**"
**Section 5, Rule 58 of the Rules of Court (as amended by A.M. No. 07-7-12-SC):**
"SEC. 5. **Preliminary injunction not granted without notice; exception.** — No preliminary injunction shall be granted without hearing and prior notice to the person or party sought to be enjoined. If it shall appear from facts shown by affidavits or by the verified application that great or irreparable injury would result to the applicant before the matter can be heard on notice, the court to which the application for preliminary injunction was made, may issue **ex parte** a temporary restraining order to be effective only for a period of twenty (20) days from service on the party or person sought to be enjoined, except as herein provided.

**If the matter is of extreme urgency and the applicant will suffer grave injustice and irreparable injury, the executive judge of a multiple-sala court or the presiding judge of a single-sala court may issue ex parte a temporary restraining order effective for only seventy-two (72) hours from issuance**, but he shall immediately comply with the provisions of the next preceding section as to service of summons and the documents to be served therewith. Thereafter, within the aforesaid seventy-two (72) hours, the executive judge shall conduct a summary hearing to determine whether the temporary restraining order shall be extended until the application for preliminary injunction can be heard. In no case shall the total period of effectivity of the temporary restraining order exceed twenty (20) days, including the seventy-two (72) hours."
**Rule 140 of the Rules of Court (as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, Feb. 22, 2022):**
"SECTION 14. **Serious Charges.** — Serious charges include:
(1) Gross misconduct constituting violations of the Code of Judicial Conduct;
(2) Bribery, direct or indirect, and extortion;
(3) Dishonesty and violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (Republic Act No. 3019);
(4) Gross ignorance of the law or procedure; [...]

SECTION 17. **Sanctions.** — (1) If the respondent is guilty of a serious charge, any of the following sanctions shall be imposed:
(a) **Dismissal from service, forfeiture of all or part of the benefits as the Supreme Court may determine, and disqualification from reinstatement or appointment to any public office, including government-owned or -controlled corporations. Provided, however, that the forfeiture of benefits shall in no case include accrued leave credits;**
(b) Suspension from office without salary and other benefits for more than six (6) months but not exceeding one (1) year; or
(c) A fine of more than P100,000.00 but not exceeding P200,000.00."
**Factual Trigger:** The conflict erupted when Respondent Judge Racoma—presiding over a single branch within the multiple-sala RTC of Daet, Camarines Norte—flagrantly exceeded his authority by issuing an **ex parte** 72-hour Temporary Restraining Order (TRO) in favor of Complainant Governor Tallado, while concurrently orchestrating illicit demands for substantial sums of money from Tallado in exchange for granting the injunctive relief and maintaining a favorable disposition in the pending suit.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Underlying Civil Proceedings:** A civil action with an application for provisional injunctive relief was initiated before the Regional Trial Court of Daet, Camarines Norte, which involved the official standing and administrative affairs of Complainant Governor Edgardo A. Tallado. The case was raffled to RTC Branch 39, presided over by Respondent Judge Winston S. Racoma. RTC Daet was, at all material times, a multiple-sala court consisting of multiple branches (Branches 38, 39, 40, and 41).
**The Ex Parte Issuance:** Notwithstanding the express limitation in Section 5, Rule 58 of the Rules of Court reserving the power to issue 72-hour TROs **ex parte** strictly to the **Executive Judge** in multiple-sala stations, Respondent Judge Racoma issued an **ex parte** 72-hour Temporary Restraining Order in the pending action.
**The Extortion Scheme:** Simultaneously with the pendency of the injunctive applications, Respondent Judge Racoma engaged in improper backchannel communications and illicit solicitations. Complainant Tallado was approached by intermediary emissaries connected to Respondent Judge, demanding millions of pesos in exchange for the issuance of the TRO and the subsequent issuance of a permanent writ of preliminary injunction to protect Tallado from administrative suspension.
**The Entrapment / Documentation:** Disturbed by the explicit and persistent monetary solicitations conditioned upon favorable judicial action, Complainant Tallado documented the solicitations, communications, and circumstances surrounding the extortion and the irregular, rushed issuance of injunctive orders by Branch 39.
**Filing of the Administrative Complaint:** Complainant Tallado formally lodged a verified Complaint-Affidavit before the Supreme Court, through the Office of the Court Administrator (OCA), charging Respondent Judge Racoma with:
1.  **Gross Ignorance of the Law and Procedure** for issuing an **ex parte** 72-hour TRO in flagrant usurpation of the exclusive statutory authority reserved to the Executive Judge in a multiple-sala station; and
2.  **Gross Misconduct, Extortion, and Violations of the New Code of Judicial Conduct** for demanding and attempting to extort monetary bribes from a litigant with a pending incident in his court.
**Respondent Judge's Comment & Denial:** Respondent Judge Racoma filed his verified Comment, categorically denying the extortion allegations as fabricated, politically motivated, and malicious. On the charge of Gross Ignorance of the Law, he maintained that he issued the 72-hour TRO in good faith, under an honest belief that extreme urgency and grave, irreparable injury justified his immediate intervention to maintain the **status quo**, and that his judicial action represented an error of judgment not subject to administrative disciplinary sanctions absent clear malice or corruption.
**OCA/JIB Evaluation & Referral:** The administrative matter was evaluated by the Court Administrator / Judicial Integrity Board. The investigating body determined that Respondent Judge's acts constituted serious infractions under Rule 140, as amended, finding undisputed documentary proof that he issued an **ex parte** 72-hour TRO in direct violation of basic remedial rules, and finding substantial evidence of gross misconduct compromising the integrity of the judicial office. The OCA recommended that Respondent Judge be found administratively liable and dismissed from the judicial service.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Complainant Edgardo A. Tallado's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Respondent Judge Winston S. Racoma committed Gross Ignorance of the Law and Gross Misconduct warranting his immediate dismissal from the judiciary, forfeiture of benefits, and disbarment, by brazenly ignoring elementary procedural rules governing injunctions and using his judicial office to extort substantial sums of money in exchange for favorable injunctive orders.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Usurpation of Injunction Powers under Rule 58:** Section 5, Rule 58 of the Rules of Court is explicit that in multiple-sala courts, **only the Executive Judge** is empowered to issue an **ex parte** 72-hour TRO upon extreme urgency. Because RTC Daet has multiple branches and Judge Racoma was merely the presiding judge of Branch 39 (and not the Executive Judge), his unilateral **ex parte** issuance was completely void and exhibited gross ignorance of elementary procedural law.
2.  **Corrupt Extortion Scheme:** Respondent Judge did not act out of innocent judicial misapprehension; his irregular issuance of the **ex parte** TRO was directly linked to illicit monetary solicitations and demands for bribes, constituting Gross Misconduct, extortion, and high corruption proscribed by R.A. No. 3019 and the Canons of Judicial Conduct.
3.  **Destruction of Judicial Integrity:** Selling justice or conditioning provisional remedies upon the receipt of payoffs destroys public confidence in the judicial system and violates the constitutional mandate of judicial integrity under Article VIII.
B. Respondent Judge Winston S. Racoma's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The administrative complaint must be dismissed because the extortion allegations are baseless, uncorroborated, and politically motivated lies, while the issuance of the 72-hour TRO was a regular judicial act performed in good faith pursuant to judicial discretion, which cannot be the subject of disciplinary punishment.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Complete Denial of Extortion/Bribery:** Respondent Judge never met, demanded, or solicited any sum of money from Complainant Tallado, whether directly or through emissaries. The accusations are retaliation for legal rulings and lack competent, direct, and substantial proof.
2.  **Good Faith Exercise of Judicial Discretion:** The **ex parte** 72-hour TRO was issued because the verified allegations in the petition presented a situation of extreme urgency where great and irreparable damage would be inflicted before a hearing could be conducted.
3.  **Judicial Remedy Doctrine:** Disciplinary proceedings cannot substitute for judicial remedies. Even assuming **arguendo** that he misinterpreted Section 5, Rule 58 regarding the exclusive authority of the Executive Judge in multi-sala courts, a judge may not be administratively disciplined for gross ignorance of the law for a mere error of judgment, absent clear, convincing, and corroborative evidence of bad faith, fraud, or corrupt motive.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Respondent Judge Winston S. Racoma is administratively liable for **Gross Ignorance of the Law and Procedure** when he, as a regular presiding judge of a single branch in a multiple-sala station, issued an **ex parte** 72-hour Temporary Restraining Order.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Respondent Judge Winston S. Racoma is administratively liable for **Gross Misconduct** for soliciting and attempting to extort monetary bribes from a litigant with a pending application for injunctive relief in his sala.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the penalty of **Dismissal from the Service** with forfeiture of all retirement benefits (except accrued leave credits) and perpetual disqualification from public office is the proper disciplinary sanction imposable under the amended Rule 140 of the Rules of Court (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC).
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Administrative Liability for Gross Ignorance of the Law and Procedure
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did Respondent Judge Winston S. Racoma commit Gross Ignorance of the Law and Procedure by issuing an **ex parte** 72-hour TRO in a multiple-sala court? **YES.** The rule restricting the authority to issue **ex parte** 72-hour TROs strictly to the Executive Judge in multiple-sala stations is elementary, mandatory, and clear; ignoring it constitutes gross ignorance of basic procedure.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Clarity of Section 5, Rule 58:** The Supreme Court emphasized that for a judge to be free from administrative liability for an error of judgment, the legal provision or rule involved must be ambiguous or open to varying judicial interpretations. Section 5 of Rule 58 is unambiguous:
In a **single-sala court**, the presiding judge may issue an **ex parte** 72-hour TRO.
In a **multiple-sala court**, **only the Executive Judge** is authorized to issue an **ex parte** 72-hour TRO upon a showing of extreme urgency and grave, irreparable injury.
2.  **Usurpation of Jurisdiction:** The RTC of Daet, Camarines Norte is unquestionably a multiple-sala court composed of Branches 38, 39, 40, and 41. Respondent Judge was merely the presiding judge of Branch 39. He was **not** the Executive Judge. Consequently, he had zero legal authority or jurisdiction to grant an **ex parte** 72-hour TRO.
3.  **Doctrinal Test for Gross Ignorance:** When a legal principle or procedural rule is so elementary, basic, and established, not to know it, or to act as if one does not know it, or to deliberately disregard it constitutes **Gross Ignorance of the Law and Procedure**. Good faith cannot shield a judge from liability where the rule is rudimentary, because competence and diligence are fundamental requirements of the judicial office. Ignorance of so basic a rule undermines the public's confidence in the competence of the courts.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"When the law or rule is so elementary, not to know it or to act as if one does not know it constitutes gross ignorance of the law, without any need of proving that the judge was motivated by bad faith, malice, or corruption."
"Under Section 5, Rule 58 of the Rules of Court, the authority to issue an **ex parte** 72-hour Temporary Restraining Order in a multiple-sala station is strictly and exclusively vested in the Executive Judge. A presiding judge of a regular branch in a multiple-sala court who arrogates unto himself this exclusive authority commits a flagrant breach of elementary procedure amounting to gross ignorance of the law."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Rule 58 sets up a hard jurisdictional fence: in a courthouse with several branches (a multi-sala court), only the **Executive Judge** can issue an emergency 72-hour TRO without notifying the other side first. Judge Racoma was only a regular branch judge, yet he went ahead and issued the emergency TRO himself. The Supreme Court ruled that this rule is so basic that claiming it was an "honest mistake" or "good faith" is unacceptable; failing to follow such a simple rule is gross ignorance of the law, pure and simple.
Issue 2: Administrative Liability for Gross Misconduct and Extortion
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Is Respondent Judge Winston S. Racoma administratively liable for Gross Misconduct for soliciting monetary bribes in exchange for favorable injunctive action? **YES.** Substantial evidence established that respondent judge engaged in corrupt, oppressive, and improper conduct by using his judicial office to extort money from a litigant, utterly debasing the integrity of the bench.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Quantum of Proof in Judicial Discipline:** The quantum of proof required in administrative disciplinary proceedings against judges is **substantial evidence**—that amount of relevant evidence which a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion.
2.  **Convergence of Irregularity and Extortion:** The Court observed that Respondent Judge's usurpation of the power to issue the **ex parte** TRO was not an isolated procedural mishap; it was intimately intertwined with the illicit monetary demands directed at Complainant Tallado. The expedited, unlawful issuance of the TRO served as the leverage and currency for the illicit payoff.
3.  Violation of the New Code of Judicial Conduct: The Canons of Judicial Conduct impose an unyielding duty on judges:
 Canon 1 (Independence)** and **Canon 2 (Integrity): A judge must exemplify personal integrity and remain uninfluenced by corrupt motives or outside inducements.
 Canon 4 (Propriety): A judge shall avoid impropriety and the appearance of impropriety in all activities.
Soliciting, demanding, or receiving money from a litigant whose case is pending before the judge's court constitutes **Gross Misconduct** of the most contemptible variety. It turns the courthouse into an extortion racket, completely destroying the public's faith in the administration of justice.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"Bribery and extortion committed by a judge constitute the highest form of judicial betrayal. A judge who uses the authority of his office to extract money from litigants in exchange for favorable orders subverts the entire judicial system and forfeits any claim to judicial office."
"Misconduct is gross if it involves a corrupt motive, a willful violation of the law, or a persistent disregard of well-known legal rules. Demanding bribes from a party to a pending suit is the very definition of gross misconduct that warrants the severest administrative sanction."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Judge Racoma did not just make a procedural error; he used that illegal TRO as bargaining leverage to extort millions of pesos from Governor Tallado. The Supreme Court held that the record clearly showed substantial evidence of this extortion scheme. Demanding money from a party with a case in your courtroom is gross misconduct and an unforgivable betrayal of judicial integrity.
Issue 3: Proper Penalty Under Amended Rule 140
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Is the ultimate penalty of dismissal from the service with forfeiture of benefits appropriate? **YES.** Under the amended framework of Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC), Gross Ignorance of the Law and Gross Misconduct are Serious Charges carrying the penalty of dismissal, forfeiture of all retirement benefits (except accrued leave credits), and perpetual disqualification from public office.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Classification of Offenses:** Under Section 14 of Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, both Gross Ignorance of the Law or Procedure and Gross Misconduct / Bribery / Extortion are classified as **Serious Charges**.
2.  **Multiplicity and Gravity of Infractions:** Where a respondent is found guilty of multiple serious charges, the Court imposes the maximum penalty. Judge Racoma's combination of an illegal **ex parte** order and corrupt solicitation struck at the very core of judicial integrity and independence.
3.  **Accessory Penalties:** Under Section 17(1)(a) of Rule 140, the penalty of dismissal carries the mandatory forfeiture of all retirement benefits (excluding accrued leave credits, which have been constitutionally and statutorily recognized as earned property) and perpetual disqualification from appointment or re-employment in any government office, including government-owned or -controlled corporations (GOCCs).
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The Court will not hesitate to wield its constitutional power of discipline to excise from the judicial ranks those who, having taken an oath to administer justice without fear or favor, brazenly monetize their judicial functions. The supreme penalty of dismissal is the only commensurate consequence."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Because Judge Racoma committed two separate "Serious Charges"—Gross Ignorance of the Law and Gross Misconduct—the Court applied the newly revised Rule 140 and imposed the ultimate punishment: immediate dismissal, total forfeiture of all his retirement pensions and benefits (keeping only his earned leave credits), and a lifetime ban from ever working in the government again.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus
**Active Subject:** Constitutional Law I
**Assigned Syllabus Topic:** III. Disciplinary Power over Lower-Court Justices and Judges
**Applied Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law (Article VIII, Sections 6 and 11, 1987 Constitution; Separation of Powers; Judicial Integrity and Self-Regulation).
Constitutional & Political Law Scrutiny
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:** The power exercised is the **Plenary Administrative and Disciplinary Authority of the Supreme Court En Banc** under Article VIII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution. Unlike executive officials who are disciplined by the President or the Ombudsman, the Constitution explicitly and exclusively insulates lower-court judges from legislative or executive discipline by vesting disciplinary supervision and removal power **solely in the Supreme Court En Banc**.
**Doctrinal Test Applied:**
 Substantial Evidence Test: Administrative guilt of judges requires substantial evidence—the quantum of relevant evidence that a reasonable mind accepts as adequate to support a conclusion.
 Gross Ignorance Doctrine: When a procedural rule or substantive statute is clear, basic, and well-settled, failure to observe it constitutes gross ignorance per se; the shield of "good faith" or "error of judgment" evaporates when the breach is elemental and coupled with bad faith or corrupt motives.
 Amended Rule 140 Retroactive / Uniform Application: Procedural and disciplinary rules governing the judiciary (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC) apply uniformly and retroactively to all pending administrative matters.
**Justiciability Audit:**
 Actual Case or Controversy: Clear administrative controversy between a citizen-litigant complaining of corruption and an incumbent trial judge.
 Constitutional Exclusivity: The Court reiterated that no other branch or agency (including the Ombudsman) can preemptively discipline or remove a sitting judge for acts connected to the performance of judicial duties without running afoul of the Supreme Court's exclusive administrative authority under Article VIII, Section 6.
Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist
1.  Elements of Gross Ignorance of the Law:
**   [x] The rule, statute, or doctrine disregarded is elementary, well-known, and established (Section 5, Rule 58 strictly reserving 72-hour **ex parte TRO authority to Executive Judges in multi-sala stations).
[x] The judge acted contrary to or in outright defiance of said clear rule (Judge Racoma, a regular branch judge, issued the order himself).
[x] The act is not a legitimate exercise of discretion or a mere forgivable error of judgment on an unsettled question of law (No room for interpretation existed; bad faith was evident).
2.  Elements of Gross Misconduct (Judicial):
[x] Transgression of an established and definite rule of action (Violation of Canons 1, 2, and 4 of the Code of Judicial Conduct).
[x] Unlawful behavior or gross negligence by the public officer.
[x] Accompanied by corruption, willful intent to violate the law, or persistent disregard of well-known legal rules (Soliciting and attempting to extort bribes from a litigant).
Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words")
 Administrative Supervision over All Courts (Art. VIII, Sec. 6)
 Disciplinary Power of the Supreme Court En Banc (Art. VIII, Sec. 11)
 Multiple-Sala Station vs. Single-Sala Station
 Exclusive Authority of the Executive Judge (Rule 58, Sec. 5)
 Ex Parte 72-Hour Temporary Restraining Order
 Gross Ignorance of the Law and Procedure
 Gross Misconduct Involving Bribery and Extortion
 Serious Charge under Amended Rule 140
 Forfeiture of Retirement Benefits (excluding accrued leave credits)
 Perpetual Disqualification from Public Office
Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer)
"In **Tallado v. Racoma** (2022), the Supreme Court En Banc exercised its exclusive constitutional power under Article VIII, Section 11 to dismiss a sitting Regional Trial Court judge. Respondent Judge Racoma, presiding over Branch 39 in the multiple-sala station of Daet, Camarines Norte, issued an **ex parte** 72-hour TRO in favor of Governor Tallado and simultaneously demanded monetary bribes in exchange for the injunction. The Court held that issuing a 72-hour **ex parte** TRO in a multi-sala court constitutes **Gross Ignorance of the Law** because Section 5, Rule 58 expressly reserves that emergency power strictly to the **Executive Judge**. Furthermore, using that illegal order to extort bribes constitutes **Gross Misconduct**. Applying the amended Rule 140, the Court meted out the maximum penalty: immediate dismissal from the judiciary, forfeiture of all retirement benefits except accrued leave credits, and perpetual disqualification from public office."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**No separate opinions filed.** The decision of the Supreme Court En Banc was rendered **Per Curiam** and was entirely unanimous.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, respondent Judge Winston S. Racoma, Presiding Judge of the Regional Trial Court, Branch 39, Daet, Camarines Norte, is found **GUILTY** of Gross Ignorance of the Law and Procedure and Gross Misconduct. He is hereby **DISMISSED** from the service, with **FORFEITURE** of all retirement benefits, except accrued leave credits, and with prejudice to re-employment in any branch or agency of the government, including government-owned or -controlled corporations.

SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Complainant Governor Tallado completely prevailed. Respondent Judge Winston S. Racoma was stripped of his judicial robes, dismissed from government service with immediate effect, stripped of all retirement pensions and monetary benefits (retaining only his earned vacation/sick leave credits), and permanently barred from ever holding any public office or working in any government-owned corporation.
