digest:
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Chavez v. Judicial and Bar Council (Resolution on Motion for Reconsideration)
**Full Official Caption:** Francisco I. Chavez, Petitioner, vs. Judicial and Bar Council, Sen. Francis Joseph G. Escudero, and Rep. Niel C. Tupas, Jr., Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 202242; April 16, 2013; 709 Phil. 478; En Banc; Ponente: Mendoza, J.
- **Voting Breakdown:** Carpio, Leonardo-De Castro, Peralta, Bersamin, Villarama, Jr., Perez, Reyes, and Perlas-Bernabe, JJ., concur; Sereno, C.J., took no part (JBC Chairperson); Velasco, Jr., J., took no part (participation in JC); Brion, J., took no part; Del Castillo, J., joined the dissent of Abad, J.; Abad, J., filed a Dissenting Opinion; Leonen, J., filed a Dissenting Opinion.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
- **Francisco I. Chavez:** Former Solicitor General of the Philippines; nominee for the position of Chief Justice of the Supreme Court following the removal of Renato C. Corona; Petitioner.
- **Judicial and Bar Council (JBC):** The constitutionally created body tasked with recommending nominees for judicial vacancies; Respondent.
- **Sen. Francis Joseph G. Escudero:** Member of the Senate of the Philippines and Chairman of the Senate Committee on Justice and Human Rights; sitting ex officio representative in the JBC; Respondent.
- **Rep. Niel C. Tupas, Jr.:** Member of the House of Representatives of the Philippines and Chairman of the House Committee on Justice; sitting ex officio representative in the JBC; Respondent.
- **Office of the Solicitor General (OSG):** Legal counsel representing Respondents Sen. Escudero and Rep. Tupas, Jr.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Motion for Reconsideration filed by the Office of the Solicitor General on behalf of Respondents Sen. Escudero and Rep. Tupas, Jr., seeking to overturn the Supreme Court En Banc's Decision dated July 17, 2012, which declared the numerical composition of the JBC unconstitutional and ordered it reconstituted so that only one member of Congress sits as a representative in its proceedings.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Article VIII (Judicial Department) → Section 8: The Judicial and Bar Council (Composition & Representation)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Review → Doctrine of Operative Fact; Principles of Constitutional Construction (**Verba Legis**, **Casus Omissus**, Separation of Powers).
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provision:**
**Article VIII, Section 8, Paragraph 1, 1987 Constitution of the Republic of the Philippines:**
"Section 8. (1) A Judicial and Bar Council is hereby created under the supervision of the Supreme Court composed of the Chief Justice as **ex officio** Chairman, the Secretary of Justice, and **a representative of the Congress** as **ex officio** Members, a representative of the Integrated Bar, a professor of law, a retired Member of the Supreme Court, and a representative of the private sector."
**Historical Landmark Rule:**
Under the **1899 Malolos Constitution (Art. 80, Title X)**, the Chief Justice and Solicitor-General were chosen by the National Assembly in concurrence with the President and Secretaries. Under the **1935 Constitution (Art. VIII, Sec. 5)**, judicial appointments were made by the President with the consent of the Commission on Appointments. Under the **1973 Constitution (Art. X, Sec. 4)**, the appointment power was vested exclusively in the President without need for legislative confirmation. The **1987 Constitution** deliberately eliminated legislative confirmation through the Commission on Appointments and instituted the JBC under Art. VIII, Sec. 8(1) to insulate appointments from political partisanship.
**Factual Trigger:**
Following the removal of Chief Justice Renato C. Corona on May 29, 2012, the JBC commenced proceedings to nominate a successor. Petitioner Francisco I. Chavez was nominated, but challenged the constitutionality of the JBC's ongoing composition—in which both a Senator and a House Representative sat simultaneously as **ex officio** members, each casting one full vote—arguing it violated the express textual limitation of Article VIII, Section 8(1) restricting Congress to "a representative."
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1987:** The 1987 Constitution is ratified. Section 8(1), Article VIII creates the Judicial and Bar Council, providing that it be composed of the Chief Justice as **ex officio** Chairman, the Secretary of Justice, and "a representative of the Congress" as **ex officio** members, alongside four regular members (a representative of the Integrated Bar, a professor of law, a retired Supreme Court Justice, and a private sector representative). Congress designates one representative, alternating between the Senate and the House of Representatives by rotation.
**1994:** The seven-member numerical balance is altered. An eighth member is introduced as the Senate and the House of Representatives begin sending two representatives to sit simultaneously, with each wielding one-half (1/2) vote.
**January 12, 2000 / May 30, 2001:** The JBC En Banc substantially changes this arrangement. It abandons the half-vote system and decides to grant each congressional representative (one from the Senate and one from the House) one full vote, effectively raising total voting members to eight.
**March 14, 2007:** Associate Justice Leonardo A. Quisumbing submits an opinion as JBC Consultant to the Chief Justice, concluding that two congressional votes violate the Constitution, run counter to the intended seven-member framework, and create the risk of deadlocks.
**March 27, 2007:** Representative Simeon A. Datumanong submits a formal position paper arguing that Congress is entitled strictly to one representative under the unambiguous terms of Section 8(1), Article VIII, and that double representation negates the equality of the three co-equal branches.
**Undated:** Secretary of Justice Agnes VST Devanadera submits a position paper affirming that the text explicitly restricts Congress to a single individual representative, and that eight members exceeds the constitutional blueprint.
**May 29, 2012:** Chief Justice Renato C. Corona is removed from office by impeachment, creating a vacancy in the Supreme Court. The JBC initiates nominations; Francisco I. Chavez is nominated as a candidate.
**July 17, 2012:** The Supreme Court renders its Decision in G.R. No. 202242, granting Chavez’s petition. It declares the JBC’s eight-member composition unconstitutional, commands the JBC to reconstitute itself with only one congressional representative, and orders the ruling immediately executory.
**July 24–31, 2012:** The OSG, on behalf of Sen. Escudero and Rep. Tupas, Jr., files a Motion for Reconsideration. The Senate passes Resolutions Nos. 111, 112, 113, and 114 urging deferral of nominations, reiterating the propriety of two representatives with full votes, requesting oral arguments, and authorizing Sen. Joker P. Arroyo to argue. On July 31, 2012, the Court sets the motion for oral argument.
**August 2, 2012:** The Supreme Court hears the parties in oral argument.
**August 3, 2012:** The Supreme Court issues a Resolution directing the parties to submit memoranda within ten days, and suspends the immediately executory nature of the July 17, 2012 dispositive portion pending review.
**April 16, 2013:** The Supreme Court promulgates its En Banc Resolution denying Respondents' Motion for Reconsideration and lifting the suspension on immediate execution.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondents' Arguments (Motion for Reconsideration via OSG)
- **Main Thesis:** Article VIII, Section 8(1) must be interpreted to allow two representatives from Congress—one Senator and one Representative—each exercising one full vote, because the legislature is bicameral.
- **Specific Contentions:**
1. **Absurdity in Bicameral Context:** Restricting Congress to one representative leads to an absurdity because a Senator cannot represent the House, and a House Member cannot represent the Senate. Each chamber has distinct constituencies, rules, organizations, and mandates.
2. **Plain Oversight Theory:** The use of the singular phrasing "a representative of the Congress" was sheer inadvertence and plain oversight by the Constitutional Commission. When the Framers shifted the legislative structure from unicameralism to bicameralism, they adjusted other provisions but inadvertently omitted modifying Section 8(1).
3. **No Danger of Partisanship:** Allowing two congressional members does not subvert the Framers' intent to insulate the JBC from partisan politics, as the Executive already exerts substantial influence over the regular members through appointment.
4. **Even-Numbered Deadlock Refuted:** The Court's premise that the JBC requires an odd seven-member framework to break ties is flawed. The JBC shortlists multiple candidates based on pluralities; it does not render binary yes/no determinations requiring a tie-breaking vote.
5. **Acquiescence / Long-Standing Practice:** The practice of having two representatives dates back years and was never questioned, demonstrating constitutional acceptance.
B. Petitioner's Arguments (Chavez Opposition & Memorandum)
- **Main Thesis:** The plain language of the Constitution is absolute; Section 8(1), Article VIII deliberately restricts Congress to only one seat and one vote in the JBC.
- **Specific Contentions:**
1. **Verba Legis:** The text clearly uses the singular indefinite article "a" ("a representative of the Congress"). Where the text is clear, there is no room for interpretation.
2. **Refutation of Oversight:** The Framers adjusted multiple other constitutional provisions when adopting bicameralism (e.g., presidential election tie-breakers, Vice-President vacancy confirmations, revocation of martial law). Their decision not to alter Section 8(1) demonstrates deliberate intent.
3. **Equal Branch Representation:** The three branches participate **ex officio** in the JBC as equal institutional departments. Congress interacts with the JBC not in its legislative capacity, but in an institutional check-and-balance function. Giving Congress two seats and two votes distorts inter-branch parity by giving the legislature twice the quantitative influence of the Executive and the Judiciary.
4. **Prohibition of Vote-Splitting:** A single representative is entitled to one full vote; dividing a vote into halves or duplicating it violates constitutional commands.
5. **Inapplicability of Estoppel:** Past unconstitutional practices, no matter how habitual or established, cannot ripen into constitutional validity under estoppel or laches.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the singular phrase "a representative of the Congress" in Section 8(1), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution permits both the Senate and the House of Representatives to seat one member each in the Judicial and Bar Council.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the failure of the 1986 Constitutional Commission to adjust Section 8(1), Article VIII upon shifting from a unicameral to a bicameral legislature constitutes a "plain oversight" that warrants judicial correction.
3. **[Secondary Substantive Issue]** Whether or not the lone congressional representative in the JBC may split their vote into one-half (1/2) each between two members of Congress.
4. **[Secondary Substantive Issue]** Whether or not long-standing practice and lack of prior challenge estop the petitioner or insulate the unconstitutional composition of the JBC from judicial nullification.
5. **[Secondary Substantive Issue]** Whether or not the declaration of unconstitutionality invalidates all prior official acts and recommendations performed by the JBC while operating with an eight-member composition.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Proper Number of Congressional Representatives in the JBC
- **(a) Short Answer: NO.** Section 8(1), Article VIII permits only one representative from Congress to sit in the JBC.
- **(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Textualism and Verba Legis:** The Constitution is the supreme direct act of the sovereign people. In interpreting it, the Court presumes the Framers meant what they said. The deliberate selection of the singular word "a" in "a representative of the Congress" demonstrates that the legislature is entitled to exactly one seat.
2. **Inter-Branch Parity in Non-Legislative Functions:** The JBC is an independent body created under judicial supervision to recommend nominees to the President. The three branches participate through **ex officio** representatives: the Chief Justice (Judicial), the Secretary of Justice (Executive), and "a representative of the Congress" (Legislative). The JBC totals seven members. In non-legislative bodies where the legislature interacts externally with co-equal branches, Congress participates as one single branch. Conferring two seats on Congress gives it two votes against one for the Executive and one for the Judiciary, subverting inter-branch equality.
3. **Constricted Representation is Not Absurd:** While the two Houses operate separately in lawmaking, appropriation, treaties, and impeachment, no internal bicameral interplay is required inside the JBC. Any member of Congress chosen to sit acts as a representative of the **entire** Congress. While this authority is constricted, it is entirely constitutional.
- **(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"The unmistakeable tenor of Article VIII, Section 8(1) was to treat each **ex-officio** member as representing one co-equal branch of government... The representatives of the Senate and the House of Representatives act as such for one branch and should not have any more quantitative influence as the other branches in the exercise of prerogatives evenly bestowed upon the three."
- **(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:** The Constitution expressly limits legislative representation in the JBC to "a representative." Because the JBC's role is non-legislative, Congress sits not as two independent chambers representing localized or national constituencies, but as a single co-equal department alongside the Executive and Judiciary; giving it two seats and two votes unconstitutionally tilts inter-branch equality.
Issue 2: Plain Oversight and Judicial Activism
- **(a) Short Answer: NO.** The omission of dual representation was not an oversight, and the Court has no power to amend the Constitution under the guise of interpretation.
- **(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Systematic Constitutional Adaptation:** The Framers demonstrated that they knew how to adapt constitutional text when switching from unicameralism to bicameralism. In multiple provisions (e.g., Art. VII, Sec. 4 [breaking presidential election ties], Art. VII, Sec. 9 [confirming Vice-Presidential vacancies], and Art. VII, Sec. 18 [revoking/extending martial law]), the text was expressly adjusted to state "both Houses of the Congress, voting separately" or "voting jointly." The absence of any such modification in Article VIII, Section 8(1) demonstrates that the singular representation was intentional.
2. **Casus Omissus Pro Omisso Habendus Est:** Under the canon of **casus omissus**, a matter omitted is held to have been intentionally omitted. Even if the omission arose from lack of foresight, courts cannot supply what they imagine the Framers would have enacted, as that constitutes improper judicial legislation.
3. **Rejection of Exuberant Activism:** The Court declined respondents' plea for judicial activism to solve practical bicameral difficulties. Judicial activism must not cross into "judicial exuberance" or constitutional alteration.
- **(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"Pursuant to this, 'the Court cannot under its power of interpretation supply the omission even though the omission may have resulted from inadvertence or because the case in question was not foreseen or contemplated.' 'The Court cannot supply what it thinks the legislature would have supplied had its attention been called to the omission, as that would be judicial legislation.'"
- **(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:** The Court cannot invoke "oversight" to rewrite the Constitution. When the Framers restored the bicameral legislature, they consciously updated multiple provisions but chose to leave the JBC composition at one congressional representative; under **casus omissus**, the judiciary cannot supply an omitted seat without impermissibly amending the Charter.
Issue 3: Validity of Vote-Splitting Schemes
- **(a) Short Answer: NO.** Dividing a single vote into two half-votes between two members of Congress is unconstitutional.
- **(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Prohibition of Indirect Evasion:** The lone representative of Congress authorized by the Constitution carries one full vote. What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.
2. **Preservation of Constitutional Symmetry:** Allowing two legislators to sit simultaneously while splitting a vote disrupts normal voting order and circumvents the textual cap. The Constitution contemplates single, individual representatives across each designated category.
- **(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"From this score stems the conclusion that the lone representative of Congress is entitled to one full vote. This pronouncement effectively disallows the scheme of splitting the said vote into half (1/2), between two representatives of Congress. Not only can this unsanctioned practice cause disorder in the voting process, it is clearly against the essence of what the Constitution authorized."
- **(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:** The Constitution designates a single representative with one whole vote. Splitting a vote into halves to allow both chambers to sit simultaneously is an impermissible circumvention of the text that compromises the integrity and order of JBC voting proceedings.
Issue 4: Estoppel and Long-Standing Practice
- **(a) Short Answer: NO.** Unconstitutional government acts cannot acquire legitimacy through passage of time, frequent practice, or official acquiescence.
- **(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Primacy of the Fundamental Law:** An act that infringes the Constitution is void **ab initio**.
2. **Inapplicability of Laches and Estoppel:** Past toleration or acquiescence by the government, the JBC, or citizens does not cure constitutional defects. Frequency and notoriety of an invalid practice cannot generate legal authority.
- **(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Well-settled is the rule that acts done in violation of the Constitution no matter how frequent, usual or notorious cannot develop or gain acceptance under the doctrine of estoppel or laches, because once an act is considered as an infringement of the Constitution it is void from the very beginning and cannot be the source of any power or authority."
- **(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:** The fact that the JBC allowed two members of Congress to sit and vote since 1994 without challenge does not create a prescriptive right; unconstitutional practices can never be legitimized by estoppel or lapse of time.
Issue 5: Validity of Past Actions Under the Doctrine of Operative Fact
- **(a) Short Answer: YES.** Under the doctrine of operative fact, all previous official proceedings, nominations, and shortlists issued by the JBC prior to the finality of this declaration of unconstitutionality remain completely valid.
- **(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Exception to Void Ab Initio Principle:** While unconstitutional acts generally confer no rights and create no offices, equity and fair play mandate exceptions when undoing past reliance would result in massive disruption and injustice.
2. **Preservation of Judicial Nominations:** Prior reliance on the invalidly composed JBC was an operative historical fact. Invalidating past JBC actions would throw into legal limbo hundreds of judicial appointments, impairing judicial stability and imposing an undue burden on the public.
- **(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"The doctrine of operative fact, as an exception to the general rule, only applies as a matter of equity and fair play. It nullifies the effects of an unconstitutional law by recognizing that the existence of a statute prior to a determination of unconstitutionality is an operative fact and may have consequences which cannot always be ignored. The past cannot always be erased by a new judicial declaration."
- **(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:** The Court invoked the doctrine of operative fact as a matter of equity to ensure that its ruling operates prospectively. All prior JBC nominations and judicial appointments made under the unconstitutional eight-member setup remain fully valid to prevent systemic chaos.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | 4. The Judicial and Bar Council | Constitutional & Political Law Lens
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
- **Governmental Act:** Congress' exercise of structural representation by sending two delegates (one Senator and one Representative) wielding two full votes in the JBC; and the JBC En Banc’s internal administrative resolutions altering its numerical composition from seven to eight members.
- **Constitutional Limitation:** Article VIII, Section 8(1) of the 1987 Constitution, restricting congressional membership to "a representative," maintaining inter-branch parity among the three co-equal departments, and enforcing the doctrine of separation of powers.
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
- **Strict Textual Construction (Verba Legis):** Applied when constitutional language is unambiguous. The word "a" commands a singular numerical ceiling.
- **Casus Omissus Canon:** A matter omitted must be treated as intentionally omitted; courts cannot supply perceived legislative omissions under the banner of interpretation.
- **Anti-Usurpation / Restraint Test:** The Court refused "judicial exuberance" or rewriting constitutional provisions under the guise of resolving bicameral anomalies.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (JBC Composition Analysis):**
- **1. Supervised Entity:** Created under the direct supervision of the Supreme Court. **(Met)**
- **2. Total Number Contemplated:** Seven (7) members total. **(Violated: expanded to 8)**
- **3. Ex-Officio Branch Representation:**
- Judiciary: Chief Justice as **ex officio** Chairman (1 seat, 1 vote). **(Met)**
- Executive: Secretary of Justice (1 seat, 1 vote). **(Met)**
- Legislative: "a representative of the Congress" (1 seat, 1 vote). **(Violated: 2 seats, 2 votes occupied by Senate and House chairs simultaneously)**
- **4. Regular Members:** Four (4) regular members representing the Integrated Bar, legal academia, retired Supreme Court Justices, and the private sector, all subject to Commission on Appointments confirmation. **(Met)**
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
- **Ex officio** representation
- **Verba legis**
- **Casus omissus**
- Inter-branch equality / Co-equal branches
- Doctrine of operative fact
- Judicial exuberance vs. Judicial activism
- Void **ab initio**
**Justiciability & Threshold Audit:**
- **Locus Standi & Actual Controversy:** Petitioner Chavez possessed standing as a citizen, taxpayer, and direct nominee for the vacancy of Chief Justice affected by the composition of the screening council.
- **Estoppel against Constitutional Challenges:** Rejected. Past unconstitutional practices, regardless of how routine or notorious, cannot ripen into legality.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
This case is the leading authority on the composition of the Judicial and Bar Council under Article VIII, Section 8(1). The Supreme Court held that Congress is entitled strictly to **one representative** and **one full vote**, rejecting the bicameral argument of "plain oversight" because the text unambiguously uses the singular article "a." Giving Congress two seats distorts inter-branch parity by giving the legislature double the quantitative influence of the Executive and Judiciary in the JBC; however, under the **doctrine of operative fact**, all prior official acts and shortlists generated by the unconstitutionally constituted eight-member council remain completely valid.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
- **Abad, J., Dissenting:** Argued that the Motion for Reconsideration should be granted. Insisted that insisting on a single representative ignores the constitutional reality of a bicameral legislature where neither House can represent the other. Pointed out that JBC representation is explicitly defined as **ex officio**, which by Senate and House rules attaches automatically to the Justice Committee Chair of each chamber; therefore, adhering to a literal reading denies real **ex officio** representation to Congress. Concluded each chamber is constitutionally entitled to one full vote, as splitting votes renders legislators "second class members."
- **Leonen, J., Dissenting:** Argued that the Constitution must be interpreted as an integrated whole (**ut magis valeat quam pereat**) rather than by hyper-focusing on the single preposition "a." Under the Charter's design, Congress exists strictly as a bicameral body; a Senator reports only to the Senate and represents a national constituency, while a Representative reports to the House and represents local/party-list constituencies. Neither can represent the other or the whole Congress. Emphasized that the Constitutional Commission records show the JBC seven-member model was discussed while the Commission was still assuming a unicameral assembly, and the Failure to adjust Section 8(1) after the 23–22 vote restoring bicameralism was a clear mechanical oversight. Argued that the JBC does not make binary decisions requiring an odd-numbered tie-breaker since it produces shortlists based on pluralities, and having eight members violates no constitutional objective.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
**"WHEREFORE**, the Motion for Reconsideration filed by respondents is hereby **DENIED**. The suspension of the effects of the second paragraph of the dispositive portion of the July 17, 2012 Decision of the Court, which reads, 'This disposition is immediately executory,' is hereby **LIFTED**."
### "SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court firmly maintained its July 17, 2012 ruling: Petitioner Francisco I. Chavez prevailed, while Respondents Sen. Escudero, Rep. Tupas, and the OSG lost. The practice of having two members of Congress sit simultaneously with full votes in the JBC was conclusively reaffirmed as unconstitutional, the immediate enforceability of the reconstitution order was reinstated, and Congress was required to designate only one member to sit and vote in the JBC.

subject: Constitutional Law I
category: Constitutional Law I | 4. The Judicial and Bar Council
digest:
Jardeleza v. Sereno
**Citation:** 741 Phil. 460 (G.R. No. 213181)
**Date of Promulgation:** August 19, 2014
**Ponente:** Mendoza, J.
**Voting Breakdown:** En Banc. Perez and Reyes, JJ., concurred; Leonardo-De Castro, Brion, and Peralta, JJ., filed separate concurring opinions; Bersamin, J., joined the separate opinions of Leonardo-De Castro and Brion, JJ.; Sereno, C.J., and Carpio, J., took no part; Villarama, Jr., J., was on official leave; Del Castillo, J., dissented on the sole ground that the decision may affect the independence of the JBC; Velasco, Jr. (Acting Chairperson) and Perlas-Bernabe, JJ., joined the dissent of Leonen, J.; Leonen, J., filed a dissenting opinion.
The Cast
**Francis H. Jardeleza:** Petitioner; incumbent Solicitor General of the Republic of the Philippines and applicant for the vacancy of Associate Justice of the Supreme Court vice retired Associate Justice Roberto A. Abad.
**Chief Justice Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno:** Respondent; Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and **ex-officio** Chairperson of the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC).
**Judicial and Bar Council (JBC):** Respondent; the constitutional body mandated to recommend appointees to the Judiciary.
**Executive Secretary Paquito N. Ochoa, Jr.:** Respondent; sued as alter ego of the President.
**Senior Associate Justice Antonio T. Carpio:** Resource person invited before the JBC **in camera** to explain a confidential legal memorandum regarding the international arbitration strategy of the Republic.
**Justice Aurora Santiago Lagman:** Incumbent regular member of the JBC who verbally contacted Jardeleza regarding the integrity objection.
**Secretary Leila M. De Lima:** Secretary of Justice and **ex-officio** member of the JBC.
How the Case Reached the Supreme Court
Petition for **Certiorari** and **Mandamus** under Rule 65 of the Rules of Court, with prayer for the issuance of a Temporary Restraining Order (TRO), seeking to declare that Chief Justice Sereno and the JBC acted with grave abuse of discretion in excluding petitioner from the shortlist of nominees submitted to the President for the position of Associate Justice of the Supreme Court, and to compel the JBC to include petitioner in the said shortlist.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Bill of Rights → Procedural Due Process; Remedial Law → Special Civil Actions → Certiorari and Mandamus
Verbatim Governing Provisions
**1987 Philippine Constitution, Article VIII, Section 8, Paragraphs (1) and (5):**
"SECTION 8. (1) A Judicial and Bar Council is hereby created **under the supervision of the Supreme Court** composed of the Chief Justice as **ex officio** Chairman, the Secretary of Justice, and a representative of the Congress as **ex officio** Members, a representative of the Integrated Bar, a professor of law, a retired Member of the Supreme Court, and a representative of the private sector.
...
(5) The Council shall have the principal function of recommending appointees to the Judiciary. It may exercise such other functions and duties as the Supreme Court may assign to it."
**1987 Philippine Constitution, Article VIII, Section 1, Paragraph 2:**
"Judicial power includes the duty of the courts of justice to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable, and **to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government.**"
**1987 Philippine Constitution, Article III, Section 1:**
"No person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property **without due process of law**, nor shall any person be denied the equal protection of the laws."
**Section 2, Rule 10, JBC-009 (Rules of the Judicial and Bar Council):**
"SEC. 2. **Votes required when integrity of a qualified applicant is challenged.** — In every case where the integrity of an applicant who is not otherwise disqualified for nomination is raised or challenged, **the affirmative vote of all the Members of the Council must be obtained for the favorable consideration of his nomination.**"
**Sections 1 and 2, JBC-010:**
"SECTION 1. The Judicial and Bar Council shall deliberate to determine who of the candidates meet **prima facie** the qualifications for the position under consideration. For this purpose, it shall prepare a long list of candidates who **prima facie** appear to have all the qualifications.
The Secretary of the Council shall then cause to be published in two (2) newspapers of general circulation a notice of the long list of candidates in alphabetical order.
The notice shall inform the public that **any complaint or opposition against a candidate may be filed with the Secretary within ten (10) days thereof.**
SEC. 2. **The complaint or opposition shall be in writing, under oath and in ten (10) legible copies, together with its supporting annexes.** It shall strictly relate to the qualifications of the candidate or lack thereof, as provided for in the Constitution, statutes, and the Rules of the Judicial and Bar Council, as well as resolutions or regulations promulgated by it.
**The Secretary of the Council shall furnish the candidate a copy of the complaint or opposition against him. The candidate shall have five (5) days from receipt thereof within which to file his comment to the complaint or opposition, if he so desires.**"
Factual Trigger
During the final selection of nominees for the vacancy created by the retirement of Associate Justice Roberto A. Abad, Chief Justice Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno verbally invoked Section 2, Rule 10 of JBC-009 (the "unanimity rule" on integrity) against Solicitor General Francis H. Jardeleza based on his legal strategy in an international arbitration case (**Republic of the Philippines v. People's Republic of China**). Although Jardeleza garnered four (4) out of six (6) votes—a qualifying majority—the JBC excluded his name from the shortlist transmitted to the President on the ground that he failed to secure the unanimous vote of the Council, after giving him only a same-day verbal summary of accusations and an immediate demand to defend himself without written specifications, sworn statements, or time to prepare.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**March 6, 2014:** The JBC announces the opening for applications or recommendations for the Supreme Court Associate Justice seat to be vacated by Associate Justice Roberto A. Abad on May 22, 2014.
**March 14, 2014:** The JBC receives a letter from UP College of Law Dean Danilo Concepcion nominating Solicitor General Francis H. Jardeleza. Jardeleza accepts the nomination.
**April 26, 2014:** The JBC publishes the list of candidates and schedules public interviews, giving the public until May 6, 2014 to submit sworn complaints or oppositions. No opposition is filed against Jardeleza.
**May 29, 2014:** Jardeleza undergoes his scheduled public interview before the JBC. No integrity issues, complaints, or questions regarding his handling of government cases are raised.
**June 5, 2014:** During an executive session of the JBC, Chief Justice Sereno manifests that Jardeleza lacks the integrity required for the post and that she will invoke Section 2, Rule 10 of JBC-009 against him. She claims that Jardeleza exhibited "disloyalty to the country" by deliberately seeking to exclude a discussion on a crucial physical feature (**Itu Aba**) in the Philippine Memorial in the UNCLOS arbitration case against China.
**June 16, 2014:** The JBC meets again in executive session. CJ Sereno reiterates her intent to invoke Rule 10. The JBC decides not to put the challenge against Jardeleza in writing because it might be "messy" and affect national interests. The Council resolves to have regular member Justice Aurora S. Lagman telephone Jardeleza to invite him to appear at the June 30 meeting.
**June 16 & 17, 2014:** Justice Lagman calls Jardeleza, informing him that CJ Sereno will invoke Section 2, Rule 10 of JBC-009 against him, and directs him to make himself available before the JBC on June 30, 2014, where the Chief Justice will disclose the objections to his integrity.
**June 24, 2014:** Jardeleza files a letter-petition (A.M. No. 14-07-01-SC-JBC) with the Supreme Court en banc, asking the Court, pursuant to its supervisory authority over the JBC, to direct the JBC to provide him at least five (5) working days written notice containing sworn specifications of the charges, allow cross-examination in public, reset the June 30 meeting, and disallow CJ Sereno from participating in the voting.
**June 25, 2014:** The Supreme Court Office of the Clerk of Court receives Jardeleza's letter-petition. However, it is not raffled immediately.
**June 30, 2014 (Morning):** The JBC convenes in executive session. Senior Associate Justice Antonio T. Carpio appears as an invited resource person to shed light on a confidential legal memorandum (prepared by international counsel Paul Reichler and Lawrence Martin) concerning the handling of the **Itu Aba** issue in the UNCLOS arbitration case. Copies of the memorandum are distributed to JBC members.
**June 30, 2014 (11:00 AM – 1:00 PM):** Jardeleza arrives at the Supreme Court ante-room as directed. Secretary of Justice Leila De Lima informs him that Justice Carpio testified before the JBC regarding his work in the international arbitration case.
**June 30, 2014 (2:00 PM):** Jardeleza is summoned before the JBC. CJ Sereno asks him if he wants to defend himself on three grounds: (1) his handling of the international arbitration case; (2) alleged extra-marital affairs while at San Miguel Corporation (SMC); and (3) alleged insider trading that led to a Philippine Stock Exchange show-cause order. (The immorality and insider trading issues were brought up by CJ Sereno for the first time during this meeting). Jardeleza refuses to answer on the spot, arguing that doing so would waive his due process rights. He demands written sworn specifications, the right to cross-examine, and a deferment pending the Supreme Court en banc session the following day. He submits a written statement and is excused after ten minutes.
**June 30, 2014 (Afternoon):** Despite a suggestion from Justice Lagman to defer voting, CJ Sereno rules that the process is complete. The JBC proceeds to vote. The tally yields: Apolinario D. Bruselas, Jr. (6 votes), Jose C. Reyes, Jr. (6 votes), Maria Gracia M. Pulido-Tan (5 votes), Reynaldo B. Daway (4 votes), and Francis H. Jardeleza (4 votes).
**June 30, 2014 (Late Afternoon):** The JBC excludes Jardeleza from the final shortlist transmitted to President Benigno S. Aquino III, concluding that because CJ Sereno invoked Rule 10, Section 2, Jardeleza failed to obtain the unanimous vote of the remaining members (needing 5 out of 5, but getting only 4). Daway, who also garnered 4 votes, is included because his integrity was not challenged.
**July 1, 2014:** Jardeleza’s June 24 letter-petition is finally raffled to a Member-in-Charge, thirty minutes before the Supreme Court En Banc session.
**July 8, 2014:** The Supreme Court En Banc issues a Resolution merely "noting" Jardeleza's letter-petition as moot due to the prior transmittal of the shortlist to Malacañang, "without prejudice to any remedy available in law and the rules." Justice Brion dissents.
**July 18, 2014:** Jardeleza files the present Petition for **Certiorari** and **Mandamus** with prayer for a TRO under Rule 65.
**July 22, 2014:** The Supreme Court requires respondents to comment within 10 days. The resolution is served on respondents on July 31 and August 1, 2014.
**August 8, 2014:** Executive Secretary Ochoa files a Comment arguing that Section 2, Rule 10 is unconstitutional and that Jardeleza should be deemed included in the shortlist.
**August 11, 2014:** The JBC files its Comment opposing the petition.
**August 15, 2014:** Jardeleza files his Reply. Minutes before office close, the JBC files a Supplemental Comment-Reply containing detailed statements from CJ Sereno and the minutes of the JBC executive sessions.
**August 20, 2014:** Expiration of the mandatory 90-day constitutional deadline under Article VIII, Section 4(1) for the President to fill the vacancy left by Justice Abad.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Francis H. Jardeleza)
**Main Thesis:** The JBC and CJ Sereno committed grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction in arbitrarily excluding Jardeleza from the shortlist through patent violations of procedural due process and the JBC’s own rules, and having obtained a qualifying majority of four (4) votes, it was ministerial on the part of the JBC to include him.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Violation of Due Process:** Jardeleza was subjected to **ex parte** accusations regarding his integrity without written notice, without specification of charges, and without reasonable opportunity to prepare a defense. The **sui generis nature of JBC proceedings does not dispense with constitutional due process.
 Violation of JBC-009 and JBC-010: Under Rule 4, Sections 3 and 4 of JBC-009, and Sections 1–5 of JBC-010, complaints or oppositions must be in writing and under oath, furnished to the applicant with a 5-day period to answer, and ventilated during public interviews. The JBC discarded these mandatory rules.
 Misapplication of Section 2, Rule 10 (Unanimity Rule): The unanimity rule cannot be invoked by a JBC member who is part of the voting collegial body. Allowing a member to object gives that member an impermissible unilateral veto power over the majority.
 CJ Sereno Acted with Egregious Bias:** CJ Sereno simultaneously acted as accuser, prosecutor, witness, and judge, violating **nemo judex in sua causa.
 Right to be Included: Having obtained 4 out of 6 votes (a majority), his inclusion in the shortlist became ministerial under Section 1, Rule 10 of JBC-009.
 Impairment of Presidential Appointing Power: Unlawfully pruning the qualified nominees from five to four unduly curtailed the President's constitutional prerogative to choose from a complete list of qualified applicants.
B. Respondent JBC's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The petition lacks procedural and substantive basis because the JBC's nomination function is purely discretionary and non-judicial, the remedies of certiorari and mandamus do not lie, and Jardeleza was accorded sufficient opportunity to be heard under the Council's **sui generis** rules.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Inappropriateness of Certiorari: Under Rule 65, certiorari lies only against tribunals, boards, or officers exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions. The JBC is a screening and recommending body exercising neither.
 Inappropriateness of Mandamus: Mandamus lies only to compel ministerial duties, not discretionary choices. Selection and inclusion in a shortlist is entirely within the JBC's discretion; an applicant has no clear legal right to be nominated.
 No Deprivation of Due Process: Jardeleza was verbally notified twice by Justice Lagman and once by Secretary De Lima. He was summoned on June 30, 2014, and offered the floor to explain, but he willfully refused and demanded trial-type formalities to which he had no right.
 Rules are Directory: Sections 3 and 4 of Rule 4, JBC-009 use the permissive word "may." The JBC has full discretion whether to hold a hearing or accept written comments, and may rely on discreet background checks.
 Correct Application of the Unanimity Rule: Section 2, Rule 10 applies whenever integrity is challenged, even by a member. CJ Sereno's vote was not counted, meaning Jardeleza needed the unanimous vote of the remaining 5 members. Since he obtained only 4, he failed to surpass the required threshold.
 Conflict of Interest: Jardeleza sued respondents while retaining his post as Solicitor General, appearing against the very government bodies and officials he is sworn to defend under the Code of Professional Responsibility.
 Injunctive Relief Unconstitutional: A TRO cannot issue to halt the mandatory 90-day constitutional deadline for presidential appointments under Article VIII, Section 4(1).
### C. Respondent Executive Secretary's Arguments (Paquito N. Ochoa, Jr.)
**Main Thesis:** Section 2, Rule 10 of JBC-009 is unconstitutional and impairs the collegial nature of the JBC; consequently, Jardeleza should be deemed included in the shortlist.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Impairment of Collegiality: The unanimity rule gives a single member an absolute veto over the majority will, destroying the collegial structure intended by the framers to shield judicial appointments from political maneuvering.
 Violation of Due Process: The rule fails to provide any clear mechanism for an applicant to refute challenges to integrity, unlike other provisions of JBC rules.
 Alternative Construction: If valid, the unanimity rule applies only when an outsider raises the objection. When an insider JBC member objects, the general majority rule must apply; otherwise, voting is rendered an absurdity.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to review the acts of the JBC via a Petition for **Certiorari** and **Mandamus** under Rule 65.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the objections raised against petitioner Jardeleza qualify as "questions or challenges on integrity" within the contemplation of Section 2, Rule 10 of JBC-009.
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the constitutional right to procedural due process is available to an applicant in JBC nomination proceedings when an objection to his or her integrity is raised.
4.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not petitioner Jardeleza is entitled to be included in the shortlist of nominees submitted to the President.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Availability of Judicial Review, Certiorari, and Mandamus Against the JBC
**(a) Short Answer: PARTIALLY MERITORIOUS.** While **mandamus** does not lie to compel the discretionary act of nomination, **certiorari** is available under the Supreme Court’s supervisory power and its expanded judicial power under Article VIII, Section 1 of the Constitution to correct grave abuse of discretion, even if the JBC does not exercise judicial or quasi-judicial functions.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Supervisory Power over the JBC:** Under Article VIII, Section 8(1) of the 1987 Constitution, the JBC is placed "under the supervision of the Supreme Court." Supervision means oversight—ensuring that subordinate officers perform their duties and that governing laws and internal rules are strictly observed and complied with. When the JBC fails to follow its own rules, the Supreme Court, as supervising authority, can order compliance.
2.  **Mandamus is Inapplicable: Mandamus** lies solely to compel the performance of a ministerial duty where the petitioner possesses a clear, well-defined legal right. The evaluation, selection, and nomination of judicial candidates by the JBC are discretionary acts. No person has a vested or demandable legal right to be nominated or included in a judicial shortlist.
3.  **Certiorari under Expanded Judicial Power:** While traditional **certiorari** under Section 1 of Rule 65 requires that the respondent exercise judicial or quasi-judicial functions, the 1987 Constitution introduced the expanded concept of judicial power under Article VIII, Section 1, Paragraph 2.
4.  **Non-Judicial Bodies Subject to Scrutiny:** Settled jurisprudence (**Araullo v. Aquino III**) establishes that **certiorari** is an appropriate procedural vehicle to question the acts of any branch, agency, or instrumentality of the government tainted with grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction, regardless of whether that body exercises judicial, quasi-judicial, or ministerial functions. Constitutional boundaries cannot be evaded by hiding behind the JBC's non-adjudicative status.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"Supervising officials see to it that rules are followed, but they themselves do not lay down such rules, nor do they have the discretion to modify or replace them. If the rules are not observed, they may order the work done or redone, but only to conform to such rules. They may not prescribe their own manner of execution of the act. They have no discretion on this matter except to see to it that the rules are followed."
"It has been judicially settled that a petition for certiorari is a proper remedy to question the act of any branch or instrumentality of the government on the ground of grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction by any branch or instrumentality of the government, even if the latter does not exercise judicial, quasi-judicial or ministerial functions."
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:**
The Supreme Court ruled that an applicant cannot use **mandamus** to force the JBC to put his name on a shortlist because choosing nominees requires human discretion. However, an applicant can file a petition for **certiorari**. Under the 1987 Constitution, the Court has broad power to strike down grave abuse of discretion committed by any government agency, including the JBC, and the Court has explicit constitutional supervisory oversight to force the JBC to follow its own written rules.
Issue 2: Scope of "Questions on Integrity" Under Section 2, Rule 10 of JBC-009
**(a) Short Answer: NO as to the original legal strategy ground; YES as to the immorality and insider trading grounds.** A professional disagreement over legal tactics in handling a government arbitration case does not constitute a challenge to an applicant’s "integrity," whereas allegations of extra-marital affairs and insider trading directly implicate moral character and fitness.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Definition of "Integrity" in JBC-009:** In the rules of the JBC, "integrity" is equated to an applicant's sound moral character, honesty, incorruptibility, irreproachable conduct, and fidelity to ethical standards. It is a virtue of moral uprightness. Therefore, the exceptional "unanimity rule" under Section 2, Rule 10 applies strictly and exclusively when moral fitness is attacked, not when an applicant’s professional judgment is second-guessed.
2.  **Legal Tactics are Not Moral Deficiencies:** CJ Sereno's initial invocation of Rule 10 on June 5, 2014 was based on Jardeleza's adoption of a specific legal strategy regarding the exclusion of **Itu Aba** in the UNCLOS Memorial. Legal strategy falls within the professional discretion of counsel. Differences in legal opinion are normal in complex litigation.
3.  **Absence of Corrupt Motive:** There was no evidence that Jardeleza’s tactical preference was linked to corruption, pecuniary gain, treason, or an intentional scheme to compromise national interest. The President, as chief architect of foreign policy, voiced no dissatisfaction with Jardeleza's loyalty. To label an attorney's debatable choice of legal theory as an "act of disloyalty" or a deficiency of "integrity" is a gross misapplication of the rule.
4.  **Immorality and Insider Trading Qualify:** In contrast, the allegations regarding an illicit extra-marital affair and insider trading (raised by CJ Sereno on June 30, 2014) directly affect a person's moral rectitude and honesty. Deliberate illicit affairs flout ethical standards demanded of judges, and insider trading is a fraudulent market manipulation. These two specific grounds properly befit "questions on integrity" that would prima facie trigger Rule 10.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Stripped of a clear showing of gross neglect, iniquity, or immoral purpose, a strategy of a legal mind remains a legal tactic acceptable to some and deplorable to others. It has no direct bearing on his moral choices... To fall under Section 2, Rule 10 of JBC-009, there must be a showing that the act complained of is, at the least, linked to the moral character of the person and not to his judgment as a professional."
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:**
The Court held that an attorney's tactical choice in presenting a government lawsuit is a matter of professional discretion and legal judgment, not a moral failure. Calling a legal theory "disloyal" does not turn it into an issue of personal dishonesty. Thus, the JBC improperly used the legal strategy issue to trigger the unanimity rule. While allegations of an illicit affair and insider trading do relate directly to moral fitness, they were improperly sprung on the applicant at the very last minute.
Issue 3: Availability of Procedural Due Process in JBC Proceedings
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Although JBC proceedings are **sui generis** and do not require a trial-type hearing, an applicant is entitled to the minimum requirements of procedural due process—namely, adequate written notice of the specific charges and a reasonable opportunity and time to answer and defend oneself.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Sui Generis Nature Does Not Extinguish the Bill of Rights:** While the JBC is an investigatory, non-adjudicative screening body, its governmental actions directly impact an applicant's reputation, character, and standing. Similar to **sui generis** bar disciplinary proceedings, the exercise of discretion by the JBC does not strip an applicant of constitutional protections.
2.  **Due Process is Demandable as of Right:** The Court rejected the JBC's argument that according an applicant due process is merely permissive or directory. While the JBC has discretion regarding whether to receive oral witness testimony, the duty to observe basic fairness and allow an applicant to explain himself against specific attacks on his moral character is mandatory.
3.  **Interplay of JBC-009 and JBC-010:** The JBC's reliance on the permissive term "may" in Sections 3 and 4 of JBC-009 was superseded by the mandatory provisions of JBC-010. JBC-010 specifically commands that "any complaint or opposition... shall be in writing, under oath," and that the Secretary "shall furnish the candidate a copy," granting him five (5) days to file a written comment.
4.  Jardeleza was Denied Due Process: The JBC completely bypassed its own published rules in JBC-010:
No written, sworn opposition was ever filed by CJ Sereno or furnished to Jardeleza.
The phone calls from Justice Lagman and Secretary De Lima provided only vague, informal notices of an integrity objection without factual specifications.
The confidential legal memorandum (Annex J) was distributed to JBC members, but was never furnished to Jardeleza prior to the June 30 meeting.
The immorality and insider trading charges were sprung on Jardeleza for the first time during the June 30 meeting.
Summoning an applicant to an executive session to instantaneously answer unexpected, serious charges on the spot, under penalty of waiver, is not a meaningful opportunity to be heard; it is a surprise ambush.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"The fact that a proceeding is sui generis and is impressed with discretion, however, does not automatically denigrate an applicant’s entitlement to due process... What precisely set off the protest of lack of due process was the circumstance of requiring Jardeleza to appear before the Council and to instantaneously provide those who are willing to listen an intelligent defense. Was he given the opportunity to do so? The answer is yes, in the context of his physical presence during the meeting. Was he given a reasonable chance to muster a defense? No, because he was merely asked to appear in a meeting where he would be, right then and there, subjected to an inquiry."
"Where the denial of the fundamental right of due process is apparent, a decision rendered in disregard of that right is void for lack of jurisdiction."
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:**
The Supreme Court ruled that even though the JBC is not a trial court, it is still bound by the constitutional guarantee of due process and its own published rules in JBC-010. Calling an applicant on the phone, refusing to put charges in writing, hiding the evidence being used, and then demanding that he defend his life and career on the spot during a 10-minute meeting is a complete denial of due process. Due process requires fair notice in advance and adequate time to gather evidence and prepare a real response.
Issue 4: Inclusion of Petitioner Jardeleza in the Shortlist Transmitted to the President
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Because the unanimity rule was improperly invoked and applied in violation of due process, its invocation was legally void; consequently, Jardeleza's qualifying majority of four (4) affirmative votes entitled him to be deemed included in the shortlist.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Nullity of the Disqualification Process:** An administrative act performed in gross violation of a person's constitutional right to due process is legally void for lack of jurisdiction. Because the invocation of Section 2, Rule 10 was tainted by the violation of JBC-010 and the denial of due process, the unanimity requirement never legally became operative against Jardeleza.
2.  **Restoration of Majority Rule:** With the unanimity rule rendered inoperative, Jardeleza’s evaluation reverted to the general rule under Section 1, Rule 10 of JBC-009, which requires an affirmative vote of at least a majority of all JBC members.
3.  **Equal Treatment with Other Candidates:** During the June 30, 2014 voting, Jardeleza garnered four (4) affirmative votes out of the six voting members present. This was the exact same number of votes obtained by candidate Judge Reynaldo B. Daway, who was successfully shortlisted under the majority rule.
4.  **Remedy Narrowly Tailored to Presidential Deadline:** Since the 90-day constitutional deadline for the President to make the appointment was expiring on August 20, 2014 (the day following promulgation), remanding the case to the JBC for a re-hearing was impossible. Because a majority of the JBC had already determined Jardeleza to be qualified, the Court declared him deemed included in the shortlist submitted to the President.
5.  **Preservation of Presidential Prerogative:** The Court emphasized that ordering his inclusion in the shortlist is not an appointment or an endorsement of Jardeleza; it merely restores the President's full constitutional discretion to select from all legitimately qualified nominees.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Having been able to secure four (4) out of six (6) votes, the only conclusion left to propound is that a majority of the members of the JBC, nonetheless, found Jardeleza to be qualified for the position of Associate Justice and this grants him a rightful spot in the shortlist submitted to the President."
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:**
Because the JBC violated due process and misapplied its own rules, the special "unanimity rule" was declared void. Jardeleza had already earned 4 out of 6 votes—a clear majority, and the exact same score as another shortlisted candidate. Because the President's deadline to appoint was only 24 hours away, the Court did not waste time sending the case back. Instead, it declared Jardeleza officially added to the list, leaving the ultimate decision of whether to appoint him entirely up to the President.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Focus:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) (Composition, Powers, Selection Process, and Due Process Constraints).
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 State Power: The constitutional authority of the JBC to recommend nominees for judicial appointments (Article VIII, Section 8) and exercise discretion in vetting applicants.
 Constitutional Limitation: (1) The Supreme Court's constitutional power of supervision over the JBC (Art. VIII, Sec. 8[1]); (2) The Bill of Rights guarantee of Procedural Due Process (Art. III, Sec. 1); and (3) The Executive's unfettered appointing power (Art. VIII, Sec. 9).
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Test Applied:** Grave Abuse of Discretion Test under the Court's expanded judicial power (Article VIII, Section 1, Paragraph 2) coupled with the Minimum Requirements of Administrative Due Process (**Ang Tibay / Ledesma** doctrine).
**Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:**
 Actual Controversy: Present, because Jardeleza was excluded from the transmitted shortlist despite winning a majority vote.
 Locus Standi: Directly established; Jardeleza suffered direct personal and reputational injury by being disqualified for lack of "integrity."
 Mootness Exception: Although the shortlist had already been transmitted to Malacañang, the issue is not moot because the President had not yet appointed, and the controversy is capable of repetition yet evading review given the strict 90-day appointment window.
**Doctrinal Checklist & Elements Matrix:**
 Supervision vs. Control: The SC has administrative supervision over the JBC. Supervision is oversight—ensuring rules are complied with without replacing them. When the JBC breaches its rules (JBC-010), the Court can compel compliance.
 Integrity Requirement: Integrity in JBC-009 refers to moral character, rectitude, and ethical conduct. Professional differences in legal strategy cannot be converted into an integrity challenge.
 Procedural Due Process in JBC Settings:** Even in **sui generis screening proceedings, if an applicant's integrity/character is attacked, the JBC must provide: (1) Written notice of specific charges under oath (JBC-010); (2) Reasonable time and opportunity to respond; and (3) Access to evidence considered. An instantaneous summons to defend oneself on the spot is unconstitutional.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"): Sui generis**, Power of Supervision, Expanded Judicial Power, Unanimity Rule, Minimum Requirements of Due Process, Delimitation of Issues, **Nemo judex in sua causa**, Capricious and Whimsical.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (30-Second Recit):**
**Jardeleza v. Sereno** establishes that while the JBC possesses wide discretion in screening applicants, its proceedings are strictly subject to the Supreme Court's supervisory power and the constitutional due process clause. An applicant's professional legal strategy cannot be treated as an "integrity" issue to trigger the Rule 10 unanimity requirement. When an applicant’s moral integrity is challenged, the JBC must strictly comply with JBC-010 by providing written, sworn specifications and reasonable time to answer; springing verbal charges on an applicant in an executive session violates due process and voids the disqualification, restoring the applicant's standing based on the majority votes garnered.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
Separate Opinions Summary
**Leonardo-De Castro, J. (Concurring):** Emphasized that procedural fairness traces back to natural justice (**audi alteram partem** and **nemo judex in sua causa**). Under JBC-010, complaints must be in writing and under oath to ensure prior delimitation of issues. A JBC member cannot act as an oppositor and a judge at the same time without an egregious conflict of interest. If a member objects, she must submit a written opposition and completely inhibit from voting on all candidates for that vacancy. She proposed a "two-step voting process" where the Council must first vote by a majority on whether an integrity issue genuinely exists before subjecting an applicant to the unanimity rule.
**Brion, J. (Concurring):** Delivered a searing critique of CJ Sereno’s actions, characterizing them as a premeditated manipulation of the JBC to deal a mortal blow to Jardeleza's candidacy. Pointed out that the SC itself was prevented from submitting recommendees because of a misleading representation by CJ Sereno. Argued that Annex J (the classified legal memo) and the Supplemental Comment were improperly filed to assassinate Jardeleza's character when he could no longer answer within the presidential deadline. He maintained that once an investigation yields an opposition, it must be in writing. The violation of due process rendered the Rule 10 invocation void **ab initio**.
**Peralta, J. (Concurring):** Concurred in full with the **ponencia** and adopted the concurring opinions of Leonardo-De Castro and Brion, JJ., affirming that Jardeleza was unduly deprived of due process and the Court's supervisory authority over the JBC must be upheld.
**Leonen, J. (Dissenting):** Voted to dismiss the petition. Argued for judicial restraint, asserting that the JBC is an independent constitutional organ whose sole prerogative is to assess qualifications and fitness. No person has a vested right to be nominated; hence, the due process clause is not triggered in the same manner as a trial. The unanimity rule was collegially accepted and applied by the entire Council, as shown by the fact that all members signed the transmittal letter without dissent. Jardeleza was given a discreet forum to explain the national interest arbitration issue but stubbornly chose to stand on procedural technicalities. Mandamus cannot compel a discretionary act, and adding a nominee unfairly dilutes the chances of the other four shortlisted candidates who were not impleaded.
Fallo (Verbatim)
**WHEREFORE,** the petition is **GRANTED.** Accordingly, it is hereby declared that Solicitor General Francis H. Jardeleza is deemed **INCLUDED** in the shortlist submitted to the President for consideration as an Associate Justice of the Supreme Court vice Associate Justice Roberto A. Abad.

The Court further **DIRECTS** that the Judicial and Bar Council **REVIEW,** and **ADOPT,** rules relevant to the observance of due process in its proceedings, particularly JBC-009 and JBC-010, subject to the approval of the Court.

This Decision is immediately **EXECUTORY.**

Immediately notify the Office of the President of this Decision.

**SO ORDERED.**
Plain-Language Outcome
Petitioner Francis H. Jardeleza prevailed. The Supreme Court nullified his exclusion from the nomination list and declared him officially included in the shortlist submitted to President Benigno S. Aquino III for the Supreme Court seat vacated by Justice Abad. The Court ordered the JBC to immediately revise its internal rules to safeguard due process, and made its decision immediately executory so the President could consider Jardeleza before the midnight appointment deadline expired the following day.
