### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Villanueva v. Judicial and Bar Council**
**Full Official Caption:** Ferdinand R. Villanueva, Presiding Judge, MCTC, Compostela-New Bataan, Compostela Valley Province, Petitioner, vs. Judicial and Bar Council, Respondent
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 211833; April 7, 2015; 757 Phil. 534; En Banc; Ponente: Reyes, J.
**Voting Breakdown:** Concurring: Carpio, Velasco, Jr., Bersamin, Del Castillo, Perez, Mendoza, JJ.; Leonardo-De Castro and Peralta, JJ. (concurred and joined the separate opinion of Brion, J.); Separate Concurring Opinions: Brion, J., and Leonen, J.; Took No Part: Sereno, C.J., and Jardeleza, J.; On Leave: Villarama, Jr., and Perlas-Bernabe, JJ.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Petitioner:** Ferdinand R. Villanueva, incumbent Presiding Judge of the Municipal Circuit Trial Court (MCTC) of Compostela-New Bataan, Compostela Valley Province (a first-level court).
**Respondent:** Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), the constitutional body created under Article VIII, Section 8 of the 1987 Constitution tasked with the screening, selection, and nomination of appointees to the Philippine Judiciary.
**Intervening / Representing Counsel:** Office of the Solicitor General (OSG), representing respondent JBC and the government.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
The case was initiated directly before the Supreme Court through a verified Petition for Prohibition, Mandamus, Certiorari, and Declaratory Relief under Rules 65 and 63 of the Rules of Court, with a prayer for the issuance of a temporary restraining order (TRO) and/or writ of preliminary injunction. The petition assailed the JBC’s long-standing, unpublished administrative policy requiring incumbent judges of first-level courts to have at least five (5) years of service in their current positions before they can qualify as applicants for promotion to second-level courts (Regional Trial Courts).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) → Powers, Functions, and Qualifications of Members of the Judiciary
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Constitutional Law I → Bill of Rights → Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses; Judicial Review & Expanded Certiorari Jurisdiction
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional & Statutory Provisions:**
**Article VIII, Section 7, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Section 7. (1) No person shall be appointed Member of the Supreme Court or any lower collegiate court unless he is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines. A Member of the Supreme Court must be at least forty years of age, and must have been for fifteen years or more a judge of a lower court or engaged in the practice of law in the Philippines.
(2) Congress shall prescribe the qualifications of judges of lower courts, but no person may be appointed judge thereof unless he is a citizen of the Philippines and a member of the Philippine Bar.
(3) **A Member of the Judiciary must be a person of proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence.**"
**Article VIII, Section 8(1) & (5), 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Section 8. (1) **A Judicial and Bar Council is hereby created under the supervision of the Supreme Court** composed of the Chief Justice as **ex officio** Chairman, the Secretary of Justice, and a representative of the Congress as **ex officio** Members, a representative of the Integrated Bar, a professor of law, a retired Member of the Supreme Court, and a representative of the private sector.
xxx
(5) **The Council shall have the principal function of recommending appointees to the Judiciary.** It may exercise such other functions and duties as the Supreme Court may assign to it."
**Article VIII, Section 1, Paragraph 2, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Judicial power includes the duty of the courts of justice to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable, and **to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government.**"
**Section 10, Republic Act No. 8557 (Philippine Judicial Academy Act):**
"Section 10. As soon as PHILJA shall have been fully organized with the composition of its Corps of Professorial Lecturers and other personnel, **only participants who have completed the programs prescribed by the Academy and have satisfactorily complied with all the requirements incident thereto may be appointed or promoted to any position or vacancy in the Judiciary.**"
**Factual Trigger:**
Petitioner, an incumbent MCTC Judge with only one year on the bench but over ten years of private practice of law, applied for vacant Regional Trial Court (RTC) judgeships. The JBC excluded his name from the list of considered candidates pursuant to an unpublished internal policy disqualifying first-level court judges who have served less than five years in their posts, prompting petitioner to challenge the policy's constitutionality before the Supreme Court.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**September 18, 2012:** Ferdinand R. Villanueva was appointed as Presiding Judge of the Municipal Circuit Trial Court (MCTC), Compostela-New Bataan, Poblacion, Compostela Valley Province, Region XI (a first-level court).
**September 27, 2013:** Having served roughly one year on the first-level bench, Judge Villanueva filed applications with the JBC for vacant Presiding Judge positions in three second-level courts: Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 31, Tagum City; Branch 13, Davao City; and Branch 6, Prosperidad, Agusan Del Sur. He had more than ten years of total experience in the practice of law.
**December 18, 2013:** The JBC’s Office of Recruitment, Selection and Nomination officially informed Judge Villanueva via letter that he was excluded from the list of candidates for the applied RTC vacancies.
**December 18, 2013:** Judge Villanueva sent an electronic mail to the JBC seeking reconsideration of his exclusion and formally protesting the inclusion of other candidates who allegedly failed to pass the Prejudicature Program examination under Republic Act No. 8557.
**February 3, 2014:** The JBC Executive Officer informed Judge Villanueva by letter that the JBC **En Banc** had noted his protest and motion for reconsideration, but nonetheless upheld his exclusion pursuant to the JBC's long-standing policy requiring incumbent first-level court judges to serve in their positions for at least five (5) years before qualifying for promotion to second-level courts.
**April 2014:** Judge Villanueva filed a petition for prohibition, mandamus, certiorari, and declaratory relief before the Supreme Court against the JBC, seeking to declare the five-year service requirement unconstitutional, compel the JBC to evaluate his application, and enjoin the JBC from disqualifying applicants similarly situated.
**April 22, 2014:** The Supreme Court directed the JBC and the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) to file their respective Comments.
**Mid-2014:** The JBC and the OSG separately submitted their Comments, arguing that the petition suffered from fatal procedural defects and that the five-year policy was a valid, rational, and constitutional exercise of JBC's mandate to ascertain "proven competence."
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The JBC’s five-year experience requirement for first-level court judges seeking promotion to the RTC is unconstitutional, ultra vires, and void because the JBC has no constitutional authority to add qualifications beyond those set by the Constitution and Congress; further, the policy violates due process, equal protection, and social justice.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Impermissible Addition of Qualifications: The Constitution (Art. VIII, Sec. 7) and BP Blg. 129 establish the qualifications for RTC judges, requiring citizenship, bar membership, and 10 years of practice of law. The JBC cannot add an extra requirement of five years of service as a first-level judge.
 Equal Protection: The policy arbitrarily discriminates against first-level court judges with less than five years of service, creating an artificial classification not imposed on other lawyers who apply directly to the RTC after ten years of law practice.
 Procedural Due Process (Lack of Publication): The five-year policy was never published in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation, nor registered with the UP Law Center Office of the National Administrative Register (ONAR).
 Social Justice & Equal Opportunity: The policy violates Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution, which mandates equal employment opportunities.
 Mandatory Prejudicature Program: The JBC unlawfully relaxed Section 10 of RA 8557 by treating the Prejudicature Program as merely directory rather than mandatory.
B. Respondent's Arguments (JBC & OSG)
**Main Thesis:** The petition is procedurally improper, and the five-year rule is a valid, reasonable, and constitutional guideline adopted pursuant to the JBC's constitutional mandate to determine "proven competence."
**Specific Contentions:**
 Impropriety of Certiorari & Prohibition: The JBC is not a judicial or quasi-judicial body exercising adjudicatory functions, making Rule 65 certiorari and prohibition inapplicable.
 Impropriety of Mandamus: Mandamus lies only to compel ministerial duties. Recommending judicial nominees is a constitutional discretion, and no applicant has a demandable legal right to be shortlisted or promoted.
 Lack of Jurisdiction over Declaratory Relief: The Supreme Court lacks original jurisdiction over petitions for declaratory relief under Rule 63, which falls within the exclusive original jurisdiction of the RTC.
 Equal Protection Justified: The classification satisfies the rational basis test. First-level judges with at least five years of service possess proven judicial experience, demonstrated ability to manage court dockets, conversance with procedural rules, and established records of integrity, probity, and independence.
 Due Process Not Violated: The policy is an internal guideline implementing constitutional standards of competence. Publication in ONAR applies only to executive agencies under Book VII of the Administrative Code, which excludes the Judiciary and bodies under its supervision.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues
1. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the extraordinary remedies of certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, and declaratory relief are procedurally appropriate vehicles to assail the qualification policies of the Judicial and Bar Council before the Supreme Court.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the JBC has the constitutional authority to establish criteria and qualifications—such as the five-year service requirement for first-level court judges—beyond the minimum statutory and constitutional requirements for appointment to the judiciary.
3. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the JBC policy requiring five years of service as a first-level court judge violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Constitution.
4. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the JBC policy violates procedural due process for failure to comply with the legal publication requirements and registration with the ONAR.
5. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the JBC unlawfully neglected its duty by allegedly treating the Prejudicature Program under Section 10 of Republic Act No. 8557 as merely directory.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Propriety of the Procedural Vehicles (Certiorari, Prohibition, Mandamus, Declaratory Relief)
**(a) Short Answer: PARTIALLY MERITORIOUS.** Certiorari and prohibition are proper under the Court’s expanded judicial power and supervisory authority over the JBC; however, mandamus and declaratory relief do not lie.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Certiorari and Prohibition under Expanded Jurisdiction: Although Rule 65 traditionally applies exclusively to tribunals, boards, or officers exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions—which the JBC does not exercise—the Court's expanded jurisdiction under Article VIII, Section 1, paragraph 2 allows certiorari and prohibition to review and correct any grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction by any branch or instrumentality of government.
 Supervisory Authority of the Supreme Court: Article VIII, Section 8(1) places the JBC "under the supervision of the Supreme Court." Supervision is the power of oversight to see that subordinate officers perform their duties and comply with existing laws and their own rules. When JBC policies are attacked as unconstitutional or contrary to its rules, the Supreme Court has the affirmative duty to inquire into the matter.
 Mandamus is Improper: Mandamus lies strictly to compel a ministerial duty where the applicant has a clear legal right. The selection and recommendation of nominees by the JBC is purely discretionary. An applicant possesses no clear legal right to judicial nomination or promotion; nomination is a mere privilege, not a demandable right.
 Declaratory Relief is Improper: The Supreme Court has no original jurisdiction over petitions for declaratory relief under Rule 63. Pursuant to Section 19 of BP Blg. 129 as amended by RA 7691, exclusive original jurisdiction over declaratory relief resides with the Regional Trial Courts.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The fact that an individual possesses the constitutional and statutory qualifications for appointment to the Judiciary does not create an entitlement or expectation that his or her name be included in the list of candidates for a judicial vacancy. By submitting an application or accepting a recommendation, one submits to the authority of the JBC to subject the former to the search, screening, and selection process, and to use its discretion in deciding whether or not one should be included in the list."
**(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:**
A candidate cannot use mandamus to force the JBC to shortlist him because screening applicants is a discretionary function, and no one has a vested constitutional right to a judgeship. While declaratory relief was filed in the wrong court, the Supreme Court nevertheless took cognizance through certiorari and prohibition by invoking its expanded judicial power to check grave abuse of discretion, combined with its constitutional supervisory authority over the JBC.
Issue 2: Constitutional Power of JBC to Establish Qualification Policies
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The JBC has the constitutional authority to establish qualifying standards and policies to determine whether an applicant possesses "proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence."
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Incidental Powers to Effectuate Mandate: The principal constitutional function of the JBC is to recommend appointees to the judiciary (Art. VIII, Sec. 8[5]). The incidental functions of searching, screening, and selecting are indispensable to this constitutional duty.
 Minimum vs. Additional Criteria:** The qualifications set forth in Article VIII, Section 7 and statutory provisions are merely the **minimum legal qualifications. The Constitution expressly mandates in Section 7(3) that every member of the judiciary must be a person of "proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence."
 Necessity of Uniform Criteria: The Constitution did not prescribe the granular mechanics for evaluating these qualities. The JBC must inevitably possess the flexibility and discretion to set uniform guidelines to distinguish the best-qualified candidates from among numerous applicants who all meet the bare statutory minimums. Setting criteria like years of experience is directly incidental to determining "proven competence."
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"While the 1987 Constitution has provided the qualifications of members of the judiciary, this does not preclude the JBC from having its own set of rules and procedures and providing policies to effectively ensure its mandate. The functions of searching, screening, and selecting are necessary and incidental to the JBC's principal function of choosing and recommending nominees for vacancies in the judiciary for appointment by the President."
**(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:**
The constitutional and statutory qualifications for judges are only minimum baselines. The JBC is constitutionally tasked to ensure nominees possess "proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence," which necessarily gives it the implied and incidental power to formulate screening policies and guidelines to separate the mediocre from the best qualified.
Issue 3: Validity under the Equal Protection Clause
**(a) Short Answer: YES (The policy is valid).** The five-year experience requirement does not violate equal protection because it satisfies the rational basis test.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Standard of Review:** The policy neither burdens a fundamental constitutional right nor targets a suspect class. Consequently, the classification must be evaluated under the **rational basis test, where a classification stands if it rationally relates to a legitimate government end.
 Legitimate Government End: The legitimate state interest is ensuring an effective, competent, and efficient administration of justice by populating the second-level bench with thoroughly tested and capable judges.
 Rational Relationship & Substantial Distinctions: Substantial distinctions exist between first-level judges with at least five years on the bench and those with less. Five years provides a tangible, verifiable track record showing an applicant's ability to manage dockets, apply procedural rules under trial pressure, craft well-reasoned decisions, and maintain irreproachable ethical conduct. It is difficult or premature to reliably assess judicial merit and stamina in an applicant with less than a year on the bench.
 Non-Exclusivity: Five years of judicial service is not an automatic ticket to nomination; it is merely a threshold screening tool used alongside comprehensive evaluations of individual merit.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Clearly, the classification created by the challenged policy satisfies the rational basis test. The foregoing shows that substantial distinctions do exist between lower court judges with five year experience and those with less than five years of experience, like the petitioner, and the classification enshrined in the assailed policy is reasonable and relevant to its legitimate purpose. The Court, thus, rules that the questioned policy does not infringe on the equal protection clause as it is based on reasonable classification intended to gauge the proven competence of the applicants."
**(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:**
The five-year rule easily passes the rational basis test because five years on the municipal bench gives the JBC a demonstrable track record to evaluate an applicant's speed, case management, and ethical endurance. It does not unfairly discriminate; it reasonably distinguishes judges with proven judicial stamina from newly appointed ones whose judicial competence is still untested.
Issue 4: Validity under Procedural Due Process and the Publication Requirement
**(a) Short Answer: PARTIALLY MERITORIOUS.** The policy is not void for lack of ONAR filing, but it is unenforceable against the public and prospective applicants without prior general publication. However, this failure did not prejudice petitioner because he has no vested right to a nomination.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Exemption from ONAR: Book VII of the Administrative Code of 1987 (requiring filing with the UP Law Center ONAR) explicitly applies only to executive branch agencies. Under Section 1 thereof, the Judiciary and bodies under its supervision—such as the JBC—are expressly excluded.
 Applicability of Tañada v. Tuvera:** Under the doctrine in **Tañada v. Tuvera, all statutes and administrative rules implementing or enforcing existing laws must be published in full to attain binding force. The only exceptions are purely internal regulations governing agency staff and interpretative circulars.
 Not a Purely Internal Rule: The JBC qualification policy directly affects prospective applicants across the legal profession and judiciary. It sets an external qualifying standard implementing the constitutional requirement of "proven competence." Therefore, the policy cannot be classified as a mere internal rule; it must be formally published in a newspaper of general circulation or the Official Gazette.
 Lack of Prejudice to Petitioner: Despite the lack of prior publication, the petition must still be dismissed because petitioner suffered no legal injury. Inclusion in the JBC shortlist is a mere privilege, not a property right or enforceable entitlement protected by due process.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Here, the assailed JBC policy does not fall within the administrative rules and regulations exempted from the publication requirement. The assailed policy involves a qualification standard by which the JBC shall determine proven competence of an applicant. It is not an internal regulation, because if it were, it would regulate and affect only the members of the JBC and their staff."
**(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:**
The JBC does not have to file rules with ONAR because it is part of the Judiciary, not the Executive. However, because its five-year rule sets qualification standards that affect potential applicants nationwide, **Tañada v. Tuvera** dictates that it must be published in a newspaper of general circulation or the Official Gazette. Even so, the Judge cannot demand his inclusion on this ground because judicial nomination is a privilege, not a vested property right.
Issue 5: Compliance with Republic Act No. 8557 (Prejudicature Program) and Social Justice Provisions
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Petitioner completely failed to substantiate his claim that the JBC neglected its legal duty under RA 8557 or violated social justice.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Unsubstantiated Allegations: Petitioner presented no factual evidence demonstrating that the JBC systematically waived or unlawfully neglected the Prejudicature Program requirement under Section 10 of RA 8557. Bare allegations carry no evidentiary weight.
 Social Justice and Equal Employment (Art. XIII, Sec. 3): The constitutional guarantee of equal opportunity for employment does not mean that every person who applies for public office must be appointed or nominated. The bench is a high constitutional office subject to rigorous state regulation and screening in the public interest.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The constitutional provision does not call for appointment to the Judiciary of all who might, for any number of reasons, wish to apply. As with all professions, it is regulated by the State. The office of a judge is no ordinary office. It is imbued with public interest and is central in the administration of justice..."
**(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:**
The claim regarding the Prejudicature Program was dismissed because the petitioner offered zero proof that the JBC ignored the law. Furthermore, the constitutional guarantee of equal employment opportunities does not mean everyone who applies for a judgeship must be shortlisted; the State has every right to subject judicial applicants to rigorous screening to protect the public interest.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | 4. The Judicial and Bar Council | Applied Lens: Constitutional & Political Law
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 Power Exercised: The constitutional mandate of the Judicial and Bar Council under Article VIII, Section 8 to search, screen, and select candidates and formulate qualification criteria to ascertain "proven competence" for appointment to the judiciary.
 Constitutional Guarantees Invoked: The Bill of Rights guarantees of Equal Protection and Procedural Due Process (Art. III, Sec. 1), the constitutional enumeration of judicial qualifications (Art. VIII, Sec. 7), and the Social Justice clause on equal work opportunities (Art. XIII, Sec. 3).
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
 Rational Basis Test: Applied to evaluate the classification created by the JBC policy. Because judicial appointment is a privilege and not a fundamental right, and first-level court judges are not a suspect class, the classification needs only to be rationally related to a legitimate state objective (i.e., fielding tested, experienced, and competent judges on the second-level bench).
**Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:**
 Actual Case or Controversy: Present; an applicant was excluded from a selection list based on an existing policy.
 Locus Standi: Present; petitioner sustained direct injury by his exclusion from consideration.
 Expanded Certiorari / Supervisory Power: The JBC does not exercise judicial or quasi-judicial functions under traditional Rule 65. Cognizance was justified by combining the Court's expanded certiorari jurisdiction under Article VIII, Section 1(2) (to check grave abuse of discretion by any government branch/instrumentality) with its general supervisory power over the JBC under Article VIII, Section 8(1).
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Proven Competence (Art. VIII, Sec. 7[3])
 Supervisory Authority vs. Control (Supervision is oversight to ensure compliance with rules, without substituting judgment)
 Rational Basis Test (Requires only reasonable classification and legitimate government objective)
 Incidental Powers (Power to screen and set criteria is incidental to the primary duty to recommend)
 Privilege, not a Demandable Right (Characterization of judicial nomination and promotion)
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
This case falls under the Judicial and Bar Council topic because it defines the scope of the JBC’s power to formulate qualification criteria beyond the minimum qualifications listed in the Constitution. The Supreme Court ruled that the JBC has the incidental constitutional authority under Article VIII to set policies—such as requiring five years of service on the first-level bench—to test an applicant's "proven competence." The policy is valid under the rational basis test of the Equal Protection Clause; however, because it sets an external qualification standard rather than an internal staff rule, the JBC is required under **Tañada v. Tuvera** to publish it before implementation.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Brion, J. (Concurring):** Elaborated extensively on the dual jurisdictional bases. Emphasized that the Court exercised its expanded certiorari jurisdiction (testing for grave abuse of discretion and finding none) and its distinct, constitutional general supervisory power over the JBC (Art. VIII, Sec. 8). General supervision is not limited to mere administrative oversight; it empowers the Court to supervise JBC's adherence to the Constitution and its own rules, and to direct the JBC to publish its regulations. Recourse under supervisory power is independent of traditional actual controversies.
**Leonen, J. (Concurring):** Maintained that Rule 65 certiorari, prohibition, and mandamus were completely improper because the JBC exercises neither judicial, quasi-judicial, nor ministerial functions. Mandamus cannot compel discretionary selection. Pointed out that petitioner had no vested legal right and failed to present a justiciable controversy. Stressed that the JBC must be afforded wide constitutional leeway to screen applicants, and that imposing a five-year requirement on first-level judges is entirely reasonable.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, premises considered, the petition is DISMISSED. The Court, however, DIRECTS that the Judicial and Bar Council comply with the publication requirement of (1) the assailed policy requiring five years of experience as judges of first-level courts before they can qualify as applicant to the Regional Trial Court, and (2) other special guidelines that the Judicial and Bar Council is or will be implementing.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Judge Villanueva lost his petition; his exclusion from the RTC nomination shortlist stood, and the five-year service policy was declared constitutional. However, the Supreme Court ordered the JBC to officially publish the five-year policy, as well as all other special qualifying guidelines it currently enforces or plans to implement in the future, in order to satisfy the constitutional requirement of due process and legal notice to prospective applicants.

digest:
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Ifurung v. Carpio Morales**
**Full Official Caption:** Rey Nathaniel C. Ifurung, Petitioner, vs. Hon. Conchita C. Carpio Morales in her capacity as the Ombudsman, Hon. Melchor Arthur H. Carandang, Hon. Gerard Abeto Mosquera, Hon. Paul Elmer M. Clemente, Hon. Rodolfo M. Elman, Hon. Cyril Enguerra Ramos in their capacities as Deputies Ombudsman, and the Office of the Ombudsman, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 232131; April 24, 2018; 831 Phil. 135; En Banc; Martires, **J.** (Voting Breakdown: Unanimous; Carpio [**Acting C.J.**], Velasco, Jr., Leonardo-De Castro, Peralta, Bersamin, Del Castillo, Perlas-Bernabe, Leonen, Jardeleza, Caguioa, Tijam, Reyes, and Gesmundo, **JJ.**, concur; Sereno, **C.J.**, on leave; no separate opinions filed).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Rey Nathaniel C. Ifurung (Petitioner):** Private practitioner suing **in propria persona** as a taxpayer, concerned Filipino citizen, and member of the Philippine Bar.
**Hon. Conchita C. Carpio Morales (Respondent):** Incumbent Ombudsman of the Republic of the Philippines.
**Hon. Melchor Arthur H. Carandang (Respondent):** Incumbent Overall Deputy Ombudsman.
**Hon. Gerard Abeto Mosquera (Respondent):** Incumbent Deputy Ombudsman for Luzon.
**Hon. Paul Elmer M. Clemente (Respondent):** Incumbent Deputy Ombudsman for Visayas.
**Hon. Rodolfo M. Elman (Respondent):** Incumbent Deputy Ombudsman for Mindanao.
**Hon. Cyril Enguerra Ramos (Respondent):** Incumbent Deputy Ombudsman for the Military and Other Law Enforcement Offices (MOLEO).
**Office of the Ombudsman (Respondent Public Office):** The independent constitutional body created under Article XI of the 1987 Constitution.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Original Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition under Rule 65 of the Rules of Court filed directly with the Supreme Court, challenging the constitutionality of Section 8(3), in relation to Section 7, of Republic Act No. 6770 (The Ombudsman Act of 1989), and praying to declare all individual respondents as **de facto** officers whose terms expired on February 1, 2015.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Constitutional Commissions → Common Provisions (Distinction between Constitutional Commissions under Art. IX and the Office of the Ombudsman under Art. XI).
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Judicial Review → Standing & Exceptions to Hierarchy of Courts; Public Officers → Term and Tenure.
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional & Statutory Provisions:**
**1987 Constitution, Article XI, Section 10:**
"The Ombudsman and his Deputies shall have the rank of Chairman and Members, respectively, of the Constitutional Commissions, and they shall receive the same salary, which shall not be decreased during their term of office."
**1987 Constitution, Article XI, Section 11:**
"The Ombudsman and his Deputies shall serve for a term of seven years without reappointment. They shall not be qualified to run for any office in the election immediately succeeding their cessation from office."
**1987 Constitution, Article IX(A) (Common Provisions), Section 1:**
"The Constitutional Commissions, which shall be independent, are the Civil Service Commission, the Commission on Elections, and the Commission on Audit."
**1987 Constitution, Article IX(B), Section 1(2):**
"The Chairman and the Commissioners shall be appointed by the President with the consent of the Commission on Appointments for a term of seven years without reappointment. Of those first appointed, the Chairman shall hold office for seven years, a Commissioner for five years, and another Commissioner for three years, without reappointment. **Appointment to any vacancy shall be only for the unexpired term of the predecessor.** In no case shall any Member be appointed or designated in a temporary or acting capacity." **(Identical rotational and unexpired term restrictions appear in Art. IX[C], Sec. 1[2] for COMELEC and Art. IX[D], Sec. 1[2] for COA).**
**Republic Act No. 6770 (Ombudsman Act of 1989), Section 7:**
"Section 7. **Term of Office.** — The Ombudsman and his Deputies, including the Special Prosecutor, shall serve for a term of seven (7) years without reappointment."
**Republic Act No. 6770, Section 8(3):**
"Section 8. **Removal; Filling of Vacancy.** —
x x x
(3) In case of vacancy in the Office of the Ombudsman due to death, resignation, removal or permanent disability of the incumbent Ombudsman, the Overall Deputy shall serve as Acting Ombudsman in a concurrent capacity **until a new Ombudsman shall have been appointed for a full term.**
In case the Overall Deputy cannot assume the role of Acting Ombudsman, the President may designate any of the Deputies, or the Special Prosecutor, as Acting Ombudsman."
**Factual Trigger:**
Following the resignation of former Ombudsman Merceditas Gutierrez in May 2011 (whose predecessor Simeon Marcelo had also resigned mid-term in 2005), President Benigno Aquino III appointed Conchita Carpio Morales as Ombudsman on July 25, 2011, for a full 7-year term ending in 2018 pursuant to Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770. Petitioner filed this action claiming that, like the staggered terms of the Constitutional Commissions interpreted in **Gaminde v. COA**, the term of the Ombudsman was permanently fixed to recurring 7-year cycles starting from February 2, 1987; hence, any successor could only serve the unexpired portion of the term (which expired February 1, 2015), making Carpio Morales and her deputies **de facto** officers overstaying past their lawful terms.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**May 1950 to January 1966:** Various presidential integrity and anti-graft bodies are sequentially formed and abolished by executive orders (President Quirino's Integrity Board; President Magsaysay's PCAC; President Garcia's PCAPE; President Macapagal's PAGC; President Marcos's PARGO).
**1969:** Congress enacts R.A. No. 6028 creating the Office of the Citizens Counselor.
**January 17, 1973:** The 1973 Constitution is ratified, providing under Section 6, Article XIII for the creation of an independent Ombudsman known as the **Tanodbayan**.
**June 11, 1978:** President Marcos issues P.D. No. 1487 creating the Tanodbayan, explicitly providing in Section 6(b) that if the office becomes vacant for any cause, an acting deputy serves until a new Tanodbayan is appointed for a **full term**. This rule is reenacted verbatim in P.D. No. 1607 (December 10, 1978) and P.D. No. 1630 (July 18, 1979).
**February 2, 1987:** The 1987 Constitution takes effect, providing in Section 11, Article XI that the Ombudsman and Deputies shall serve for a term of seven years without reappointment.
**July 24, 1987:** President Corazon C. Aquino issues Executive Order No. 243 pursuant to Section 6, Article XVIII (transitory legislative powers), setting the organizational framework of the Office of the Ombudsman and providing in Section 6 that the Ombudsman and Deputies shall have the rank and salary of Chairman and Members of Constitutional Commissions.
**May 1988:** Conrado M. Vasquez is appointed as the first Ombudsman under the 1987 Constitution, serving until May 1995.
**November 17, 1989:** Congress enacts R.A. No. 6770. Section 8(3) provides that any successor appointed due to death, resignation, removal, or permanent disability of the Ombudsman shall be appointed for a **full term** of seven years.
**August 4, 1995:** Aniano A. Desierto is appointed Ombudsman, serving until August 3, 2002.
**October 10, 2002:** Simeon V. Marcelo is appointed Ombudsman, but resigns in November 2005 before finishing his 7-year term.
**December 1, 2005:** Ma. Merceditas Navarro-Gutierrez is appointed Ombudsman. She resigns effective May 6, 2011, during her term.
**July 25, 2011:** Conchita Carpio Morales is appointed Ombudsman to a fresh 7-year term pursuant to Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770. Deputies Carandang, Mosquera, Clemente, Elman, and Ramos are appointed to their respective deputy positions for full 7-year terms.
**February 1, 2015:** According to petitioner's theoretical schedule of recurring 7-year cycles originating from February 2, 1987, the supposed fourth 7-year cycle of the Ombudsman ends.
**July 2017:** Rey Nathaniel C. Ifurung files the instant petition for certiorari and prohibition before the Supreme Court seeking the nullification of Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770 and the ouster of respondents as overstaying **de facto** officers.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770 unconstitutionally grants a fresh 7-year full term to newly appointed Ombudsmen and Deputies upon a mid-term vacancy, directly violating Section 11 in relation to Sections 8 and 10 of Article XI of the 1987 Constitution; all respondents are **de facto** officers whose lawful unexpired terms ended on February 1, 2015.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Intent to Equalize Status: The framers intended to elevate the Office of the Ombudsman to the same stature, clout, and independence as the three Constitutional Commissions (CSC, COMELEC, COA) and the CHR.
 Application of Gaminde Doctrine:** Under **Gaminde v. COA, the terms of all constitutional bodies uniformly started on February 2, 1987. The Ombudsman cannot be an exception. Successors appointed upon mid-term vacancies are limited strictly to the unexpired term of the predecessor.
 General Constitutional Architecture:** All constitutionally created offices (President, Vice President, Senators, District Representatives, and Commissioners) only allow successors to serve unexpired terms. The Ombudsman is not **sui generis.
 Prevention of Executive Abuse: Allowing a fresh 7-year term allows an outgoing President to execute midnight or strategic appointments, tying the hands of the incoming President.
 Proscription on Acting Appointments: Section 8(3)'s designation of the Overall Deputy as Acting Ombudsman violates the express command in Article IX that in no case shall any member be appointed in an acting capacity.
 Procedural Propriety:** Direct resort via Rule 65 is warranted due to the transcendental importance of determining the correct tenure of constitutional guardians, which justifies bypassing the hierarchy of courts. Standing exists as a taxpayer and concerned citizen protesting illegal disbursement of public salaries to **de facto officers.
B. Respondents' Arguments (via Office of the Solicitor General)
**Main Thesis:** Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770 is wholly consistent with Section 11, Article XI of the 1987 Constitution, which prescribes a plain 7-year term without distinction or provision for staggered rotational replacements; the petition is procedurally fatal as an improper collateral attack on title to office.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Verba Legis and No Distinction:** Section 11, Article XI states that the Ombudsman and Deputies shall serve for seven years without reappointment. Unlike Article IX, it contains no clause restricting appointments in case of vacancies to the unexpired term. **Ubi lex non distinguit nec nos distinguere debemus.
 Ombudsman is Not a Collegial Body: The Constitutional Commissions require staggered expiration intervals (7-5-3 years) to preserve collegiality and prevent one President from packing the body. The Office of the Ombudsman is not collegial; each deputy has separate territorial or sectoral jurisdiction, making rotational staggered appointments structurally impossible.
 Gaminde Inapplicable:** The **Gaminde fixed-base date (February 2, 1987) was established exclusively to safeguard the operational cycle of collegial Constitutional Commissions under Article IX.
 Rank and Salary vs. Term: Section 10, Article XI equalizes the Ombudsman only in "rank" and "salary" with the Chair of a Constitutional Commission for classification purposes, which does not encompass tenure or term limits.
 Improper Remedy:** Certiorari and prohibition cannot be used to unseat public officers on title; the exclusive remedy is **quo warranto** under Rule 66 initiated by the Solicitor General or public prosecutor (**Topacio v. Ong).
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not a Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition under Rule 65 is the proper remedy to assail Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770 and challenge respondents' title to office.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to take direct cognizance of the petition despite the doctrine of hierarchy of courts and the non-joinder of indispensable parties.
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770 is unconstitutional for providing a full 7-year term to an Ombudsman or Deputy appointed to fill a vacancy, in alleged contravention of Section 11, in relation to Sections 8 and 10, Article XI of the 1987 Constitution and the **Gaminde** doctrine governing Constitutional Commissions.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Propriety of the Remedy (Certiorari/Prohibition vs. Quo Warranto)
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Certiorari and prohibition under Rule 65, pursuant to the Court's expanded judicial power under Section 1, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution, is the proper remedy because the petition directly mounts a facial constitutional attack on a statute rather than an individualized qualification contest.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**   The OSG's reliance on **Topacio v. Ong** is misplaced. In **Topacio, the petitioner collaterally attacked an Associate Justice's title to office based strictly on his personal citizenship qualifications under Section 7, Article VIII. Here, petitioner does not dispute the individual qualifications of Morales or the deputies under Section 8, Article XI.
Instead, the petition directly attacks the constitutionality of a legislative enactment—Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770. Petitioner claims Congress exceeded constitutional parameters established in Article XI.
**   Under the expanded concept of judicial power (Section 1, Article VIII), petitions for certiorari and prohibition are appropriate vehicles to correct grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction by any branch or instrumentality of the government, including legislative and executive acts, whenever a positive constitutional infringement is seriously alleged (**Tañada v. Angara**, **Araullo v. Aquino).
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Clear from his petition was that the petitioner beseeches the Court for a declaration primarily as to the unconstitutionality of Sec. 8(3) in relation to Sec. 7 of R.A. No. 6770, and as a consequence thereof, a pronouncement that the incumbent Ombudsman and the deputies are **de facto** officers and whose offices are vacant. The petition does not task the Court to scrutinize the qualification of the respondents to hold office as Ombudsman and deputies but rather to determine the constitutionality of Sec. 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770 in so far as their term of office is concerned."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** An action that challenges whether a law itself complies with the Constitution is an attack on the statute, not a collateral attack on the appointee's title. **Quo warranto** tests personal qualifications (like citizenship or age), whereas Rule 65 under the Court's expanded jurisdiction tests whether the Legislature acted unconstitutionally in establishing the term of the office.
Issue 2: Jurisdiction, Hierarchy of Courts, Standing, and Indispensable Parties
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The Court properly assumed original jurisdiction because the petition presents an actual, ripe controversy of transcendental importance that falls squarely within the established exceptions to the doctrine of hierarchy of courts; standing is recognized due to alleged unconstitutional expenditure of public funds.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Requisites of Judicial Review Met:** (1) **Actual Controversy & Ripeness:** If petitioner's theory is correct, incumbent respondents have unlawfully overstayed since February 2015, resulting in unauthorized official acts and illegal continuous disbursements of public funds to pay their salaries. (2) **Locus Standi:** Under **Funa v. Villar, procedural standing is relaxed for taxpayers alleging illegal disbursements and concerned citizens raising issues of transcendental importance.
 Hierarchy of Courts Relaxed:** While adherence to the hierarchy of courts is ordinarily mandatory (**Bañez v. Concepcion**), direct resort to the Supreme Court is permitted under well-established exceptions (**Diocese of Bacolod v. COMELEC): where genuine issues of constitutionality must be resolved immediately, cases of first impression exist, public welfare demands it, and the acts of a constitutional organ are challenged.
 Non-Joinder of Parties Curable: Although petitioner failed to implead the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), Congress, or the Office of the President, the OSG entered its appearance and robustly represented the legal interests and constitutionality of the enactments on behalf of the government, fully satisfying due process.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The Court holds that the present petition involves an actual case or controversy and that the same is ripe for judicial determination... Of prime consideration, too, if petitioner's position is correct, is the alleged pervasive noncompliance and non-observance of the constitution relative to the seven-year term of office of the Ombudsman and the deputies... It should likewise be taken into account... that there are continuing illegal disbursements of public funds to pay the salaries of the **de facto** Ombudsman and deputies."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Even though the Supreme Court shares concurrent jurisdiction with lower courts over Rule 65 petitions, it will entertain direct filings when the dispute involves the constitutional legitimacy of a high constitutional body, involves taxpayers protesting continuous illegal salary disbursements, and presents questions of transcendental legal importance that lower courts cannot authoritatively resolve.
Issue 3: Constitutionality of Section 8(3), R.A. No. 6770 (The 7-Year Full Term)
**(a) Short Answer: NO, the provision is NOT unconstitutional.** Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770 is fully constitutional. The Office of the Ombudsman is structurally distinct from the Constitutional Commissions; it is not a collegial body and does not operate under a staggered rotational system. Successors are entitled to a full 7-year term.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Presumption of Constitutionality:** A legislative measure is presumed valid unless shown to palpably breach the fundamental law beyond reasonable doubt (**Estrada v. Sandiganbayan).
 Ombudsman is Not an Article IX Constitutional Commission: Article IX, Section 1 expressly enumerates only three independent Constitutional Commissions: CSC, COMELEC, and COA. These bodies are strictly **collegial** (they decide by majority vote under Art. IX[A], Sec. 7) and are structured around a synchronized rotational cycle (staggered 7-5-3 year terms for the first appointees) with an express command: **"Appointment to any vacancy shall be only for the unexpired term of the predecessor."** In sharp contrast, the Office of the Ombudsman (governed by Article XI) is **not a collegial body**. The Ombudsman and Deputies have separate, independent geographic and sectoral jurisdictions (Luzon, Visayas, Mindanao, MOLEO, Special Prosecutor).
 Gaminde Inapplicable:** The doctrine in **Gaminde v. COA**, fixing the starting base line to February 2, 1987, exists exclusively to preserve the mathematical rotational plan (a vacancy occurring every two years to prevent a single President from appointing the majority of a collegial board). Because the Ombudsman has no rotational system and no collegial board, the **Gaminde rationale is entirely inapplicable.
 Plain Meaning of "Rank and Salary" (Verba Legis):** Section 10, Article XI states that the Ombudsman and Deputies have the "rank of Chairman and Members, respectively, of the Constitutional Commissions, and they shall receive the same salary." The Records of the Constitutional Commission reveal that this clause was intended purely as an administrative benchmark for government salary grade classification. Under **expressio unius est exclusio alterius** and **casus omissus pro omisso habendus est, the express mention of "rank" and "salary" necessarily excludes "term of office."
 Section 11, Article XI Stands Alone:** Section 11 unequivocally provides: **"The Ombudsman and his Deputies shall serve for a term of seven years without reappointment."** It does not contain an "unexpired term" proviso. Where the organic law does not distinguish between a regular expiration vacancy and an involuntary mid-term vacancy, the courts cannot introduce one (**ubi lex non distinguit nec nos distinguere debemus).
 Historical Precedents Confirm Full Term: Under the 1973 Constitution, P.D. No. 1487, P.D. No. 1607, and P.D. No. 1630 all expressly declared in Section 6(b) that upon a vacancy for any cause, an acting official serves until a successor is appointed for a **full term**. Congress merely codified this continuous legislative and constitutional tradition when it enacted Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770.
 Article IX Temporary Appointment Ban Inapplicable: Petitioner’s memorandum argument that an "Acting Ombudsman" violates Article IX's prohibition against temporary appointments fails because that specific prohibition governs only the Constitutional Commissions under Article IX, not Article XI officers.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Unlike the constitutional commissions in the 1973 and 1987 Constitutions, the Ombudsman and the deputies do not make a collegial body thus, making it implausible to apply the regular rotation or cycle in its membership... Granting that the regular rotation applies to the Office of the Ombudsman and that the first appointed Ombudsman shall enjoy a seven-year term, then these queries are posed: Will the seven-year term likewise apply to the first appointed deputies? Who among the first appointed deputies shall take the five-year term? Or the three-year term? Obviously, the 1987 Constitution does not provide the answers plainly because there is nothing specific in the fundamental law that provides for the regular rotation of seven-five-three-year term of office in the Office of the Ombudsman."

"Harmonizing Sec. 11, Art. XI of the 1987 Constitution with Sec. 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770, in any vacancy for the positions of Ombudsman and the deputies, whether as a result of the expiration of the term or death, resignation, removal, or permanent disability of the predecessor, the successor shall always be appointed for a **full term of seven years**."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The unexpired-term rule in **Gaminde** applies only to the three Constitutional Commissions (CSC, COMELEC, COA) because they are collegial bodies designed with staggered 7-5-3 year terms to ensure regular rotational cycles. Because the Office of the Ombudsman is an Article XI non-collegial office without a rotational schedule, its constitutional 7-year term does not restart on fixed historical calendar cycles; whenever an Ombudsman leaves office prematurely, the newly appointed successor is entitled by law and Constitution to a fresh, complete 7-year term.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Assigned Syllabus Topic: The Constitutional Commissions - Common Provisions.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Comparative Checklist (Art. IX Commissions vs. Art. XI Ombudsman):**
 Exclusivity of Art. IX Identity: Art. IX, Sec. 1 establishes only three Constitutional Commissions (CSC, COMELEC, COA). The Ombudsman is created under Art. XI (Accountability of Public Officers).
 Collegiality Test:** Art. IX Commissions must decide cases by a majority vote of all members (**en banc collegiality). The Office of the Ombudsman is non-collegial; each deputy has separate jurisdiction and the Ombudsman exercises singular hierarchy.
 Rotational Plan Requisites (Republic v. Imperial):** Staggered terms require: (1) terms of first appointees start on a fixed common date, and (2) mid-term vacancies are filled **only for the unexpired portion. Present in Art. IX; completely absent in Art. XI.
 Temporary/Acting Appointment Prohibition: Art. IX expressly prohibits designating members in an acting capacity. Art. XI contains no such prohibition, making Section 8(3)'s Acting Ombudsman designation lawful.
 Constitutional Limitation Borrowing:** Art. XI, Sec. 10 borrows **only** the "rank and salary" from Art. IX; it does **not adopt the Art. IX structural term limitations.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Collegial body
 Rotational system of appointment / Staggered terms (7-5-3 year intervals)
 Unexpired term of the predecessor
 Verba legis non est recedendum (from the words of a statute there should be no departure)
 Expressio unius est exclusio alterius (express mention of one excludes others)
 Casus omissus pro omisso habendus est (a thing omitted is intentionally omitted)
 Ubi lex non distinguit nec nos distinguere debemus (where the law does not distinguish, we should not distinguish)
 De facto officer
**Constitutional & Political Law Analytical Directives:**
 State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation: Plenary legislative power of Congress under Article VI to enact Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770 versus the constitutional checks on term lengths in Section 11, Article XI.
 Level of Judicial Scrutiny:** Strong presumption of constitutionality (**"To doubt is to sustain"); statute upheld as having a clear reasonable and historical basis.
 Justiciability & Review Audit:
 Actual Case:** Ripe due to imminent claims of **de facto tenure and active public disbursements.
 Standing:** Relaxed via citizen/taxpayer standing under **Funa v. Villar due to transcendental importance.
 Hierarchy of Courts:** Direct resort permitted under **Diocese of Bacolod exceptions.
 Lis Mota: The constitutionality of Section 8(3) was inescapable because petitioner's request to unseat respondents depended entirely on whether Section 8(3) was void.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"This case is placed under the Constitutional Commissions because it delineates the precise boundary between the common provisions of Article IX and other constitutional offices. The Supreme Court held that the unexpired-term rule and staggered rotational cycles set in **Gaminde v. COA** apply exclusively to the three collegial Constitutional Commissions (CSC, COMELEC, and COA). Because the Office of the Ombudsman under Article XI is non-collegial and its constitutional text does not provide for staggered expirations, Congress acted within its constitutional bounds when it enacted Section 8(3) of R.A. No. 6770, granting every newly appointed Ombudsman and Deputy a fresh, full 7-year term upon assuming a vacancy."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed. (Acting Chief Justice Antonio T. Carpio and twelve other Associate Justices concurred without separate writing; Chief Justice Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno was on leave).
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is DISMISSED.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court dismissed the petition for lack of merit, expressly upholding the constitutionality of Section 8(3) of Republic Act No. 6770. Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales and her deputies were declared legitimate, **de jure** public officers lawfully serving their respective, full seven-year terms from their individual dates of appointment, and were not overstaying in office.
