### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: CSC v. Sojor**
**Full Official Caption:** The Civil Service Commission, Petitioner, vs. Henry A. Sojor, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 168766; May 22, 2008; 577 Phil. 52; 105 O.G. No. 17, 2472; En Banc; Ponente: Reyes, R.T., J. Voting: Puno, C.J., Quisumbing, Ynares-Santiago, Austria-Martinez, Corona, Carpio-Morales, Azcuna, Tinga, Chico-Nazario, Velasco, Jr., Nachura, Leonardo-De Castro, and Brion, JJ., concurred. Carpio, J., was on leave. No separate opinions filed.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Civil Service Commission (CSC) / CSC Regional Office No. VII (CSC-RO VII):** Petitioner; the central personnel agency of the Philippine Government constitutionally vested with disciplinary authority over all officers and employees of the civil service.
**Dr. Henry A. Sojor:** Respondent; President of Central Visayas Polytechnic College (CVPC), subsequently converted into the Negros Oriental State University (NORSU).
**Jose Rene A. Cepe and Narciso P. Ragay:** Complainants in ADMC DC No. 02-20(A); CVPC faculty members.
**Jocelyn Juanon and Carolina Fe Santos:** Complainants in ADM DC No. 02-20; CVPC instructors/professors.
**Rose Marie Palomar:** Complainant in ADM DC No. 02-21; former part-time instructor of CVPC.
**Board of Trustees (BOT) of CVPC / Board of Regents (BOR) of NORSU:** The collegiate governing board of the state collegiate/university institution established under Republic Act (R.A.) No. 8292 and R.A. No. 9299.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure assailing the June 27, 2005 Decision of the Court of Appeals (CA) in CA-G.R. SP No. 85552, which annulled and set aside CSC Resolution No. 040321 (March 30, 2004) and Resolution No. 040766 (July 6, 2004) and permanently enjoined the CSC from proceeding with the administrative investigation against respondent Sojor.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Constitutional Commissions → The Civil Service Commission → Disciplinary Jurisdiction over State University Presidents / Concurrent Jurisdiction with University Governing Boards
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Administrative Law → Administrative Cases → Jurisdiction of the CSC vs. Corporate/Charter Powers of SUC Governing Boards → Academic Freedom & Condonation Doctrine Inapplicability
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article IX-B, Section 2 (1), 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Section 2. (1) **The civil service embraces all branches, subdivisions, instrumentalities, and agencies of the Government, including government-owned or controlled corporations with original charters.**"
**Section 4 and Section 7, Republic Act No. 8292 (Higher Education Modernization Act of 1997):**
"Sec. 4. **Powers and Duties of Governing Boards.** — The governing board shall have the following specific powers and duties in addition to its general powers of administration and the exercise of all the powers granted to the board of directors of a corporation under Section 36 of Batas Pambansa Blg. 68, otherwise known as the Corporation Code of the Philippines:
...
(h) to fix and adjust salaries of faculty members and administrative officials and employees subject to the provisions of the revised compensation and classification system and other pertinent budget and compensation laws governing hours of service, and such other duties and conditions as it may deem proper; to grant them, at its discretion, leaves of absence under such regulations as it may promulgate, any provisions of existing law to the contrary not withstanding; **and to remove them for cause in accordance with the requirements of due process of law.**"
**Section 4 and Section 7, Republic Act No. 9299 (Charter Converting CVPC into NORSU):**
"Sec. 4. **Administration.** — The University shall have the general powers of a corporation set forth in Batas Pambansa Blg. 68, as amended, otherwise known as 'The Corporation Code of the Philippines.' **The administration of the University and the exercise of its corporate powers shall be vested exclusively in the Board of Regents and the president of the University insofar as authorized by the Board.**

Sec. 7. **Powers and Duties of the Board of Regents.** — The Board shall have the following specific powers and duties **in addition to its general powers of administration** and the exercise of all the powers granted to the Board of Directors of a corporation under existing laws:
...
(i) To fix and adjust salaries of faculty members and administrative officials and employees, subject to the provisions of the Revised Compensation and Position Classification System and other pertinent budget and compensation laws governing hours of service and such other duties and conditions as it may deem proper; to grant them, at its discretion, leaves of absence under such regulations as it may promulgate, any provision of existing law to the contrary notwithstanding; **and to remove them for cause in accordance with the requirements of due process of law.**"
**Factual Trigger:** State university faculty members filed administrative complaints against their college president before the CSC Regional Office for dishonesty, payroll falsification, and nepotism. The president challenged the CSC's authority to investigate and suspend him, asserting that as an appointee of the university's governing board under a special charter, he was exclusively subject to the disciplinary authority of the Board of Regents or the Office of the President, and that subjecting him to CSC jurisdiction violated institutional academic freedom.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**August 1, 1991:** President Corazon C. Aquino appoints Dr. Henry A. Sojor as President of the Central Visayas Polytechnic College (CVPC) in Dumaguete City.
**June 1997:** Republic Act No. 8292 ("Higher Education Modernization Act of 1997") is enacted, creating a Board of Trustees (BOT) as the governing board of state colleges.
**September 1998:** The CVPC BOT appoints Sojor as College President for a four-year term running from September 1998 to September 2002.
**June 26, 2002:** CVPC faculty members Jose Rene A. Cepe and Narciso P. Ragay file an administrative complaint (ADMC DC No. 02-20[A]) against Sojor before CSC-RO VII in Cebu City for Dishonesty, Grave Misconduct, and Conduct Prejudicial to the Best Interest of the Service, alleging Sojor approved the release of salary differentials without the required Plantilla, Salary Adjustment Form, or valid appointments.
**July 10, 2002:** Faculty members Jocelyn Juanon and Carolina Fe Santos file an administrative complaint (ADM DC No. 02-20) against Sojor before CSC-RO VII for Dishonesty, Misconduct, and Falsification of Official Documents, alleging malicious antedating and falsification of the reclassification differential payroll to the prejudice of instructors/professors seeking academic rank adjustments.
**August 13, 2002:** The CVPC BOT approves and adopts the reappointment of Sojor for a second four-year term (expiring September 24, 2006), with his formal appointment signed on September 23, 2002, by Commission on Higher Education (CHED) Chairman Ester A. Garcia pursuant to Section 6 of R.A. No. 8292.
**August 15, 2002:** Former part-time instructor Rose Marie Palomar files an administrative complaint (ADM DC No. 02-21) against Sojor before CSC-RO VII for Nepotism, alleging Sojor appointed his half-sister, Estrellas Sojor-Managuilas, as a casual clerk in violation of the Administrative Code.
**August 20, 2002:** Prior to filing his counter-affidavits, Sojor files a Motion to Dismiss before CSC-RO VII regarding the first two complaints, alleging lack of jurisdiction, bar by prior judgment, and forum shopping. He asserts he is a presidential appointee in the unclassified service subject exclusively to the Office of the President, that the Civil Service Law lacks procedures to discipline presidential appointees, and that the Ombudsman had already resolved the matter.
**September 4, 2002:** CSC-RO VII issues a Resolution denying Sojor’s Motion to Dismiss for lack of merit; Sojor moves for reconsideration.
**October 28, 2002:** Following the denial of his motion for reconsideration by CSC-RO VII, Sojor files an appeal with the Commission Proper (CSC). Simultaneously, CSC-RO VII formally charges Sojor in the three administrative cases: (1) Dishonesty, Misconduct, and Falsification of Official Document; (2) Dishonesty, Grave Misconduct, and Conduct Prejudicial to the Best Interest of the Service; and (3) Nepotism.
**March 30, 2004:** The CSC En Banc issues Resolution No. 040321 dismissing Sojor’s appeal. It holds that Sojor is not a presidential appointee but a BOT appointee, that the CSC holds concurrent disciplinary jurisdiction with the BOT, and that having first assumed jurisdiction, CSC excludes the BOT. It adopts the formal charges issued by CSC-RO VII, directs CSC-RO VII to conduct the formal investigation within 105 days, and places Sojor under 90-day preventive suspension.
**June 25, 2004:** CVPC is converted into the Negros Oriental State University (NORSU) under R.A. No. 9299. A Board of Regents (BOR) replaces the BOT as the governing body.
**July 6, 2004:** The CSC En Banc issues Resolution No. 040766 denying Sojor's Motion for Reconsideration with finality.
**August 2004:** Sojor files a Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition with prayer for injunctive relief before the Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. SP No. 85552), asserting lack of jurisdiction in the CSC, violation of academic freedom, and exclusive disciplinary authority lodged in the BOT/BOR.
**September 29, 2004:** The CA issues a Writ of Preliminary Injunction directing the CSC to cease and desist from enforcing its March 30, 2004 and July 6, 2004 Resolutions, halting the CSC-RO VII formal investigation.
**June 27, 2005:** The CA renders a Decision granting Sojor's petition, annulling and setting aside CSC Resolutions Nos. 040321 and 040766, and making the preliminary injunction permanent. The CA holds that the power to appoint carries the power to remove, that R.A. No. 9299 is a special law granting exclusive disciplining power to the BOR which prevails over the general provisions of the Administrative Code (E.O. No. 292), leaving the CSC without jurisdiction.
**July 2005:** The CSC petitions the Supreme Court for review on certiorari.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Civil Service Commission)
**Main Thesis:** The CSC possesses constitutional and statutory disciplinary jurisdiction over all officers and employees in the civil service, including state university presidents who belong to the non-career service. The disciplinary authority granted to state university governing boards is concurrent, not exclusive, and does not oust the CSC of its primary constitutional mandate.
**Specific Contentions:**
The CA gravely erred in ruling that the CSC acted without jurisdiction. Under Article IX-B, Section 2(1) of the 1987 Constitution and the Administrative Code of 1987 (E.O. No. 292), the civil service embraces all government branches, agencies, and chartered institutions.
State universities with original charters (like CVPC/NORSU) fall squarely under civil service coverage; their personnel are subject to civil service disciplinary rules.
Sojor is not a presidential appointee exempt from CSC rules; he was appointed by the CVPC BOT pursuant to Section 6 of R.A. No. 8292.
The CSC and the BOT/BOR possess concurrent original jurisdiction over administrative disciplinary complaints against school officials. Under settled jurisdictional rules, the body that first takes cognizance of the complaint acquires jurisdiction to the exclusion of the other. Because the complaints were lodged directly with the CSC-RO VII, the CSC lawfully acquired jurisdiction.
The invocation of academic freedom is baseless because the charges involve statutory offenses (dishonesty, falsification, misconduct, and nepotism) rather than educational, pedagogical, or admission policies.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Henry A. Sojor)
**Main Thesis:** The CSC lacks jurisdiction to entertain, investigate, formally charge, or preventively suspend a state university president. Disciplinary power is exclusively lodged in the university's governing board (BOT/BOR) under its specific charter, or alternatively within the Office of the President.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Presidential Appointee Status: Under his initial appointment, and because the BOT is chaired by the CHED Chairperson who is an alter ego of the President, Sojor claimed status as a presidential appointee in the unclassified/non-career service, cognizable only by the Office of the President.
 Special Law Precedence: R.A. No. 8292 and R.A. No. 9299 are special laws that explicitly grant governing boards (BOT/BOR) the power to appoint and remove faculty, administrative officials, and employees for cause. Under principles of statutory construction, this special charter grant supersedes the general civil service authority under P.D. No. 807 and E.O. No. 292.
 Exclusivity of Administration:** Section 4 of R.A. No. 9299 expressly vests the administration of the university and corporate powers **exclusively in the BOR and the university president, thereby excluding outside interference from the CSC.
 Academic Freedom: Assumption of jurisdiction by an outside administrative agency over the university president encroaches upon the constitutionally guaranteed academic freedom of higher educational institutions.
 Condonation Doctrine:** His subsequent reappointment by the BOT/BOR as President of NORSU in 2004, despite the pendency of the administrative complaints, operated as a condonation of the alleged prior misconduct under the doctrine established in **Aguinaldo v. Santos** and **Salalima v. Guingona.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Civil Service Commission has administrative disciplinary jurisdiction over the president of a state university.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the statutory power of a state university's Board of Regents or Board of Trustees to discipline and remove its officials and employees is exclusive, thereby stripping the CSC of concurrent disciplinary jurisdiction.
3.  **[Secondary Substantive Issue]** Whether or not the assumption of disciplinary jurisdiction by the CSC over a state university president violates the constitutional guarantee of academic freedom.
4.  **[Secondary Substantive Issue]** Whether or not the reappointment of a state university president by its governing board operates as a condonation of alleged administrative misconduct committed during a prior term.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: CSC Disciplinary Jurisdiction over State University Presidents
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the Civil Service Commission has administrative disciplinary jurisdiction over the president of a state university. **YES.** As an appointed officer of a chartered state institution holding a fixed-term office, a state university president is a non-career civil service officer subject to the constitutional and statutory disciplinary jurisdiction of the CSC.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Constitutional Scope: The 1987 Constitution (Art. IX-B, Sec. 2[1]) and the Administrative Code of 1987 (E.O. No. 292) mandate that the civil service embraces every branch, agency, subdivision, and instrumentality of the government, including government-owned or controlled corporations with original charters.
 Classification of Positions: The civil service is classified into career and non-career services. Career positions require entrance via competitive merit/fitness or technical qualifications with security of tenure. Non-career positions are characterized by entrance without competitive examination and tenure limited by law, coterminous with the appointing authority, or subject to pleasure. Non-career service expressly includes chairmen and members of commissions and boards with fixed terms, as well as contractual and emergency personnel.
 Status of Respondent: Sojor is not a presidential appointee. His appointment was made and approved by the CVPC Board of Trustees pursuant to Section 6 of R.A. No. 8292 (Higher Education Modernization Act of 1997), signed by CHED Chairman Ester Garcia acting in her capacity as head of the Board. Because he was appointed to a fixed term by a governing board of an institution with an original charter, Sojor is a non-career civil service officer.
 Regulatory Competence: Under Section 4, 5, and 6 of the Revised Uniform Rules on Administrative Cases in the Civil Service, the CSC has final authority to pass upon the removal, separation, and suspension of all officers and employees in the civil service. The CSC Proper retains disciplinary jurisdiction over third-level officials who are not presidential appointees. Consequently, Sojor is directly within the disciplinary ambit of the CSC.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"It is evident that CSC has been granted by the Constitution and the Administrative Code jurisdiction over all civil service positions in the government service, whether career or non-career. ... Respondent, a state university president with a fixed term of office appointed by the governing board of trustees of the university, is a non-career civil service officer. He was appointed by the chairman and members of the governing board of CVPC. By clear provision of law, respondent is a non-career civil servant who is under the jurisdiction of the CSC."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** A state university president is not a presidential appointee just because the CHED Chairman signs the paper; the appointment comes directly from the university's Board of Trustees under R.A. No. 8292. Because the university exists by an original legislative charter, its officers belong to the civil service (specifically the non-career service). Therefore, the CSC holds full constitutional authority to investigate and discipline them.
Issue 2: Exclusivity of BOR/BOT Disciplinary Powers vs. Concurrent CSC Jurisdiction
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the statutory power of a state university's Board of Regents or Board of Trustees to discipline and remove its officials and employees is exclusive, thereby stripping the CSC of concurrent disciplinary jurisdiction. **NO.** The power of a university governing board to remove officers is an administrative power that runs concurrently with, and does not extinguish, the general disciplinary jurisdiction of the CSC.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Presumption of Concurrency:** When the law vests an agency with authority to hear and decide cases on specific matters, the jurisdiction is presumed to be exclusive **unless another body is also vested with the same jurisdiction, in which case both bodies exercise concurrent jurisdiction.
 Statutory Construction of Charters:** Section 4 of R.A. No. 8292 and Section 7 of R.A. No. 9299 empower the Board to fix salaries and "remove them for cause in accordance with the requirements of due process of law." While Section 4 of R.A. No. 9299 states that the **administration of the university is vested exclusively in the BOR and the President, Section 7 clarifies that the power to remove is conferred "in addition to its general powers of administration." The legislature did not specify that the disciplinary/removal power was exclusive.
 Controlling Precedents:** In **University of the Philippines v. Regino**, the Court squarely rejected the claim that the UP Board of Regents held exclusive disciplinary jurisdiction, ruling that chartered institutions are civil service components subject to CSC disciplinary authority. In **Camacho v. Gloria, the Court reaffirmed that complaints against state university officials may be filed either with the university’s Board of Regents or directly with the CSC.
 Priority in Concurrent Jurisdiction: Because the CSC and the BOR/BOT possess concurrent original jurisdiction, the body that first acquires jurisdiction retains it to the exclusion of the other. The complaints were directly instituted before CSC-RO VII; thus, the CSC validly acquired jurisdiction over Sojor's administrative cases to the exclusion of the BOR.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Verily, the BOR of NORSU has the sole power of administration over the university. But this power is not exclusive in the matter of disciplining and removing its employees and officials. Although the BOR of NORSU is given the specific power under R.A. No. 9299 to discipline its employees and officials, there is no showing that such power is exclusive. When the law bestows upon a government body the jurisdiction to hear and decide cases involving specific matters, it is to be presumed that such jurisdiction is exclusive unless it be proved that another body is likewise vested with the same jurisdiction, in which case, both bodies have concurrent jurisdiction over the matter."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The university charter grants the BOR exclusive **administrative** authority over the school, but not exclusive **disciplinary** authority over personnel. Under settled administrative law doctrines (**UP v. Regino** and **Camacho v. Gloria**), the BOR and the CSC share concurrent jurisdiction over administrative cases involving university staff and officials. Since the complainants chose to file their charges directly with the CSC Regional Office, the CSC acquired primary jurisdiction to hear the case to the exclusion of the university board.
Issue 3: Invocation of Academic Freedom
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the assumption of disciplinary jurisdiction by the CSC over a state university president violates the constitutional guarantee of academic freedom. **NO.** Academic freedom relates to institutional autonomy regarding who may teach, what may be taught, how it shall be taught, and who may be admitted, and cannot serve as a shield against administrative liability for statutory and civil service violations.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 The Four Essential Freedoms: Under prevailing jurisprudence, institutional academic freedom encompasses four fundamental institutional determinations: (1) who may teach, (2) what may be taught, (3) how it shall be taught, and (4) who may be admitted to study.
 Nature of the Charges: The administrative complaints against Sojor did not touch upon academic standards, curriculum design, faculty pedagogical discretion, or student admissions. The charges were purely administrative infractions under civil service rules: nepotism (appointing his half-sister), dishonesty, misconduct, and falsification of payroll documents to prejudice academic rank reclassifications.
 Limitation on Autonomy: Academic freedom does not bestow unbridled license upon university officials to violate statutory civil service mandates. Institutional independence does not operate as an immunity card shielding school officers from investigations of corruption and grave misconduct.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Contrary to the matters traditionally held to be justified to be within the bounds of academic freedom, the administrative complaints filed against Sojor involve violations of civil service rules. He is facing charges of nepotism, dishonesty, falsification of official documents, grave misconduct, and conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service. ... This Court has held that the guaranteed academic freedom does not give an institution the unbridled authority to perform acts without any statutory basis. For that reason, a school official, who is a member of the civil service, may not be permitted to commit violations of civil service rules under the justification that he was free to do so under the principle of academic freedom."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Academic freedom protects an educational institution's intellectual choices—who teaches, who is admitted, and what is studied. It has nothing to do with falsifying payroll documents, dishonesty, or appointing a half-sister to a clerk position. A civil servant cannot evade prosecution for grave offenses by claiming academic freedom.
Issue 4: Inapplicability of the Condonation Doctrine
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the reappointment of a state university president by its governing board operates as a condonation of alleged administrative misconduct committed during a prior term. **NO.** The condonation doctrine applies exclusively to elective officials whose reelection reflects the sovereign will of the people, not to appointive officials reappointed by a governing board.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Electoral Basis of Condonation:** The condonation doctrine established in **Aguinaldo v. Santos** and **Salalima v. Guingona** is anchored on the democratic principle of **vox populi est suprema lex. When voters elect an official despite known misconduct during a prior term, the electorate condones the offense and strips the state of the right to remove the official for acts committed prior to the reelection.
 Appointive vs. Elective Office: The doctrine applies strictly to elective officials. Appointed non-career officials, such as a state university president reappointed by a collegiate board (BOT/BOR), do not draw their mandate from the sovereign will of the voters.
 Absence of Popular Will: Reappointment by an administrative body does not represent the sovereign will of the people. Consequently, reappointment cannot condone administrative offenses or extinguish pending administrative disciplinary liability.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Under the principle of **vox populi est suprema lex**, the re-election of a public official may, indeed, supersede a pending administrative case. The same cannot be said of a re-appointment to a non-career position. There is no sovereign will of the people to speak of when the BOR re-appointed respondent Sojor to the post of university president."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Condonation requires a mandate from the voting public at the ballot box. Because Sojor was an appointed official whose second term was granted by an administrative board, no sovereign will was exercised. An administrative reappointment never washes away prior administrative misconduct.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Active Subject Context:** Constitutional Law I | Assigned Syllabus Topic: Administrative Cases | Applied Lens: Constitutional & Political Law
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 State Power Invoked: Executive/Administrative Disciplinary Power exercised by the Civil Service Commission under Article IX-B, Sections 1, 2(1), and 3 of the 1987 Constitution, and Section 47, Chapter 6, Subtitle A, Title I, Book V of E.O. No. 292 (Administrative Code of 1987).
 Constitutional / Structural Limitations Invoked: Institutional Academic Freedom (Art. XIV, Sec. 5[2], 1987 Constitution), the constitutional boundary on the scope of the Civil Service Commission over non-career positions, and the statutory distribution of corporate administrative autonomy under university charters (R.A. No. 8292 and R.A. No. 9299).
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
 Jurisprudential Test on Concurrent Administrative Jurisdiction: The Rule of Prior Cognizance. When two administrative bodies are endowed with concurrent original disciplinary jurisdiction over the same official/subject matter, the tribunal or commission that first takes cognizance of the administrative complaint acquires jurisdiction to the exclusion of the other.
 Statutory-Harmonization Test: General Law vs. Special Law in Charters. A special corporate charter granting administrative and removal powers to a university governing board does not automatically divest or repeal the general constitutional and statutory oversight of the CSC unless an explicit, irreconcilable legislative intent to strip concurrent authority is established.
**Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:**
 Actual Case or Controversy: Present; ripe for adjudication because the CSC issued formal charges and a 90-day preventive suspension order, creating an immediate and tangible legal injury.
 Lis Mota: The constitutionality and statutory reach of CSC's disciplinary authority over non-career officers of chartered state colleges was essential to resolving the validity of the CA's permanent injunction.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
1.  Civil Service Coverage Requisites (Art. IX-B, Sec. 2[1]):
Agency/Subdivision/Instrumentality of Government OR Government-Owned or Controlled Corporation. (Met: CVPC/NORSU is a chartered state educational institution).
With an Original Charter. (Met: Created by special legislative acts—R.A. No. 8292/R.A. No. 9299).
2.  Concurrent Administrative Jurisdiction Requisites:
Conferment of disciplinary/removal power on an internal agency/board. (Met: Section 4, R.A. No. 8292 and Section 7, R.A. No. 9299 confer disciplinary authority upon the BOT/BOR).
**   Absence of explicit legislative language making the internal power "exclusive." (Met: Charters designate "exclusive" authority only for corporate **administration**, not for **discipline/removal).
Prior Assumption: The complainant must invoke the jurisdiction of one tribunal before the other acts. (Met: Complainants filed formal charges directly before CSC-RO VII before any BOR proceeding).
3.  Academic Freedom Defense Requisites (Institutional):
Subject matter must relate directly to institutional autonomy: (a) who teaches, (b) what is taught, (c) how it is taught, or (d) who is admitted. (Failed: Administrative charges involved payroll falsification, nepotism, and dishonesty).
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Concurrent Jurisdiction
 Non-Career Service
 Government-Owned or Controlled Corporations with Original Charters
 Rule of Prior Cognizance / Primary Jurisdiction
 Institutional Academic Freedom
 Vox Populi Est Suprema Lex
 Condonation Doctrine (inapplicable to appointive positions)
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**CSC v. Sojor** establishes that the president of a state university is a non-career civil servant under Article IX-B of the 1987 Constitution and is directly subject to the disciplinary authority of the Civil Service Commission. While a university's charter grants its governing board (BOT/BOR) power to remove university personnel, this authority is concurrent with, rather than exclusive of, the CSC; thus, under the rule of prior cognizance, the CSC properly acquired jurisdiction by receiving the complaints first. Finally, institutional academic freedom cannot be invoked to shield civil servants from administrative liability for corrupt acts, and the condonation doctrine is strictly confined to elective officials re-elected by the sovereign people, never applying to appointed officers reappointed by an administrative board.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed.
**Verbatim/Near-Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is GRANTED. The Decision of the Court of Appeals is REVERSED and SET ASIDE. The assailed Resolutions of the Civil Service Commission are REINSTATED.

SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Civil Service Commission, reversing and setting aside the Court of Appeals Decision and dissolving the permanent injunction. CSC Resolution No. 040321 and Resolution No. 040766 were reinstated, fully empowering CSC Regional Office No. VII to resume its formal administrative investigation against Dr. Henry A. Sojor and enforcing his 90-day preventive suspension.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Civil Service Commission v. Court of Appeals and Guevarra (2012)
**Full Official Caption:** Civil Service Commission, Petitioner, vs. Court of Appeals, Dr. Dante G. Guevarra, and Atty. Augustus F. Cezar, Respondents (G.R. No. 176162); Atty. Honesto L. Cueva, Petitioner, vs. Court of Appeals, Dr. Dante G. Guevarra, and Atty. Augustus F. Cezar, Respondents (G.R. No. 178845).
**Citation & Metadata:** 696 Phil. 230; G.R. Nos. 176162 & 178845; Promulgated October 9, 2012; En Banc; Mendoza, J. (Ponente). Voting: Concurring: Carpio, Leonardo-De Castro, Del Castillo, Villarama, Jr., Perez, and Perlas-Bernabe, JJ.; Dissenting: Velasco, Jr., J. (joined by Sereno, C.J., Brion, Bersamin, and Abad, JJ.); No Part: Peralta and Reyes, JJ.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Civil Service Commission (CSC):** Petitioner in G.R. No. 176162; the central personnel agency of the Philippine Government claiming concurrent original disciplinary jurisdiction.
**Atty. Honesto L. Cueva:** Petitioner in G.R. No. 178845; then-Chief Legal Counsel and Dean of the College of Law of the Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP); original complainant against university officials.
**Dr. Dante G. Guevarra:** Respondent; then-Officer-in-Charge/President of PUP; accused of dishonesty and falsification for answering "NO" to having criminal/administrative records on a public bond application.
**Atty. Augustus F. Cezar:** Respondent; then-Vice President for Administration of PUP; endorsed and recommended approval of Guevarra's bond application.
**Court of Appeals (CA):** Nominal respondent; nullified CSC formal charges for lack of jurisdiction.
**Board of Regents (BOR) of PUP:** The governing board of PUP under its charter and Republic Act (R.A.) No. 8292.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Consolidated Petitions for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 assailing the December 29, 2006 Decision of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 95293, which granted Guevarra and Cezar's Rule 65 Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition, nullified CSC Resolution Nos. 060521 and 061141, and ruled that the CSC lacked original jurisdiction over an administrative complaint filed by a public employee against state university officials.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Constitutional Commissions → Civil Service Commission → Disciplinary Jurisdiction (Original Concurrent vs. Appellate)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Administrative Law → Administrative Agencies & Public Officers → Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies → Disciplinary Powers of State University Governing Boards (R.A. No. 8292 vs. E.O. No. 292)
**Full Text of Governing Provisions:**
**Article IX-B, Section 2(1), 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"The civil service embraces all branches, subdivisions, instrumentalities, and agencies of the Government, including government-owned or controlled corporations with original charters."
**Executive Order No. 292 (Administrative Code of 1987), Book V, Title I, Subtitle A, Chapter 7, Section 47:**
"SECTION 47. Disciplinary Jurisdiction.—(1) The Commission shall decide upon appeal all administrative disciplinary cases involving the imposition of a penalty of suspension for more than thirty days, or fine in an amount exceeding thirty days’ salary, demotion in rank or salary or transfer, removal or dismissal from office.
**A complaint may be filed directly with the Commission by a private citizen against a government official or employee in which case it may hear and decide the case or it may deputize any department or agency or official or group of officials to conduct the investigation.** The results of the investigation shall be submitted to the Commission with recommendation as to the penalty to be imposed or other action to be taken.
(2) **The Secretaries and heads of agencies and instrumentalities, provinces, cities and municipalities shall have jurisdiction to investigate and decide matters involving disciplinary action against officers and employees under their jurisdiction.** Their decisions shall be final in case the penalty imposed is suspension for not more than thirty days or fine in an amount not exceeding thirty days’ salary. In case the decision rendered by a bureau or office head is appealable to the Commission, the same may be initially appealed to the department and finally to the Commission and pending appeal, the same shall be executory except when the penalty is removal, in which case the same shall be executory only after confirmation by the Secretary concerned."
**Republic Act No. 8292 (Higher Education Modernization Act of 1997), Section 4(h):**
"Section 4. Powers and duties of Governing Boards. – The governing board shall have the following specific powers and duties in addition to its general powers of administration and the exercise of all the powers granted to the board of directors of a corporation under Section 36 of Batas Pambansa Blg. 68 otherwise known as the Corporation Code of the Philippines:
...
(h) to fix and adjust salaries of faculty members and administrative officials and employees... and **to remove them for cause in accordance with the requirements of due process of law**."
**Factual Trigger:**
Dr. Dante G. Guevarra, as Officer-in-Charge/President of PUP, accomplished General Form No. 58-A (Application for Bond of Accountable Officials and Employees) to engage in fiscal transactions for the university, answering "NO" to Question No. 11 ("Do you have any criminal or administrative records?") despite having 17 pending anti-graft cases under Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 before the Sandiganbayan; Vice President Cezar endorsed the form knowing of the pending charges, prompting PUP Chief Legal Counsel Cueva to bypass the PUP Board of Regents and file an administrative complaint directly with the CSC.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1978:** Presidential Decree (P.D.) No. 1341 converts PUP into a chartered state university, establishing it as a government-owned or controlled corporation with an original charter governed by Civil Service law.
**2005:** Dr. Dante G. Guevarra serves as OIC/President and Atty. Augustus F. Cezar serves as Vice President for Administration of PUP. At this time, both face 17 pending criminal cases before the Sandiganbayan for alleged violation of Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019.
**Mid-2005 (Bond Application):** Guevarra accomplishes General Form No. 58-A (Application for Bond of Accountable Officials and Employees of the Republic of the Philippines) to obtain fiscal bonding required for university disbursements. In answer to Question No. 11 ("Do you have any criminal or administrative records? – If so, state briefly the nature thereof"), Guevarra writes "NO" to both queries. Cezar endorses and recommends approval of the application.
**September 27, 2005:** Atty. Honesto L. Cueva, PUP Chief Legal Counsel and Dean of the College of Law, directly files an administrative complaint with the CSC against Guevarra and Cezar charging gross dishonesty, grave misconduct, falsification of official documents, conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service, being notoriously undesirable, and violating Section 4 of R.A. No. 6713.
**Pre-Charge Proceedings before the CSC:** Guevarra and Cezar submit to CSC jurisdiction by filing a Joint Counter-Affidavit, explaining that they interpreted "criminal or administrative records" to mean final conviction, and that their negative answer was executed in good faith because the Sandiganbayan cases remained undecided.
**March 24, 2006:** The CSC issues Resolution No. 060521 finding a **prima facie** case and formally charging Guevarra with Dishonesty and Cezar with Conduct Prejudicial to the Best Interest of the Service.
**Post-Charge Pleadings:** Guevarra and Cezar file a "Motion for Reconsideration and Motion to Declare Absence of Prima Facie Case," praying to suspend the administrative proceedings. Cueva files an Urgent Ex-Parte Motion for Preventive Suspension and an Omnibus Motion to add the omitted charges.
**June 30, 2006:** The CSC issues Resolution No. 061141 denying Guevarra and Cezar's motion as a prohibited motion to dismiss under Section 16 of the Uniform Rules on Administrative Cases in the Civil Service (URACCS), denying Cueva's motion to add charges, and placing Guevarra under 90-day preventive suspension to prevent undue influence over witnesses.
**Mid-2006 (Court of Appeals Petition):** Guevarra and Cezar file a Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition (CA-G.R. SP No. 95293) before the CA, raising for the first time the CSC's lack of original jurisdiction, arguing that under Section 47 of E.O. No. 292 and R.A. No. 8292, exclusive original disciplinary jurisdiction belongs to the PUP Board of Regents, and that Cueva failed to exhaust administrative remedies.
**December 29, 2006:** The CA renders a Decision nullifying and setting aside CSC Resolution Nos. 060521 and 061141 for lack of jurisdiction. The CA rules that Section 47 of E.O. No. 292 restricts direct filing before the CSC exclusively to complaints filed by "private citizens," meaning complaints initiated by fellow civil service employees must be filed before the agency head (PUP BOR).
**Early 2007:** CSC (G.R. No. 176162) and Cueva (G.R. No. 178845) file separate Rule 45 petitions before the Supreme Court, which are consolidated.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments (Civil Service Commission & Atty. Honesto L. Cueva)
**Main Thesis:** The CSC, as the constitutional central personnel agency of the government, possesses original concurrent jurisdiction along with state university governing boards over administrative disciplinary complaints instituted against chartered state university officials, regardless of whether the complainant is a private citizen or a civil service employee.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Statutory Mandate: Under Section 12(11), Chapter 3, Subtitle A, Title I, Book V of E.O. No. 292, the CSC is explicitly granted the power to hear and decide administrative cases instituted by or brought before it "directly or on appeal" without qualification as to complainant identity.
 Rejection of Literal/Plain Meaning Construction: Restricting direct filings under Section 47(1) of E.O. No. 292 to "private citizens" operates unreasonably and leads to absurdity, effectively disenfranchising public servants by denying them administrative recourse against erring superiors and colleagues before the central personnel agency.
 Reconciliation with Agency Powers: Section 7 of the URACCS explicitly recognizes that heads of agencies share "original concurrent jurisdiction, with the Commission, over their respective officers and employees."
 Judicial Precedent:** Pursuant to **Hilario v. CSC**, **Camacho v. Gloria**, **CSC v. Alfonso**, and **CSC v. Sojor, the disciplinary authority granted to state university boards under university charters and R.A. No. 8292 does not divest the CSC of its constitutional supervisory and disciplinary power.
 Estoppel by Laches: Guevarra and Cezar fully submitted to the CSC's jurisdiction by participating in preliminary investigation proceedings and submitting a Joint Counter-Affidavit, barring them from belatedly challenging jurisdiction after receiving adverse resolutions.
B. Respondents' Arguments (Dr. Dante G. Guevarra & Atty. Augustus F. Cezar)
**Main Thesis:** The CSC possesses only appellate jurisdiction over disciplinary cases involving chartered state university personnel unless a complaint is directly initiated by a private citizen; because complainant Cueva was a public officer subject to PUP authority, original jurisdiction belongs exclusively to the PUP Board of Regents.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Plain Meaning Rule (Verba Legis): Section 47(1) of E.O. No. 292 explicitly states that direct complaints may only be filed before the CSC by a "private citizen." Cueva, being the PUP Chief Legal Counsel, is not a private citizen.
 Exclusive Agency Head Jurisdiction: Section 47(2) of E.O. No. 292 dictates that agency heads have jurisdiction to investigate and decide disciplinary matters over their officers and employees, rendering CSC jurisdiction strictly appellate.
 Special Law Over General Law: Section 4(h) of R.A. No. 8292 (Higher Education Modernization Act of 1997) explicitly and specifically vests in the Board of Regents the disciplinary power to remove university officials and personnel for cause, superseding general provisions of the Administrative Code.
 Administrative Rules Cannot Expand Substantive Law: Section 4 and Section 7 of the URACCS cannot grant original concurrent jurisdiction over employee complaints because an administrative rule cannot enlarge or modify statutory jurisdictional boundaries established by E.O. No. 292.
 Failure to Exhaust Administrative Remedies:** Cueva breached administrative hierarchy by bypassing the PUP Board of Regents, relying on **Gaoiran v. Alcala to argue that disciplinary complaints against academic personnel must be instituted within the school's administrative structure.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Civil Service Commission has original concurrent jurisdiction, along with the governing boards of chartered state universities, over administrative disciplinary cases directly initiated by a public officer against fellow government officials.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the enactment of Section 4(h) of R.A. No. 8292 divested the CSC of its disciplinary jurisdiction over administrative offenses committed by state university personnel.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondents are legally estopped from challenging the jurisdiction of the CSC after submitting their Joint Counter-Affidavit and participating in the initial preliminary proceedings.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: CSC's Original Concurrent Disciplinary Jurisdiction over Direct Complaints
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the CSC has original concurrent jurisdiction over administrative cases filed directly with it against officials of a chartered state university by a public employee. **YES.** The CSC possesses concurrent original disciplinary jurisdiction with agency heads over complaints against civil service personnel, and its authority to take direct cognizance of such cases is not restricted to complaints filed by private citizens.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Constitutional Scope: Under Section 2(1), Article IX-B of the 1987 Constitution, the civil service embraces GOCCs with original charters. PUP was established as a chartered state university under P.D. No. 1341; thus, its officers and employees are civil servants subject to E.O. No. 292 and CSC disciplinary authority.
 Rejection of Absurd Plain Meaning:** Although Section 47(1), Chapter 7, Subtitle A, Title I, Book V of E.O. No. 292 uses the phrase "complaint may be filed directly with the Commission by a private citizen," a strictly literal construction must be rejected under **Secretary of Justice v. Koruga. Statutory interpretation must not defeat legislative intent or yield unjust, absurd results.
 Disenfranchisement Doctrine:** Interpreting Section 47(1) to mean that **only private citizens may file direct complaints would strip the CSC of its broad original disciplinary powers granted under Section 12(11), Chapter 3, Subtitle A, Title I, Book V of E.O. No. 292 (which authorizes the CSC to hear cases brought before it "directly or on appeal" without limitation). Such a reading absurdly disenfranchises government employees by denying them an alternative forum against abusive officials.
 The Complainant's Identity is Immaterial:** Relying on **Hilario v. CSC, the Court held that nothing in the law prevents a public officer from filing an administrative complaint directly with the CSC against a fellow employee. The identity of the initiator is legally immaterial to the CSC's acquisition of jurisdiction.
 Harmonization of Rules and Statutes: Under Section 4 and Section 7 of the URACCS, agency heads and the CSC exercise original concurrent jurisdiction. Section 5 of the URACCS is purely directory and implementary; it does not truncate or restrict the broad statutory jurisdiction of the CSC Proper. Under concurrent jurisdiction, the body that first takes cognizance of the complaint exercises jurisdiction to the exclusion of the other.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"A literal interpretation of E.O. 292 would mean that only private citizens can file a complaint directly with the CSC. For administrative cases instituted by government employees against their fellow public servants, the CSC would only have appellate jurisdiction over those. Such a plain reading of the subject provision of E.O. 202 would effectively divest CSC of its original jurisdiction, albeit shared, provided by law. Moreover, it is clearly unreasonable as it would be tantamount to disenfranchising government employees by removing from them an alternative course of action against erring public officials."

"It cannot be overemphasized that the identity of the complainant is immaterial to the acquisition of jurisdiction over an administrative case by the CSC. The law is quite clear that the CSC may hear and decide administrative disciplinary cases brought directly before it or it may deputize any department or agency to conduct an investigation."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Supreme Court refused to read Section 47 of the Administrative Code literally because doing so would bar public employees from reporting corrupt superiors directly to the Civil Service Commission, forcing them to complain only to their own agency heads. Section 12(11) of the Administrative Code gives the CSC unqualified power to hear administrative cases brought directly before it. Therefore, the CSC and the PUP Board of Regents share concurrent original jurisdiction, and because Cueva filed first with the CSC, the CSC validly acquired jurisdiction to the exclusion of the university board.
Issue 2: Impact of R.A. No. 8292 on CSC Disciplinary Authority
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not R.A. No. 8292 (Higher Education Modernization Act of 1997) granted state university governing boards exclusive disciplinary jurisdiction, thereby implicitly divesting the CSC of original jurisdiction. **NO.** R.A. No. 8292 confers disciplinary authority upon university governing boards, but that authority is concurrent with, and not exclusive of, the constitutional disciplinary powers of the CSC.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Harmonization of Statutes (Interpretare et concordare leges legibus): Under settled statutory construction, laws concerning the same subject matter must be harmonized to create a coherent legal system. An implied repeal is never favored; the enactment of a subsequent statute does not abrogate an earlier law absent irreconcilable inconsistency.
 Application of Precedent (CSC v. Sojor and CSC v. Alfonso):** In **CSC v. Sojor** and **CSC v. Alfonso, the Court expressly resolved that while Section 4(h) of R.A. No. 8292 empowers governing boards to discipline and remove personnel for cause, this power is not exclusive. When a statute vests disciplinary power in a specific administrative body without words of exclusivity, that power is presumed concurrent with the central personnel agency.
 Distinction of Inapplicable Jurisprudence: Gaoiran v. Alcala** is entirely distinguishable because it turned on whether an unsworn letter-complaint was validly cured when the CHED issued its formal charge; it did not confer exclusive jurisdiction on university boards. Similarly, **UP v. Regino affirmed CSC appellate jurisdiction after UP BOR proceedings had concluded, but never stripped the CSC of its concurrent original jurisdiction over direct filings.
 Administrative Burdens and Deputization: Addressing concerns that the CSC would be overwhelmed with trivial complaints, the Court pointed out that concurrent jurisdiction gives priority to whichever body first assumes cognizance, and Section 47 of E.O. No. 292 explicitly empowers the CSC to deputize the agency itself to conduct fact-finding investigations.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Be that as it may, we cannot interpret the creation of such bodies nor the passage of laws such as – R.A. Nos. 8292 and 4670 allowing for the creation of such disciplinary bodies – as having divested the CSC of its inherent power to supervise and discipline government employees, including those in the academe. To hold otherwise would not only negate the very purpose for which the CSC was established, i.e. to instill professionalism, integrity, and accountability in our civil service, but would also impliedly amend the Constitution itself."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Higher Education Modernization Act (R.A. No. 8292) gives university regents disciplinary power over their personnel, but it does not make that power exclusive. All university employees are still civil servants under the Constitution, meaning the CSC retains its overarching authority to discipline them. The two statutes coexist harmoniously: the board has disciplinary power under its charter, but it shares concurrent original jurisdiction with the CSC.
Issue 3: Estoppel from Questioning Jurisdiction
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not respondents Guevarra and Cezar were estopped from questioning the CSC's jurisdiction before the Court of Appeals. **YES.** By submitting their Joint Counter-Affidavit and seeking affirmative relief from the CSC during the preliminary investigation, respondents submitted to the CSC's jurisdiction and were barred under the doctrine of estoppel from later attacking that authority.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Submission to Authority:** Just as in **CSC v. Alfonso, respondents Guevarra and Cezar voluntarily submitted to the authority of the CSC by filing their Joint Counter-Affidavit and submitting a "Motion for Reconsideration and Motion to Declare Absence of Prima Facie Case" seeking substantive dismissal on the merits.
 Opportunistic Attack on Jurisdiction Barred: A litigant cannot actively participate in proceedings before an administrative tribunal, invoke its jurisdiction to secure affirmative relief, and then—upon receiving an adverse preliminary determination (the issuance of a formal charge and preventive suspension)—repudiate that same jurisdiction on appeal. Such conduct violates principles of fair play and constitutes estoppel.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Equally significant is the fact that he had already submitted himself to the jurisdiction of the CSC when he filed his counter-affidavit and his motion for reconsideration... At the very least, respondent's active participation in the proceedings by seeking affirmative relief before the CSC already bars him from impugning the Commission's authority under the principle of estoppel by laches."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Respondents did not challenge the CSC's authority at the start; they answered the charges, argued they acted in good faith, and asked the CSC to dismiss the case for lack of a **prima facie** showing. Only when the CSC formally charged them and placed Dr. Guevarra under preventive suspension did they run to the CA to question the CSC's jurisdiction. Under established law, participating on the merits and seeking affirmative relief bars a party from belatedly attacking administrative jurisdiction.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → Constitutional Commissions → Civil Service Commission → Administrative Cases / Disciplinary Powers
**Applied Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 Governmental Power Exercised: The constitutional mandate and disciplinary power of the Civil Service Commission as the central personnel agency under Section 3, Article IX-B of the 1987 Constitution and Book V of E.O. No. 292.
 Check / Limitation Invoked: State university institutional autonomy and statutory self-governance under R.A. No. 8292 (Higher Education Modernization Act of 1997), along with statutory agency head primary disciplinary authority under Section 47(2), Book V of E.O. No. 292.
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
 Statutory Harmonization Test (Interpretare et concordare leges legibus): Reconciling overlapping grants of quasi-judicial disciplinary authority between a constitutional commission and special statutory governing boards without declaring an implied repeal.
 Absurdity / Unreasonableness Canon:** Overriding the literal "plain meaning" (**verba legis) rule where an uncompromising textual reading would disenfranchise public officers and impair the constitutional design of the Civil Service Commission.
 Rule of Concurrent Administrative Jurisdiction: In administrative law, where two tribunals possess concurrent original jurisdiction over the same subject matter, the tribunal that first takes cognizance of the case exercises jurisdiction to the exclusion of the other.
**Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:**
 Actual Case or Controversy: Present; an actual formal charge and 90-day preventive suspension order were issued by the CSC against university executive officers.
 Exhaustion of Administrative Remedies: Respondents argued complainant Cueva failed to exhaust remedies by bypassing the PUP Board of Regents; the Court rejected this, holding that because the CSC has original concurrent jurisdiction, direct filing with the CSC is a complete and valid administrative recourse.
 Estoppel to Impugn Jurisdiction: Respondents submitted their Joint Counter-Affidavit and sought affirmative relief before raising the jurisdictional challenge in the CA, barring their collateral jurisdictional attack.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Central Personnel Agency (referring to the constitutional status of the CSC)
 Original Concurrent Jurisdiction (shared baseline authority between agency heads and the CSC)
 Chartered State University (status under P.D. No. 1341 bringing PUP under Art. IX-B, Sec. 2(1))
 Exclusion Rule in Concurrent Jurisdiction (the tribunal first acquiring cognizance excludes all others)
 Interpretare et concordare leges legibus est optimus interpretandi modus (harmonizing statutes)
 Estoppel by Laches / Estoppel to Deny Jurisdiction (active participation bars belated jurisdictional challenges)
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"In **CSC v. CA and Guevarra**, the Supreme Court held that the Civil Service Commission exercises original concurrent jurisdiction with the governing boards of chartered state universities over administrative disciplinary complaints, regardless of whether the complaint is instituted by a private citizen or a fellow public officer. Although Section 47 of Book V of the Administrative Code references direct complaints by a 'private citizen,' the Court rejected a literal reading because it would absurdly disenfranchise civil servants from seeking direct administrative redress against erring officials before the central personnel agency. Furthermore, R.A. No. 8292 does not vest exclusive disciplinary power in state university regents; because the CSC took cognizance of Cueva's direct complaint first, it acquired jurisdiction to the exclusion of the PUP Board of Regents."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Dissenting Opinion of Velasco, Jr., J. (joined by Sereno, C.J., Brion, Bersamin, and Abad, JJ.):**
 Strict Adherence to Plain Meaning (Verba Legis):** Justice Velasco maintained that where statutory language is plain and unambiguous, courts must apply it strictly. Section 47 of Book V of E.O. No. 292 creates a general rule of CSC **appellate** jurisdiction over administrative disciplinary cases, accompanied by a single, explicit exception: direct original complaints filed before the CSC must be brought by a **private citizen.
 Exclusive Primary Jurisdiction in Agency Heads: Because Cueva was the Chief Legal Counsel of PUP and not a private citizen, original jurisdiction belonged exclusively to the PUP Board of Regents under Section 47(2) of E.O. No. 292 and Section 4(h) of R.A. No. 8292.
 Rules Cannot Enlarge Statutory Jurisdiction: The Uniform Rules on Administrative Cases in the Civil Service (URACCS) cannot expand substantive statutory jurisdiction. An administrative regulation issued under quasi-legislative authority cannot grant the CSC original concurrent jurisdiction over employee-initiated complaints when the governing statute denies it.
 Harmonization and Administrative Floodgates: Limiting direct CSC filings to private citizens properly harmonizes R.A. No. 8292 with E.O. No. 292, allowing university governing boards to discipline their own staff while preserving CSC oversight on appeal, and prevents the CSC from being overwhelmed with thousands of localized intra-agency complaints.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petitions are GRANTED. The December 29, 2006 Decision of the Court of Appeals is hereby REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Resolution Nos. 060521 and 061141 dated March 24, 2006 and June 30, 2006, respectively, of the Civil Service Commission are REINSTATED.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Civil Service Commission and Atty. Cueva, completely overturning the Court of Appeals. The administrative formal charges of Dishonesty against Dr. Guevarra and Conduct Prejudicial to the Best Interest of the Service against Vice President Cezar, as well as Dr. Guevarra's 90-day preventive suspension, were fully reinstated, allowing the CSC to proceed with the disciplinary prosecution.
